name: California
title: We went to court to check on California illegal voting cases. Here’s what we learned
authors: By Marek Warszawski of KVPR; Eli Chavez of KCRW of Tyche Hendricks, KQED and Noah Abrams, KRCB
description: Experts say the federal government must prove that noncitizens intentionally violated election law. Regardless, defendants may face dire immigration consequences.
text:
In summary
Experts say the federal government must prove that noncitizens intentionally violated election law. Regardless, defendants may face dire immigration consequences.


A 51-year-old business owner and father of seven was the first of more than three dozen California residents to appear in court to face allegations by the federal government that they violated voting laws because they are not U.S. citizens.
Camilo Giles Jimenez, a U.S. legal permanent resident from Mexico who, according to the criminal complaint, has lived outside Kerman, in Fresno County, since at least 2017, pleaded not guilty to three misdemeanor counts Wednesday afternoon in federal court in downtown Fresno. The government charges say he voted in three elections in violation of the law that bans noncitizens from voting for president or Congress. 
During the 10-minute hearing before Judge Stanley A. Boone, federal public defender Erin Snider said Jimenez, who was dressed in a peach polo shirt, faded jeans and white Nike sneakers, owns a paving company. Neither Jimenez nor Snider answered questions from reporters.
Justice Department officials announced the charges against Jimenez and 27 other California residents on Oct. 19 as part of a coordinated effort they said was designed “to root out fraud” in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity. On Monday, the department announced charges against 12 more people in California. 
Many of the defendants are not charged with illegally voting, but with illegally registering to vote or lying on their naturalization applications. 
More court appearances are set for the coming days and weeks. 
Legal experts say that to gain convictions for illegal voting prosecutors must prove that these people willfully committed a crime, which could be difficult. Regardless of any criminal convictions, even legal residents could be deported whether or not they knew they were breaking the law.
The cases
Twenty-three of hose accused are from Southern California, six are from the Bay Area, four are from the Sacramento region and seven are from Fresno County and the Central Valley. 
One of those arrested in the mid-October sweep, 72-year-old Omar Muñoz of Commerce, told KCRW that six police vehicles, a helicopter and at least six reporters arrived at his home just after 5 a.m. on Oct. 19. 
“It’s a show,” Muñoz told the station. “I said, ‘Wow!’ I said, ‘I’m not a killer.’”
Omar Muñoz is one of over two dozen people in California charged with voter fraud. Photo by Eli Chavez, KCRW
Muñoz was still wearing pajamas when he was shackled around the waist and legs and transported to downtown Los Angeles. He was released that afternoon but would not speak to the specifics of the charges against him.
Justice department officials have said these indictments are the tip of the iceberg in what they allege is widespread voter fraud in California. 
“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a news release. “Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today’s charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk.”
Wednesday, a federal judge sided with California by rejecting a bid by the Trump administration to separate out any ballots sent in from people on that list. The decision by U.S. District Judge David Carter is a setback for the federal government in its efforts to exert more control over state-run elections ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm. On Monday, the Supreme Court denied an appeal by the Department of Justice to wade into its fight with California over voter rolls.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote in his 26-page decision. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”
The California Newsroom tried to speak with many of the defendants, and their lawyers, but except for Muñoz, all inquiries were turned down or received no response.
In its case against Jimenez, the government alleges the Fresno County resident submitted a voter registration application to the Fresno County Registrar in 2022, and checked a box indicating he is a U.S. citizen. Jimenez is also accused of voting in recent elections.
The complaint says Jimenez subsequently told agents that he registered to vote after receiving his green card. Jimenez also said that he had been voting since 2023, according to the complaint, although he denied ever claiming he was a citizen.
Standard of proof
To prove its case against Jimenez and the other defendants, the government must show they deliberately broke federal law by voting as noncitizens, according to UCLA law professor Rick Hasen.
The federal statute prohibits anyone who isn’t a U.S. citizen from voting to elect the president or members of Congress. Doing so is punishable by up to one year in prison, a fine or a combination of both.
“In order to violate the statute, there has to be proof that the person did so intentionally,” Hasen said. “That is, they knew they were not eligible, and they did it anyway.”
For example, Hasen said it is not necessarily considered intentional if a government office, like the Department of Motor Vehicles, mistakenly offers someone who is not a citizen the chance to register to vote.
“Suppose you are told by a government official you can register to vote, even if you’re not a citizen, and the person registers, then they might be doing so knowing that they registered but not knowing that they were violating the law,” Hasen added.
Even a statement that a defendant makes acknowledging that he or she voted would not automatically prove the government’s case, Hasen said. Prosecutors must still show defendants were knowingly and willfully breaking the law.
He said successful prosecutions or guilty pleas by noncitizens accused of voter fraud are rare.
“It seems to be a very small problem relative to the number of voters in the country,” Hasen said, adding that it is more about, “trying to make an example of some people, rather than showing evidence that there’s a massive problem of election fraud in the United States.”
Potential immigration consequences
While intentionality is key to a criminal case, it may not matter when it comes to immigration consequences. Regardless of whether someone meant to break the law, unlawful voting and falsely claiming to be a citizen, including by signing a voter registration form, can be grounds for deportation and for denial of an application for U.S. citizenship. 
Many of the people charged have lived in the U.S. legally for years and are in the process of applying for citizenship, according to the federal complaints against them. That could now be denied to them, even if the government doesn’t move to deport them.
Stanford University Law Professor Jennifer Chacón says that one reason noncitizen voting is rare, is because the price to pay is so steep.
“The fact that these individuals can be criminally prosecuted, barred from naturalization, subject to deportation, all demonstrates why, as a general rule, noncitizen voting is not a problem,” she said, “because there are many, many consequences to it, and people are generally aware of that.”
Federal prosecutors said that the names they provided in California are only a small fraction of a wider problem. “We are investigating thousands of more similar cases throughout the nation,” Bill Essayli, U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, told reporters. 
While the Department of Justice has emphasized that the number of noncitizens charged with voting and related offenses has grown to more than 150 in this Trump term from a total of 13 under Biden’s entire term, other analysts point out that it is small compared to the number of registered voters.
California has 23 million voters, Attorney General Bob Bonta noted, saying those who face charges in the state are “just a drop in the bucket numerically, and it makes the point that there is no widespread voter fraud.”
Speaking on KQED’s Forum program, Hasen cast doubt on the federal government’s statements. “What I think they’re actually trying to do,” he said, “is to project the image that there’s a widespread voter fraud problem in this country, and to kind of mimic the claims that President Trump has made, that noncitizens are voting in droves and affecting the outcome of elections.”
This story was reported by KVPR, KCRW and KQED with The California Newsroom, a collaboration of public media outlets that includes NPR, CalMatters, KQED (San Francisco), LAist and KCRW (Los Angeles), KPBS (San Diego) and other stations across the state.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Our polling shows strong support for statewide restrictions on cellphones in schools. Will the Legislature act?
authors: Tatishe Nteta, Jesse Rhodes, Jesse Usher-Barrett, and Sydney Brake
description: Local school districts, including the state’s largest district, are increasingly moving forward on their own, creating a patchwork of local policies in the absence of statewide action.
text:
IN RECENT YEARS, support for restricting cellphone use in the nation’s public schools has grown dramatically. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 42 states, Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico have passed legislation restricting cellphone use in K-12 public schools.
Proponents of these bans cite studies that find they improve classroom dynamics, with teachers in schools that have instituted stricter restrictions reporting greater satisfaction, less disruption, and more focused classrooms. 
However, opponents note that research on student outcomes, including test scores, attendance, and bullying, has found limited effects. They point to studies showing that, in the years after these bans were instituted, some schools saw increases in disciplinary actions such as suspensions, and argue that these bans adversely affect parents’ ability to communicate with their children, particularly during emergencies and for children with medical conditions or disabilities.   
In the Commonwealth, about 80 percent of the state’s school districts have adopted some form of cellphone policy or restriction, according to the Massachusetts Association of School Superintendents. Boston Public Schools, the state’s largest school district, recently announced plans for a “comprehensive bell-to-bell ban on all personal electronic devices,” which includes phones, laptops, tablets, smartwatches, and smartphones, beginning at the start of the 2027-28 school year. 
Are these policies popular among residents of the Bay State?  Since 2024, we have asked a representative sample of Massachusetts residents, “Do you support or oppose restricting the use of cellphones by public school students during official school hours, except for an emergency or a medical condition or disability?”  We find widespread support for these restrictions, with about 3 in 4 residents expressing support for the ban in four surveys since October 2024, as shown in the figure below

In our most recent poll, close to eight in 10 expressed support for these restrictions, and the policy is supported by majorities of all gender, generational, class, and racial groups. 



Restrictions on cell phones are overwhelmingly popular among Democrats (79 percent), Republicans (80 percent), independents (74 percent), liberals (83 percent), moderates (75 percent), conservatives (79 percent). Put in terms of the last presidential contest, restrictions are backed by identical shares of Harris (79 percent) and Trump (79 percent) voters. 



Notably, parents are especially supportive, with 86 percent of adults with children under 18 supporting restrictions, compared with 76 percent of those without children under 18. 
Our findings are largely consistent with a December 2025 EdTrust-Massachusetts poll conducted by the MassINC Polling Group, which also found broad majority support for a ban on cellphones and smartwatches.   
To date, the Legislature has debated the issue, but not passed legislation.  
Proposals to restrict cellphone use in schools have passed in different forms in the House and Senate. They must be reconciled by a conference committee of House and Senate members before the session ends on January 5 or the process will have to start over in the new two-year legislative session begins after that date.   
Meanwhile, local school districts, including the state’s largest school district, are increasingly moving forward on their own, creating a patchwork of local policies in the absence of statewide action. 
With the public strongly in support of restricting cellphone use in schools, state legislators on Beacon Hill can be confident that legislation creating a uniform, statewide policy on cellphone use would be well-received. 
Tatishe Nteta is Provost Professor of Political Science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and director of the UMass Poll. Jesse Rhodes is a professor of political science at UMass Amherst and co-director of the UMass Poll. Jesse Usher Barrett is a PhD student in political science at the UMass Amherst and a graduate research fellow for the UMass Poll. Sydney Brake is a PhD student in political science at UMass Amherst and a graduate research fellow for the UMass Poll.

name: Nevada Current
title: Trump administration touts NV worker heat protections as national model, analysis suggests otherwise
description: Business and industry groups have held up Nevada’s worker heat protection standard as a national model, but Nevada’s own workers say otherwise, according to an analysis released last month.  In Nevada, there is no specific temperature at which employee heat protections are required to start. Instead, employers have sole discretion to decide when to provide [[...]
text:
Nearly half of heat complaints in Nevada came from just three sectors: hotels, casinos and restaurants; retail; and warehousing and delivery. (Stock photo via Canva)Business and industry groups have held up Nevada’s worker heat protection standard as a national model, but Nevada’s own workers say otherwise, according to an analysis released last month. 
In Nevada, there is no specific temperature at which employee heat protections are required to start. Instead, employers have sole discretion to decide when to provide heat protections for their workers.
Nevada’s heat standard kicks in when working conditions create “the reasonable likelihood that heat illness could occur” and requires employers to prepare their own “one-time, written job hazard analysis to assess working conditions that may cause occupational exposure to heat illness.”
In practice, that means two construction crews performing the same task on the same day could be subject to different temperature thresholds.
Employers and industry groups argue that flexibility is needed to ensure regulations don’t burden businesses, while allowing more tailored standards across states with different climates. 
But a new analysis commissioned by the Natural Resources Defense Council and conducted by researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health calls that model into question.
The analysis — which reviewed 2,561 records of heat complaints and referrals logged by Nevada OSHA from Jan. 2015 through Nov.  2025 — found that workers’ heat complaints across almost every industry in Nevada start climbing at about 90°F air temperature, contradicting Nevada regulators’ claim that no single threshold works.
The analysis found that the odds of a complaint more than tripled between 90°F and 100°F, and were nearly 8 times higher at 105°F. 
Barrak Alahmad, a senior research scientist for the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said that decades of scientific evidence show that thresholds are a foundational component of an effective heat standard.
“We don’t think this should be the model going forward, and that the Nevada model, in fact, if anything, should have some basic thresholds that, when exceeded mandate water rest breaks and basic stuff,” Alahmad said. 
Alahmad, who co-authored the study, said he was motivated to analyze Nevada’s heat complaints after industry groups held up Nevada’s heat standard as a possible national model. 
That findings reveal there is a data-driven threshold when working in extreme heat without protections becomes dangerous, said Alahmad.
“What we showed is that, yeah, even in Nevada, these thresholds exist,” Alahmad said. 
Temperature thresholds were at the center of federal OSHA hearings last year, and proved unpopular among employers and industry groups. 
 In September, the U.S Small Business Administration Office of Advocacy sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Labor, asking federal regulators to model any new federal regulations on Nevada’s model, citing the need for “flexibility.”
The Department of Labor indicated it intends to publish a revised proposal by the end of the year, with expectations for a finalized standard by October 2027. Although the deadlines are not mandatory. 
Under the current OSHA proposed standards, when workplace conditions reach a heat index of 80°F, employers would be required to implement heat hazard protection. However, Alahmad said “that is not the rule of the land right now, and there doesn’t seem to be an appetite for it with the current administration.”
Alahmad said his analysis revealed the need for clear state and federal workplace heat standards based on specific, data-driven temperature thresholds. 
Nearly half of heat complaints in Nevada came from just three sectors: hotels, casinos and restaurants (23%), retail (14%), and warehousing and delivery (nearly 8%). Just over 80% of complaints came from Clark County, Nevada’s most populous region and home to Las Vegas. 
But official records almost always undercount heat-related issues among workers, Alahmad said. 
Many workers, particularly those in small, nonunionized, or precarious workplaces, may never report dangerous heat hazards out of fear of retaliation, said Sara Evans, the chair of SEIU Local 1107’s Climate Justice Caucus. 
Evens argued Nevada’s regulation focused on “reasonable likelihood” is subjective and allows too much employer discretion, adding that workers without union support may be less likely to report concerns because of retaliation fears and economic pressures.
Unionized workers are more likely to lodge health and safety complaints with OSHA than nonunionized workers, likely because they have a better understanding of their rights on the job and are better protected from illegal retaliation by employers, said Evans. 
Only about 13% of private sector workers in Nevada are represented by unions. 
Evans said she got involved with advocating for stronger heat protections in Nevada after seeing that Nevada’s standards were not enough to protect more vulnerable workers.
“It’s super alarming that the only people that are reporting heat-related concerns at work are usually people within unions,” Evans said. “We don’t even know what’s going on in these non-unionized areas.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: It’s Election Day: Here’s why 12 election monitors are in Utah
description: Election officials say they’re not worried, but advocates see cause for concern.
text:
Signs direct people to a voting location at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)As 1,000 federal election monitors fan out across the country, 12 of them are assigned to Utah — and all within Salt Lake County, according to the county’s top elections official.  
Many of her fellow Democrats, some Republicans and voting rights groups see cause for alarm with the Department of Justice sending more monitors to the states than ever before. But Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman summed up her take in two words: “No concerns.” 
“I don’t want our voters to feel concerned about their right to casting their vote,” Chapman said in an interview last week. She’s assuring them that everyone who’s eligible will have a chance to cast a ballot in the midterm elections. 
DOJ is sending election monitors to Utah polls this November

Chapman said she didn’t know which of the county’s 40 voting centers the monitors will go to. Their presence was expected only for Election Day, she said, and not during early voting. 
Election monitors have long kept an eye on compliance with federal voting rights laws, but not in every state at once. Critics of the plan point out it follows recent moves by the Trump administration to claim federal authority over state-run elections. 
The Justice Department sued Utah and more than two dozen other states in an attempt to obtain voter lists with sensitive data like driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The Utah case is one of at least 20 that have been dismissed.
A Justice Department spokesperson told Stateline that “every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day.” 
Voting rights advocates in Utah are raising concerns the program could intimidate voters just the same and say its specific objective isn’t clear.  
“We don’t believe it’s needed,” said Helen Moser, director of voter services for the Utah League of Women Voters. She noted the effort comes on the heels of the Trump administration’s unsuccessful legal fight for access to Utah’s unredacted voter rolls. 
“And so it seemed really very arbitrary and kind of capricious,” Moser said. 
Her organization was working with the ACLU and other groups to recruit poll watchers before the announcement that federal monitors were coming, and now plans for those volunteers to also keep an eye on the monitors through Election Day, she said. So far, the coalition’s organizers have trained roughly 150 observers. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The mandate for the federal election monitors is to watch and take notes, while not intruding or interfering with voting, a DOJ attorney informed Utah’s top elections officer, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, in a letter last week. They’ll also introduce themselves to the poll manager, present ID, dress in business casual attire, and won’t carry guns or wear pins or uniforms identifying them as Justice Department employees. 
“Generally, we are monitoring for compliance with the federal voting rights statutes that fall within the jurisdiction of the Civil Rights Division,” the letter states. 
Alison Griffith, director of community engagement for the ACLU of Utah, said she doesn’t expect monitors to break the rules, but says the anticipation of their presence could be enough to make voters uneasy. 
“But they haven’t given any specificity about what they’re doing in Utah and why. And I think it’s the unknown that creates confusion. It creates concern. It creates anxiety,” Griffith said. “That lack of knowledge about why they’re here and what they’re doing lends itself to potential for intimidation, so we’re hoping that having poll watchers out there as well can balance that out.”
Chapman, the Salt Lake County clerk, said she feels confident after speaking with Justice Department representatives that the agency won’t overstep in her county — heavily Democratic and the state’s most populous. 
“However, they will be held strictly to what our law allows,” Chapman said. “And if anything goes above or beyond that, we will take care of it very quickly.” 
And she notes they won’t be traveling very far to do the job. 
“While they do work for the federal government, these are our neighbors by and large, so they’re Utah residents that will be here monitoring,” Chapman said. 
She said the federal monitors are expected to look at whether election workers are following federal law requiring Spanish language voting materials and compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. 
State officials in California and Minnesota are assigning their own observers in response, but Utah is not planning to do the same, Henderson, Utah’s Republican lieutenant governor, has said. 
Her office is working with elections officials in Utah’s 29 counties to develop “contingency plans” for if issues arise, she said late last month. 
“I’m always worried about people feeling intimidated about voting,” Henderson told reporters. “I don’t want that to be the case, so I’m trying to help the public understand that while the scope and scale of this is maybe not normal, the fact that election monitors from the Department of Justice go to states every election year is normal.”
She does not expect the 12 in Utah, which she told KUER will work in pairs at six or seven voting locations, to alter the environment as voters come and go. 
“I think that they probably won’t notice,” Henderson said.



What federal monitors can’t do
They’re bound by standard rules for poll watchers, Henderson’s office says. 
That means they’re not allowed within 6 feet of voting booths and ballot boxes. 
Observers, including federal monitors and poll watchers, are prohibited by state law from making a recording that violates a voter’s right to cast a secret ballot. 
Broadly, they’re barred from interfering with voting, divulging information regarding vote counts, revealing how someone voted, or attempting to influence someone’s vote. 
If voters spot any violations, Henderson is directing them to get in touch with their county clerk.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: It’s Election Day. Here’s what you need to know.
description: Finally, it’s arrived. Some common questions, answered. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. If you’re in line by 8, you can vote. You can type your address in here and get your answer. You don’t need to show ID, but don’t try voter fraud, as it can result in a felony […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at Lyndale Community School in south Minneapolis during the primary election Tuesday, August 11 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Finally, it’s arrived. Some common questions, answered.
How much time do I have?
Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. If you’re in line by 8, you can vote.
Where do I vote?
You can type your address in here and get your answer.
What if I forget my ID?
You don’t need to show ID, but don’t try voter fraud, as it can result in a felony conviction.
Do I need to be registered?
No! You can show up at your polling station and register. Here’s how to register on Election Day.
How can I be sure my absentee ballot is being counted?
You can track it here.
What if I have an absentee ballot but never sent it in?
Per the secretary of state: You may drop off your ballot no later than 5 p.m. on Election Day; just return it to the office that sent the ballot, during office hours.
Or, just throw away the ballot and go vote at your precinct.
Who is on the ballot?
The constitutional offices — governor and lieutenant governor, who run as a ticket; attorney general; secretary of state; state auditor. All 201 legislative seats, plus Congress: Minnesota’s U.S. House seats and a U.S. Senate contest to replace U.S. Sen. Tina Smith, who is retiring at the end of the year. A statewide ballot measure. Some local races, too.
Check out your sample ballot.
Our voter guide has info, and will point you to Reformer coverage.
Seems like a lot of people voted early.
Yes, Secretary of State Steve Simon reports that as of 9 a.m., Monday, local election officials have accepted 886,427 absentee and mail ballots.
How many people voted in 2022?
2,525,873, or about 61% of elibible voters, which was fewer than the 2018 high but still among the highest in the nation. That’s typical for Minnesota. Lots of room to grow, however: More than 3.2 million Minnesotans cast ballots in the presidential election of 2024.
OK, who’s running?
U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party is running for governor against Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth. What’s certain is that Minnesota will have its first female governor.
Read a Reformer profile of Demuth. who is hoping to become Minnesota’s first Republican governor in 16 years.
And Klobuchar.
In the U.S. Senate race, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is running against Republican Michele Tafoya.
DFL Attorney General Keith Ellison is running for a third term against Ron Schutz, a patent lawyer and conservative activist. The attorney general is the state’s chief legal officer and protects Minnesotans against consumer fraud, among other duties.
Just as important for setting Minnesota’s course during the next two years will be control of the Legislature. The House has been 67-67 during the 2025-26 sessions, while the DFL has controlled the Senate 34-33. The Legislature writes the two-year state budget, which will come in around $60 billion, and determine how much we spend on schools, roads, parks, health care and social services. Republicans want to cut taxes and spending, while Democrats will push to support education and health care.
Here’s some key House and Senate districts that will determine control of the two chambers.
When do we find out who won?
Results will start to trickle in after 8 p.m. We often know who won within a couple hours, and typically it’s all done by early Wednesday. In 2024, control of the Minnesota House took weeks to sort out, and they wound up in a 67-67 tie.
Nationwide, you can get a decent idea of how things are going with chart #6, compiled by Washington insider Bruce Mehlman.
Can I trust the results?
Yes. Post-election audits, which are available to the public, entail a hand count in at least two precincts in every county and 3% of the total precincts in the biggest counties. Historically, the results are nearly identical to the machine results. Minnesota also has the top-ranked election administration system, according to MIT’s Elections Performance Index.
What about recounts?
The state will pay for a recount if the difference between the candidates is less than one-quarter of 1%, or 0.25% in a federal race, like for Congress, or a statewide constitutional race, like for governor.
If it’s a legislative race, the state pays if the difference is one-half of 1%, or 0.5%. But given how accurate the machine tallies are relative to hand counts, recounts rarely change an outcome.
When does the new governor take office?
The inauguration is on the first Monday in January.
If Klobuchar wins, what happens to her Senate seat?
If she resigns before her inauguation, then Gov. Tim Walz would appoint her successor, but Walz can and most likely would defer to Klobuchar, who would appoint her own successor. Some potential appointees include Secretary of State Steve Simon and U.S. Rep. Kelly Morrison, though the subject tends to spark lively debate.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri could approach turnout record as ballot measures drive interest
description: Missouri election officials say brisk early voting could push Tuesday’s turnout close to — or beyond — the state record for a nonpresidential election. The benchmark is 2018, when 2,442,306 Missourians cast ballots. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins expects about 55% of the state’s 4.4 million registered voters to participate, spokeswoman Anne Marie Moy said [...]
text:
Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon, right, checks in a voter Oct. 23 at the Boone County Government Center in Columbia (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Missouri election officials say brisk early voting could push Tuesday’s turnout close to — or beyond — the state record for a nonpresidential election.
The benchmark is 2018, when 2,442,306 Missourians cast ballots. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins expects about 55% of the state’s 4.4 million registered voters to participate, spokeswoman Anne Marie Moy said in a text to The Independent. 
That would mean about 2.42 million ballots, just short of the 2018 total. A slightly higher turnout rate could set a new record.
With no hotly contested statewide candidate race, local election officials say voters are being drawn to the polls by the three controversial statewide ballot questions and, in some areas, expensive legislative races.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
No-excuse absentee voting began Oct. 20 and concluded when local election authorities closed their offices Monday afternoon. Polls open at 6 a.m. Tuesday and close at 7 p.m. Anyone in line by 7 p.m. will be allowed to vote.
Platte County has averaged 1,000 voters a day since early voting began, said Chris Hershey, director of elections for the Platte County Board of Elections. Hershey estimated that 72% of Platte County’s more than 80,000 voters will cast ballots.
There is a targeted Missouri House race in Platte County and the state Senate race in the 34th District has become unexpectedly competitive.
“Folks have shown they are motivated to vote,” Hershey said. “We’ve stayed consistently busy.”
Turnout in previous nonpresidential elections this century has ranged from 35% in 2014, when Democrats did not contest the state auditor’s race, to 58% in 2018. That year, a U.S. Senate race costing more than $100 million combined with controversial ballot measures on legislative redistricting and medical marijuana to motivate turnout.
Presidential elections typically draw about 3 million Missouri voters.
Spending on this year’s ballot measures — Amendment 3, to ban most abortions, Amendment 6, to limit the power of lawmakers to change measures passed by initiative and Proposition A, the referendum on redistricting — totaled $55 million through Friday. 
Of that, almost $17 million has been spent on broadcast advertising, according to tracking by The Independent.
St. Louis County, which has the most registered voters, keeps a tally of absentee ballots received available online. When early voting stopped Monday, 173,484 people — more than one-fourth of the county’s voters — had cast ballots. 
The Independent contacted election officials from both parties across the state, who reported strong interest in early voting and projected substantial Election Day turnout.
The 35,000 ballots received in St. Charles County are double the number cast early in 2022 — the first year it was available — and about half the number who voted early in 2024, elections director Kurt Bahr said.
There are three Missouri House races targeted by both parties in St. Charles.
“This shows both that the midterm turnout will be lower than the presidential year and that the two weeks of no excuse voting is becoming more popular,” Bahr said.
In Jackson County, where spending in the 8th District state Senate race is approaching $6 million, there have been 21,049 ballots been cast through Friday morning.
“Turnout is great,” said Tyler Spencer, Republican director of the Jackson County Election Board. “We love when people get out and vote.”
The other multimillion-dollar state Senate race is in Greene County. The candidates and their supporters have also combined to spend $6 million in the 30th District. There are also three Missouri House districts targeted by both parties.
Almost 2,300 votes were cast Saturday and almost 21,000 ballots have been received, Greene County Clerk Shane Schoeller said. He expects turnout between 58% and 59%. 
That would almost match the 2018 turnout of 60.7%. In 2014, turnout in Greene County was 33.2%
“This election is unusual, as you know, because state auditor is the only statewide race on the ballot,” Schoeller said. “The issues on this ballot are drawing more interest than those in 2014, and we have a competitive state Senate race in Greene County that wasn’t on the 2014 ballot.”
In Franklin County, a reliably Republican county without competitive legislative races targeted by either party, about 4,500 people had cast ballots by Friday morning, Clerk Tim Baker said.
There is no comparison data for 2022 “because it wasn’t used that much,” Baker said. This year so far is about half of the early vote in 2024, he said.
“Turnout is steady and I would say we should be close to the state prediction of 50 to 55%,” Baker said.
In Boone County in central Missouri, a Democratic-leaning county, Clerk Brianna Lennon said her office had received about 10,500 ballots by the end of the day Thursday, about half the number cast by this point in the 2024 election. 
She expects about 57% of voters to cast ballots, she said, which would be comparable to 2018.
“I expect we’ll land at double the amount of November 2022 and half the amount of November 2024,” Lennon said. “A healthy splitting of the middle.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri election 2026: What to know before heading to the polls
description: Missouri voters will decide whether to ban most abortions, approve a new congressional map and strengthen protections for citizen-led ballot measures Tuesday, along with choosing representatives in Congress and the state legislature. Before heading to the polls for the Nov. 3 general election, it’s worth taking a few minutes to check your polling location, r[...]
text:
The Missouri Independent has answers to some common Election Day questions (Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star).Missouri voters will decide whether to ban most abortions, approve a new congressional map and strengthen protections for citizen-led ballot measures Tuesday, along with choosing representatives in Congress and the state legislature.
Before heading to the polls for the Nov. 3 general election, it’s worth taking a few minutes to check your polling location, review your ballot and make sure you have the identification you need.
The Missouri Independent has answers to some common Election Day questions.
 What time do polls open?

Polls across Missouri open at 6 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. Voters in line by 7 p.m. are entitled to cast a ballot.
 Where do I vote?

Before heading out the door, check your voter registration and polling location at GoVoteMissouri.com.
Most Missouri voters must cast their ballots at an assigned polling place, though some jurisdictions have voting centers where residents can vote at multiple locations.
If you have questions about your polling location or the information listed on the state’s website, contact your local election authority.
 How do I find out what’s on the ballot?

Local election authorities provide sample ballots that voters can review, mark and bring with them on Election Day as a guide.
Sample ballots are typically available on county election websites and may also be found through the state’s voter information lookup system.
Researching your ballot ahead of time can help reduce the time you spend at the polls. Voters may bring printed notes or a sample ballot into the voting booth.
 What are acceptable forms of ID to vote?

To cast a regular ballot, registered Missouri voters must present acceptable photo identification issued by Missouri or the federal government.
Accepted forms of identification include:
– A Missouri driver’s license or nondriver identification card that is unexpired or expired after Nov. 5, 2024.
– A military identification card, including a veteran identification card, that is unexpired or has no expiration date.
– An unexpired U.S. passport or passport card.
– Another photo identification issued by Missouri or the federal government that is unexpired or expired after Nov. 5, 2024.
Student IDs and driver’s licenses issued by other states are not accepted.
Registered voters without acceptable identification may cast a provisional ballot. That ballot will count if the voter returns to the polling place before polls close on Election Day with acceptable photo identification or if the local election authority determines that the signature on the provisional ballot envelope matches the signature in the voter’s registration record.
Voters who cast provisional ballots receive a stub with instructions for checking whether their ballots were counted.
 Can I wear a T-shirt with my candidate’s name on it?

No. Missouri prohibits campaign apparel advocating for a candidate or ballot issue inside a polling place.
State law also prohibits electioneering within 25 feet of the building’s closest outside door. Under a law that took effect in August, local election authorities may extend that restriction to 50 feet if they provide the required public notice.
 Can I take a picture of my ballot?

Voters should not photograph or share a marked ballot. Missouri law prohibits intentionally revealing a ballot to show how someone voted or intends to vote.
 What if I need help casting my ballot?

Voters with disabilities can request assistance from election workers or bring someone to help them vote. Polling places must provide accessible voting equipment, and voters with limited mobility may request curbside voting.
If you make a mistake while marking your ballot, you can ask an election judge for a replacement.
 Who can I call if I need help?

Voters can call the Missouri Secretary of State’s election complaint hotline at 1-800-669-8683 to report suspected violations of election laws.
The nonpartisan Election Protection hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683) also has trained volunteers available to answer voting questions and help resolve Election Day problems.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska races to watch for the 2026 midterms
description: Polls open for 12 hours at 8 a.m. Central time/7 a.m. Mountain time. Mail-in ballots must be returned by the time polls close.
text:
Voting booths at the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April, 24. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Election Day is here. Nebraska has received more national attention than usual, as a handful of races in the Cornhusker State are viewed as competitive. Here are some key races to watch closely. 
Polls open for 12 hours at 8 a.m. Central time/7 a.m. Mountain time. Mail-in ballots must be returned by the time polls close.
 Who will win the bitter Senate race?

Nebraska will finally know who wins the heated Senate race between incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, a Republican, and registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn. Three other third-party candidates are also on the ballot. This race has seen plenty of twists and turns (and campaign songs!).
Osborn lost to Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 by about 7 percentage points; the former labor leader hopes to improve on that margin. The Ricketts’ campaign hopes its strategy of labeling Osborn as a Democrat works. 
The last time Nebraska elected a non-Republican to the Senate was in 2006, when Ricketts handily lost to then-Democratic Sen. Ben Nelson. 
That was also the last time a Democrat won any election statewide. Osborn has repeatedly said he wouldn’t caucus with either party in the Senate. 
 The governor’s race: Jim Pillen vs. Lynne Walz

Few national pundits, pollsters or leading political figures, from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance to Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, had the race for Nebraska governor on their map.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, a Republican, is running for reelection, and similar to Ricketts, he’s received national support to boost his chances, including $2 million from the Republican Governors Association. Former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz, however, has also received support, including more than $500,000 from the Democratic Governors Association, which Beshear chairs.
Pillen and Walz also face former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom, running under the America First Party, and Rick Beard of the Legal Marijuana NOW Party.
Walz would need to follow in the footsteps of Nelson, who unseated Republican Gov. Kay Orr in 1990. He would go on to safely win reelection in 1994 before being elected to the Senate in 2000.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Will NE-02 go blue or again defy expectations?

Nebraska’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district has dimmed a bit in terms of the national spotlight as the race is viewed as one of the easiest pickups for Democrats this cycle. Still, the red-leaning 2nd Congressional District has fooled political analysts before under retiring Rep. Don Bacon. 
Bacon beat Brad Ashford, the last Democrat to represent the district, in 2016; since then, Bacon has won five terms.  
The question is whether Denise Powell can regain the seat for Democrats or if Brinker Harding can bring it home like Bacon. 
 Omaha-area legislative races

A trio of Omaha-area Republican legislative incumbents faces tough reelection fights: state Sen. Brad von Gillern vs. registered nonpartisan Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek (Legislative District 4), state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston vs. Democrat Christy Knorr (Legislative District 12) and state Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue vs. Democrat Darin Tompkins (Legislative District 36). All three districts are in the 2nd Congressional District.
Von Gillern and Holdcroft fell below their opponents in the low-turnout primary, while Riepe faced three Democrats but hovered below 50%. Von Gillern has been eyed as the potential next speaker of the Legislature. His fate could decide a cascade of leadership positions for the 2027 session.
If Republicans face a tough night, Democrats are eyeing two pickup opportunities for open seats: Legislative District 18, between Democrat Jess Goldoni of Omaha and Taylor Royal of Bennington, and Legislative District 14 in neighboring Sarpy County, between Republican Bill Bowes of La Vista and Democrat SuAnn Witt of Papillion.
Conservatives, meanwhile, are still trying to pick up seats, starting in the Omaha-Bennington Legislative District 10, between Democrat Cindy Johnson and Republican Rebecca Rens. Republicans are also trying to unseat Democratic incumbents in Omaha’s Legislative District 20 (state Sen. John Fredrickson vs. Republican Chris Anderson) or Lincoln’s Legislative District 26 (state Sen. George Dungan vs. Republican Tobias Howard).
The Legislature is currently split with 33 Republicans, 15 Democrats and one progressive nonpartisan. 
It takes 33 votes to overcome filibusters and advance certain legislation, and 30 votes to overcome a gubernatorial veto or change legislative rules. Lawmakers don’t caucus by party, and a candidate’s party isn’t on the ballot.
 Three honorable mentions

Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District between Rep. Mike Flood and Democratic challenger Chris Backemeyer has gotten a bit of attention as the national political environment for Republicans has deteriorated. Watch for a closer margin than Flood’s last two races (or an upset, which would mean a historic night for Democrats).
Nebraska voters will choose a new secretary of state from Scott Petersen (Republican), Sarah Slattery (Democrat), Paul Rumbaugh (Working People Party) and Bob Krist (America First Party). Incumbent Secretary of State Bob Evnen lost the GOP primary to Petersen, a challenger from Evnen’s right. The other candidates have criticized Petersen for echoing election-integrity concerns raised by President Donald Trump and others, which could split the vote. 
Voters will weigh in on proposed Constitutional Amendment 1 on their ballots to decide whether to allow state lawmakers to serve up to three consecutive four-year terms, instead of the current limit of two terms. But in an anti-incumbent environment, the sponsor of the measure, state Sen. Rob Dover of Norfolk, is less optimistic about the chances. The proposal advanced from the Legislature 39-10, but many lawmakers now expect it to fail, perhaps even more than in 2012 when voters rejected a similar proposal.
Voting ends at 8 p.m. Central Time Tuesday.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: It’s Election Day in Iowa: What to know as you go to vote
description: After a competitive and expense election cycle, it’s finally Election Day in Iowa. Voters in Iowa will get to cast their ballots Tuesday for statewide and federal offices, as well as having the chance to weigh in on a proposed amendment to the state constitution and whether to retain certain judges. Iowa is expected to host […]
text:
A table hosted "I voted" stickers for voters to pick up after casting their ballots at the Polk County Election Office in Des Moines on the first day of early voting, Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)After a competitive and expense election cycle, it’s finally Election Day in Iowa.
Voters in Iowa will get to cast their ballots Tuesday for statewide and federal offices, as well as having the chance to weigh in on a proposed amendment to the state constitution and whether to retain certain judges.
Iowa is expected to host several of the most competitive races in the country, according to election forecasters, that could be pivotal in determining which party controls the U.S. House and Senate. This year, Iowans are also voting in more races with open seats than in previous recent elections — both Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds and U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, two Republicans, are not seeking reelection, leaving the top-of-ticket races for U.S. Senate and governor without an incumbent.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Additionally, two of the state’s four U.S. House seats have no incumbent, as U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, currently representing the 2nd District, runs to replace Ernst in the Senate, and U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra in the 4th District made an unsuccessful bid to become the GOP gubernatorial nominee.
Early voting participation has been high, with 464,216 absentee ballots received and counted by the Iowa Secretary of State’s office as of Monday morning. This represents a roughly 36% increase as of 341,237 absentee ballots received as reported by the secretary of state the day before the election by Nov. 7, 2022 — but it’s below the 497,085 ballots received by secretary of state in the 2018 midterms reported Nov. 5, 2018 — the midterm election cycle during President Donald Trump’s first term in office.
More Iowans are expected to vote Tuesday, when polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. across the state.
If you haven’t voted yet — or if you’ve requested an absentee ballot but have not yet returned it — there’s still time to cast your ballot. Here’s what you need to know:
Where do I vote?
Voters can find their precinct polling locations using the Iowa Secretary of State’s website. Polling locations are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday. Voters who are in line at their polling place at 8 p.m. must be allowed to vote.
Who can vote in Iowa?
In order to participate in Iowa elections, people must register to vote. A qualified voter in Iowa must be:

An Iowa resident.
A U.S. citizen.
18 years old by Election Day.

There are also restrictions on voting for certain individuals in Iowa. Voters cannot be:

A convicted felon, unless their voting rights have been restored.
Judged mentally incompetent to vote by a court.
Claiming the right to vote in any other place.

A person who is eligible to vote but is not yet a registered voter has the option to register on Election Day at their precinct voting location. In order to register, a qualified voter must provide proof of identity using ID like an Iowa driver’s license, non-operator’s ID or U.S. passport, as well as proof of residence using documents like a residential lease, paycheck or utility bill listing their current address.
Check your voter registration status online here.
I’m registered to vote. What do I need to bring to the polls?
Voters who are already registered to vote still need to bring a form of identification with them to their polling place in order to participate. Accepted forms of identification include:

Iowa driver’s license
Iowa non-operator ID
Out-of-state driver’s license or non-operator ID
U.S. passport
U.S. military or veteran ID
ID card issued by employer
Student ID issued by Iowa high school or college
Tribal ID card/document

If a person does not have a valid ID when they go to vote, they are still allowed to cast a ballot if another registered voter at the precinct attests for their identity. Voters can also bring Election Day registration documents to confirm their identity.
People who do not have accepted IDs or a person willing to attest for them can cast a provisional ballot. People who cast provisional ballots will have their voter registration record and related evidence reviewed by the absentee and special voters’ precinct board. Individuals casting provisional ballots can provide proof of ID or other confirmation of their eligibility to the board up until the time of county canvass of votes, which this year is Nov. 12.
I have an absentee ballot that I haven’t returned. What should I do?
Iowans who have sent in their absentee ballots can track the ballot’s status on the Secretary of State’s website. But for people who have not yet returned their ballot, there’s still time to participate in this year’s election.
Absentee ballots can be returned to a voter’s local county auditor’s office by 8 p.m. on Election Day to be valid. These ballots cannot be delivered to precinct polling locations on Election Day.
If a voter cannot go themselves to return the ballot, Iowa has some restrictions on who can return it in their stead — voters can designate another person to return their absentee ballot if they are an immediate family member or member of the household. Voters with disabilities can also designate someone outside of these categories to return their ballot.
There’s also options available for people who have requested — but not returned — absentee ballots to vote in-person on Election Day. Voters can cast regular ballots if they bring in their absentee ballot to the precinct polling place and surrender it. If a person requested an absentee ballot but cannot return it, they are allowed to cast a provisional ballot.
What’s on the ballot?
In addition to the races for U.S. Senate and House members, Iowans will weigh in on their choices for statewide elected officials. This includes the Iowa gubernatorial election, as well as races for state auditor, attorney general, secretary of agriculture, secretary of state and treasurer. Learn more about the candidates running for these offices through Iowa Capital Dispatch’s 2026 voter guide.
There are also numerous races for the Iowa Legislature and for local elected office on the ballot.
On the back of the ballot, voters will also be able to choose whether to retain certain judges in Iowa. You can learn more about the judges on the retention ballot by reading the 2026 Judicial Performance Review, a report prepared by the Iowa State Bar Association. Voters will also choose whether or not to add language to the Iowa Constitution that would require two-thirds majority approval of the Iowa Legislature to raise personal or corporate income taxes in Iowa.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Author chronicles the most decorated air mission in US history
description:
Best-selling author Adam Makos's new book is about Operation Tidal Wave in which those  involved received five Medals of Honor, 56 Distinguished Service Crosses and more than 1,700 Distinguished Flying Crosses — one for each man who flew on the World War II mission.
.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
It is the most decorated air mission in U.S. history and yet many Americans today know nothing about it.
Best-selling author Adam Makos has corrected that oversight with his riveting new book about Operation Tidal Wave. Those involved received five Medals of Honor, 56 Distinguished Service Crosses and more than 1,700 Distinguished Flying Crosses — one for each man who flew on the mission.
Mississippians may best know Makos for his book, “Devotion,” which told the Korean War story of the friendship between Navy Lt. Tom Hudner, who passed up Harvard University to fly for his country, and Ensign Jesse Brown, a Hattiesburg native who became the Navy’s first Black carrier pilot. The book was adapted into a 2022 film for Columbia Pictures.
The author’s latest book, “Tidal Wave: The Pilots, the Princess, and the Enemy Ace,” tells the story of one of the most dangerous air missions during World War II — sending B-24 Liberator bombers to blow up Romanian refineries that fueled Adolf Hitler’s armies.
But the rest of the plan sounded suicidal: have the B-24s fly as low as 50 to 100 feet to bomb the Ploesti oil complex.
The lumbering B-24s usually carried out attacks from 20,000 feet to avoid anti-aircraft fire, but in this case, Allied leaders wanted the pilots to blow up the refineries from an extremely low altitude in hopes of crippling Hitler’s war machine.
The leaders thought they would surprise the soldiers in Nazi-controlled Romania, but when the B-24s flew in, the soldiers were far from surprised and began firing immediately.
The book includes a host of memorable characters from these courageous aviators to Romania’s top fighter ace to a real-life princess living in the war-torn land, and the improbable story leads to an improbable ending as well.
Nearly a decade ago, Makos and his team began looking to see if any of the more than 1,700 men involved in the operation were still alive. The only survivor they could find was Ernie Poulson, the copilot on the bomber that crash-landed on the princess’ estate. 
“A copilot isn’t just any crew member,” Makos said in an interview. “He literally had his hands on the controls of the bomber and a hand in the fate of all aboard.
“But would he talk to us? And did his memory still hold the story?
“When we reached out to Ernie Poulson, he was 97 years old but still sharp and spry. He’d risen to the rank of colonel in the Air Force and afterward became a professor at the University of Utah.”
When Makos asked Poulson if he would talk to them, the World War II hero replied, “Come on out. My door is open.”
At that moment, Makos said, “We knew we had a book there. And not only that, but Ernie had written his own memoir of the events that was never published.”
Finding a 97-year-old eyewitness to one of the greatest events in military history “was like winning the lottery,” Makos said. “And that was nine years ago.”
There’s only one reason “you spend this long on a story,” he said. “It’s just that good.”
This review was published in partnership with the Clarion Ledger.
Jerry Mitchell grew up surrounded by aviation. His father was a Top Gun pilot in the Navy during the early days of the Vietnam War. Mitchell is the author of “Race Against Time” and now serves as senior investigative reporter for Mississippi Today.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyomingites head to the polls today. Here’s what to know.
description:
Voters will decide whether to dramatically cut their property taxes and choose the Equality State’s next governor.
The post Wyomingites head to the polls today. Here’s what to know. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming voters will head to the polls today to elect the state’s next governor and decide whether to dramatically reduce residential property taxes at the expense of local revenue. They’ll also cast ballots for a bevy of statewide and local races, from secretary of state to sheriff.
While Republican dominance in the Equality State means that many key races are effectively decided during the August primary, there are still several contests with important consequences in today’s general election. (And if you need more information before heading to the polls, check out our election guide.)
WyoFile reporters and editors will be working throughout the day and late into the night, keeping you updated on the latest developments. Here’s what we’ll be watching.
Will voters cut their property taxes?
In the years following the pandemic, property values in Wyoming jumped — and likewise, so did the property taxes that people paid. That increase was not uniform. Teton County, for example, experienced a 111% spike, while Sweetwater County saw a more modest 19.5% increase. Lawmakers responded with a series of relief measures, including one last year that created a 25% exemption on the first $1 million of a primary residence’s fair market value. 
But some believe those measures didn’t go far enough. They’re supporting Proposition 1, a ballot measure that would exempt 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value. There would be no cap on the value of the home: A fixed-income retiree in a one-bedroom bungalow in Casper and a wealthy Jacksonite in a multi-million-dollar mansion would both benefit.
Some condominiums at Teton Village, the base of the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, are valued at more than $7 million and subject to annual property taxes of almost $50,000. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Advocates say Proposition 1 will help homeowners who can’t keep up with rising property tax bills. They also say that local governments would do just fine with less revenue generated by property taxes. But critics — including Gov. Mark Gordon and a host of local officials — say a 50% reduction “would have an immediate and devastating effect on the services most Wyoming citizens rely upon in their communities,” as the governor put it in a recent editorial.
There’s been no public polling on the measure, so we really have no idea which argument voters will find most compelling. It is worth noting that opposition to the ballot measure has been well organized and well funded.
Which Republican will become Wyoming’s next governor?
Technically, there is only one Republican in this race: Sen. Eric Barlow won the GOP nomination in August, fending off two high-profile challengers. But members of Wyoming’s far right have questioned whether Barlow is conservative enough in ruby red Wyoming.
Enter Rebecca Bextel. A conservative activist from Teton County, she was perhaps best known at the start of the year for advocating against affordable housing mitigation fees and for her unsuccessful bid to serve as leader of the Wyoming Republican Party. Then in February she became the face of the Checkgate controversy after a Democratic lawmaker photographed her handing out checks to Freedom Caucus lawmakers on the House floor. The check passing dominated the session, resulting in two investigations and rule changes. Lawmakers determined the checks did not constitute bribery, but voted unanimously to adopt a report that admonished Bextel’s conduct. 
Constitution Party candidate for Wyoming governor Rebecca Bextel takes her opening question on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, during the Wyoming PBS gubernatorial debate in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Undaunted, Bextel in May announced she would run for governor as the Constitution Party’s nominee, but only as an insurance policy should Barlow triumph in the primary. When he did, she launched her bid, campaigning as the true conservative in the race. Suddenly, Republicans had to choose between Barlow, their actual nominee, or Bextel, who argued she better represented their views. Many notable Republican figures, including Gordon and Wyoming’s congressional delegation, lined up behind Barlow. Others, like former GOP Chair Frank Eathorne, backed Bextel.
History favors Barlow. No third-party candidate has ever won a statewide race in Wyoming. 
If Bextel performs well, will the Constitution Party break through?
In Wyoming, a minor political party can gain major-party status if one of its candidates for governor, secretary of state or U.S. House earns at least 10% of the total votes in a general election. So whether Bextel upsets Barlow or not, she could still give the Constitution Party a victory if she crosses that threshold.
There is some recent precedent for minor-party success. The Constitution and Libertarian parties earned major-party status after their candidates reached the necessary threshold in the 2014 secretary of state’s race. But those successes were only temporary. Both parties lost their major-party status after a single election cycle.
Yes, there are legislative races that matter.
Most of Wyoming’s legislative races are decided in the primary. That’s because Democrats are not competitive in many parts of the state, meaning the only race that effectively matters is between hard-line and more traditional Republicans in the primary. That reality means we knew before a single general election ballot was cast that the statehouse will be dramatically different next year after most Freedom Caucus candidates lost their seats in August.
Still, we’re watching a handful of key races today. Fremont County’s House District 33 is one of the state’s few swing districts, and this year features a race between incumbent Rep. Ivan Posey, a Democrat and Eastern Shoshone educator, and Republican challenger Justin Morgan, a veteran who owns a horse training business.
Rep. Ivan Posey, D-Fort Washakie, during the first meeting of the House Special Investigative Committee on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
Farther to the south in Albany County’s House District 14, incumbent Democrat Rep. Trey Sherwood faces Republican challenger Emily Study. While Laramie is one of Wyoming’s few blue bubbles, the rural district north of town was represented by Republicans prior to Sherwood’s victory in 2020.
For more on the legislative races we’re following, click here.
What’s turnout going to be like? 
Unlike many parts of the country, Wyoming’s congressional races have drawn little attention. Democrats face long odds against Harriet Hageman and Chuck Gray, respectively the Republican U.S. Senate and House nominees. 
So what does that mean for turnout? There are early signs that the lack of a high-profile congressional race won’t deter voters from heading to the polls. Early and absentee voting are ahead of 2018 and 2022 — the last midterm elections — according to the Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office. More than 65,000 Wyomingites had already cast ballots as of Thursday.
Voting booths fill up during the 2026 Wyoming primary elections at Laramie County Community College on Tuesday, Aug. 18, in Cheyenne. (Dan Cepeda for Oil City News and WyoFile)
Voters in Cheyenne may see U.S. Department of Justice observers outside polling places. Two DOJ election monitors, who appeared at a Cheyenne polling place on primary election day, caught the governor and others off guard. Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee expects the general election to go differently.
“Unlike their visit during the Primary Election, however, monitors won’t be allowed inside polling places and must remain 100 yards from the polls, in accordance with state law and a recent Wyoming Attorney General’s opinion,” Lee said in a press release last week. 
Where can I get the election results? 
Fear not, dear reader. WyoFile has you covered. As in past elections, we’ll have up-to-the-minute results throughout the evening. Look for a link to our results page to pop up at the top of WyoFile.com shortly after 7 p.m.

title: Today is Election Day in Idaho. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot.
description: Here’s what you need to know this Election Day in Idaho. Even though the president isn’t on the ballot this year, it’s still a big election year for the state. All statewide offices — such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state controller and state treasurer — are up for grabs, along […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots for the May 19, 2026, primary election at Fox Hollow Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Here’s what you need to know this Election Day in Idaho.
Even though the president isn’t on the ballot this year, it’s still a big election year for the state.
All statewide offices — such as the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state superintendent, state controller and state treasurer — are up for grabs, along with three congressional seats in the U.S. House and Senate, and all 105 state legislative seats. So are local races like for county commissioners, highway district officials, magistrate judges and even a runoff election for an Ada County judge. 
But perhaps the biggest race this year is Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights. That’s one of several ballot measures that voters can decide on, along with a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow only the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana, which is called HJR 4; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language, which is called HJR 6; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What is a general election?

Today, Idahoans cast votes to decide the winners for races to political offices. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
In years where the president isn’t being elected, which are called midterm elections, fewer voters tend to turn out. But early data shows high amounts of Idahoans are casting ballots already through early and absentee voting. Across the nation, voters cast early ballots at record levels for a midterm election, States Newsroom reported. 
 Who’s on my ballot?

To find out which races and candidates are on your ballot, plug your information into this tool on VoteIdaho.gov. That tool will show you your sample ballot. 
 When and where can I vote?

Polls are open between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. local time in Idaho. If you are in line before 8 p.m., you will be able to vote. 
To find your polling location, type your address into this tool on VoteIdaho.gov.
 How do I register to vote on Election Day?

To register to vote, you need a current photo ID and a document proving you live in Idaho. 
Here’s what works:

Two types of documents: A form of approved photo identification, and proof that you live in Idaho.
Photo ID types allowed: An Idaho driver’s license, or free state identification card; a passport or federal ID; a tribal ID card; or a concealed weapons license, issued by an Idaho county sheriff.
Proof of residence allowed: If the photo ID you plan to use has your current address, you’re likely covered here. But if not, you need a separate proof of residence. That could include a mortgage, lease, or rental agreement; proof of insurance; utility bills, besides for a cellphone; a property tax bill or assessment; a statement from your credit card or bank; a paycheck or paystub; an enrollment letter from an Idaho high school or university; an intake document to a care facility; or a letter from a social service agency.

To register to vote, you must be a U.S. citizen, at least age 18, who has lived in Idaho for at least 30 days before the election. People who have been convicted of felonies cannot register to vote until they have completed the terms of their sentence. 
 How do I check my voter registration status?

You need to update your voter registration when you move, change your name, or have not voted in the past four years. 
Want to check if you’re registered to vote? Look it up online on VoteIdaho.gov. (You’ll need your driver’s license handy.)
 When are absentee ballots due?

Absentee ballots are due when polls close, at 8 p.m. local time. That means that election officials must have received them by then, not just that the ballots are dropped in the mail by 8 p.m. local time.
If you still need to turn in an absentee ballot, the best way to ensure it gets counted at this point is to drop it off at a ballot drop box or hand deliver it to your county clerk’s office. 
 How do I find information on candidates and issues?

Idaho’s top officials keep getting these common election questions. Here’s the answers to your FAQs.

Visit the Idaho Capital Sun’s voter guide for information on candidates for statewide offices, such as the governor and attorney general; for congressional seats; and for select legislative seats, along with information on ballot measures.
For more information on ballot measures, visit the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office’s online voter pamphlet, which doesn’t have much info on candidates. 
To see news articles about the 2026 election, visit the Idaho Capital Sun’s website. 
 When will election results come in?

Election officials don’t start counting votes until after all the polls close in Idaho, which is at 9 p.m. Mountain time and 8 p.m. Pacific time. Then, the results that trickle in will be unofficial, until they are officially certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which typically takes a few weeks. 
On Election Day after polls close, it can take several hours for all precincts to report results for local races, such as for state legislative seats. For larger races, such as ballot measures and statewide offices, the Associated Press calls the winners of races. 
Tune into the Idaho Capital Sun’s website for live updates on election results, and stories on individual races.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Permitting reform bill will decimate protections in the National Historic Preservation Act
description: On September 30, 2026, a permitting reform bill was introduced in the U.S. Senate that would significantly weaken the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The NHPA was passed in 1966 after thousands of historic places around the U.S. were demolished during urban renewal efforts in 1950s and 1960s. The loss of buildings like Penn Station […]
text:
Because archaeological resources in Michigan are often buried, Sec. 106 reviews require identification through methods such as shovel testing or excavation. This photo, courtesy of the Michigan State Historic Preservation Office, is of work being conducted in the Detroit neighborhood known as Paradise Valley.On September 30, 2026, a permitting reform bill was introduced in the U.S. Senate that would significantly weaken the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The NHPA was passed in 1966 after thousands of historic places around the U.S. were demolished during urban renewal efforts in 1950s and 1960s.
The loss of buildings like Penn Station in New York City produced fierce public outcry because the demolition had occurred without any public review process. In Michigan, it was the destruction of Old City Hall in Detroit 1961 and the demolition of whole neighborhoods for new highways that prompted Michigan’s own reckoning.
Because of these demolitions when the NHPA was passed it included a provision known as Section 106 which required that any federally funded, licensed, or permitted project be evaluated to determine if  historic properties would be negatively affected and it requires that state and local governments, Tribal Nations, and the public be provided the opportunity to comment on these projects.
Public input is a specific remedy baked into the NHPA after we learned hard lessons in the rubble of our discontent, the realization dawning that  we had no means to preserve our significant places while we sorted through the actual rubble of Penn Station, Old City Hall, and thousands of other places.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act obliterates the public notice and input requirements that were purposefully inserted into the NHPA. Imagine a data center project that requires a federal permit because it’s close to a wetland: if passed, this bill will remove the requirement that federal agencies solicit the public’s input, rather, the public will only learn about federally permitted destruction when the bulldozers arrive on site.
The bill contains additional, highly concerning provisions including narrowing the project types that trigger the Section 106 process in the first place. For instance, it excludes projects that utilize federal loans, grants, and other financial assistance which means that Federal Highway Administration projects, (which are typically funded by grants distributed to states) will largely be excluded from the Section 106 process.
Perhaps some of the most egregious changes in this bill pertain to Tribal Nations. Today, Tribal Nations are key constituents in the Section 106 process because they steward their sacred places and ancestral lands. To ensure these places are accounted for, the Section 106 process requires archeological survey for areas where ground disturbance is proposed. For example, in 2026, an FCC-permitted cell phone tower project in Charlevoix County required ground disturbance and, during the survey work, a Native American burial place was discovered.
After discussing this discovery with the State Historic Preservation Office and the Little Traverse Bay Band of Odawa Indians, it was decided that the best path forward was to redesign the project to avoid the burial site completely. This early identification exemplifies the importance of the Section 106 process under the current law which requires consultation with interested parties like Tribal Nations.
In new collaborations, tribes become stewards of parks and monuments

But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will gut this process as it relates to Tribes because it will make consultation with Tribal Nations optional and it would allow federal agencies to unilaterally decide which Tribal sites are sacred enough to protect. Moreover, the bill has provisions that violate tribal sovereignty because it will allow the federal government to take over tribal preservation offices if they function in a way that displeases the federal government.
This bill was hastily written. Key terms are not defined and, when asked what certain terms mean, the drafters admitted they couldn’t agree on definitions, leaving courts to sort it out. This bill will not streamline projects; it will cause confusion and prompt excessive litigation.
Most people likely don’t realize that architects, archaeologists, architectural historians, and Tribal Nation leaders work every day to protect historic places via the Section 106 process, quietly enfranchising diverse voices in the process.
At a time when some of our most important historic places are under threat, it is vital that we speak up when bad legislation is proposed and this bill is about as bad as it gets for historic places, places we cannot put back together once the wrecking ball starts swinging.
