name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania’s legislature is losing its climate champion
description: In what might have been his last hearing as chair of Pennsylvania’s House Environmental and Natural Resource Protection committee, long-time Democratic state Rep. Greg Vitali seemed to have little interest in soaking it all in.
text:
State Rep. Greg Vitali listens to a budget address on Feb. 3. (Photo courtesy of the Pennsylvania House of RepresentativesThis article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. 
In what might have been his last hearing as chair of Pennsylvania’s House Environmental and Natural Resource Protection committee, long-time Democratic state Rep. Greg Vitali seemed to have little interest in soaking it all in.
During the October hearing, Vitali instead furrowed his brow as he watched a parade of witnesses discussing “roadspreading,” a practice in which some oil and gas companies dump waste brine from drilling on rural roadways, ostensibly to help control dust.
The regulations governing roadspreading are riddled with complex loopholes, and Vitali called the hearing after state officials issued a roadspreading permit he took issue with. That move proved the most recent example of a recalcitrance that may have contributed to ending Vitali’s decades-long career in Pennsylvania’s legislature earlier this year.
But if his loss in a competitive primary in his suburban Philadelphia district was humbling, Vitali seems determined to keep advocating for the climate and environmental issues he has always cared about. For the past 34 years, no one in the state legislature has spoken out more consistently or forcefully for fossil fuel regulation or clean energy alternatives in Pennsylvania, even as political polarization and the rise of the gas industry made those positions increasingly embattled. Vitali was the first Pennsylvania lawmaker to introduce climate change legislation and a chief advocate pushing for a “severance” tax on gas drilling in the state during the fracking boom.
David Hess, a former secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, said what really sets Vitali apart is his willingness to act as a thorn in the side of even his own party’s leadership.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“I think, in some ways, he became sort of the conscience of the Democratic caucus on a lot of environmental issues,” Hess said. “Some people admired him for that. Some people didn’t admire him for that because he was very plain-spoken.”
Now Pennsylvania will find out what it’s like not to hear his voice in Harrisburg at all. Some of Vitali’s critics welcome his impending exit at the end of November, contending that his principled stands made it more difficult to forge the kind of compromises that are necessary to pass laws in a divided government. His allies think the state will be worse off without his dedication to the environment and sense of moral clarity.
With the House’s current term winding down, Democratic state Rep. Danielle Friel Otten said Vitali’s calling of the October hearing was like a teacher assigning homework on the penultimate day of school: Otten was one of just six lawmakers present from the 27-member committee. Even after Republican Minority Chair Rep. Jack Rader Jr. closed the hearing by thanking Vitali for his time in office, which began in 1992, Vitali signaled he still has miles to go.
“Oh, we’ve got almost two months left,” Vitali said with a wry smile. “You’re not done.”
 Filling a leadership vacuum

Vitali’s career in politics began with a recycling regulation. In 1988, Pennsylvania passed Act 101, requiring large municipalities to provide curbside recycling for the first time. In Vitali’s view, his local Haverford Township was only doing the “bare minimum” the law required. He said he had an interest in environmental topics dating to when they rose to the top of the priority list for Democratic activists following the Vietnam War. Then a young lawyer, Act 101 became his personal call to action.
“I actually set up my mother’s card table by a recycling center and got signatures on a petition for the township to do more recycling, and took those to a township meeting,” Vitali said, adding the effort was ultimately successful. “It struck me that people wanted to make a contribution, but not be the prime mover or leader. And I felt I was filling a leadership vacuum.”
That solo effort grew into a drive to push surrounding Delaware County to establish a household hazardous waste collection program, which in turn provided the political base on which Vitali launched his first campaign for the State House in 1992. That year, he won the open seat for Pennsylvania’s 166th House District, previously held by a Republican. When the next session began, Vitali made the environment committee his first choice and got the assignment.
The first half of his career in Harrisburg was relatively fruitful. In 2004, he was among the Pennsylvania House members who voted for the Pennsylvania Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards, among the first regulations in the country to require electric utilities to purchase power from renewable sources like wind and solar. That same year, he introduced the legislature’s first-ever climate specific bill to require the state DEP to develop an inventory of greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2008 co-sponsored a similar bill that passed both chambers and became law.
That same year also saw the passage of Act 129, a so-called “smart metering” bill that supported statewide energy efficiency measures for utilities. John Hanger, then secretary of the DEP, said Vitali played a “significant role in its passage.”
Then came seismic shifts: Pennsylvania’s Marcellus Shale natural gas boom took off, enabled by advances in hydraulic fracturing, just as national political discourse began to polarize in the wake of the Obama presidency. Since then, even Vitali acknowledges his legislative track record has been more limited.
“It’s very difficult doing climate policy in Pennsylvania. Obviously, it has a lot of coal and oil and natural gas. So when you choose climate policy as the most important thing to work on, your life is not going to be filled with victories,” Vitali said. “It’s been frustrating. I like to give myself credit for being at the plate swinging.”
Exhibit A is Vitali’s crusade to pass a severance tax. As Pennsylvania shale gas production took off in the late aughts, efforts to institute a tax on its production followed soon after. Democrats managed to approve a House measure to institute a tax when they controlled the chamber in 2009, but the measure died acrimoniously when negotiations between the Republican-controlled Senate and outgoing Democratic Gov. Ed Rendell broke down.
Vitali introduced another severance tax proposal the next session. But by then Republicans had won full control of state government, and a separate, less-lucrative impact fee on natural gas wells was instituted. (Vitali, like most Democrats, was a “No” vote.)
Before long, Vitali also found himself battling it out with members of his own party. In June 2016, three years after he became minority chairman of what was then the House Environmental Resources and Energy Committee, Vitali blasted then-Gov. Tom Wolf, a Democrat, over his perceived wavering on oil and gas regulations. He also criticized the governor for the exit of DEP secretary John Quigley, who left office a month earlier after emails surfaced in which Quigley forcefully urged environmental groups to fight for the regulations. Later that year Vitali again criticized Democratic colleagues in the legislature, including over a proposal to ban fees on plastic bags.
He found himself in the office of then-House Minority Leader Frank Dermody, who stripped Vitali of his chairmanship and stuck him in a different committee. But if the goal was to teach Vitali a lesson, it failed.
State Rep. Greg Vitali (center) listens to testimony from David Hess, a former secretary of the state’s Department of Environmental Protection, during a committee hearing on Oct. 5. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)
 The costs of consistency

Two years after his demotion, Vitali returned to his committee position because, he said, no one else wanted the job. In 2023, he had another stroke of luck when the Democrats won the House, and Vitali suddenly found himself for the first time as majority chair of the committee he’d served on for two decades.
Democratic colleagues on his committee speak favorably of his leadership. Friel Otten recalled how Vitali helped her navigate her own low point as a freshman lawmaker in 2018, when she was criticized for posting controversial statements on social media. Vitali, she said, offered advice to regularly connect with constituents in order to cut through the noise of the internet and politics. Vitali told her that he tries to knock on 25 doors every day he’s in his district in order to take the pulse of people’s opinions.
“I share that advice with people all the time,” Friel Otten said.
State Rep. Joe Webster, another Democratic committee member, said he believes that respect for Vitali crosses party lines due to the consistency of his principles, even when others don’t agree with them.
“I think because he’s faithful to that, that they respect that,” Webster said of Republican lawmakers.
But as is often the case for political firebrands of all stripes, there are persistent questions about how effective Vitali has proven at converting ideas into actual policy in Pennsylvania. Legislation he introduced focusing on natural gas drilling, roadspreading, and the tech industry over the past four years failed to become law, including a bill to remove hundreds of millions of dollars in tax breaks for data centers that passed the House 197-5 this year before stalling in the Senate.
The commonwealth is currently one of just four states with a divided legislature, as Democrats hold the House and Republicans the Senate. Democrats also hold just a three-member majority in the lower chamber, a razor-thin margin that requires policy buy-in from centrist Democrats hailing from gas-rich communities.
State Rep. Paul Takac, a Democratic member of Vitali’s committee from the center of the state, said the political landscape has proven tricky to navigate.

“We have a very diverse caucus in the House Democrats. We have everybody from urban and suburban to rural,” Takac said. “It’s difficult to build consensus around some of these highly politicized issues.”
Others argue that Vitali has demonstrated an ability to cut a deal. The 2004 Pennsylvania Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards also created subsidies for fossil fuel sources like waste coal, which environmental advocates have worried about ever since.
Hanger, who served as DEP secretary from 2008 to 2011, said Vitali’s “Yes” vote on the bill shows he could compromise when there were willing partners. But since that time, Hanger argued, the Republican Party drifted nationally toward climate denialism, while there are now fewer centrist Republicans in Pennsylvania willing to cut a deal.
“I know he does make compromises,” Hanger said of Vitali. “But he was also fearless about saying things that needed to be said, fearless in challenging powerful industries and powerful figures that needed to be challenged.”
In his four years as majority chair, allies said, Vitali was more effective than some may realize.
Rob Altenburg, a former senior director of energy and climate for the nonprofit PennFuture, notes that in 2023, Vitali sought to eliminate similar tax breaks for cryptomining operations as part of a larger regulatory package that ultimately received pushback, including from his own party, and failed to pass. The next year, Vitali managed to slip language eliminating the tax breaks into another bill anyway.
“So there wasn’t a formal sponsorship there on his part,” Altenburg said. “But on issues like that, he’s been willing to sit down and think, ‘What’s the right [strategy] in this situation?’”
Vitali also said he saw a lot of his job while committee chair as playing defense, including advocating against cuts to DEP funding come budget time. Regardless, the job slipped from Vitali’s grasp.
In 2025, House Democratic leadership created a new Energy committee, removing that aspect of Vitali’s portfolio and giving it to state Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler, a Philadelphia Democrat with a swift-rising reputation as an effective lawmaker whose wins include bipartisan measures that provide funding to put solar panels on schools and require utilities to consider energy efficiency measures.
Things got worse for Vitali when a 41-year-old township commissioner named Judy Trombetta announced this January she would run for his seat.
Trombetta went on to win the endorsement of the local Delaware County Democratic Committee and defeated Vitali handily in a May primary. Some insiders speculate Trombetta’s candidacy was championed by the party establishment in retaliation for Vitali’s outspokenness.
State Sen. Katie Muth, another Southeast Pennsylvania Democrat and firebrand on environmental issues, said she believes Vitali’s ousting was retributive and will have a chilling effect on other members.
“He’s being taught a lesson: ‘If you don’t [expletive] fall in line, we’re going to teach you a lesson. We’re going to make an example out of you,’” Muth said.
The Delaware County Democrats did not respond to a request for comment about their endorsement. The group also endorsed Vitali’s opponent in 2022, unsuccessfully, and Trombetta told local media outlets that while she respected Vitali as an environmental champion, she also believed he had “neglected numerous other constituencies on numerous other topics.”
Spokespersons for Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and House Speaker Joanna McClinton both spoke favorably of Vitali in emailed statements to Inside Climate News.
If Vitali holds any animosity about his fall from power, he doesn’t show it.
“Nothing retributive,” Vitali said of his ousting. “My primary opponent had her own career ambitions.”
The Pennsylvania Capitol in downtown Harrisburg on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
 Looking ahead

Vitali said during an October interview in Harrisburg that he believes the state will struggle to pass stronger environmental policy even if Democrats win a trifecta in next month’s elections, and even if he was still part of the legislature in January.
The state’s oil and gas lobby has always been powerful, even among Democrats, he said.
He believes labor interests have also amassed too much power within his party in recent years, and that Shapiro is focused on running for president in 2028. (The governor has not yet declared his intentions and consistently says he remains focused on his current job.)
“Unions look at all issues through the lens of their own jobs. … They won’t let basic stuff pass,” Vitali said. “And the governor looks at all issues through the lens of his presidential ambitions, quite frankly. He values being aligned with labor more than he values being aligned with enviros.”
Rosie Lapowsky, Shapiro’s spokesperson, said the governor wishes Vitali well and “appreciates his long standing commitment” to environmental issues.
“Governor Shapiro is proud of his Administration’s record of protecting clean air and water, plugging abandoned wells, expanding clean energy, and holding polluters accountable,” Lapowsky wrote in an email. “There is more work to do, but the biggest obstacle to further progress has been Senate Republicans, who have repeatedly blocked commonsense proposals to expand clean energy and lower costs.”
The true impact of Vitali’s legacy may be borne out in the years ahead. Vitali said he sees promise in younger lawmakers, like Fiedler and several members of his committee.
“No one is irreplaceable,” he said.
But for advocates who have fought for years beside Vitali for better environmental and energy policy in Pennsylvania, his absence will be noticeable, especially as the state confronts a newer threat to clean air, water and land: data centers.
Altenburg said many Pennsylvania lawmakers on both sides of the aisle believe that building even more natural gas infrastructure should be the preeminent policy solution to power the controversial industry.
Vitali has been one of the few challenging that narrative, and it’s not clear who will pick up the mantle once he leaves office in late November, Altenburg said. “I think if we don’t have a voice like Greg’s, if we don’t have somebody telling people that that’s not the only solution, it’s hard to see a pathway to change.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: It’s Election Day in Florida
description: LAKELAND — Donald Trump’s sagging public approval numbers have led to an expectation that Democrats will have a big night around the country on Tuesday. But the essential question in Florida is whether any sort of “blue wave” makes its way to the Sunshine State? That didn’t happen during Trump’s first midterm election as president […]
text:
Campaign signs outside of a polling location in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)LAKELAND — Donald Trump’s sagging public approval numbers have led to an expectation that Democrats will have a big night around the country on Tuesday. But the essential question in Florida is whether any sort of “blue wave” makes its way to the Sunshine State?
That didn’t happen during Trump’s first midterm election as president in 2018, when Democrats prospered nationally but not in Florida. And that was when registered Democrats outnumbered registered Republicans by more than 250,000.
Now Republicans hold a more than 1.5 million voter-registration advantage.
 
Florida 2026 Voter Guide

But Democrats have been strong in the combined early vote and vote-by-mail tallies, prompting concern among Florida Republicans. More than 5.4 million Floridians have already cast ballots either by mail or in early voting, which concluded Sunday. Registered Republicans have a 2.4% lead in votes cast over registered Democrats, 40.2% to 37.8%. NPA and third-party voters have cast 22% of all votes.
“We need to have massive Republican turnout tomorrow,” Florida Republican Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia exhorted a group of Republicans in Polk County Monday afternoon, on the last full day of campaigning. “Everyone up and down the ticket needs your help to get them to the polls tomorrow.”
In recent election cycles, Republicans have dominated on Election Day, and there’s no question GOP officials believe they can duplicate those results Tuesday.
Democratic Party strategist Steve Schale wrote Sunday on his Substack site that in 2022 (when Ron DeSantis won reelection by 19 points), Republicans won Election Day turnout in Florida by 600,000 voters. He noted that they have about 700,000 more voters who have voted in the past three general elections — 2020, 2022, and 2024 — than the Democrats do.
And in the Aug. 18 primary, Republican election day turnout was double the number for Democrats (60%-30%).
 Polk County
Ingoglia participated in Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donald’s campaign swing Monday that, in addition to Polk County, made stops in Pasco, Sarasota, and Lee counties.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly added a stop in Polk Monday in addition to three other appearances he had previously scheduled (his appearance in Brevard County was cancelled due to heavy rainfall and flooding).
Polk County is where DeSantis expressed angst about GOP turnout last week on social media. It’s a district he won by 30 points in 2022, that Trump won by 20 points in 2024, and has nearly 60,000 more registered Republicans than Democrats. Going into Election Day, however, registered Republicans had cast fewer than 2 percentage points more than had registered Democrats.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds in Lakeland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix).
 ‘Pure tossup’
Florida voters will also choose whether they want to formally approve of DeSantis’ choice of Republican Ashley Moody for the U.S. Senate, or go with Democrat Angie Nixon to serve the remaining two years of the term originally won by Marco Rubio in 2022.
All 28 congressional seats are also on the ballot, although many of the boundaries of those seats changed this year after the GOP-controlled Legislature enacted a new redistricting map designed to add to their ranks.
(Voting rights groups filed a lawsuit to challenge that new map, contending it violates the Fair Districts Amendment approved by voters in 2010. The Florida Supreme Court upheld the map for this year’s midterm, while the legal case will continue).
Donalds leads Jolly by an average of around 4 points, according to the RealClearPolitics average.
“I expected this race to be close and it is,” Insider Advantage pollster Matt Towery said  in a press release Friday. His poll shows Donalds up over Jolly, 49%-45%.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly in Polk County on Nov. 2, 2026 (Photo from Jolly campaign).
Jolly told reporters in Pasco County Saturday that he thought the race was “a pure tossup right now,” adding he believed that while Donalds had the money advantage, “we’ve got the momentum.”
Donalds has raised nearly $174 million from his two campaign accounts. Jolly less than $27 million.
Moody leads Nixon by an average six points, 52%-46%, according to an aggregation of 30 individual polls by pollstergraph.com.
Voters will decide three constitutional amendments, all put on the ballot by the Florida Legislature. The highest-profile measure is Amendment 3, to raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and make other changes that would reduce local revenue, with projected annual reductions reaching nearly $12 billion after five years.
Floridians will choose members of the state House and Senate. Democrats are desperate to overcome thes uperminority status they’ve been in for four years.
Races to watch there include the rematches of two special elections that Democrats won in majority Republican-leaning districts in March: Democratic incumbent Brian Nathan versus Republican Josie Tomkow in Florida’s Senate District 14 in Hillsborough County, and Democratic incumbent Emily Gregory versus Republican Jon Maples in House District 87 in Palm Beach County.
Additionally, three Florida Cabinet seats are on the ballot.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A camera is not a conscience
description: What kind of society do we want to live in? Is it one that functions because everyone knows they are being watched?
text:
Imagine someone finds a wallet on the sidewalk and returns it to its owner. Now, imagine they know a camera is recording what they do. In both scenarios, the outcome is the same. The wallet is returned. But what we learn about the person who returned it is quite different.
In the first case, their actions tell us something about their character. In the second, we cannot distinguish whether they acted out of concern for a stranger or because they knew that their actions could be traced back to them. This example raises an important point about society today. While surveillance can make people more likely to cooperate, it also allows us to secure that cooperation without actually having to trust one another.
Social scientists have spent decades studying the relationship between cooperation and trust in society. Findings reveal a distinction between getting people to behave cooperatively and getting people to trust one another. In a study published in Management Science, participants behaved more cooperatively when they anticipated monitoring, but acted more selfishly when they expected that their actions would go unobserved.
Importantly though, others often mistook someone’s strategic compliance for genuine trustworthiness. Other research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology found that punishment systems could encourage cooperation while making people less likely to believe others would have cooperated on their own. Another study involving more than 4,000 participants across four countries found that monitoring not only affected trust, but could change how people understood their relationships. When monitoring was introduced, relationships based on mutual care began to feel more like transactions.
Taken together, these studies suggest that surveillance is not socially neutral. It can change how we interpret one another’s actions and what we come to expect from our relationships. That matters because cooperation is about much more than following rules. Think about everything a functioning community depends on that cannot be compelled or reliably monitored, such as volunteering, extending the benefit of the doubt, or working together when no one is required to do so. These are not small things. They are part of the infrastructure of community life.
These ideas are especially relevant to the ongoing debate over automated license plate readers in Connecticut’s cities and towns. Police officials have defended the technology as valuable for criminal investigations. But, whether a technology helps investigators solve specific crimes is not the same question as whether its widespread use is appropriate for a community. Automated license plate readers collect information about vehicles passing through public spaces, regardless of whether their occupants are suspected of wrongdoing. That is a consequential change in the relationship between people and their government. We should ask more than whether cameras help police. We should ask what the public gives up when we use them.
Routine surveillance of Connecticut residents should not become a permanent feature of civic life. At its heart, this debate goes far beyond one company’s cameras or one town’s contract and raises the bigger question of what kind of society we want to live in. Is it one that functions because everyone knows that they are being watched? Or one in which people have the freedom to demonstrate to one another that they can be trusted? Public safety is not just about catching people who do wrong. It also depends on people who choose to do right even when no one is watching.
Jennifer McLeer is a sociological social psychologist and assistant professor of psychology at the University of Hartford.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The election result Americans refuse to imagine: losing
description: In modern politics, an overwhelming majority of voters expect their “side” to win.
text:
With the outcome of the midterm elections fast approaching, it’s only natural that many of us have taken up political forecasting as something like a second job.
Will Democrats win the Senate? How deep into Trump country can their House candidates compete? Why does Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine, seem so resilient?

Seth Warner

Obviously, election outcomes are an uncertain matter. Opinion polls can provide clues about what may happen, but elections today are decided by tiny margins, and the methodological choices about which polls, weights, or turnout models to trust make knowing what’s about to happen even harder.
However, it’s not terribly difficult to predict what a given person expects to happen. In modern politics, an overwhelming majority of voters expect their “side” to win.
That’s the headline finding from my new research article in the journal Political Behavior. Today, ahead of presidential elections, about 90% of voters expect their preferred candidate to win, and the pattern appears similar ahead of this year’s midterms.
Of course, unwarranted optimism isn’t a new phenomenon (your author is a Mets fan). Going back nearly a century, we have known that people occupy information bubbles that make them likely to expect victory. An early study found 71% of Herber Hoover voters expected him to win in 1932, despite the ravaging effect of the Great Depression.
Yet over the past 15 years, what I refer to as “partisan wishful thinking” has grown to an all-time high. Throughout the mid-20th century and into the early 2000s, the percentage of voters expecting their candidate to triumph hovered in the low-70s by percentage. That spiked with the tea party’s ascent ahead the 2012 cycle and has grown even stronger across the three elections featuring Donald Trump.
My article uses seven decades of survey data to study the factors that predict this optimism, and to see what has changed about voters today. The core finding is that the more a person wants an outcome, the more they are likely to expect it. Historically, this has taken the form of wanting your own side to win, but more recently, people also want the other side to lose.
Indeed, much of political behavior today is driven by what we call negative partisanship, or animosity toward supporters of the “other side.”  While this animosity can increase participation, and some may be necessary to ensure social progress, the downsides are huge. People who actively dislike the other party are more gullible in the face of misinformation, accepting of their own party’s bad behavior, and willing to dehumanize people with whom they disagree.
What’s scary about sky-high wishful thinking is that it may make this polarization worse. The problem with everyone expecting to win, of course, is that few are prepared to lose — even though one of them must.
Using surveys that interviewed people before and after presidential elections between 1996 and 2024, I found that people suffering from “dashed hopes” came out with greater animosity toward the other side in most of these elections. Importantly, this was not merely a Trump-era effect; disappointed Bob Dole and John Kerry supporters also showed the same dynamics.
So, what does this mean ahead of the coming election? As my grandfather would tell me before the Mets took the field each April, “Don’t get your hopes up.”
While Democrats lead in generic ballot polls, the difficulties forecasting who shows up to vote are well-documented, and Democratic Senate candidates will need to win in red states to wrest control of Congress.
The ideal posture for a small-d democrat — one committed to seeing our democracy succeed — would be to consider good-faith reasons why their party may lose. Research shows that intellectual humility can be a valuable bulwark against polarized politics.
For my part, I can see Republicans losing because they oversee an economy with drastically higher gas prices than a year ago, seemingly because of a war that most view as optional. Then, amid the president’s use of his pardon powers to help allies, Americans perceive corruption in government to a greater degree than at any point in recent history.
Democrats, meanwhile, seem to be “running against Trump” for the 10th consecutive year, and are struggling to make an affirmative case for themselves. They ended their last presidency as failed defenders of the gerontocracy, and when they belatedly got a younger candidate in Kamala Harris, had trouble articulating a coherent agenda on the economic issues that swing voters care most about.
None of this is to say there aren’t reasons to get excited about the midterms or see good in a party’s positions. But with more modest expectations, and ideas about how our own side can improve, we can help make democracy self-improving no matter how the results turn out.
Seth Warner is an Assistant Professor of Political Science at the University of Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Voting — the most powerful form of resistance
description: I want to make a plea, and I mean it as a desperate one: Please vote.
text:
For most of my life, I believed certain things about America were permanent. Not perfect, never that, but permanent.
I believed that whatever our failings, the world looked at us and saw a nation that stood for justice, for equality, and above all for reason. A country where institutions outlasted the people who ran them and the rule of law was more than a slogan.
I no longer take that for granted. And I don’t think you should either.
After the Second World War, America leaned into peace. We invited the nations of the world to gather on our own soil and placed the United Nations in New York, a promise that countries could argue and negotiate rather than destroy each other. Our foreign aid made its share of missteps, but for generations it fed the hungry and vaccinated children in places most Americans will never see. American strength came with American generosity.
So how did we get here? How is it that we now find ourselves trading tariffs and insults with Canada, our closest friend, our neighbor along the longest peaceful border on earth? Canadians stood with us after September 11th. They took in our stranded travelers. If we can turn that friendship into a quarrel, what relationship is safe?
America was also a promise to the people who came here. For generations, immigrants arrived with little more than hope, and they found a country where they could build a life for themselves and their families that they could never have imagined in the country they left. They worked, they saved, they sent their children to school, and their children became teachers and soldiers and business owners. That promise built this nation. Today too many people who came here chasing it are made to feel unwelcome in the only home their children have ever known.
These commitments are eroding. Not in one dramatic stroke, but steadily, the way a shoreline disappears. A reputation built over 80 years can be spent in a handful.
So I want to make a plea, and I mean it as a desperate one.
Please vote on November 3.
Vote as if everything this country has stood for is on the line, because the things we assumed were permanent are proving they are not. Vote as if the erosion is real, because it is. And vote as if the loss can still be stopped, because it can.
Marches have their place. But the most powerful act of resistance in a democracy is quiet. It happens behind a voting booth curtain, one citizen at a time.
The revolution will not be televised. It never was. The revolution that pushes back against this erosion happens in the voting booth.
I have lived long enough to see America at its best and to know what we stand to lose. This November, your vote may matter more than it ever has.
Joseph Luciano lives in Bridgeport.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Democrats make election eve plea for voters to help them flip Congress
description: At an election eve rally in Springfield, New Jersey Democrats rallied mostly for Democrat Rebecca Bennett in her bid to unseat GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr.
text:
House hopeful Rebecca Bennett (D), a former Navy helicopter pilot, holds up the American flag patch she wore on her flight uniform for 10 years during a rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]SPRINGFIELD — With control of Congress at stake, New Jersey’s top Democrats gathered Monday for an election eve rally, painting Republicans as a corrupt party beholden to billionaires that has lost touch with regular people and deserves to be swept from office on Election Day.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill, Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, and others rallied in two-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr.’s district, hoping their get-out-the-vote pleas will help deliver a victory Tuesday for his Democratic challenger, Rebecca Bennett.
Kim told supporters packed into the Raymond Chisholm Community Center that he agreed with Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat who described himself as “nauseously optimistic” as Election Day approached.
“We’re hopeful. We’re hopeful, but it’s nerve-wracking, right? Because we know that so much is at stake. So much is at stake,” Kim said. “Right now we do not have three functioning branches of government. We have one branch of government that’s just trying to dominate the other two branches. That’s not the Constitution. That’s not America. That’s not our democracy.”
Kim and his fellow Democrats bashed President Donald Trump and his MAGA faithful, with Sherrill and Bennett referencing the $2 billion Trump has gained since his second White House term began.
“Has anybody else gained $2 billion in net worth in the last two years? Yeah, I don’t think so,” Bennett said. “And we have career politicians like Congressman Tom Kean Jr. who have been in office for 25 years, who are doing absolutely nothing to solve the issues that we are facing in this country. That’s ultimately, I think, part of the problem, is that we have a bunch of career politicians in Washington who are putting their personal interests over the needs of all of us.”
Harrison Neeley, a Kean spokesman, did not respond to a request for comment.

Sherrill told the crowd that when America has bad government, working people suffer.
“Everything is on the ballot tomorrow. If you care about working people having a shot in this country, if you care about getting costs down, if you care about protecting people’s rights, if you care about a future for our kids that we can be proud of, every single thing is on the ballot,” Sherrill said.
Speaking in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Trump accused Democrats of being committed “to the same radical agenda.”
“The Democrats want to blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists, and the United States Congress will not allow that to happen. Got some big races tomorrow. I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow is Election Day, more traditional, and we can’t let that happen,” he said.
Sen. Cory Booker speaks at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFIlippo/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, laughs at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Sen. Cory Booker and Rebecca Bennett, both Democrats, smile at Booker's phone, which he used to record a live video for his social media followers during an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Sen. Andy Kim speaks at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFIlippo/New Jersey Monitor)The crowd listens to speakers at a Democratic rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) House hopeful Rebecca Bennett (D) speaks to supporters at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Democrat Rebecca Bennett, center, talks with reporters alongside Sen. Andy Kim and Gov. Mikie Sherrill at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Democrat Rebecca Bennett waits to speak to supporters at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. Bennett is seeking to oust GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
In Springfield, Bennett displayed the American flag patch she wore on her flight uniform for the decade when she served as a Navy helicopter pilot. It always reminded her she served the United States of America, not any specific president or party, she said.
“I brought this patch with me tonight because I want to remind everyone in this room that this flag does not belong to a political party. It does not belong to Donald Trump. It belongs to all of us,” she said.
Earlier, Bennett told reporters she’s confident but “definitely not measuring the drapes before tomorrow night. We got to make sure we’re sprinting through the finish line.”
Kim urged the crowd to help get her there.
“I see a lot of cowardice,” Kim said. “When I see Speaker Johnson just continuing to allow Donald Trump to do whatever he wants, here’s what I’ll say: On Tuesday, we got to rack up the votes so high for Rebecca and these candidates around the country, I want to make sure none of us have ever had to say after Tuesday the phrase ‘Speaker Johnson’ ever again. Never again!”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Alaska fishers need clean energy solutions to lower fuel costs
description: I have fished out of Sitka, Alaska, for more than 40 years. I know the challenge of running a business where every cost increase is a risk to my bottom line. This past summer, the rapidly escalating cost of fuel added stress to an increasingly unpredictable business. For a fisherman, fuel is not optional. It […]
text:
The sunrise lights the sky over Thomsen Harbor and Mt. Edgecumbe in Sitka in this 2011 photo. The city is among the communities surrounded by the Tongass National Forest. (Photo by Jeffrey Wickett/U.S. Forest Service)I have fished out of Sitka, Alaska, for more than 40 years. I know the challenge of running a business where every cost increase is a risk to my bottom line. This past summer, the rapidly escalating cost of fuel added stress to an increasingly unpredictable business.
For a fisherman, fuel is not optional. It powers the boat that is our workplace, and every increase comes straight out of a narrow margin. The war in Iran has sent fuel prices soaring, and that increase took a toll on my business and all the other small-scale fishing businesses that power Alaska’s rural economy.
The Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association, a non-profit I run when I am not fishing, is working to reduce the fishing fleet’s dependence on fossil fuels. Ocean acidification is a threat to our fisheries, and along with lowering costs we want to reduce our emissions. For close to a decade, we have been helping the fleet identify energy efficiencies, and this year worked with project partners to install the first hybrid propulsion system in a commercial fishing boat. We are working on a second hybrid boat now, and also assessing energy-efficiency and cost-saving opportunities in the seafood processing sector. This work has been guided by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, and mostly funded by two Department of Energy grants.
This season, our first hybrid boat, a 50-foot longline/troller, saved an estimated 20%on fuel costs. The second hybrid will be electric propelled with a small diesel generator to recharge batteries at sea if needed. His estimated fuel savings will be 80%or higher.
That’s what smart federal investment looks like: a small business spending less on energy and keeping more of what it earns. But these boats are the exception. In recent years, more than 401 clean energy projects nationwide have been canceled, delayed or stripped of grant funding, taking over 42,000 megawatts of planned power with them, enough for nearly 22 million homes. In Alaska, three canceled projects would have generated 45 MW, enough for 9,000 homes.
When less power comes online, bills go up. Household electric bills are up 15% nationally since 2024. Utilities have raised or sought rate increases totaling more than $101 billion, reaching more than 116 million electric customers and 59 million natural gas customers. Some Alaskans are paying an additional $45 per month on their electricity bill. Small businesses are squeezed from both directions: paying more for fuel while losing the federal support that could help us use less of it.
This summer, fish prices in Alaska were relatively strong, helping fishermen bear the higher fuel costs and the burden of tariffs. If the prices paid to fishermen drop next season, the number of boats fishing will also drop. That means less fish to market, fewer paychecks spent in local shops and more risk in an already dangerous job. In Sitka, where a half-gallon of milk can cost $8, every dollar saved on energy helps keep a boat working, crew employed and a town whole.
Fishermen are not asking for special treatment or subsidies. We want policies that promote energy efficiency, stabilize supply and bring costs down. Our future depends on healthy fisheries and affordable operating costs. We are doing our part to address ocean acidification and drive energy transition, but we cannot do it on our own. Energy modernization deserves federal and public investment. The businesses that anchor our rural communities cannot keep absorbing costs they did not create.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Care Callers, ‘speed friending,’ other efforts to help Marylanders combat loneliness
description: Health leaders warned that the social isolation and loneliness of the COVID-19 era could take a physical and emotional toll. The social distancing may be gone, but the loneliness remains, which is why health groups are running programs to reduce that loneliness.
text:
The loneliness epidemic that began during the COVID-19 lockdown remains and can cause physical as well as emotional damage, officials say, which is why some organizations are taking steps to reach out to isolated or lonely individuals. (Photo by Halfpoint Images/Getty Stock photo)In the social distancing days of the COVID-19 pandemic, national health leaders warned that social isolation and loneliness not only bring emotional wounds but also take a physical toll on the body, increasing risks of premature death and other health outcomes.
The social distancing days may be gone, but experts say that social isolation is still a problem, particularly for seniors but also for people with disabilities and teens to young adults.
One hospital CEO says there may be a simple solution, which also has its roots in the pandemic — just pick up the phone.
Meritus Health CEO Maulik Joshi created a pilot program in the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic in which volunteers called patients who identified as lonely to simply check in on them – ask about their day, bond over shared interests like sports, and build an ongoing connection.
“Five years ago, we thought ‘let’s try something simple.’ And that was to just call people and talk to them on the phone and make a connection with them,” Joshi said in a recent interview. “Loneliness and social isolation really are of epidemic proportions — COVID didn’t cause it, but it certainly accelerated that.”
Since launching in November 2021, the Care Caller program has had about 1,800 patients participate. Today, 60 active volunteers and four contracted callers connect with over 350 people who use the care caller services.
Guns, drugs, budget cuts, AI join traditional maladies at public health forum

Joshi himself participates as a volunteer, regularly speaking with one of the first patients to take part in the program.
“We really believe that these practical, pragmatic interventions can go a long way,” he said. “Who would have thought that just a phone call here and there would make a difference? … All the little stuff we do does add up to big health outcomes.”
He said that Care Caller patients span all ages and demographics, though about 60% of the participants are 60 years old or older. An AARP survey found that Marylanders over age 50 may have the nation’s highest rates of feeling lonely or left out.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, about half of adults reported experiencing loneliness, according to an official advisory issued in 2023 by then-Surgeon General Vivek H. Murthy. In that advisory, “Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation,” Murthy warned that loneliness is “more than just a bad feeling.” It also comes with greater risks of cardiovascular disease, dementia, depression and premature death, among other concerns.
“The mortality impact of being socially disconnected is similar to that caused by smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day, and even greater than that associated with obesity and physical inactivity,” the report said. “We have an opportunity, and an obligation, to make the same investments in addressing social connection that we have made in addressing tobacco use, obesity, and the addiction crisis.”
That advisory brought national attention to health outcomes that accompany social isolation — defined as objectively having few social relationships and infrequent social interactions — and loneliness, “subjective distressing experience that results from perceived isolation or inadequate meaningful connections.”
Nationally, about 54% of adults aged 18 and older reported in 2025 that they feel isolated from others, according to an American Psychological Association report on stress due to societal division and loneliness.
The APA also reports that almost 69% of adults say that they needed more emotional support than they received over the last year, up from 65% reported in 2024.
But statistics show a persistent and growing challenge of older residents facing loneliness and social isolation.
The AARP, an advocacy group for retirement-aged people, said in a December report that 40% of adults aged 45 and older report being lonely, up from 35% in 2018, revealing that “loneliness is not only persistent but growing.”
The AARP worked with NORC at the University of Chicago, a nonpartisan research organization, to report geographic variations in loneliness reported across the United States. It finds that that Maryland has the largest share of residents aged 50 and older who report frequently feeling left out or isolated compared to other states.
Dan Martin, chief public policy officer for the Mental Health Association of Maryland, says older adults have the greatest need for programs that combat social isolation and loneliness. (Photo by Danielle Brown/Maryland Matters)
The data creates a “loneliness score” based on how often people aged 50 and older reported feeling a lack of companionship, isolated or left out. Almost 29% of older Marylanders had a high loneliness score, trailing only Washington, D.C., where 33.3% of older residents reported higher instances of feeling alone.
It’s why mental health advocates often have anti-loneliness programs more tailored to senior populations, said Dan Martin, chief public policy officer at the Mental Health Association of Maryland.
“The biggest impact is in the older adult community,” Martin said.
He said the association often coordinates events at senior living spaces or senior centers to facilitate social interactions.
“One of our really popular activities is what we call ‘speed friending’ — which gives participants a structured and welcoming opportunity to meet people, share experiences and build friendships,” Martin said.
“They develop new friendships through ‘speed friending’ that continue to this day,” he said. “It reinforces the value of creating the opportunity for older adults to connect with others in their communities and giving them those places to meet new people.”
The conversation on loneliness and social isolation was more concentrated during the early COVID-19 years. But Del. Joe Vogel (D-Montgomery) said that Murthy’s surgeon general advisory and the experience of reduced face-to-face interactions due to social distancing measures brought more awareness to the importance of staying connected.
“I think in some ways that was also eye-opening for all of us of what it’s like to feel socially isolated — how that impacted our mental health and our physical health,” Vogel said.
Del. Joe Vogel (D-Motngomery) sits with Del. Bernice Mireku-North (D-Montgomery) in the General Assembly during 2023 legislative session. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)
“I heard from constituents, especially older folks in my district, individuals with disabilities, there’s many communities that really struggle with this issue of social isolation and loneliness and it has real health consequences,” he said. “I think as a state we could be doing more to address those issues.”
This past session, Vogel sponsored a bill that would have created a new grant program to help expand programs in the state already trying to reduce social isolation and loneliness.
But in the tight budget challenges the state of Maryland faced in the 2026 session, the bill did not get voted out of committee.
“The investment we could be making to create or expand programs that focus on social connection and addressing loneliness that many in our communities feel – that is money that we’re actually then saving on healthcare,” Vogel said.
“If we can strategically invest in these programs that are working, and replicate them across the state, I think in the long run we’re actually saving money and helping Marylanders along the way,” he said.
Vogel said he may revisit the issue of social isolation and loneliness in the upcoming session, either through reintroducing the proposal for a new grant program or through similar legislation. The state’s budget woes will likely continue into the 2027 session, however, which could hinder such efforts.
“I think this is a really important step that we should be taking to invest in our communities to support those most at risk,” Vogel said, “and address this, often, neglected public health crisis of social isolation and loneliness.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Howard County Executive Calvin Ball steps down to take over Baltimore City Community College
description: After making history as Howard County’s first Black county executive, Calvin Ball announced Monday he will step down this month to become interim president at Baltimore City Community College.
text:
Howard County Executive Calvin Ball (D) in the State House for the 2025 State of the State address. Ball announced Monday he will step down from the executive's post to become interim president at Baltimore City Community College. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)After making history as Howard County’s first Black county executive, Calvin Ball announced Monday he will step down this month to become interim president at Baltimore City Community College.
Ball, 51, returns to the city’s two-year college where he worked as director of its Complete College program before being elected county executive in 2018. The Complete College program provides resources to help students transition to a community college career.
“To return to an institution that holds such a special place in my heart is a full-circle moment,” said Ball, who has a doctorate in education from Morgan State University.
“BCCC is a place of possibility, where dreams can be nurtured, barriers broken, and futures are transformed,” he said. “I am grateful to the Board of Trustees for placing its trust in me and for the opportunity to once again serve this extraordinary community.”
Ball wrote on Facebook that he plans to step down Nov. 16, just three weeks before the new county executive is scheduled to be sworn in. Brandee Ganz, the county’s chief administrative office, will serve as acting county executive until the new executive takes office Dec. 7.
Baltimore City Community College leader defends school against audit

Ball, who is term-limited after serving two four–year terms, served as president of the Maryland Association of Counties (MACo) between 2023-24. Ball often traveled to Annapolis during the 90-day legislative session and testified before various General Assembly committees. He joined other Black men in Annapolis almost two years ago, encouraging them to get out and vote during the 2024 presidential election.
Ball takes over after a state audit released in June found that the college apparently awarded $264,000 in financial aid to 145 potentially fictitious or “ghost students,” and didn’t adhere to procurement laws. The audit also said the school could not account for more than 20,000 missing items, such as laptops and other computer equipment, worth a total of about $20 million.
In August, the community college’s faculty union ratified its first-ever contract. Part of the contract with members represented by United Academics of Maryland Local 6628, an affiliate of American Federation of Teachers-Maryland, includes a 3.25% raise and a $1,000 bonus in the first year.
Slightly more than two weeks later, on Sept. 9, BCCC President Debra McCurdy testified before the legislature’s Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee, and defended the school against the state audit. McCurdy attributed some of the challenges to a vacancy rate that exceeds 25% for BCCC positions, and said new leadership has been hired to help get the school back on track.
According to The Baltimore Banner, McCurdy emailed faculty and staff Friday she will step down at the end of the year.
Ball said Monday he plans to bring “that same spirit of service, collaboration, and compassion to BCCC, building upon the progress made under Dr. McCurdy’s leadership, and working alongside our faculty, staff, and students to strengthen pathways to opportunity and success.”
“I plan to continue leading with love, listening with intention, and working together to ensure that every student who walks through BCCC’s doors has the opportunity to realize their potential and build a brighter future,” his statement said.
Voters on Tuesday will choose Ball’s successor, with Democrat Vanessa Atterbeary and Green Party nominee Nater Kane squaring off for the job.

title: Judge blocks Tennessee from denying driver’s licenses to immigrants with work permits
description: A Nashville judge temporarily blocked Tennessee officials from denying driver’s licenses and license renewals to immigrants authorized by the federal government to live and work in the United States.  Chancellor Russell Perkins, in an order issued Monday, wrote several factors weighed in favor of the temporary restraining order, including the threat of irrep[...]
text:
A Nashville judge has temporarily blocked new Tennessee rules denying driver's licenses to immigrants with valid federal work permits. Pictured: ICE agents take a  man into custody during a May 2025 sweep of a predominantly immigrant Nashville neighborhood as a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer looks on. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Nashville judge temporarily blocked Tennessee officials from denying driver’s licenses and license renewals to immigrants authorized by the federal government to live and work in the United States. 
Chancellor Russell Perkins, in an order issued Monday, wrote several factors weighed in favor of the temporary restraining order, including the threat of irreparable harm and the public interest.
Perkins set an initial hearing in the case for Nov. 14. 
The Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights and six immigrants with valid work permits filed suit on Friday, alleging the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security violated state law and exceeded its authority in implementing new rules for what immigration documents are necessary to obtain a temporary driver’s license. 
Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits

The rules exclude a federally-issued employment authorization card as an acceptable document for the purposes of demonstrating an individual is authorized by the federal government to legally work and be present in the country. 
For many immigrants, including asylum seekers and so-called Dreamers — individuals who were brought to the country as children and are now protected from deportation — the work authorization document serves as the only proof they have of their immigration status. 
Hundreds of Tennessee residents have been denied temporary licenses and license renewals since the department first began implementing the new rules in recent weeks. Immigrants without permanent legal status are only eligible for temporary licenses in Tennessee. 
In a statement issued late Monday, the Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights said that, under the temporary order, state driver’s license clerks cannot require that people provide a “visa or I-94” in order to get a license, referring to immigration documents the state is now requiring. The documents are not issued to many classes of immigrants the federal government has authorized to live and work in the country. 
Lawsuit seeks to block TN from denying driver’s licenses to immigrants legally allowed to work 

“Instead, the Department has to comply with its regulations and practice of many years and accept work permits and other federal documents as proof of federally authorized presence when issuing temporary driver’s licenses,” the statement said.
A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security, which administers driver’s licenses, last week cited a Tennessee law that requires applicants for the temporary licenses to provide documentation that establishes a specific period of lawful status in the United States. The employment authorization card, the spokesperson said, does not. 
The law cited by the department was first enacted nearly 20 years ago then revised by lawmakers in 2025. Neither the original nor the revised law specifies which documents are acceptable or unacceptable forms of proof of immigration status. 
The legal challenge alleges state officials abruptly changed rules for driver’s licenses without following state law and without public notice. Thousands of immigrants statewide with federally-issued work permits are at risk for losing drivers’ licenses that enable them to legally drive to work and school.

title: Nebraska’s 28 ‘opportunity zones’ OK’d by U.S. Treasury aim for private investment, growth
description: LINCOLN — Federal officials have approved 28 Nebraska census tracts as “opportunity zones” eligible for a new tax incentive program that starts in January and is intended to boost economic development. The tracts span the state from Scottsbluff to Omaha and include both rural and urban areas. The batch was submitted earlier this year to […]
text:
U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner, flanked by Gov. Jim Pillen, visits the Micro Market in the Highlander redevelopment site in May. He was in North Omaha in part to promote opportunity zones. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Federal officials have approved 28 Nebraska census tracts as “opportunity zones” eligible for a new tax incentive program that starts in January and is intended to boost economic development.
The tracts span the state from Scottsbluff to Omaha and include both rural and urban areas. The batch was submitted earlier this year to the U.S. Treasury as Gov. Jim Pillen’s recommendations for the second version of the federal opportunity zone program, which replaces the first iteration established by Congress in 2017. 
Made permanent in the One Big Beautiful Act of 2025, the purpose of  Opportunity Zones 2.0 is to promote private investment and drive development in low-income and economically disadvantaged communities.
Pillen announces picks for tax incentive-eligible ‘opportunity zones,’ a slate stretching statewide

Pillen expects the program to help create jobs and bolster construction of affordable workforce housing by providing investors in the designated geographies with incentives such as deferrals or reductions on capital gains taxes.
“These identified tracts are now poised to benefit from investment that will help spur housing, jobs and attract talent,” Pillen said. 
Ten of the tracts are in Omaha, five are in Lincoln, the state’s two most populated and urban cities. Others are in Alliance, Ogallala, North Platte, McCook, Lexington, Hastings, Columbus, Norfolk, Fremont, Bellevue, Crete, Scottsbluff and Beatrice. All three congressional districts are represented.
Cities across the state earlier submitted applications for 107 of the 112 tracts eligible for the designation under federal criteria. Nebraska was allowed to nominate a quarter of that number, officials said.
Mayor John Ewing Jr. and Greater Omaha Chamber CEO Heath Mello, in a joint statement Monday, said they expect the Omaha designations and opportunity zone funds to expand housing and business development in neighborhoods with potential for growth.
“These designations provide another tool to help move promising projects forward,” they said.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming tribe reclaims access after asking church to leave Wind River Reservation
description:
Workers dismantle the driveway to Foundations For Nations Church where the pastor criticized sacred Northern Arapaho spiritual traditions. It’s the latest in a standoff that’s seen months of protest.
The post Wyoming tribe reclaims access after asking church to leave Wind River Reservation appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—A backhoe quietly pulled up to Foundations For Nations Church along Rendezvous Road on the Wind River Reservation and started digging Thursday morning.
Multiple police agencies responded to the scene as protesters and onlookers gathered.
The construction came as a strong statement. The Northern Arapaho Tribe dismantled the church’s Rendezvous Road driveway access, digging up culvert pipes, then adding fill, giant concrete barriers, and erecting two tall flag poles, tribal flags billowing in the sky.
The tribe has essentially cut off the church’s main driveway access, though the property also has an access point along Mission Road. It’s the latest in a standoff between the church, which is on private deed land on the reservation, and tribal members outraged by a July sermon that criticized sacred Northern Arapaho spiritual traditions.
The Rendezvous Road driveway has been at the heart of a very physical standoff over those remarks. Protesters have gathered there every Sunday for the last 16 weeks.
Police have been called over claims some have trespassed in the driveway or blocked service-goers from entering; church leaders have erected signs banning trespassing. The tribe maintains the church doesn’t have ownership or right-of-way authorization of the access point, and on Thursday, it reclaimed the space as protesters cheered.
The move came alongside a flurry of construction work on the church’s property, as Foundations works to finish its large youth center adjacent to the church building.
While the tribe has told Foundations For Nations Church it is no longer welcome on the reservation, Foundations Founders and Co-Pastors Jason and Sarah Lucas have insisted they are committed to continuing their work spreading the gospel at the Christian compound. 
In addition to their Sunday services, Foundations operates an off-reservation food pantry in Riverton and has traditionally offered a variety of youth programs at the church site. Since the July 5 sermon and persistent protests, Foundations has scaled back those kids’ services, though construction on the youth center continues.
“But God!!! Please be praying for our church and our lawyers as we deal with this situation!” Sarah Lucas shared on social media following the construction of the driveway blockade. “We are going to have worship and prayer tonight at church. This is how we fight our battles!”
On Friday, just before press time, the Northern Arapaho Business Council offered a statement on what it called the tribe affirming its sovereign authority to “regulate access and rights-of-way on tribal lands.”
The Northern Arapaho Business Council reviewed the legal issues and consulted with federal agencies, the council wrote, and “determined certain individual landowners have not obtained the necessary authorization or approved rights-of-way to access and utilize tribal lands.” 
The council also “emphasizes that private ownership of adjoining fee lands does not, by itself, authorize individuals to enter, cross, or utilize tribal lands without necessary legal authorization.”
Both the church and the Northern Arapaho Business Council have exchanged legal threats since the July 5 sermon, with no indication that a resolution is in sight.
The sermon
On July 5, the Northern Arapaho people were just coming out of the Sundance ceremony, a deeply spiritual tradition for tribal members.
Pastor Sarah Lucas’ message to parishioners that day focused on parts of that spiritual tradition. She called the Northern Arapaho pipe, which is used in the Sundance ceremony, an “idol,” and encouraged tribal members to reject such spiritual practices in favor of exclusively worshipping Jesus.
“I pray as the people coming out of Sundance – today is their last day, Father God. They’re going back into the community, Father God,” she said in a video that quickly went viral. “You have generations – generations, centuries – of people doing this offering, going in and being, making, vows to change Father God. And we see no fruit … Where it says ‘tear down the altars, tear down the idols.’ And this nation gathered this week and they prayed, and they prayed to pipes, and prayed to their ancestors believing that this is their way for their freedom, to get free from addiction, for people to be healed from their sickness … Jesus is the chain-breaker. He is the only god that we should be praying to. The pipe cannot hear your prayers. It’s just a piece of material, right? And this is a cycle that they’re caught up in, and this is all they’ve ever known. And the Lord is saying ‘tear down the idols, tear down the altars, the idol worship.'”
By July 7, several hundred protesters gathered outside the church. It was the first of many to come.
Full-steam friction
By that Friday, Foundations For Nations leaders met with the Northern Arapaho Business Council and other tribal officials at the Wind River Casino, when the council told Foundations to leave the reservation.
The Lucases said they’d remain steadfast in their mission at the property, telling members they’d hold fast “on the truth of the Word of God concerning idol worship,” describing intense backlash they’d faced in the days since the sermon — including online death threats. They requested donations to help fund an expected legal battle ahead. “We are in contact with legal counsel and are preparing to pursue this matter in federal court as soon as possible in order to uphold our Constitutional rights to preach the Gospel,” they explained, adding, “We are not stopping.”
In late July, both the Northern Arapaho Business Council and Eastern Shoshone Business Council announced new policies aimed at governing outside organizations, requiring them to “consult” with the tribes before conducting organized activities on the reservation. The Northern Arapaho Business Council stated Foundations had never received permission to establish the church on the reservation; the Lucases shared emails with The Ranger dating back years showing communication with former council officials, some of whom expressed enthusiasm for the church’s activities at the site – including the construction of the youth center.
In August, the Northern Arapaho Business Council and Lucases coordinated another meeting, this time to address the requirements of the new tribal policy and consult with the tribe about the church’s activities on the reservation. The Lucases, citing what they called a hostile initial meeting with the business council, attempted to suggest a more neutral location than the casino or to attend via Zoom, but the council declined and held the meeting without them.
Then, the Northern Arapaho Business Council produced a “findings of fact, conclusions of law, and final decision” document, announcing that Foundations For Nations did not have approval to “initiate or expand” its activities on the reservation. The Lucases contend they never asked for it.
Meanwhile, the controversy spilled over to the church’s food pantry. Shortly after the July sermon, a complaint was filed with the Food Bank of Wyoming, which had partnered with the church’s food program in supplying bulk food under a contract. The complainant claimed that Sarah Lucas’ sermon amounted to discrimination, and Food Bank of Wyoming pulled the plug on the partnership.
Foundations quickly consulted with Florida-based Christian litigation and policy nonprofit Liberty Counsel, and announced it had filed a discrimination complaint of its own; this time, with the USDA. The complaint said the sermon was protected by the First Amendment, and that the food pantry had never denied a person food based on any protected class.
In September, Sarah Lucas filed petitions for stalking orders of protection against Darci Quiver and Alice Thomas — two of a handful of prominent protesters who have spent more than a dozen Sundays standing along Rendezvous Road with protest signs demanding Foundations leave the reservation. Those petitions are still awaiting a December court hearing, after questions about jurisdiction arose during a preliminary hearing in circuit court.
“I’ve never threatened her,” Thomas explained in an interview. “I’ve never voiced that I was going to cause her bodily harm. I’ve never gone out of my way to seek [the Lucas family] out, other than to protest on the side of the road at the church.” 
The Lucases, in an earlier interview, described persistent online threats and the need to take legal action. 
“[There are] posts of them scalping me and burning down our church. And so you don’t know if that’s going to be true or not,” Sarah Lucas said. 
She said her family had been in contact with the Riverton Police Department, Bureau of Indian Affairs, FBI and Fremont County Sheriff’s Office.
“We’re going to start moving forward with the law on harassment charges and things like that,” she said.
Many of those agencies stood by as the driveway blockades were erected Thursday. Fremont County Undersheriff Mike Hutchison said deputies were there in an effort to keep the peace as protesters assembled, and church leaders stood in the parking lot, looking on in surprise.
“Deputies were told that tribal officials had decided to remove a driveway entrance to the property at 20 Mission Road, which had previously provided access to the property from Rendezvous Road,” he said, adding that there’s still access to the property along Mission Road. “Deputies and [Wind River BIA] police officers stood by while the work was completed without incident.”
