name: California
title: Former Assembly staffer claims retaliation, hostile work environment in lawsuit
description: A former employee of Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco sued the Downey Democrat and her chief of staff, alleging that they retaliated against him for requesting medical leave and whistleblowing, subjected him to a baseless theft investigation and excluded him from meetings.
text:
In summary
A former employee of Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco sued the Downey Democrat and her chief of staff, alleging that they retaliated against him for requesting medical leave and whistleblowing, subjected him to a baseless theft investigation and excluded him from meetings.


A former staffer for Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco, a Downey Democrat, has sued the lawmaker and her chief of staff, alleging they created a “hostile and abusive” work environment and retaliated against him for complaining about it.
Ari Ruiz Reyes, a former district director for Pacheco, alleges in a lawsuit filed last month in Los Angeles Superior Court that Pacheco and chief of staff Nikki Johnson subjected him to a “baseless” theft investigation immediately after he returned from medical leave. 
After he reported them to the Legislature’s Workplace Conduct Unit, which investigates retaliation and harassment complaints, Pacheco’s office stripped him of his job duties, excluded him from meetings and abruptly fired him in June, Ruiz Reyes said in the lawsuit. 
He is also suing the state Assembly and its Rules Committee, which serves as the Assembly’s human resources department and is chaired by Pacheco. 
Ruiz Reyes began working for Pacheco in 2024. He previously worked as an aide to U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters and, from 2016 and 2022, as a district staffer for former Assemblymembers Autumn Burke and Blanca Rubio, according to his LinkedIn page. 
Pacheco declined to comment, citing the need to protect employee privacy, but said she would respond to the lawsuit “through the appropriate legal channels,” her spokesperson Alina Evans said in a statement. Johnson also declined to comment.
Lia Lopez, chief administrative officer of the Assembly rules committee, said the Assembly “dispute(s) the allegations and intend(s) to defend against it” and declined further comment.
In August 2025, Ruiz Reyes was injured in a car crash during work, which left him with chronic back pain, the lawsuit said. After he returned from sick leave in September, the lawsuit alleges that Pacheco and Lopez met with him to investigate him for a missing office camera, excluded him from an all-staff meeting and directed his subordinates to report to Johnson’s assistant.
Sam Yebri, Ruiz Reyes’ attorney, declined to clarify what happened to the theft investigation. 
Within weeks, Ruiz Reyes went on leave again, between September and December, for what the lawsuit describes as stress-related medical conditions caused and worsened by the defendants’ conduct, including stress-induced hair loss. 
Ruiz Reyes filed a complaint with the workplace unit on Nov. 7, 2025 and submitted another complaint a month later. The unit closed the case without investigating in February, stating in a letter obtained by CalMatters there was not enough information “to support a connection to a protected class.” 
The WCU did not immediately return a CalMatters request for comment.
In those complaints, Ruiz Reyes accused Johnson of asking a staff member to take her to a hair salon during work hours and of allowing Capitol staff to work remotely while requiring district staff to work from the office. 
The case was closed “without conducting any investigation and without interviewing a single witness or requesting a single document,” Ruiz Reyes said in the lawsuit.
After he returned to work on Dec. 5, he said “the retaliation escalated,” and Johnson stripped him of the authority to approve expenditures, excluded him from the hiring of his subordinate and criticized him for his tone. Pacheco, he said, fired him despite knowing his concerns about Johnson.
“Mr. Ruiz is a career public servant with nearly a decade of legislative experience,” Yebri said in a statement. “California has enacted strong protections for workers and for legislative whistleblowers, and those protections should apply fully to those who work in the Legislature’s own offices.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Secretary of State: About 50% of Louisiana voters will take part in midterms
description: Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry expects turnout among registered voters to reach 48% to 52% once voters go to polls one Election Day, matching levels for midterm election cycles over the past 12 years, her spokesman said.
text:
Voter turnout in Louisiana for the Nov. 3, 2026 election is expected to be around 50%, according to the Secretary of State's office. (Photo by Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry expects turnout among registered voters to reach between 48% and 52% once voters go to polls Tuesday, matching levels for midterm election cycles over the past 12 years, her spokesman said. 
Trey Williams, Landry’s communications director, shared the projected numbers with a reporter Monday afternoon.
Midterm elections take place halfway through a presidential term when congressional candidates are on the ballot. Their outcomes are often interpreted as a referendum on the president and ruling party’s policies. 
Voter turnout for statewide elections during the midterms in Louisiana was 46.7% in 2022, 50.8% in 2018 and 51.5% in 2014. Like this year, a U.S. Senate race was at the top of the ballot in 2014 and 2022. 
Presidential elections typically generate the highest turnout. For example, 70.1% and 66.3% of Louisiana registered voters participated in the 2020 and 2024 presidential races, respectively, according to information on the Secretary of State’s website. 

This year, the U.S. Senate race between Congresswoman Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, and Democrat Jamie Davis of Tensas Parish is expected to generate the most interest. 
Elections for the U.S. House, the Louisiana Public Service Commission, and state Board of Elementary and Secondary Education are also taking place, in addition to several judicial and local government races. Voters statewide also have 10 constitutional amendments to decide. 

Polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday. Any voter in line to vote at 8 p.m. will be allowed to cast a ballot even if they haven’t gotten into a voting booth yet, according to the Secretary of State’s office. 

Louisiana residents can check to see if they are registered to vote at GeauxVote.com or the smartphone application of the same name. The website and the app provide information about what races are on the ballot for individual voters. 

In a statement Monday, Landry requested the public respect election commissioners working at polling places Tuesday. She also warned that lines to vote may be longer than usual because there are several races and the constitutional amendments that will take time for voters to consider in the booth. 

Political campaigning is not allowed within 600 feet of a polling location between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. on Election Day. People are not allowed to wave signs, hand out literature or wear campaign shirts, buttons and hats in these “campaign-free” zones, according to state law. 

Violators can face fines of up to $500 or six months in jail for their first offense. 
Voters with questions about the election can contact the Secretary of State’s Election Hotline at 1-800-883-2805.

name: California
title: Supreme Court declines to hear Trump’s California 20,000 ballot case. Here’s what to know
description: The U.S. Supreme Court declined to issue an emergency ruling in the Trump Administration’s case to sequester 20,000 ballots.  Here’s what to know about the ongoing, unprecedented legal attack on California’s elections.
text:
In summary
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to issue an emergency ruling in the Trump Administration’s case to sequester 20,000 ballots.  Here’s what to know about the ongoing, unprecedented legal attack on California’s elections.


On the eve of Election Day, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a last-minute legal challenge from the Trump administration that would have forced California to not count over 20,000 ballots that the administration had flagged as being cast by possible noncitizens.
The rejection came the same day prosecutors filed new federal charges against noncitizens accused of voting improprieties.Here’s where things stand on the unprecedented legal war the federal government is waging on California’s elections.
U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump 
On Monday — a day before the election — the Trump Administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which almost immediately rejected the federal government’s request to force California to set aside the 20,000 ballots.None of the judges dissented, and no explanation was provided.
The ruling came after U.S. District Court Judge David O. Carter issued a blistering ruling last week declaring that the Trump administration’s efforts were likely unconstitutional.“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” wrote Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton.
The Trump administration immediately appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. A three-judge panel on the appellate court for the second time in a week rejected the administration’s claims.
Background on the case
For years, President Donald Trump has claimed, without evidence, that potentially “millions” of noncitizen voters are rigging elections for Democrats. His federal prosecutors in California have been aggressively trying to prove him right, even as independent experts and election officials say noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare.
In mid-October, the Trump administration sent a letter to California’s secretary of state and Los Angeles County election officials demanding they set aside the 20,000 ballots. The letter demanded the ballots not be counted until the voters’ citizenship can be verified.
California refused.The Trump administration sued and urged a federal court to issue an order forcing California to comply. Meanwhile, it also sent similar demand letters and grand jury subpoenas to county elections offices warning that election workers could be charged if they allow noncitizens to vote.
New arrests on eve of Election Day
Also on Monday, the federal government announced charges against another 12 noncitizens for registering to vote or voting in California elections after previously charging 28 green California card holders for similar crimes. 
“Voting is the essence of American citizenship,” Bill Essayli, Trump’s top prosecutor in Los Angeles, said at a press conference Monday. “Illegally attempting to infiltrate and influence our political determinations is not only wrong, it’s a crime.”California officials have been quick to point out that the arrests represent a fraction of a percent of California’s 23 million registered voters — hardly proof of a sweeping election-rigging conspiracy as Trump has so often claimed.
“They said, ‘Aha! Look at this widespread voter fraud,’” and then they made 28 arrests,” Democratic California Attorney General Rob Bonta said last week. “I mean, talk about a fizzle.” 
Moria Dahan, one of the people charged on Monday, made her first appearance in federal court shortly after the charges were announced. Dahan was shackled at the ankles and led into the courtroom by U.S. marshals. Dahan, an Israeli national who lives in West Hills, spoke through a Hebrew interpreter as she acknowledged the charges against her. She was released minutes later.
Her attorney, Tiffany Feder, said her client didn’t “intend to defraud, intend to conceal, or falsify any kind of documents. She didn’t know what she was filling out.”  
Judge blocks election worker threats
Another federal court judge issued an order Friday blocking the Trump administration’s unprecedented targeting of election workers, after their union filed a legal challenge asking the court to halt the administration’s threats.
U.S. District Court Judge Trina L. Thompson, a Joe Biden appointee, said the law “favors the protection of election staff, who are working diligently to ensure that all citizens can cast their votes.” She ordered the administration not to threaten or pressure election officials to withhold or segregate ballots and barred the federal government from criminally charging workers based on claims of ineligible voters. 
The ruling is in response to federal prosecutors sending letters to all 58 county election officials demanding they set aside ballots from the list of 20,000 suspected noncitizens or face potential criminal charges. Prosecutors also have served some county election officials with federal grand jury subpoenas.
Experts, counties question Trump’s numbers
Several county officials say they have done spot checks on the federal list, and they say the data is riddled with inaccuracies.The UCLA Voting Rights Project also submitted a brief to a federal court saying its data scientists found that 42% of the 20,000 names were “not anywhere to be found on the current California voter file.” The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government’s list.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Red flag’: Voter inactivations surge in midterms since secretary of state adopted unverified Experian data to clean voter rolls
description: Carolyn Johnson fills out her ballot at Briarwood Presbyterian Church on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, during Mississippi’s federal primary election in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Voter inactivations surged ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, the first since the Mississippi Secretary of State’s Office authorized unverified data from the credit bureau Experian for counties to use statewide when cleaning their voter rolls.
A Mississippi Today analysis of voter data from the secretary of state found that in the eight months since the March primaries, inactivations more than doubled in some jurisdictions, leaving up to 1 in 5 voters in counties such as DeSoto and Wilkinson one step closer to being purged from the rolls. Over 230,000 voters statewide — or about 1 in 9 — are now inactive ahead of Election Day as Mississippi stares at an increasingly competitive U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom.
For years, county election officials relied on verified government data to do the routine job of identifying and inactivating voters who moved or died. But since Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson last year announced a $50,000 deal to use Experian’s data statewide to “strengthen the integrity of elections,” Mississippi Today found incorrect information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters ahead of the primaries.



Watson previously said his office’s rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful,” but voting rights advocates and election experts question whether the latest surge in inactivations indicates mistakes in the data have put a larger number of legitimate voters at risk. The secretary of state’s office did not answer questions about the reason behind the spike in time for Mississippi Today’s publication of this article.
“Our office is busy prepping for the federal midterm election, and we will be happy to address your questions in a more realistic timeframe after the election,” Assistant Secretary of State Elizabeth Jonson wrote in an email.
Advocates warn surge could create barriers to ballot box
While inactive voters can still cast a ballot, they have to go through additional hurdles to make sure their vote counts, such as filling out an affidavit ballot. Advocates are concerned that many of these voters won’t find out they’ve been inactivated until they go to the polls, where confusion, frustration or fear may prevent them from exercising their right to vote.
“There may be a lot of disenfranchisement tomorrow from people who are showing up to vote,” Nsombi Lambright, executive director of the Jackson-based nonprofit One Voice, said Monday. “My concern is that their vote may not be counted.”
Michael Watson gives a speech as he announces his campaign for Mississippi lieutenant governor at a Hilton Garden Inn in Pascagoula on Tuesday, April 7, 2026. Credit: The Sun Herald
The additional steps inactive voters must take at the polls has made Amir Badat, a Mississippi voting rights attorney with Fair Fight Action, concerned that the surge could disrupt election operations Tuesday by creating long lines, depleting affidavit ballots and straining the county election commissioners responsible for conducting the elections.
“It’s just a totally unnecessary burden on voters and election commissioners that the state has created,” Badat said. “Voters are going to be, like, ‘Wait, why is my name not on the poll book? Why do I have to vote this separate process?’ People are going to have less confidence that their ballot will be counted.”
DeSoto County emerges as ‘hotspot’ for inactivations
Voting rights advocates are watching DeSoto County, which accounted for over a third of all inactivations in Mississippi’s 82 counties from the primaries to the midterms. There, election commissioners removed over 15,000 voters from the active rolls, doubling the number of inactive voters in just months.
To election researcher Thessalia Merivaki, who previously taught at Mississippi State University, an increase of that scale raises a “red flag.” She said the secretary of state’s rollout of commercial data could have driven the surge, instead of the traditional methods election commissioners have used to identify whether voters have moved, such as information from the U.S. Postal Service or an undeliverable jury summons.


“Is it reasonable to expect that all these voters that are inactive, they were asked to do jury duty, or they moved out of the county, or they moved within the county in six months?” Merivaki said.
The surge in inactive voters also pushed DeSoto County Democratic Party Chair Deborah Williams to raise concerns to the election commission responsible for inactivating voters. Williams said after she asked about it, commissioners ordered more affidavit ballots to ensure there wouldn’t be a shortage on Election Day.
The DeSoto County Election Commission did not respond to a request for comment.
As voting rights advocates seek answers on the reason behind the surge, Lambright said the most immediate concern is ensuring inactive voters still know they have the right to vote. Her organization, One Voice, last week announced the launch of a website with the Mississippi Poor People’s Campaign for voters to search whether they’ve been inactivated or purged.
Since entering the partnership with Experian, the secretary of state’s office last week wrote in a statement to WAPT that it has replaced the credit bureau’s data with another company, IDI Data.
You can check your voter registration status before heading to the polls at the secretary of state’s Y’all Vote website.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Draft bill to appoint Public Service Commissioners heading to 2027 session
description: State Sen. Gayle Lammers has been talking with Montanans about legislation to change the way the Public Service Commission is formed — to appoint members rather than elect them. Some people worry about taking away the ability to vote for a commissioner, but they also see problems at the agency, Lammers said. Recently, for example, […]
text:
(Screenshot from a PSC social media page.)State Sen. Gayle Lammers has been talking with Montanans about legislation to change the way the Public Service Commission is formed — to appoint members rather than elect them.
Some people worry about taking away the ability to vote for a commissioner, but they also see problems at the agency, Lammers said.
Recently, for example, one commissioner was suspended for professional misconduct.
Lammers said he opens up the newspaper and reads reports of one “fumble” after another by the agency, made up of five commissioners elected by district.
The 2027 Montana Legislature kicks off in January, and among draft legislation in the queue is LC0500, to change the PSC to an appointed body.
“I’ve been having a hard time finding people that don’t like this bill,” said Lammers, R-Hardin.
Lammers was a member of the Energy and Technology Interim Committee, which approved the plan for a draft bill.
The top recommendation from the Governor’s Energy Task Force also was to consider an appointed PSC.
The PSC regulates monopoly utilities such as NorthWestern Energy, and it is currently all Republican.
The 2027 session is still a couple of months away, but bills that come out of committee have momentum, at least to be introduced for debate.
As drafted, LC0500 would create a nomination committee, which would forward candidates to the governor, who would appoint commissioners. Appointees would be subject to confirmation by the Senate with a vote of at least three-fifths of the body.
The nominations committee would have seven members — one each appointed by the speaker of the House, House minority leader, Senate president, Senate minority leader, head of Department of Environmental Quality, head of Department of Commerce, and tribal representative appointed by the state director of Indian affairs.
The draft also would set qualifications that commissioners be “industry experts.”
Rep. Bob Carter, D-Missoula, also a member of the interim committee, said the draft bill is designed to put experienced professionals into office, people who are not politicians but have bipartisan support.
“These are highly qualified people,” Carter said. “These are not people who are running for office and therefore making promises that they can’t keep.”
In most states, utility regulators are gubernatorial appointments. Carter said just 10 states still elect commissioners, although a couple of states have a hybrid system.
“In the last 100 years, no states have gone from appointed to elected, but there have been many examples of states going from elected to appointed (commissioners),” Carter said.
Anne Hedges, with Montana Environmental Information Center, said her organization sees shortcomings with the current Public Service Commission, such as a lack of expertise.
“We need people to walk in the door and know what they’re doing as opposed to learning on the job,” Hedges said.
However, Hedges said she doesn’t believe the structure being proposed will be the best fix for the PSC. MEIC is a conservation and energy watchdog group in Montana.
Hedges said the process in the draft bill language allows “gamesmanship by the governor,” and it doesn’t ensure the PSC will be made up of professionals that will look out for affordability.
“We need people who are on the job from day one and see through the utility smokescreens,” Hedges said.
Gov. Greg Gianforte recently appointed a commissioner temporarily — for one year — after allegations of misconduct led the PSC to request he suspend Brad Molnar, an elected commissioner.
The PSC is an executive branch agency even though the commissioners are elected. The suspension was unprecedented — and followed unprecedented behavior, Gianforte said.
Gianforte selected a former PSC commissioner, Kirk Bushman, to serve during Molnar’s absence.
Kaitlin Timken, a spokesperson for Gianforte, didn’t comment on the draft bill to appoint the PSC, but she said the governor is proud of the work of his energy task force.
In response to a proposal to change the way the PSC was made up in 2025, Gianforte said it’s important to have a regulatory climate that offers predictability and stability for consumers and producers.
But previous proposals to modify the formation of the PSC never got far enough to land on his desk.
In a phone call Monday, Lammers said the energy industry is complex, with new nuclear options, coal, transmission issues, and data centers all in play.
“We really gotta get a Public Service Commission that’s up for these 21st-century issues that are coming up in Montana,” Lammers said.
As he sees it, a change to an appointed PSC wouldn’t be taking away people’s ability to vote for a commissioner, it would be giving the public a PSC that does its job well.
“You’ve got to have a Public Service Commission that’s functional,” Lammers said.

name: Nevada Current
title: NV turnout so far on pace with last midterm, but may lag this year’s national record-setting trend
description: More than 735,000 people have already cast ballots in this year’s midterm election, according to the Nevada Secretary of State’s Office. As of midday Monday, the SOS was reporting approximately 308,000 Nevadans had cast ballots in person during the state’s two-week early voting period, which ended Friday, and 427,000 had voted via a mail ballot. […]
text:
(Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)More than 735,000 people have already cast ballots in this year’s midterm election, according to the Nevada Secretary of State’s Office.
As of midday Monday, the SOS was reporting approximately 308,000 Nevadans had cast ballots in person during the state’s two-week early voting period, which ended Friday, and 427,000 had voted via a mail ballot.
Turnout creeps to more than three-quarters of a million people if you count mail ballots that have been returned to county offices but not yet processed and accepted.
Early voting has been setting midterm records nationally this year, though Nevada may end up being an outlier as a state with no U.S. Senate race to help drive turnout.
In Nevada, early in-person voting numbers this year exceeded the last midterm election in 2022. But whether turnout this year exceeds the last midterm will depend on Election Day turnout and the number of mail ballots outstanding.
In 2022, Election Day voters made up 21% of total voter turnout. Mail ballots made up 51%, and in-person early voting made up 28%.
The 2022 general election turned out 1,025,854 people.
Election Day is Tuesday, with polls open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Anyone in line by 7 p.m. is allowed to cast a ballot.
Additional mail ballots will also be received and accepted via physical dropboxes and the United States Postal Service. State law allows for any ballots postmarked by USPS on Election Day to be accepted and counted up to four days after Election Day.
Despite that buffer time, the SOS recommends voters physically deliver them to a dropbox rather than rely on mail delivery. Dropboxes can be found at vote centers on Election Day.
More than 5,500 mail ballots across the state have been flagged for signature issues and need to be cured by voters.
Voters can track the status of their ballot at myballot.nv.gov.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​Jared Polis’ final budget request as Colorado governor seeks to limit Medicaid growth
description: Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released his final budget proposal on Monday, once again calling for the Legislature to significantly restrict Medicaid growth in the state. The Democrat, who is in his last few months as governor, wants to limit program growth to 4.3% during the next budget year, compared to an expected 15% with current […]
text:
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis presents his budget request for the 2027-2028 fiscal year in his office at the state Capitol in Denver on Monday. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released his final budget proposal on Monday, once again calling for the Legislature to significantly restrict Medicaid growth in the state.
The Democrat, who is in his last few months as governor, wants to limit program growth to 4.3% during the next budget year, compared to an expected 15% with current spending trends. Medicaid costs have more than doubled since the 2021-2022 fiscal year and could soon eat up around 40% of the state’s entire general fund. It is propelled in part by rising healthcare costs and an aging population that needs more services. The health insurance program for low-income people serves around 1 in 5 Coloradans.
“Absent changes, Medicaid growth will crowd out everything else, including education,” Polis told reporters. “That would be unsustainable. Based on what I’ve seen, I don’t believe low-income Coloradans would be any healthier under this scenario.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A 4.3% growth would match the rate that state spending is allowed to grow under the state’s Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. That rate of increase is based on inflation and population growth.
Polis’ proposal includes a $250 million general fund increase for Medicaid, but he also outlines almost 30 program cuts and other actions to save around $988 million in total spending and $290 million in general fund spending. That includes the entire elimination of adult dental benefits, reductions for long-term services and supports, reinstatement of prior authorization for behavioral health, and lower hospital medical education payments.
“We oppose any way to reduce Medicaid expenditures by throwing people off of Medicaid,” he said. “That’s not what this is about. We actually want to protect and get even more people who are eligible to access Medicaid. That’s a basic value.”
Critics were quick to push back on the changes in the budget proposal. Adam Fox, the deputy director at the Colorado Consumer Health Initiative, said in a statement that the plan puts “the health of vulnerable Coloradans at risk.”



Quotation







Absent changes, Medicaid growth will crowd out everything else, including education ... That would be unsustainable. Based on what I've seen, I don't believe low-income Coloradans would be any healthier under this scenario.


– Jared Polis, Colorado governor


The Health Initiative supports Amendment 87, a ballot measure that would establish a graduated income tax and could raise much more revenue for the state to spend, depending on what other measures pass on Election Day. Polis is opposed to Amendment 87, as is the Democratic nominee for governor, Attorney General Phil Weiser.
“Polis, who has passed pro-consumer healthcare policies and expanded access to Medicaid, is now proposing more cuts to lifesaving programs rather than supporting a viable solution,” Fox said. “Cuts aren’t a solution for Coloradans struggling to afford healthcare or other basic necessities.”
The explosion of Medicaid spending has been a driving force in Colorado’s perpetual budget shortfalls the last few years. A 10-member commission has met throughout the summer and fall to consider policy changes that could make the program more efficient. Next year, lawmakers will need to solve another $1 billion-plus gap between the amount the government can spend under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights and how much it would cost to keep program funding steady.
This final budget request of the Polis administration is for $18.9 billion in general fund spending, up 2.6% from the current budget. The general fund is where Colorado has its discretionary spending.
In the proposal, Polis also suggests the Legislature refer a ballot measure next year to pay for food and nutrition assistance. Under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year, states have to pay more into the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. That’s expected to be about $100.5 million for Colorado. The state already keeps some tax revenue for the universal school meal program, and Polis wants voter permission for the state to retain more to partially cover those SNAP costs.
Responsibility will pass to new governor
The budget would also increase per-pupil funding by $488 for public education, and continue to put money towards a new school finance formula passed in 2025. Polis also called for $16.8 million to hire more nurses and clinical staff in prisons across the state and $12.4 million to reopen part of the private Huerfano County Correctional Center in Walsenburg.
Polis’ proposal is a starting point for the bipartisan Joint Budget Committee’s work to craft a balanced state budget for the entire Legislature to vote on, usually in late March.
But Polis, who is term-limited, won’t actually be around for all that. His successor will be elected Tuesday, and after he submits a revision in January for this budget proposal, the responsibility will pass to the next governor. The governor’s request is always due Nov. 1, election year or not.
“Obviously, if a governor doesn’t bring Medicaid spending in line with growth, then there would be cuts to K-12 or higher education,” he said. “But I believe that they would share the same values of funding our schools and and not throwing people off of Medicaid.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: After months of preparation, Pa. county elections officials ready for big day
authors: Ian Karbal, Emily Previti, Whitney Downard, Peter Hall
description: Pennsylvania has been in a national spotlight in the weeks leading up to midsterms, with the election for governor, four highly competitive congressional races, and nearly 250 state legislative seats on the ballot.
text:
Voters fill out their ballots at the Board of Elections office in Kittanning, Armstrong County, Pa. October 20, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Across the commonwealth Monday, election workers in 67 counties were preparing for midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the state and federal governments for the next two years. 
Pennsylvania has been in the national spotlight in the weeks leading up to midsterms, with the election for governor, four highly competitive congressional races, and nearly 250 state legislative seats on the ballot.
As the Trump administration has filed lawsuits to intervene in other states’ elections, cracked down on a small number of cases involving noncitizen voting and pursued detailed state voter rolls earlier this year, voting rights watchdogs have been on the lookout for any potential disruptions.
Despite efforts to improve ballot access and security, voters are wary for a variety of reasons that depend on their political orientation, said Committee of 70 President & CEO Lauren Cristella.
“There’s probably more questioning about the integrity of our elections, and people just don’t know what to believe or where to get their information or (whether) what they’re seeing is true,” Cristella said.
The Trump administration sued in Alaska to set aside election results if incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the state’s ranked-choice election because another candidate by the same name is on the ballot. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed that lawsuit and the administration said it will appeal.
In California, the administration took its fight to the U.S. Supreme Court. But, the court denied the administration’s  effort to block officials from counting mail-in ballots from 20,000 people who federal officials allege are likely noncitizens who are ineligible to vote.   

Voter Guide: 2026 Pennsylvania General Election


Election officials in two of the four Pennsylvania counties where the U.S. Department of Justice is sending election monitors Tuesday say that’s not unusual. 
The DOJ sent monitors to Luzerne County in 2022 and 2024. And organizations like political parties, campaigns and civil rights groups also use poll watchers. 
“Our voters should know that their vote is safe, and the process is transparent and fair, and not to have any fears if they go to the polls,” Luzerne County Manager Romilda Crocamo said. “We’re not allowing monitors into the polling places, whether it’s the ACLU or the DOJ. Once you’re outside of the polling place, if they ask you questions, you have to make a choice of whether you’re going to answer those questions or not.”
Lehigh County is also expecting DOJ poll monitors this year, and county Director of Elections Mike Paston said the only difference is the number of observers will be greater. There will be eight federal observers working in pairs or trios across the county’s 158 precincts.
“It’s not the first time we’ve had monitors, probably won’t be the last,” said Paston. “There’s no reason, from what they’ve said and done, there’s no reason to think their motives are anything but aboveboard and normal.”
Election monitors are required to stay away from the entrances to polling stations and may not be armed. They’re not allowed to question voters entering the polling place but may question voters leaving the polls.
“The level of preparation that has gone into this election is quite high. Perhaps that’s why we’re hearing of so few problems,” said League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania Executive Director Amy Widestrom, who was a political science professor at Arcadia University prior to taking her current role three years ago. “It’s really quiet. I hope it stays quiet tomorrow.”
A sign directs voters to where they can cast their ballots at Allegheny County Election office in Pittsburgh on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Widestrom said counties and non-partisan organizations like the League have also worked to recruit more poll and canvassing monitors, in addition to poll workers. 
“Voters are paying attention. They seem to be engaged,” said Widestrom, pointing to a higher mail-in ballot return rate (83 percent as of Monday).
The flip side of that is vitriol against county election workers. 
“The demagoguery against election officials – it’s probably the worst I’ve seen since 2020, from both sides,” Lycoming County Election Director Forrest Lehman said. “We’ve got the right-leaning sphere out there accusing election officials (of) harboring non-citizen voters. DOJ is sending threatening letters out to state officials, threatening to prosecute them. And then on the left-leaning side, we’ve got them accusing election officials of voter suppression at the drop of a hat on issues like ballot curing and drop boxes.”
Trump also signed an executive order in March that would have required the postal service to block delivery of mail ballots to voters not on lists submitted by state election officials. The U.S. Supreme Court in September upheld a lower court’s decision freezing the restrictions.
As that requirement was looming, officials in some counties in the state took steps to give voters more alternatives to requesting and submitting ballots through the mail. While Pennsylvania does not have true early voting, many counties allow voters to obtain a mail ballot “on demand,” complete it and return it in the same location ahead of Election Day.
Bucks County spokesperson Jim O’Malley said the Board of Elections added four locations for the county’s 487,000 registered voters to request on-demand mail ballots, bringing the total to seven.
“The county wanted to do this to expand access for folks but also to make it more convenient,” O’Malley said, noting officials have provided more than 4,500 on-demand ballots.
The new locations are at the three campuses of Bucks County Community College, in the southern, central and northern parts of the county, plus the Warminster Township public library. Previously, voters had to visit one of the county offices in Doylestown, Warminster or Quakertown. 
Lehigh added five drop boxes for ballots this cycle and now has ten options for voters, Paston said.
“During the summer there was a lot of distrust (with) the post office and what they may or may not do. That’s gone away and, actually, the post office is very cooperative,” said Paston. “But during that period, we decided to increase the boxes for people who were concerned about mailing their ballot back and didn’t want to vote in person.”
The declaration on the return envelope of a Pennsylvania mail-in ballot. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
In Chester County on Monday, the district attorney’s office announced initial testing by the FBI determined a mail-in ballot with a foreign object inside the envelope flagged last week by an election worker is not hazardous. The discovery caused a county office building where ballots are processed to be locked down briefly Friday.
For election workers across the commonwealth, preparing for the unexpected is part of business as usual. 
Dauphin County Commissioner Justin Douglas, who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination to run for Congress in the 10th District this spring, said part of the work includes running tabletop exercises where staff from each department with a role in Election Day work together to gameplan responses to a variety of scenarios.
They game out what would happen if there’s snow on election day, if a polling place loses power or runs out of paper ballots, or if there’s an issue with a voting machine. And plans have been put in place to respond to such issues quickly.
This year, Douglas said, they also ran through what might happen if the federal government gets involved.
“We talked through what our channels of communication would be in that particular case, and have a plan,” he said. “But that’s kind of internally what happens with every election. And, obviously, with midterm and presidential elections there’s just a lot more focus and attention.”
According to York County President Commissioner Julie Wheeler, the days and hours before the election are all about ensuring everything is in place after months of planning.
“There’s certainly a lot of flurry,” she said. “We had to have the machines delivered to the polling locations, we have materials that need to be prepared for the judge of elections — ballots, folders, markers, all those types of things. We had to prepare the poll books for the polling locations. That’s all the election day prep.”
But the county, she said, is in good shape, and most of that planning will never be noticed by voters. 
County staff Wheeler called “rovers” will be standing by in cars with backup supplies in case a polling place runs out. Others will be counting mail-in ballots. And staff from county departments like Information Technology, Emergency Preparedness, and the Sheriff’s Office will be ready to respond if there are issues.
“We pride ourselves in providing good customer service to voters,” Wheeler said. “We want the voter to have a positive experience at their polling location.”
Polls in Pennsylvania will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Any voter who is in line before polls close will be allowed to vote.
Mail-in ballots that haven’t been returned must be dropped off at a return location in their county. The Department of State’s website has information on where that is in each county.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Parents of 1-year-old fatally shot by police protest at building that houses Mississippi attorney general’s office
description: Activists pray inside lobby of the downtown Jackson building that houses the Mississippi Attorney General's Office on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, to protest the fatal police shooting of Kohen Wiley in Senatobia in June.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The parents of a 1-year-old boy who was shot and killed by a police officer in Mississippi led a protest Monday at the office of the state’s attorney general, who ruled last month that the shooting was justified.
Cries of “our baby’s life mattered” echoed through the office’s lobby as Kohen Wiley’s parents and a small group of activists demanded to speak to Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch.
Marquell Bridges, an activist who has been working with Kohen’s parents, said they wanted Fitch to look Kohen’s parents in the eyes and tell them why the shooting was justified.
“These people work for us. We pay their salaries. We vote. We put them in office, and our people have to understand that we have the power,” Bridges said.
They were met in the lobby by Fitch’s chief of staff, who said Fitch was not in the office. An email seeking comment was sent to the attorney general’s office Monday.
Vellesiya Wiley pictured with Kohen Wiley, who was her only child.   Credit: Ben Crump Law
Kohen Wiley was killed in June when a police officer in the small town of Senatobia about 40 miles south of Memphis, Tennessee, fired his gun into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call.
Body-worn cameras show Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen as she and another woman run across the parking lot of a Senatobia Walmart and enter their vehicle. 
Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop.
The vehicle then accelerates forward as Senatobia Sgt. Hunter Foster steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother’s lap.
The shooting sparked months of mourning and calls for justice, both nationally and in Senatobia.
Kohen would have turned 2 on Sunday.
Sitting outside the attorney general’s office, Kohen’s father, Davion Williams, said the passing of Kohen’s birthday was “the worst feeling ever.”
“It’s hard. It’s just hard to even express and talk about,” Williams said. “Now we have to keep his name alive.”
Williams said he wants Foster prosecuted and Fitch out of office. He wore a T-shirt with Kohen’s face that read “Kohen should be 2. Vote in his honor.”
Fitch, a Republican, is running for governor in 2027.
Foster’s attorney, Martin Zummach, has said his client had “no choice” but to shoot at the vehicle because it was going to hit him. The Mississippi Attorney General’s office said its monthslong probe found that Foster’s use of force was appropriate.
The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, meanwhile, was investigating an arson fire on Saturday that damaged the Senatobia police building. It was unclear what caused the fire. Emails to the ATF and the state fire marshal’s office Monday were not immediately returned.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Satanic Temple wins right to stage holiday event in Iowa Capitol’s rotunda
description: The ACLU of Iowa has won a preliminary injunction that clears the way for The Satanic Temple to stage a holiday event next month in the Iowa Capitol rotunda. In August, the ACLU filed a lawsuit against the state in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa over the state’s repeated refusal […]
text:
The Iowa State Capitol. (Photo by Perry Beeman/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The ACLU of Iowa has won a preliminary injunction that clears the way for The Satanic Temple to stage a holiday event next month in the Iowa Capitol rotunda.
In August, the ACLU filed a lawsuit against the state in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa over the state’s repeated refusal to grant permission for the temple to stage what the ACLU calls “a family-friendly winter holiday event.” The ACLU of Iowa cited the fact that other religious and civic groups are allowed to stage events in the rotunda.
Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, said Monday that “state officials have made it clear that they denied The Satanic Temple permission to hold events in the Capitol rotunda because they disagreed with their religious viewpoint. It is a foundational principle that the government cannot restrict speech in this way, favor one religion over another, or discriminate against religious groups because they don’t agree with them … We are glad that the court decision today upholds the principles of free speech that we all hold dear and requires the state to act in line with the constitutional requirements of the First Amendment.”
Named as defendants in the ongoing case are the director of the Iowa Department of Administrative Services, Mark Campbell; the department’s former director, Adam Steen; and the department itself.
The lawsuit has sought to have the court declare that state officials’ denials violated The Satanic Temple’s constitutional rights under the First and 14th Amendments as well as their rights under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and Iowa Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
In agreeing Monday to issue a preliminary injunction in the case, Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose noted that in December 2023, The Satanic Temple was permitted to hold a holiday display in the rotunda, alongside other holiday displays such as a Christian nativity scene.
Beginning in 2024 and continuing through 2026, the state denied The Satanic Temple’s applications. The state would later allege that the 2024 denial was based, at least in part, on a concern that participants in the event would be part of a costume contest and that the costumes would involve carrying bundles of sticks that might then be used as weapons against children.



Quotation







Steen coordinated the (permit) denial with the governor’s office, emphasized Satanic symbols, hymns and rituals when he described the event to the public, and explained his policy change as a way to avoid losing a free-speech argument.


– Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose, commenting on Adam Steen's actions


But in his public statements about his denial of the permit, Steen didn’t reference the sticks and outlined a different reasoning for the decision, Rose noted in her ruling.
“No more marketing to children,” Steen said at the time. “No more trying to get them to create Satanic symbols, sing Satanic hymns, partake in Satanic rituals. No more having youth involved in costume contests and defending weapons used to abuse youth.”
Rose also noted that Steen testified under oath that The Satanic Temple’s religious beliefs played no part in his denial of the permit, and that when he was asked why he had publicly emphasized Satanic symbols and hymns, he testified he could not recall the reason.
“Steen coordinated the (permit) denial with the governor’s office, emphasized Satanic symbols, hymns and rituals when he described the event to the public, and explained his policy change as a way to avoid losing a free-speech argument,” Rose stated in her ruling.
The decision under court review was not the 2024 decision made by Steen but the 2026 denial made by his successor, Campbell. In her ruling, Rose pointed out that Campbell gave somewhat conflicting accounts as to the rationale for his decision on the temple’s planned 2026 event.
“When the court asked whether his ‘entire reasoning’ and ‘sole reason’ for the denials was that the applications matched the 2024 application, he agreed,” Rose stated. “Moments later, defense counsel asked whether he had ‘independently reviewed and thought about’ the applications or had ‘just rubber-stamped a prior decision.’ He then offered a different explanation: Department staff had told him the 2024 application was denied for ‘fear of harm to children,’ and he looked at the application and he concurred.”
State officials, Rose found, “never looked into whether the sticks posed any real danger” and said Steen admitted not knowing whether the sticks were real or props.
Campbell had “performed no independent evaluation of whether the costumes posed any risk,” Rose concluded. “Meanwhile, the Capitol already guards against the very danger the department invokes. Everyone who enters passes through metal detectors staffed by security personnel who examine what visitors bring in and can stop items that are not allowed.”
In issuing the injunction, Rose barred Campbell from denying The Satanic Temple’s application to stage an event at the Capitol on Dec. 12, 2026, as described in the organization’s March 2026 permit application.
Campbell may impose on the event only those restrictions or conditions the state would apply to other indoor events at the Capitol, such as security, insurance and damage-deposit requirements.
Despite the injunction, litigation in the case continues, with the ACLU of Iowa seeking a finding of constitutional violations and violations of the Iowa Civil Rights Act and Iowa Religious Freedom Restoration Act. As part of the lawsuit, the ACLU of Iowa is seeking an award for damages resulting from past violations.
Representatives of the state, who have said they do not comment on pending litigation, have denied any wrongdoing in the matter.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill stumps for Zack Mullock as Democrats push to oust Jeff Van Drew
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill said “momentum is growing” for Democrats as she stumped for Zack Mullock in the 2nd Congressional District.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherril stumps for Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor and the Democratic nominee in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]VINELAND — Gov. Mikie Sherrill stumped for Democratic Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock on the eve of Election Day as he seeks to unseat GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew before Van Drew can claim a fifth term in the House.
Though Democrats have held South Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District for only one year out of the last 30, they have been heartened in recent days by the party’s strong performance in pre-Election Day voting that they believe shows they may be able to oust an entrenched Republican who last won reelection by nearly 17 points.
“From everything I’ve seen, the momentum is growing,” Sherrill said at a Mullock rally on Monday. “We are seeing better and better numbers each day, and I think part of it is because we have such fantastic candidates.”
As of Monday morning, 109,080 New Jerseyans had voted in the 2nd District race, according to a New Jersey Monitor review of pre-Election Day returns.
Democrats hold the overall preelection edge. Among that party’s registered voters, 51,358 had cast ballots by mail or during the state’s nine-day in-person early voting period, compared to 37,766 for Republicans and 19,492 for unaffiliated voters.
The turnout represents a decline among Republicans and a slight increase among Democrats as compared to 2025, when New Jersey’s governorship and all 80 seats in the General Assembly came up for a vote. That year, 45,696 Republicans voted in advance of Election Day, and 48,170 Democrats did the same.
Mullock said the early returns are a mark of Democratic enthusiasm that could be seen even outside the figures.
“Everywhere we go, people are excited, and they’re willing to jump out and do these canvasses and do these phone banks,” he said. “I just think it’s hard to measure that energy in a poll. What I’m seeing on the ground is a lot of momentum. Hopefully that lasts through tomorrow.”
With Election Day so near, campaigns don’t have much to do aside from ensuring their voters cast their ballots, and Mullock said he intended to spend the time before polls close on Tuesday pushing them to do just that.
Sherrill was sending the same message, urging voters to turn out even as she acknowledged New Jersey’s 2nd District is difficult ground for Democrats.
“That’s what we’re working on today: getting out every single vote. Every vote counts,” she said, adding, “This is a hard place to win, but we can do it.”
Gov. Mikie Sherrill stands on a folding chair as she stumps for Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor and the Democratic nominee in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor and the Democratic nominee in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, speaks to supporters in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor and the Democratic nominee in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, applauds at a campaign event in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Zack Mullock (D), left, who is running to oust Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R), shares a moment with Gov. Mikie Sherrill as Sherrill campaigned for Mullock in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Van Drew captured the district for Democrats when he was still in the party in 2018, but he switched his party affiliation to Republican over what he said was a values split with the Democratic Party.
Ron Filan, Van Drew’s campaign manager, said it was unsurprising to see a Democratic governor campaign for a member of her own party.
“It’s not the first time the governor has been here to campaign against Congressman Van Drew, nor will it be the last,” Filan said.
Despite the indicators of strong Democratic turnout, the 2nd District remains a steep uphill climb for the party.
Though Van Drew won it as a Democrat in 2018, its boundaries were redrawn in 2021 to make it more Republican. It shed all of its municipalities in Camden and Burlington counties — areas Democrats wanted to use to make the 3rd Congressional District safer for their party — and gained deeply Republican portions of Ocean County in exchange.
Trump won the 2nd District by 13 points in 2024, when Van Drew took it by nearly 17.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Historic flooding keeps overwhelming southeastern Utah — here’s how to donate
description: As historic flooding continues to overwhelm San Juan County and southeastern Utah and a flood watch extends to Monday night, donations for the rural and tribal communities there are still needed. But, amid road closures and other limitations, some instructions are changing. Most efforts are being organized by organizations like Utah State University Blanding[...]
text:
Drone footage shows flooding in Bluff, Utah, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Video by Raini Pachak/Bluff Community Foundation)As historic flooding continues to overwhelm San Juan County and southeastern Utah and a flood watch extends to Monday night, donations for the rural and tribal communities there are still needed. But, amid road closures and other limitations, some instructions are changing.
Most efforts are being organized by organizations like Utah State University Blanding, the Bluff Community Foundation and Navajo Strong.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Leah Swenson, program director at Navajo Strong, said on Monday morning that the organization is working with USU and Blanding to deliver items that were donated last week.
“But we’re still getting donations, monetary donations. We’re planning on taking some down, hopefully soon, again, because I know it’s supposed to rain again tomorrow,” Swenson said on Monday.
Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson visited the area with other top state officials last week and met with local leaders and residents to coordinate short and long term relief efforts, she said on social media. 
“These communities have faced devastating home, property, and business losses. Their needs are significant and we are all pulling together to help,” Henderson said at the time. “As a result of our visits today, state agencies have mobilized manpower, water pumps, and UDOT trucks to build a gravel road to access families stranded by the breach of the San Juan River.”
After a “rough night” in San Juan County, Henderson returned to the area on Monday “to ensure adequate resources are in place for the election tomorrow,” she said in another social media post.
“Roads flooded, a bridge washed out, a town evacuated — all on the back of last week’s flooding,” Henderson wrote, asking for prayers for the region.



Let us know what you think...


 


Homes and businesses were damaged after water inundated Bluff Monday morning, including the Bluff Community Foundation’s headquarters, the organization said in a news release. The center “served as a collection point and storage for thousands of donated items for area flood relief.”
“More importantly,” the release says, “those in our community were greatly impacted, and we stand ready to continue assisting families and businesses in Bluff.”
Big USU donation drive
Utah State University is hosting a donation drive at its Career and Technical Education building in Blanding, located at 860 S. Main Street, every weekday from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. until Nov. 6. 
Suggested donations include non-perishable food items, unopened baby formula, cases of water and electrolyte drinks, as well as personal hygiene, clothing and bedding items and cleaning supplies — including N95 masks, which will be used for clean-up efforts.
Because there are limited volunteers sorting through and washing used clothing and bedding, organizers are asking the community to prioritize donations of new items and other necessities on the university’s list of suggestions.
“So used clothing, blankets, even if they’re slightly used, I would just hold off. I know they are looking for new stuff at the moment,” Swensen, of Navajo Strong, said. “I mean, I know the community wants to help out. It’s just one of those things where they are getting way more items than they should be getting, and they have to go through them.”
Other items needed by the community include batteries, flashlights, phone chargers and freezer bags. The USU drive is not accepting cash donations, pet and school supplies or medications. 
Navajo Strong is putting a hold on its drop-off donation efforts in West Valley City while its volunteers travel to the flood site. But it is still accepting monetary donations on the organization’s Venmo, @NavajoStrong-1. Questions about donations can be directed to Swensen via email at Leah@navajostrong.org.
Bluff Community Foundation has a monetary donation platform on its website that accepts different types of cards and other payment options for the relief efforts.
According to a San Juan County update posted Monday, damage assessments are still underway, as there are road closures and limited access to some affected areas.
“We recognize that flooding has affected multiple communities throughout the county, and additional information about relief efforts and opportunities to assist may become available as needs are identified,” the county wrote on social media.

name: VTDigger
title: In Kirby, a potluck and debate night brings neighbors together
description:
Residents said events like this are important for a healthy democracy.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In Kirby, a potluck and debate night brings neighbors together.
text:
Kirby residents gathered for a potluck followed by a moderated House candidate debate on Oct. 15 at the Kirby Town Hall. Photo by Juliette Dutton/Community News Service

This story by Finn McDonough and Juliette Dutton was first published by Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship, on Nov. 2, 2026.
KIRBY — A potluck and a debate. That’s how Kirby, a small town in the Northeast Kingdom, got ready for Election Day.
Kirby has 575 residents, according to the 2020 census. Dozens of them gathered Oct. 15 at the Kirby Town Hall to eat meatballs and casseroles and to hear from all five candidates vying for two seats in the Vermont House from the Caledonia-Essex district.
Democrats Amanda Cochrane and Heather Whitemore Young are running, along with two Republicans — Rep. Deborah Cordz Dolgin, who is seeking reelection, and her husband, Steven Dolgin — and independent Brandolyn Bradley.
Kirby covers about 24 square miles in Caledonia County. It doesn’t have a village center, and residents live far apart.
“Our town has no school, no church, no Quik Stop, pretty much nothing to hold us together,” said John McClaughry, a former state legislator who has moderated Kirby’s Town Meeting since 1967.
But lately, neighbors have been creating spaces to connect.

The five candidates for the Caledonia-Essex House seats participated in a moderated debate following a potluck at the Kirby Town Hall on Oct. 15. The debate was moderated by Dana Gray of the Caledonian Record. Photo by Juliette Dutton/Community News Service

It started over the summer, when resident Tracy Sherbrook helped organize a townwide party for the nation’s 250th anniversary in July.
“We had an RSVP of about 78 people; 180 people came,” Sherbrook said. “So we realized there was a real need for more community events that brought people together.”
Sherbrook and a few neighbors started a series they call Potluck Plus. Each event is a shared meal plus an activity. She and resident Alex Donn organized the debate night, which was moderated by Dana Gray of the Caledonian Record.

A sign directing residents to the potluck and debate event at the Kirby Town Hall on Oct. 15. Photo by Juliette Dutton/Community News Service

“A debate and a potluck just kind of galvanizes people,” said resident Melanie Finn. “This is such a spread-out community— you can see people on the road, you give them the two-finger wave off the steering wheel, but I think it’s really nice for people to come together, particularly for something like this.”
Resident Thomas De Carlo said events like this one are important for a healthy democracy.
“We’re in a very politicized time where people, you know, they put on their party face,” he said. “And this kind of relaxes people and makes it more of a community event. And that’s the whole point of what we should be doing: talking, and sharing views, and seeing how the other people think.”

The Kirby Town Hall at dusk on Oct. 15. Photo by Juliette Dutton/Community News Service

Resident Nelia Rath brought her daughter to the event. She said nothing brings people together like food.
“Sharing, breaking bread together, you know, it’s biblical,” Rath said. “People have done that since the beginning of time. And of course, engaging in civic debate is really important, and being able to model that for my fifth grader is really important.”
At the debate, candidates discussed housing, tax rates and affordability for families. Attendees said they didn’t know whether the event would have an effect on the election, but they do hope this Potluck Plus will be the first of many.
The next one, a potluck and land use presentation, is scheduled for Nov. 12.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Millionaire game postponed, state lottery says
description: The Montana State Lottery experienced a “continued technical issue” this weekend in its Montana Millionaire game, which the state agency postponed on Nov. 1. Each year, the state lottery runs a game that picks several winners for a prize of $1 million. This year, the lottery was set to pick six tickets that would win […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.The Montana State Lottery experienced a “continued technical issue” this weekend in its Montana Millionaire game, which the state agency postponed on Nov. 1.
Each year, the state lottery runs a game that picks several winners for a prize of $1 million. This year, the lottery was set to pick six tickets that would win $1 million each and additionally one person to win $250,000 and thousands of other smaller cash prizes.
Tickets were on sale starting at 5:30 a.m., on Nov. 1 and Montanans routinely line up for hours ahead of the tickets going on sale. Last year, 620,000 tickets sold out in just six hours.
This year, ticket sales were chaos, according to news outlets around the state, and it remained a topic of discussion in gas stations, bars, and social media across the state on Monday.
Problems began early Sunday morning, according to Q2 in Billings, with the system crashing shortly after sales started.
At 11 a.m. on Sunday, the state lottery made the “difficult decision to postpone the game,” it said in a Facebook post, adding that a new date and time for sales would be forthcoming. The lottery has not announced a new sales date as of Monday.
In a statement to the Daily Montanan, Montana Lottery said it would provide information out about a new date when it was decided, adding it would “provide adequate notice” before the game starts.
“A new sales date and time will be announced once the technical issues have been fully resolved and the Montana Lottery can ensure that all sales and game data have been properly validated,” a state lottery Facebook post said.
On social media, the state lottery blamed issues related to the game’s vendor, Bally’s Intralot. State contracts with that company have been under intense scrutiny by lawmakers in recent years.
In a statement, Montana Lottery said the system “experienced performance issues due to the high volume of transactions occurring simultaneously.” It also added “Instant Win” prizes were being awarded more frequently than intended while sales were briefly ongoing on Sunday.
Information about the Montana Millionaire game was also not displaying correctly on its website and mobile platforms.
Those who did buy Montana Millionaire tickets are asked to hang on to them as they are still valid. There were 12,919 Montana Millionaire tickets sold before the postponement announcement, Montana Lottery said.
Instant wins can still be redeemed by players. No winning Montana Millionaire tickets have been drawn, the state lottery said.
“The sales agent must scan the barcode of the instant win coupon so the appropriate accounting can take place,” the lottery said in a press release. “Players that received Montana Millionaire tickets need to hold onto them because they will still be a part of the prize pool once sales resume.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Grinnell College Poll shows increased confidence in correct vote counts for midterms
description: More Americans are confident in the integrity of vote counts for the midterm elections than in past election cycles, according to a poll authored by Grinnell College students and faculty. The Grinnell College Poll, delivered every two years since 2018, was administered by YouGov through a web survey in mid-October and recorded responses from 1,500 […]
text:
The Grinnell College Poll gathered responses on voting and other topics from 1,500 U.S. residents. (Photo courtesy of Grinnell College) More Americans are confident in the integrity of vote counts for the midterm elections than in past election cycles, according to a poll authored by Grinnell College students and faculty.
The Grinnell College Poll, delivered every two years since 2018, was administered by YouGov through a web survey in mid-October and recorded responses from 1,500 U.S. residents over 18. It runs the gamut of current political topics, asking respondents about the election and national issues like the economy, immigration and technology.
According to a news release announcing the poll results, 64% of respondents are confident that votes will be counted correctly in Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Iowans will cast their vote for the state’s next governor and federal and state lawmakers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Peter Hanson, Grinnell political science professor and director of the Grinnell College Poll, said confidence in the correct counting of votes grew in this poll by 4 percentage points from the previous survey in March 2024, which placed confidence at 58%. Hanson’s students help co-author questions for the Grinnell College Poll, he said, and they’re paying close attention to the midterm races.
That increase came mainly from Republicans, of which 41% reported confidence in the vote in 2024 and 66% indicated the same in this year’s survey. Just under three-quarters of Democrats and respondents who reported leaning that direction this year reported feeling either somewhat or very confident in the vote.
“We have about a 25-point jump in Republican confidence in the vote, and I think that’s really primarily a function of Donald Trump being president,” Hanson said. “Now, with him being president, they think it’s more likely that votes will be counted as intended.”
It’s an interesting finding when looking at the “constant drumbeat of attacks from the president questioning the integrity of our elections,” Hanson said. As Democrat confidence in the vote has remained high through previous iterations of the poll, he said he interprets that to mean that they didn’t believe President Donald Trump’s claims, which have not been substantiated.
Close to 90% of respondents, regardless of party leaning, stated they believe it’s very important that “free and fair elections are conducted without fraud, led by Democrats at 91% and followed by Republicans at 89% and independents at 82%. This is one of the “core democratic values” the poll touches on, Hanson said, and provides a contrast to responses to a question of American democracy.
A majority of both political parties, as well as independent voters, reported their agreement with the statement, “American democracy is in crisis,” with somewhat or strong agreement from 84% of Democrat respondents, 60% of Republicans and 66% of independents.
“We have this contrasting view of the electorate, where they say they believe deeply in core democratic values, but they are very worried about the state of American democracy,” Hanson said.
Only 5% of Democrat respondents said they approve of Trump’s handling of his job leading the U.S., compared to 78% of Republican respondents and 22% of independents.
When it comes to the midterm elections and how political parties could potentially come out, Hanson said that when “looking at the structure of the political environment… it’s very clearly a very good year for the Democrats,” based on Trump’s 35% approval rating in the Grinnell and other polls and perceptions of the economy.
The poll asked respondents about their expectations for the U.S. economy in the next 12 months, to which 43% of Republicans, 12% of Democrats and 10% of independents reported their belief that it will be better. More than half of both Democrats and independents responded that they expect the economy to be worse, compared to 15% of Republicans.
Hanson said his go-to line about elections is that they’re decided by turnout and persuasion. He thinks the Democrats have the turnout advantage. Democratic voters are “likely to show up to vote in larger numbers than Republicans,” he said, as they’re motivated and “deeply concerned about the state of the country.”
“Then in terms of persuasion, that’s really a story about independents, and independents have really soured on President Trump,” Hanson said. “They disapprove of the job he’s doing in office. They’re very concerned about the economy, and those are things that are likely to lead them to vote for Democrats in larger numbers than they would for Republicans.”
