name: Kansas Reflector
title: At Kansas election eve rallies, Masterson and Holscher seek to propel supporters to get out the vote
description: Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher, the Kansas gubernatorial candidates, urge voters to keep charging until polls close Tuesday.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Ty Masterson offers closing thoughts on Nov. 2, 2026, to a group of supporters in Lenexa. He is competing against Democratic candidate Cindy Holscher in the 2026 race for Kansas governor. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)LENEXA — Republican Ty Masterson spoke Sunday night to Johnson County conservatives in defense of President Donald Trump’s policies and the perils of allowing Democrat Cindy Holscher to win Tuesday’s election for Kansas governor.
“I understand President Trump’s personality, right?” Masterson said. “I understand. He’s a flavor. And, some people like him and some people hate him. But, you know, even the haters that I run into, none of them hate what he’s done. None of them say, ‘Oh, no. I wish he hadn’t closed the border.’ Because you know what? You’re safer.”
Masterson, a state senator from Andover near Wichita, asked 150 or so people in the crowd to think back to July 13, 2024, when an assassin bloodied Trump’s right ear in Pennsylvania, but defiantly raised a fist and mouthed the word “fight.” That’s the attitude Kansas Republicans need to carry into final hours of the 2026 election, Masterson said.
“Our battlefield is the ballot box. You guys are at the front of the battle in Johnson County,” Masterson said. “I do not expect to win Johnson County, but I sure expect to lose by a lot less than everybody else thinks.”
Several hours and a few miles to the south during a loud gathering of Democrats in Lenexa, Holscher outlined a case against electing Masterson to fill the shoes of term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Holscher punctuated her closing argument with a blend of defensive and offensive strategies to serve the state’s interests as governor.
Holscher, an Overland Park senator who repeatedly won election in red-leaning districts, chose a renovated timber barn for her get-out-the-vote rally. She was joined by Kelly, former Gov. Kathleen Sebelius and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.
“Together, we are going to build a Kansas where hard work pays off, where our schools are strong and where every family gets a fair shot,” Holscher said. “I’m going to lower property taxes and bring down the cost of living. I’m gonna protect our seniors, stand up for our farmers, because they’re the backbone of this state.”
On Monday, the latest New York Times poll gave Holscher a 1 percentage point edge on Masterson with little more than 24 hours before polls closed.
Voter registration in Kansas tips election scales in favor of Republican candidates. The state has 900,000 Republicans, 580,000 independents and 520,000 Democrats. That deficit for Democrats didn’t prevent Kelly from winning back-to-back terms as governor in 2018 and 2022. In the past 30 years, Kansas voters have steadfastly sent Republicans to the U.S. Senate, but alternated between Democratic and Republican governors. If the trend held, Masterson would prevail.
 
Kelly backing Holscher
Holscher, who once walked from Johnson County to Topeka to bring attention to lack of public school funding, vowed to deliver collaborative state government to Kansans finding it harder to make ends meet as the rising cost of food, fuel and other essentials outpaced stagnant incomes. She touted policies with bipartisan appeal in Kansas, including Medicaid expansion, full funding of K-12 special education, abortion rights and legalization of marijuana.
Holscher took a dig at Trump’s endorsements for Masterson, including a full-throated version Sunday night for several thousand people at a MAGA rally in Salina. She has criticized the president’s war with Iran, which is blamed for the spike in fuel prices at the pump.
She reminded the crowd that she was part of the legislative coalition that voted in 2017 to repeal state income tax cuts championed by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback, who recently endorsed Masterson. The resulting steep decline in tax revenue starved state programs for five years. Holscher said voters should keep in mind Masterson has continued to defend Brownback’s tax initiative.
Kelly said Holscher had enough momentum to compete with Masterson and put herself in a place to win the race for governor.
“I want somebody who cares about Kansas,” Kelly said. “I want somebody who will protect our schools. I want somebody who understands and will work for and always pay attention to our rural communities. I want somebody who’s not a wholly owned subsidiary.”
In the August primary, Kelly endorsed state Sen. Ethan Corson of Johnson County, but switched her allegiance to Holscher after votes were counted.
Beshear, who chairs the national Democratic Governors Association, said he was impressed by Holscher.
“I think Laura and I are living, breathing proof that Democrats can win anywhere,” Beshear said. “I’m so proud of the race Cindy has run. She is scrappy in all the right ways.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher makes a final pitch for votes Nov. 2, 2026, to a crowd of enthusiastic supporters in Lenexa. She faces Republican nominee Ty Masterson in the governor’s race on Tuesday. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
Lombardi and Reagan
Dayton Moore, the former general manager of the Kansas City Royals, spoke at the Lenexa campaign stop on Masterson’s behalf. He said legendary football coach Vince Lombardi believed winning was the only thing that mattered. It’s that type of attitude supporters of Masterson had to carry into waning hours of a campaign, he said.
“His principle of leadership, his Judeo-Christian beliefs uniquely prepare him to bring our community of leaders, our educators, our farmers, our politicians together to solve issues,” Moore said. “We’re thankful that (Tuesday) we get to go out and do something that many people around the world don’t get to do, and so we encourage those of you that are registered voters to get out there and vote. Protect this God-given right to voice your opinion.”
During the Sunday appearance with Trump in Salina, Masterson said he was reminded of a comment by President Ronald Reagan about how freedom was potentially one generation away from elimination.
“I don’t think it’s ever been more relevant than it is today,” Masterson said.  “This isn’t about an individual candidate. It is about the direction of this country and this state. So, you got a personal issue with any one of us? Anybody that’s running? Look past it. Because it is directional.”
Masterson complained political operatives such as Our Heritage Matters and Stand Your Ground were flooding Kansas with campaign messages to divert conservative votes away from Republican candidates.
“It’s all nefarious to get you to go out and shave off votes from the Republicans,” Masterson said. “They say they’re the real conservatives, but they’re not attacking the left. They’re attacking the right.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: At election eve rally, Cindy Holscher drives message of economic and healthcare renewal for Kansas
description: Republican Ty Masterson and Democrat Cindy Holscher, the Kansas gubernatorial candidates, urge voters to keep charging until polls close Tuesday.
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher makes a final pitch for votes Nov. 2, 2026, to a crowd of enthusiastic supporters in Lenexa. She faces Republican Ty Masterson in the governor's race. (Photo by Tim  Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)LENEXA — Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher stood united with Gov. Laura Kelly on the eve of Tuesday’s election to deliver closing arguments on economic, healthcare and education issues in the tense campaign against Republican Ty Masterson.
Holscher, an Overland Park state senator who repeatedly won election in red-leaning districts, packed supporters into a renovated timber barn for a get-out-the-vote rally with Kelly, former Gov. Kathleen Sebelius and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear.
“Together, we are going to build a Kansas where hard work pays off, where our schools are strong and where every family gets a fair shot,” Holscher said. “I’m going to lower property taxes and bring down the cost of living. I’m gonna protect our seniors, stand up for our farmers, because they’re the backbone of this state.”
On Monday, the latest New York Times poll gave Holscher a 1 percentage point edge on Masterson with little more than 24 hours before polls closed.
Holscher, who once walked from Johnson County to Topeka to bring attention to lack of public school funding, vowed to deliver collaborative state government to Kansans finding it harder to make ends meet as the rising cost of food, fuel and other essentials outpaced stagnant incomes. She touted policies with bipartisan appeal in Kansas, including Medicaid expansion, full funding of K-12 special education, abortion rights and legalization of marijuana.
Holscher took a dig at President Donald Trump’s series of endorsements for Masterson, including a full-throated version Sunday night for several thousand people at a MAGA rally in Salina. She has criticized the Republican president’s war with Iran, which is blamed for the spike in fuel prices at the pump. The state senator has denounced global tariffs advanced by Trump that undercut the bottom line for ranchers and farmers.
She reminded the crowd that she was part of the legislative coalition that voted in 2017 to repeal state income tax cuts championed by GOP Gov. Sam Brownback, who recently endorsed Masterson. The resulting steep decline in tax revenue, without equivalent reductions in spending, starved state programs for five years. Holscher said voters should keep in mind that Masterson, the Andover Republican serving as Kansas Senate president, continued to defend Brownback’s tax initiative and the budget-cratering consequences.
Voter registration in Kansas tips election scales in favor of Republican candidates. The state has 900,000 Republicans, 580,000 independents and 520,000 Democrats. That registration deficit for Democrats didn’t prevent Kelly from winning back-to-back terms as governor in 2018 and 2022.
Kelly said the quality of Democratic candidates up and down the ballot resonated with Kansas voters. Kelly said she was confident Holscher had the momentum to challenge Masterson and to follow her in the governor’s office.
“I want somebody who cares about Kansas,” Kelly said. “I want somebody who will protect our schools. I want somebody who understands and will work for and always pay attention to our rural communities. I want somebody who’s not a wholly owned subsidiary.”
In the August primary, Kelly endorsed state Sen. Ethan Corson of Johnson County, but switched her allegiance to Holscher after votes were counted.
Beshear, who chairs the national Democratic Governors Association, said he was optimist Democrats would perform well in dozens of governor races.
“I think Laura and I are living, breathing proof that Democrats can win anywhere,” Beshear said. “I’m so proud of the race Cindy has run. She is scrappy in all the right ways. She has pushed through. She has done the tough things. She has knocked on doors. She has worked her tail off.”
Masterson’s end-of-campaign rally was scheduled for later Monday evening several miles away in Johnson County.
Ty Masterson speaks before President Donald Trump takes the stage at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
During a Sunday appearance with President Donald Trump in Salina, Masterson said he was reminded of a comment by President Ronald Reagan about how freedom was potentially one generation away from extinction.
“I don’t think it’s ever been more relevant than it is today,” Masterson said. “It has blown my mind the stark directional change that we’re considering in this election.”
Masterson urged rally participants to work until the poll closed Tuesday to get out the conservative vote.
“I need you to get out. It is that important,” he said. “This isn’t about an individual candidate. It is about the direction of this country and this state. So, you got a personal issue with any one of us? Anybody that’s running? Look past it. Because it is directional.”
He said organizations with conservative-sounding names were working to persuade Kansas voters to embrace Libertarian Party candidates.
“Don’t let anybody buy that, all because you might have some disillusionment with the Republican Party,” he said. “Don’t go off and waste your vote and vote for some third-party person. It is a vote for socialism as much as it is a vote for that Democratic candidate.”
He said Trump was successful in tightening border security and reducing federal taxes. Eventually, he said, the price of fuel at the pump would decline. He said high gasoline and diesel prices shouldn’t be blamed on Trump’s war with Iran. The culprit was climate-change activists responsible for inhibiting construction of refineries.
“That’s what causing you so much pain at the pump,” Masterson said. “Not the Iran war. That is a glitch in time. It will be solved. If you want affordability back, you don’t have a choice but to vote Republican. Because that is the only way to go.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Gulf Coast states could get more flexibility to manage red snapper limits
description: The way Gulf Coast states manage their catch limits for red snapper, a popular catch among recreational anglers, is poised to change next year as fisheries management officials recommend adding more flexibility for states into federal rules.
text:
Red snapper displayed on a dock in 1978.  (NOAA NMFS SEFSC Panama City Beach Laboratory)The way Gulf Coast states manage their catch limits for red snapper, a popular catch among recreational anglers, is poised to change next year as fisheries management officials recommend adding more flexibility for states into federal rules. 
The Gulf Fishery Management Council took action last week to alter how red snapper catch limit “paybacks” are done at their meeting in Galveston, Texas. The council advises the federal government on managing species in its Gulf of Mexico waters. Its members include sportfishers, commercial harvesters and scientists. 
Gulf states are each allotted a specific amount of fish per species that recreational anglers may pull from the water every season. It’s done to ensure anglers don’t take too many, which can destabilize the population or even lead to a species’ extinction. 
Previously, if a state went over its seasonal catch limit for red snapper, it had the overage amount taken away from its limit the following season, known as a payback.
The Gulf Council will change the regulations to require payback in only some instances. It will apply when a state exceeds its catch limit by more than 10%, surpasses its limit twice within three years or goes beyond its individual state limit in a year where the total catch limit for all Gulf States is surpassed.
Kesley Banks, a fisheries scientist and chair of the Gulf Council, said the change is being made to avoid punishing states that go over their catch limits by insignificant amounts. 
“It’s an estimate. There’s a margin of error on either side,” Banks said about the statistical modeling used to set catch limits. The added flexibility allows states that consistently obey catch limits to fall back on their good track records to avoid being “punished” when they fall within the margin of error, she added. 
“This is one way we can address that without opening that long, convoluted process” of reworking the standards from scratch, Banks said. 
The new rules go next to the U.S. Department of Commerce, where its secretary will decide whether to approve the council’s recommendation. The council fashioned the rule changes after a public comment period, and the public will get another chance to provide feedback when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick officially opens the comment period, lasting 16 to 30 days.
In all, the process is expected to take seven to 10 months, Banks said, with the rules becoming official around mid-year 2027. 
The Gulf Council is one of eight regional fishery management groups that Congress established in 1976. They all set and revise regulations for federal waters to keep fish populations from being overexploited and maintain healthy ecosystems.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma high court questions why Secretary of State hasn’t shown its work
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Some Oklahoma Supreme Court justices seemed skeptical Monday about the process the Secretary of State’s Office used to strike tens of thousands of signatures from a citizen-led initiative petition. They questioned why the agency has been unwilling to explain why each of the more than 57,000 signatures were rejected if artificial intelligence [...]
text:
Cedric Bond, an attorney representing Oklahoma Secretary of State Benjamin Lepak, argues to the state Supreme Court over a challenge to disqualified signatures for an initiative petition on Nov. 2, 2026. (Screenshot)OKLAHOMA CITY — Some Oklahoma Supreme Court justices seemed skeptical Monday about the process the Secretary of State’s Office used to strike tens of thousands of signatures from a citizen-led initiative petition.
They questioned why the agency has been unwilling to explain why each of the more than 57,000 signatures were rejected if artificial intelligence technology and human error played a role in the process.
The state’s high court heard nearly two hours of oral arguments that could determine not only the fate of State Question 836, which proposes changing the state’s primary system, but also how the Secretary of State’s Office handles signature verification efforts moving forward. The court did not immediately rule Monday.
An attorney representing Oklahoma Secretary of State Benjamin Lepak argued the state had complied with a new law passed in 2024 that increased the number of data points a signature must meet to be considered valid. But those challenging the office’s rejection of what they say are tens of thousands of legitimate voters’ signatures argued Lepak’s office unlawfully placed the burden of proof on proponents of the state question. 
State Question 836 would place all candidates on one primarty ballot, allowing voters to select any one candidate – regardless of their party affiliation. The top two voter getters would advance to the general election. Oklahoma law currently bars independent voters from voting in partisan primaries unless the party files paperwork to allow it. 
Supporters of State Question 836 said they collected more than the number of signatures state law required to place items on a future ballot.
Cedric Bond, an attorney representing Oklahoma Secretary of State Benjamin Lepak, argues to the state Supreme Court over a challenge to disqualified signatures for an initiative petition on Nov. 2, 2026. (Screenshot)
But in March, Lepak rejected the open primaries initiative petition, saying it fell short of the required number of valid signatures. The office reported that only 142,567 of the more than 209,000 submitted signatures were valid. This was met with two separate legal challenges in June, which asked for Lepak’s office to point out which signatures were rejected and explain why.  
Vice Chief Justice Dana Kuehn and Justice Noma Gurich both questioned why Lepak’s office hadn’t provided the report in response to requests from proponents of the state question. 
“I always didn’t like it when my math teacher told me I had to show my work,” Kuehn said. “I just wanted to write the answer, and you had to take me for my word that I knew how to do the math. So why don’t you all want to show your work? Can you show your work?”
Cedric Bond, an attorney representing Lepak, said the office does not object to providing a report of which specific signatures were rejected if the court orders it, nor does it object to allowing the proponents to review individual signature data.
He said some older artificial intelligence technology was used to help verify signatures, but the process had human oversight at “every step of the way” and still couldn’t match 57,841 signature lines with 80% confidence. 
State law requires that at least 4 of 5 voter data points be verified for a signature on an initiative petition to be considered valid. Those include legal first name, legal last name, zip code, house number, numerical month and date of birth. 
“I would also like to point out here that the secretary is not the protestant to this initiative petition,” he said. “The secretary does not oppose this, it’s not a policy preference question in this at all. The secretary has a ministerial role, and that role is given by the Legislature, which was acting under its constitutional mandate.” 
Frederic Dorwart, an attorney representing proponents of the state question, said Lepak’s office has unlawfully burdened the proponents with proving the validity of signatures and has not provided “competent evidence” of the reason for rejection 29% of the submitted signatures. 
“If it were 5%, we probably wouldn’t be here,” he said. “If it were 5%, we would probably live with the result. But it was 29%, and that is an implausible number to think that those 57,841 people were not legal voters when they signed that petition.”
Each signature sheet has bold, oversized letters that tells people it’s a felony to sign if they’re not a valid, legal voter, Dorwart said. It’s not plausible that so many people were not valid voters, he said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New round of flooding leads to damage, evacuations in northern New Mexico, Navajo Nation
description: Unrelenting rainfall in northern New Mexico over the weekend prompted additional flooding in areas already inundated, along with numerous evacuation orders for those near the banks of the San Juan, La Plata, Animas and Chama rivers.
text:
Additional flooding over the weekend of Oct. 31, 2026, inundated northern New Mexico homes and roadways that were already underwater from floods earlier in October, including San Juan County, pictured above Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)Unrelenting rainfall in northern New Mexico over the weekend prompted additional flooding in areas already inundated, along with numerous evacuation orders for those near the banks of the San Juan, La Plata, Animas and Chama rivers. 
Areas of northern New Mexico including San Juan County and Rio Arriba County and the Navajo Nation near Shiprock have been hit with floods in recent weeks, with rivers rising far above their banks at historic levels. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Before the flooding this weekend, at least 10,000 homes in San Juan County and elsewhere suffered some flooding damage, according to state officials. Damage estimates from a new round of flooding since Saturday were not immediately available, though a National Weather Service database details floodwaters breaching homes at several locations in San Juan County, including an RV park. 
According to the National Weather Service, San Juan and Rio Arriba counties bore the brunt of the additional flooding over the weekend. The service received dozens of reports of flooded roadways and other damage in Farmington, Chama, Abiquíu, Bloomfield and elsewhere. 
Swiftwater rescue crews saved one couple who was briefly swept away by floodwaters near the La Plata River on Sunday afternoon, according to the National Weather Service database.
Officials in the village of Chama just south of the Colorado border issued mandatory evacuation orders Sunday and closed all roads into town. On Monday afternoon, they alerted the public of potential sewage contamination and told residents to avoid any contact with Rio Chama water. 
National Weather Service flood warnings are in effect through Wednesday, concentrated at rivers that run along the northernmost portion of the state.
Flooding-related issues have caused numerous water and power outages on the Navajo Nation, including in Shiprock and the Red Mesa areas in New Mexico. The Navajo Department of Emergency Management on Monday afternoon listed 17 sites that lost water and six that lost power in that region alone. 
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Thursday announced she’d authorized up to $55 million in state emergency funds to counties and pueblos in northern New Mexico that are reeling from the floods. 
On Monday, the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office issued an election advisory about the severe weather saying it had been in contact with county clerks in parts of the state impacted by the weather and that all polling places as of Monday remain open to voters. 
In the event of severe weather impacting polling spots for Tuesday’s election, the Secretary of State noted that registered voters can cast ballots at any polling location within the county.

title: Trump promotes Reflecting Pool renovation the day before the election
description: WASHINGTON — One day before his party is forecast to lose control of the U.S. House, and possibly the Senate, President Donald Trump gathered guests and press at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to tout the “magnificent” renovation of the monument — a monthslong project plagued by algae, reclosure and false accusations of vandalism.Trump spoke for roughl[...]
text: WASHINGTON — One day before his party is forecast to lose control of the U.S. House, and possibly the Senate, President Donald Trump gathered guests and press at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to tout the “magnificent” renovation of the monument — a monthslong project plagued by algae, reclosure and false accusations of vandalism.Trump spoke for roughly 45 minutes, bouncing from topic to topic. His remarks included but were not limited to unfounded allegations of “unprecedented” vandalism to the pool’s lining, accusations that former FBI Director James Comey is a “dirty cop,” a mention of “rave reviews” for the new White House helipad, and assertions that “we got Greenland on an unlimited basis” and “we won” the war with Iran that moments later he said is “not a war.”The president did not mention the midterm elections until 23 minutes into his delivery, when he said Democrats are running the “most dangerous candidates ever put up,” including “jihadists and Muslim Brotherhood members.”The remark is a continuation of the president’s persistent  verbal attacks, called racist by critics, on Michigan’s Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed, an Arab American. The candidate, who is leading in the latest New York Times/Siena poll, has denounced accusations that he could be connected to extremist Islamists.Trump could lose GOP trifecta controlThe midterms are slated to be the most expensive on record, and depending on the forecast, Democrats stand a chance to gain Senate seats in reliably Republican states. Trump’s party is expected to lose roughly 15 to 25 seats in the U.S. House, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to record lows in the months leading up to the election, as Americans face high gas prices and inflation largely due to global oil market disruptions caused by the Iran war, and the president’s steep tariffs.The Democrats, Trump said, “are all committed to the same radical agenda,” which he defined as raising taxes by “trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilation of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas,” among other claims.He also repeated his promise to give voters cash if Republicans retain control of Congress.“Every adult is going to get $5,000. But you have to spend it in the United States of America,” he said.The plan would cost $1.2 trillion, and ultimately Congress would need to appropriate the money.“The Democrats want to blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists, and the United States Congress will not allow that to happen. Got some big races tomorrow. I guess some of the voting has already gone on, but tomorrow is Election Day, more traditional, and we can't let that happen,” he said.Voting breaks recordsMidterm voting is well underway, with more than 57 million Americans having already cast early ballots in person or by mail as of 4 p.m. Eastern Monday. The early turnout smashed the all-time high-water mark for early midterm voting, which crested at 46 million in 2022.Trump’s Monday appearance on the National Mall followed a whirlwind month of campaigning in mostly Republican stronghold states, where he delivered lengthy speeches, veering off script and repeatedly mentioning Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s backside. The president wrapped up his campaign travel this past weekend with two final rally appearances in Kansas and Iowa. During his last in-person midterm campaign stop in Dubuque, Trump trailed off during his endorsement of Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ashley Hinson and began discussing her weight and physique.According to his official schedule, Trump had already appeared at two telerallies Monday prior to his visit to the Reflecting Pool. He was scheduled to do seven more telerallies through the evening.Reflecting Pool sagaIn his final in-person appearance before the midterm culmination, the president dredged up his political grievances, listed his administration’s projects in the nation’s capital and repeated false claims that vandalism was the culprit for the lengthy Reflecting Pool repairs.Trump’s own hand-picked U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, dropped the government's case against a former Olympian canoeist who had been accused of damaging the pool’s lining. Pirro dismissed the charges after finding the grand jury was not provided with all the evidence, namely that the damage had occurred because of “contractor error.”“The pipes have just been changed. The whole thing is in great shape, and we're going to make sure nobody vandalizes it,” Trump said Monday, intermittently holding up enlarged photos of pipes and surfacing for the crowd to see. “And I'm going to ask the Park Police, the people, to really watch cause a lot of people are sort of watching as this group of people slashed the hell out of it,” he said, trailing off to say “a weird feeling came upon them, and they didn’t, didn’t get it. But we learned a lot.”Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum also spoke during the event, which wrapped up in just under an hour.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Should Oklahoma lower school class sizes? Educators, experts weigh in.
description: OKLAHOMA CITY —  Having only 18 students last year was “a dream” for Choctaw Elementary teacher Monica Short. This school year, her roster swelled to 26 fourth graders as a result of redistricting in Choctaw-Nicoma Park Public Schools. Short said she still loves her job, but “it’s hard,” even as an experienced teacher. “Two weeks […]
text:
Students raise their hands in a fourth-grade classroom at Cleveland Elementary in Oklahoma City on March 6. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY —  Having only 18 students last year was “a dream” for Choctaw Elementary teacher Monica Short.
This school year, her roster swelled to 26 fourth graders as a result of redistricting in Choctaw-Nicoma Park Public Schools. Short said she still loves her job, but “it’s hard,” even as an experienced teacher.
“Two weeks ago, I got my 26th student,” Short told state lawmakers last week. “I have always said I felt called to this profession, so I’m like, ‘If the good Lord is going to give me a kid, I’ll take the 27th, and I’m not going to complain about it.’ But I want you to know it is tough. It is tough.”
House legislators heard from experts and educators speak about the impact of class sizes during an interim study last week at the state Capitol.
Last year, Short finished each school day feeling great about what she and her students had accomplished, she said. Now, dedicating one-on-one time to each student, managing classroom behaviors, giving individual feedback on classwork and organizing small-group instruction is more challenging.
The larger the class, “the more difficult it is to have that student success across the board,” she said.
Oklahoma law permits no more than 20 students per classroom at the elementary level, but it allows broad exemptions, said Brent Rowland, executive director of the Oklahoma Appleseed Center for Law and Justice.
For example, districts that have borrowed 85% or more of their bonding capacity are exempt from class size limits, he said. That rule alone would apply to 185 districts, including many of the state’s largest, which educate just under half of all students enrolled in Oklahoma public schools, Oklahoma Appleseed found. 
Kindergarten students sit on a rug in their classroom at Thelma R. Parks Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 13, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Research is not conclusive on whether lower class sizes lead to better academic results, Rowland said. However, Oklahoma teachers have reported in statewide surveys that large class sizes are one of the top challenges they face, along with disruptive student behavior.
Rowland encouraged state lawmakers to seek out more data, particularly on which districts are using class size exemptions, before making policy decisions.
“Class size, one of the biggest factors in a teacher’s capacity, is regulated here but largely not measured and consistently enforced,” he said during the interim study. “These are not separate problems. Literacy, behavior, teacher capacity all come together in the classroom.”
Choctaw Elementary teacher Susan Johnson said she has 21 third graders in a high-need and high-trauma classroom this year.
One student is reading at an eighth-grade level and another at a kindergarten level, she said. Four of her students have active cases with the Department of Human Services, and two are involved in court proceedings.
“It’s a lot,” Johnson said. “You’re trying to create an environment and have student engagement — meaningful, deep student engagement — with kids that are coming with a lot, and you’re expected to teach them eight subjects every day. Having a complex classroom does impact learning, and you have to really rise to that.”
Rep. Ronny Johns, R-Ada, said he requested the interim study after hearing complaints from teachers in his House district about classroom disruptions and a need for more support. 
Rep. Ronny Johns, R-Ada, speaks during a House Education Oversight Committee meeting March 5, 2025, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Johns, a former teacher and principal, said class sizes are even more relevant with the state implementing new laws focused on child literacy.
Oklahoma’s Strong Readers Act will require students to repeat third grade if they score below a basic reading level on statewide tests, starting in the 2027-28 academic year. This past spring, 44% of Oklahoma third graders, or 21,100 students, would have been at risk of repeating the grade had the law already been in effect, based on 2025-26 test scores.
Johns said “we’ll see” whether it’s feasible for the Legislature to add more funding to lower class sizes. Providing a strong early education is worth the money, he said.
“It’s about investment,” Johns said after the study. “I get a little aggravated when I hear, ‘Well, we’re just throwing money at education.’ Really, to me, it’s an investment.
“A good third-grade reader is not going to end up in prison. And so we’re either going to invest now, or we’re going to be throwing money in other ways.”
Policymakers should focus more on improving the system of support that surrounds each teacher rather than on the size of that teacher’s class, said Tim Lewis, a professor from the University of Missouri College of Education & Human Development.
Although Lewis acknowledged there’s a class-size “sweet spot” of about 20 students, he said the resources that help teachers provide individualized instruction to students who most need it are even more crucial.
“Spend 99.9% of your time and energy focused on what happens in that classroom and how do we as a state or as a district support that individual teacher,” he told lawmakers during the interim study. “You heard the importance of retaining those highly qualified teachers. They’re going to leave if they’re not successful. They can be successful, but we cannot expect a single teacher to meet and solve this issue.”

name: VTDigger
title: I nearly died because I couldn’t find a primary care doctor
description:
Health insurance doesn’t mean anything if there’s no doctor to see. Universal primary care would close that gap for every Vermonter.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  I nearly died because I couldn’t find a primary care doctor.
text:
Dear Editor,
To understand why universal primary care is so important, you have to experience what it is like to have a life-threatening disease without access to a primary care doctor. Twenty years ago, that was me. I nearly lost my life because of it. The breathtaking question is why our political system — federal and state  — has been so cavalier about the awful injustice of our healthcare mess. 
I was one of the lucky ones back then. I had employer-sponsored health insurance. Still, that didn’t matter. Health insurance is not healthcare. It is a long story, but the insurance company’s networked providers did not include any primary care doctors in state. When I finally found a doctor, it was almost too late. If we had universal primary care, I would not have reached the state where I came close to being “a goner.” 
Universal primary care will, of course, not cure every problem in our healthcare system. Critics always cite its costs. But they never count the cost of lives lost or forever scarred because people couldn’t get care at the most vulnerable time in their lives, or had to fight for it through a forest of claim denials, co-pays, deductibles and so on. Why do we keep spending enormous sums to subsidize vast hospital and private insurance company bureaucracies while arguing that publicly funded access to basic care is too expensive?   

READ MORE

Unlike means-tested public assistance programs, universal primary care would not tell working Vermonters, like me, who pay taxes out of every paycheck, that they earn too much to qualify for the benefits their taxes help support. 
I learned the hard way how high these stakes really are. Vermont has an opportunity to build a system that finally puts people first. It’s long past time to choose life over profit or operating revenue — and introduce primary care for all Vermonters.
Walter Carpenter Montpelier, Vt.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Dueling rallies, heavy turnout mark last day of 2026 campaigns in Arkansas
authors: Antoinette Grajeda, Tess Vrbin, Ainsley Platt
description: Arkansas’ statewide and congressional candidates held dueling rallies and met with voters throughout the state Monday, on the eve of a midterm election where Democrats hoped to break Republicans’ lock on the top elected offices.  More than 500,000 Arkansans cast a ballot early in person or absentee by Monday. Secretary of State Cole Jester’s office […]
text:
Voters make their selections on touchscreen machines on the last day of early voting for the midterm election at the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo By Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas’ statewide and congressional candidates held dueling rallies and met with voters throughout the state Monday, on the eve of a midterm election where Democrats hoped to break Republicans’ lock on the top elected offices. 
More than 500,000 Arkansans cast a ballot early in person or absentee by Monday. Secretary of State Cole Jester’s office has predicted that at least 50% of the state’s 1.8 million registered voters will cast a ballot in this year’s midterm election.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Democrats haven’t won statewide or federal office in Arkansas in 16 years, but the party is hopeful that President Donald Trump’s low approval numbers and concerns about affordability could create an opening in the solidly Republican state.
Appearing at a get-out-the-vote rally in Rogers Monday morning, Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said she wants to continue serving Arkansans, and touted her success reforming the state’s education system and cutting taxes. 
“We’re not just winning races, we’re investing in the next generation,” Sanders said. “This isn’t just about the next election, it’s about the future of our state and the future of our country.”



Democratic state Sen. Fred Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby are challenging Sanders, who urged attendees to support other Republican candidates. 
Sanders planned to end her election campaigning with a Little Rock rally alongside Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who is being challenged by Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin.
Shoffner and Chris Jones, the Democrat hoping to unseat Republican Rep. French Hill in central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, planned to hold a separate rally Monday night in Little Rock. 
Greeting voters and waving a sign near a polling site in downtown Little Rock Monday morning, Jones said his focus between now and the end of voting Tuesday is to encourage people to go out and vote. After 12 years of being represented by Hill, voters in the district want change, Jones said.
“We are seeing more young people go vote, we’re seeing the … infrequent voters showing up,” Jones said. “People are struggling. They’re hurting. They’re in pain because the gas prices are too high. They’re in pain because groceries are too high.”
A poll worker directs a voter to a voting machine inside the Benton County Election Commission office in Rogers on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Heavy turnout with Election Day storms looming
Turnout was heavy at the Pulaski County Regional Building’s early voting site, with a line stretched down the block. 
Several people turned around in the face of the long line instead of joining it. Others stepped out halfway through, needing to return to work.
Arkansas faces the possibility of a soggy Election Day, with much of the state at risk of severe weather, according to the National Weather Service. 
Wendell Griffen, Democratic nominee for Pulaski County judge, arrived around lunchtime and called the long line at the Little Rock site “extraordinary.” He suspected people voted early to avoid bad weather forecast for Tuesday.
Sharrolean Cobbs of Little Rock declined to say who she voted for when departing the downtown Little Rock polling place, but expressed hope that Democrats and Republicans could work together again.
“I hope we can start working toward the same thing, and not have any divisions like we have,” Cobbs said. “Because I believe people are people, and we just need to start working together.”
But in Benton County, Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack warned voters that Democrats are going “to pull out all stops” to halt what the president and Republican-led Congress are doing “to right the ship in America.”
“And it’s up to us to make sure that we get our voters to the polls to ensure that this American Dream continues, that’s our job,” he said at the GOP rally with Sanders.
Womack is running for reelection in northwest Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District against Democrat Robb Ryerse and Libertarian Bobby Wilson.
Jill Griess, a Bella Vista resident and rally attendee, said she supports Sanders and values “the beauty of Arkansas.” Outdoor recreation has been a focus for Sanders, as well as legislation prohibiting China from owning agricultural farm land in Arkansas, the latter of which Griess said she supports. 
Republican U.S. Rep. Steve Womack speaks at a rally in Rogers on Nov. 2, 2026 as (from left) First Gentleman Bryan Sanders, U.S. Sen. John Boozman, state Sen. Bart Hester and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders listen. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Busy scene at northwest Arkansas polling site
About four miles from the rally, the Benton County Election Commission office was buzzing midmorning as voters cast ballots in the front of the building, officials processed absentee ballots in the back and election equipment was loaded onto trucks outside and delivered to the county’s 34 Election Day voting centers. 
Benton County Election Coordinator Kim Dennison said, “the morning was really crazy,” but overall, early voting has gone smoothly with nearly 70,000 residents casting ballots by Saturday. 
The county has just over 204,000 registered voters, including Maribel Hurtado, a Rogers mother of four who said she was concerned about the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. 
Prior to voting, Hurtado said she attended a nearby church service where a man said his wife —  who was seeking permanent residency — was deported this year during an immigration appointment. 
“We pray that everyone opens their hearts and thinks about families staying together,” Hurtado said.
Rogers City Council candidate Mallory Sanders was one of two people holding signs across from the polling center. Northwest Arkansas’ rapid population growth has been a concern for voters, said Sanders, who’s running for the first time to ensure officials are “making positive decisions for the future as our city’s growing.”
“The city has served my family well and I want to make sure it does the same for our kids and then our kids’ kids in the future,” she said. 
Sanders, an attorney, faces Chris Collins and Robert Gaffigan in the race for the Ward 1 Position 1 seat. 
Christian Orton of Conway voted on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026 at the Faulkner County Library’s main branch. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)
Contrasting views of Senate race in Faulkner County
Dozens of voters lined up outside the Faulkner County Library in Conway during Monday afternoon’s drizzly weather.
In her six decades voting, Mary Kay Sullivan said she’s rarely seen political ads as “vicious” as the ones against Shoffner.
In September, Cotton’s team began running TV ads quoting Shoffner saying in a podcast interview that Arkansas farmers would “trade five Americans for just one” undocumented immigrant worker. Shoffner said she was relaying another farmer’s words rather than speaking for herself.
Sullivan said she was impressed by Shoffner’s composure and preferred her over Cotton, whom she called “a puppet for Trump.”
Christian Orton said he was most excited to vote for Jones and Shoffner. He said Hill and Cotton have “spent their entire careers doing little for everyday Arkansans.”
“They could be replaced with someone who’s a scientist and another person who’s a farmer,” Orton said. “I can’t think of better representatives of this state.”
Jones and Shoffner have pitched themselves as agents of change Arkansas needs, but Dustin Tinkler said he doesn’t believe the state needs a change in representation and he would be fine with reelecting Hill and Cotton.
Tinkler said he is not registered with a political party but typically votes conservative. He also said the issue of lower taxes was more important to him than any candidate in any race.
“I generally vote against all new taxes or raising taxes, regardless of what they would be for,” Tinkler said.
Sullivan and Tinkler both said they didn’t believe Issue 1, also known as “The Citizens Only Voting Amendment,” was necessary. The measure, proposed by the state Legislature in 2025, proposes amending the state’s constitution to prohibit noncitizens from voting in state or local elections held in Arkansas. Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.
Sullivan said all four ballot measures frustrated her because none of them were straightforward.
“If you voted for them, there were still bad contradictions in it,” she said.

text:

The 2026 DIAA Field Hockey Tournament brackets for both division one and division two were released on November 2. Tournament games will begin on November 4. 
 
The 2026 high school field hockey regular season is in the rearview mirror and thus begins the 2026 postseason for both division one and division two schools.
The Cape Henlopen Vikings claimed the top spot in the division one bracket with an undefeated regular season and a 10-0 win over Lake Forest in the Henlopen Conference Championship game. The top-seed in division two belongs to the Tower Hill Hillers who finished the regular season, 14-1. The Hillers’ only loss of the year came against the Vikings.
The division two field includes 12 teams with the top four seeds receiving a bye in the first round. The other teams receiving a first round bye include Newark Charter, Caravel and Archmere. The division one field includes only eight teams so there is no first round. The division one tournament begins with the quarterfinal round.
Here’s a look at the matchups for division two’s round one and both quarterfinal rounds for the 2026 DIAA Field Hockey Tournaments:
Division 2
Round One: 
No. 5 Indian River vs No. 12 Mount Pleasant: These two teams will meet for the first time this season on Wednesday, November 4, at 2:30 p.m. Indian River will host the matchup.
No. 6 Wilmington Friends vs No. 11 Delaware Military Academy: Friends and DMA will play each other for the first time this season on Wednesday, November 4, at 2:30 p.m., at Wilmington Friends. The Quakers won the division two championship last season.
No. 7 Concord vs No. 10 Sussex Academy: The Raiders and Seahawks will match up for the first time this season on Wednesday, November 4, at 5:00 p.m. This game will be played at Odyssey Charter. 
No. 8 Lake Forest vs No. 9 Ursuline: This is the first meeting between the two teams this season. The game will be played at Lake Forest on Wednesday, November 4, at 4:00 p.m.
Quarterfinals: (All games will be played on Saturday, November 7, at 11:30 a.m.)
No. 1 Tower Hill vs Winner of No. 8 Lake Forest/No. 9 Ursuline: The game will be played at Tower Hill
No. 2 Newark Charter vs Winner of No. 7 Concord/No. 10 Sussex Academy: The game will be played at Newark Charter.
No. 3 Caravel vs Winner of No. 6 Wilmington Friends/No. 11 Delaware Military Academy: The game will be played at Caravel.
No. 4 Archmere vs Winner of No. 5 Indian River/No. 12 Mount Pleasant: The game will be played at Archmere.
Division 1
Quarterfinals:
No. 1 Cape Henlopen vs No. 8 Appoquinimink: This will be the first meeting between the Vikings and Jaguars this season. The game will be played at Cape Henlopen on Friday, November 6, at 2:30 p.m.
No. 2 Caesar Rodney vs No. 7 Charter School of Wilmington: The two teams will match up for the first time this season on Friday, November 6, at 3:00 p.m. The Riders will host the game.

No. 3 Padua vs No. 6 Milford: Padua and Milford will meet in the postseason for the second year in a row when they play on Friday, November 6, at 2:30 p.m. The game will take place at Tatnall. The Pandas defeated the Buccaneers, 2-1, in last year’s postseason.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Galvin uncertain about beating voter turnout in 2022, 2018
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: There's been "a dramatic increase" in early in-person voting, Galvin said at a State House press conference, while the mail-in voting rate is about the same as it was in 2022.
text:
MORE THAN 1.1 MILLION people have already voted in Massachusetts as of Monday morning, according to Secretary of State William Galvin, though he didn’t offer a figure for just how many Bay Staters he thinks will turn out in total. 
There’s been “a dramatic increase” in early in-person voting, Galvin said at a State House press conference, while the mail-in voting rate is about the same as it was in 2022.
Massachusetts voters this year face many uncontested races but also decisions on nine potential ballot laws and a race for governor between Republican Mike Minogue and Gov. Maura Healey.
“The significance of the in-person, I think, is it speaks to the desire of voters to have the opportunity to vote on the questions slowly, at least take as much time as they need, and it also probably is eating in to some extent to the people who are going to show up tomorrow – would have shown up tomorrow,” Galvin said. 
“A lot of people have to show up to vote in person” Tuesday to hit 2022’s turnout of 2.5 million or 2018’s turnout of 2.7 million, Galvin said. The number of people visiting his website to see the location of their polling place, which he uses as an indicator, is down compared to past years, though he thinks “there’s a momentum that is hard to project, especially given the circumstances that we have that there aren’t intense races here.” 
Voter turnout in the 2018 State Election was just over 60 percent, and voter turnout in 2022 was about 51.4 percent, according to data from Galvin’s website. 
Galvin said there haven’t been many elections where he has felt this kind of uncertainty about turnout, but that indicators are often wrong. He pointed to the state primary in September, during which Democrats turned out higher than he anticipated and Republican turnout underperformed his estimates. 
While the election in Massachusetts hasn’t been as intense as others, he said, “Then again, I look back to ’18, and Governor [Charlie] Baker was running for election. There wasn’t much intensity in that either, but we had a great turnout.”
“There, I think the national atmosphere was such. Now the national atmosphere is intensified, but are voters thinking in other directions?” Galvin continued. “Are they frustrated? I don’t know. I wish I could say, ‘This is the number and that’s what’s going to be.’ I can’t be that confident.”
Ahead of midterm elections where control of Congress is up for grabs, Galvin told reporters he thinks the election has become “a referendum on the economy, the direction of our nation and in fact the direction of the world.” 
“It’s a measured study of where the country is and what it’s thinking, what it’s expecting,” Galvin said. “It’s not simply about the policies of this administration, it’s about where are we going? And what are we going to do? And that’s certainly the questions we have to confront here in Massachusetts. And so, for all those reasons, I think would have increased turnout. I think it’s an important thing to have certainty in place for the 2028 presidential cycle.”
Healey and Minogue have raised and spent millions of dollars during their contentious gubernatorial race. Though Galvin didn’t mention that contest specifically, national politics have seeped into it from both sides of the aisle. 
“The question is, will we come up with another 1.5 million people tomorrow? It’s a hard question for me to answer. Usually, I’m offering a number. I’m simply not going to do that today because I think there are cross indicators,” he continued. He said he doesn’t think turnout will reach much higher than 2.5 million. 
“As I often say, I hope I’m wrong,” Galvin said. “I want a big, big turnout, but on the other hand, I’m really not sure what it’s going to bring this year.”
There were concerns that the volume of ballot measures would slow or complicate the process or spur confusion. Galvin told reporters that he doesn’t think the amount of ballot cards will delay the election process or keep people in line, and that it appears most voters who voted in-person prepared for the polls. 
Galvin said that he’s concerned “but not terribly worried” about federal interference or law enforcement presence at polling locations in Massachusetts, and that he’s “had communication” with the federal authorities.  
“Observers are, of course, a part of the process and are welcome,” he said. “Federal observers are something that we’ve always had here, so that’s fine. I don’t think it’ll be interference. I’m almost as concerned, to be honest, about some of the observers who are supposedly protecting people from them interfering or creating issues.”
There are 57 contested legislative races among the 200 seats on the ballot Tuesday, and 18 seats are open, eight of them contested. Even if Republicans won every race in which they’re challenging a Democrat, Democrats would retain their supermajorities in both chambers for the 2027-2028 session.
Two incumbents, both Democrats, lost their seats in the primary: Sen. Michael Rush, who lost to challenger Persis Yu, and Rep. Francisco Paulino, who was ousted by Celina Reyes. There are 49 incumbents facing a challenge Tuesday, 10 senators and 39 representatives, or about a quarter of the Legislature.
According to the numbers as of Friday, more than 733,000 early votes were by mail and more than 336,000 were cast in-person. The figures combined to represent about 20.5 percent total voter turnout in a state with 5,230,765 registered voters.
Galvin also noted that he thinks the measure he’s backing to legalize Election Day registration, Question 4, is going to do well based on polling and comments from voters. A Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll of 500 registered voters in mid-October found more than 59 percent of respondents’ supported Question 4. A UMass/WCVB poll conducted October 5 through October 12  found that 67 percent of 800 registered voters supported the measure. 
Commenting on the diversity of ballot measures, Galvin said, “It’s been a phenomenal experience in democracy.” 
“We feel that, you know, the voters are prepared. The book has been widely read. It’s a bestseller this year for some reason,” Galvin said of his office’s red voter information pamphlet. “The bottom line is, people have looked into what the impact of the questions are. There remain close races in the questions.”

title: Tennessee Supreme Court paves way to cut Metro Council, give state control of airport authority
description: The Tennessee Supreme Court denied a constitutional challenge to a new state law cutting the Metro Nashville Council in half and, separately, dismissed a case challenging a state takeover of Nashville’s airport authority. The court issued the opinions Monday, giving approval of the legislature’s move to cap Metro Nashville’s legislative body at 20 and permit[...]
text:
The Tennessee Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a state law that will allow Metro Nashville Council to be cut from 40 members to 20. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Tennessee Supreme Court denied a constitutional challenge to a new state law cutting the Metro Nashville Council in half and, separately, dismissed a case challenging a state takeover of Nashville’s airport authority.
The court issued the opinions Monday, giving approval of the legislature’s move to cap Metro Nashville’s legislative body at 20 and permitting the law that gives state officials a majority of appointments on the Metro Nashville Airport Authority.
In the Metro Council case, the court dismissed a claim by the plaintiffs who sued the state that the law violated Tennessee’s home rule provision prohibiting the legislature from targeting governments without local approval. The legislature amended the law so it would apply to all metropolitan governments in the state after the Supreme Court granted a review of the measure.
With that part of the argument removed, the court decided the 20-member cap doesn’t violate a clause exempting metropolitan councils from constitutional requirements, nor does it prevent the legislature from imposing restrictions.
Previously, a three-judge panel overruled a Davidson County Chancery Court’s decision that the move violated two sections of the state Constitution, including the home rule amendment and a clause exempting metro governments from a 25-member cap.
“I am deeply troubled that Nashville’s voters can repeatedly choose the government they want and still have that choice taken from them,” said Metro Councilmember Brenda Gadd, who represents a portion of West Nashville, in a statement. 
Tennessee has only two other local governments with metropolitan forms of government, Moore County and Trousdale County.
The Republican-controlled legislature started targeting Metro Nashville in 2021 with a spate of bills designed to give the state greater control of the local government, including reducing the size of the council, in part because of conflict over the council’s refusal to try to bring the Republican presidential convention to Nashville.
In the airport authority case, the Supreme Court dismissed Metro’s constitutional challenge as moot after lawmakers passed a bill this year making it applicable to all airport authorities in Nashville, Chattanooga, Memphis, Knoxville and the Tri-Cities.
Metro argued that under federal law the Federal Aviation Administration had to approve a change in operation at the airport if the current board didn’t agree to the move.
A three-judge panel previously blocked the legislature’s first effort to take control of the Nashville airport, saying it violated the home rule amendment.
The decision is likely to affect a similar lawsuit over operation of the Chattanooga airport.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ‘This is our year’: Will a blue wave swing Pueblo back to Colorado Democrats?
description: The last time Pueblo, Colorado, was represented in Congress by a Democrat — Rep. John Salazar, who served three terms before losing reelection in 2010 — Aaron Gutierrez was a young staffer in Salazar’s Washington, D.C., office. Now an attorney, father and cancer survivor, Gutierrez is his party’s nominee for a crucial state Senate district […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Jason Crow, a Democrat from Aurora, speaks at a canvass launch event at the Pueblo County Democratic Party's headquarters on Sunday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)The last time Pueblo, Colorado, was represented in Congress by a Democrat — Rep. John Salazar, who served three terms before losing reelection in 2010 — Aaron Gutierrez was a young staffer in Salazar’s Washington, D.C., office.
Now an attorney, father and cancer survivor, Gutierrez is his party’s nominee for a crucial state Senate district centered on Pueblo, and his hometown could be a linchpin in Democrats’ efforts to set a new high-water mark for their recent electoral dominance in the Centennial State.
“This is our year. I think we can do it,” Gutierrez, who faces Republican Dana Charles in the Senate District 3 race, told a small crowd of volunteers inside the Pueblo County Democratic Party’s headquarters on Sunday. “A lot of people have counted out Pueblo because Trump has won here twice … But we know if people actually turn up and vote, we’re going to win.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Even as Democrats have succeeded over the last decade in painting the former swing state of Colorado a solid shade of blue, Pueblo County has moved in the opposite direction: Once a Democratic stronghold, it’s become one of the state’s top battlegrounds and a national bellwether. In 2016, Donald Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry the county since Richard Nixon in 1972. Joe Biden narrowly swung it back to Democrats four years later, only for Trump to win it again in 2024, by a wider margin than before.
Without Trump’s name on the ballot, the marquee race in Pueblo in the 2026 midterms is the 3rd Congressional District contest between incumbent U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, a first-term Republican from Grand Junction, and Democratic challenger Dwayne Romero, an Army veteran and business owner from Aspen.
As polls show voters turning against Republicans over the cost of living, the war in Iran and other issues, Hurd has billed himself as a “voice of independence,” highlighting disagreements with Trump over his denial of disaster aid and a February vote against some of the president’s tariffs. That vote led Trump to briefly pull his endorsement from Hurd and back a primary challenger, before he reversed himself a month later and endorsed Hurd again.
“Doing the right thing in Washington isn’t easy,” Hurd tells voters in an ad airing in the final days of the campaign. “But that’s the job.”
U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, a Republican from Grand Junction, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 18. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
To Democrats, Hurd’s occasional breaks with Trump mean little compared to his votes in favor of Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending law, which included steep cuts to Medicaid, food assistance and other social programs, along with the Iran war and most of the rest of Trump’s domestic and foreign policy agenda.
“Jeff Hurd ran on a campaign of expanding rural access to healthcare, and all of his votes in Congress have done the exact opposite,” Nick Voss, chair of the Pueblo County Democrats, said in an interview. “People aren’t dumb.”
3rd District showdown
“It’s important that we get out there and talk to people, because every vote’s going to count, especially for Dwayne’s race,” Gutierrez told the small crowd of canvassers at party headquarters.
Any Democratic candidate’s hopes of winning the 3rd District hinge on Pueblo, where its largest concentration of Democratic voters is found. Even when he was soundly defeated in the midst of a Republican wave in the 2010 midterms, Salazar carried Pueblo County by more than 14 percentage points. No Democrat has come close to that margin in the last decade.
Pueblo County Republican Chair Michelle Gray said she was busy training volunteers of her own at the party’s headquarters on Monday.
“We’re feeling pretty good as the Republican Party. People want change,” Gray said, but declined an interview until after the election. “We’re in the thick of it.”
Until recently, Hurd and his supporters, including several deep-pocketed Republican super PACs, had massively outspent Romero and Democratic campaign groups in the 3rd District race. Romero — a late recruit for Democrats who only launched his campaign in March — raised and spent $1.1 million and had languished without support from Democratic super PACs.
The lack of investment in the 3rd District race has surprised some Colorado political observers — especially when contrasted with the resources and attention Democratic groups have lavished since last year on the 5th District, where Democratic challenger Jessica Killin, a well-connected D.C. insider, is challenging Rep. Jeff Crank.
In that race, in a district centered on Colorado Springs, Democrats are hoping El Paso County’s palpable leftward shift in recent elections has primed Killin for an upset victory in a district that has never before elected a Democrat to Congress.
Dwayne Romero, center, a Democratic candidate for Congress in Colorado’s 3rd District, knocked doors with U.S. Rep. Jason Crow in Pueblo on Sunday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Pueblo and Colorado Springs have been on opposite political trajectories — at least in part because of the migration, Voss said, of older and more conservative voters from El Paso County to exurban communities in Pueblo County, like the sprawling Pueblo West development near Lake Pueblo north of town.
While Hurd and Republicans still enjoy a nearly 2-to-1 financial advantage in the race, Romero has benefited from a late infusion of $2.5 million in outside spending on his behalf by the House Majority Project, the main Democratic House super PAC, beginning in the final week of October.
The sprawling 3rd District, which extends from Pueblo across the San Luis Valley and much of Colorado’s Western Slope, can be a difficult place for campaigns to spend money efficiently. It’s split between three different Colorado media markets, complicating TV ad-buying efforts, and field organizing is even more of a challenge.
“As an organizer, you go where population density is,” Voss said. “CD5 is a population-dense area. CD3 is one of if not the largest geographical congressional district in the United States, which makes it very, very hard to put in the miles, to go out there and have the conversations that need to be had.”
A ‘level playing field’
More than any other place in Colorado, Pueblo — a steel town once dubbed “the Pittsburgh of the West,” which has struggled economically since a major contraction in the industry in the 1980s — resembles the Rust Belt communities where Democrats’ electoral fortunes have collapsed in the Trump era.
With a population that’s over 40% Latino, it’s also the kind of community where Trump and Republicans made substantial gains in the 2024 election, raising GOP hopes of a durable new coalition of younger, more diverse and more working-class voters. With polls showing many of those voters having turned sharply against Trump, Democrats are confident they’ll win many of them back on Tuesday.
The Pueblo County Democratic Party’s headquarters is pictured on Sunday. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
As they prepared to fan out into Pueblo neighborhoods to canvass voters, Democrats joked about the chilly reception they might receive at some doors. One speaker advised volunteers that if they hurried, they could finish before the Broncos game started. As motivation, a field organizer alluded to a statistical model, based on early ballot return data, that showed Romero could be on track to lose the race by as few as 68 votes.
“We are gaining back ground,” said state Rep. Tisha Mauro, who is running for a third term in Pueblo’s House District 46. “We had a couple slips during those Trump years, but we’re bringing it back where it needs to be, as a team.”
U.S. Rep. Jason Crow addressed the group and likened Pueblo to the working-class part of rural Wisconsin where he grew up. An Army veteran like Romero, he said Democrats should appeal to voters who want a “level playing field,” rather than “a handout” or for “anyone to solve our problems for us.”
“That’s why I’m supporting Dwayne Romero, and (county commissioner candidate) Angela (Giron), and Aaron, and Tisha, and the whole group,” Crow said. “Those are the types of Democrats we are. We’re the level-playing-field folks. We want to unrig the system.”
Romero said in an interview that he hopes the 2026 election can “galvanize” the work that Democrats have done to reassert themselves in Pueblo, and “tap into the potential that has always been here.”
“Pueblo has such a great, diverse set of economies and cultures,” Romero said. “It makes a great community, but it’s also a community that needs to tend to staying together. And I believe that’s what I’m seeing.”

title: Wyoming Highway Patrol limited mileage and overtime to offset budget overrun, transportation department says
description:
The overtime budget overrun was “caught early enough” and didn’t “reach an unmanageable level,” department spokesperson says. 
The post Wyoming Highway Patrol limited mileage and overtime to offset budget overrun, transportation department says appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Highway Patrol offset a 2026 budget overrun by limiting mileage and overtime, according to the Wyoming Department of Transportation. 
The department’s spokesperson, Doug McGee, noted that the agency “operates on a balanced budget and would not carry over a negative balance.” The highway patrol’s 2025-2026 budget biennium ended in September. 
“It’s worth noting that the anticipated overrun was caught early enough that the actual shortfall did not reach an unmanageable level,” McGee said via email. 
In 2025, the Wyoming Department of Transportation restricted the highway patrol’s overtime hours after staff found that the agency had overspent its funds, the Wyoming Tribune Eagle reported. The agency had roughly $3.2 million budgeted for overtime in 2025 and 2026. But by December 2025, it had spent nearly $4.9 million, though the biennium continued through September 2026. 
Former Wyoming Highway Patrol Col. Tim Cameron, who retired in March and was replaced last month by Col. KC Ramsey, attributed the overspending to fewer vacancies and increased wages, the Wyoming Tribune Eagle reported. 
The transportation department imposed mileage and overtime limits on the Wyoming Highway Patrol as well as the Ports of Entry program to offset the overrun, according to McGee. 
As of Oct. 1, the highway patrol is on a new budget for fiscal year 2027. The patrol’s new biennium budget is $93 million, a $13.6 million increase from the last biennium budget, according to McGee. That increase is meant to cover Legislature-approved salary boosts and internal reorganization — changes in staffing structure to facilitate “more boots-on-the-ground supervisor availability” and tweaks to district boundaries aimed at improving response times, McGee said. 
The transportation department also increased the highway patrol’s budget by roughly $4 million to cover operational budget increases like training costs and vehicle use, as well as one-time purchases of equipment like car and body cameras and vehicle radars.  
“We are forcing them to ensure that they can stay within their budget,” Wyoming Department of Transportation Director Darin Westby told lawmakers at a meeting last week. That includes continuing to cap the number of miles troopers drive. 
“At the end of the day, we have a budget. We got to stick with it. And if we have to stay within x number of miles, we have to stay within x number of miles.” 
The mileage limits have sometimes forced troopers to be stationary in medians. Staffing shortages and budget constraints have also contributed to gaps in Wyoming Highway Patrol coverage, according to local law enforcement. But when it comes to major incidents, like the June shooting in Baggs, Westby said troopers will respond regardless of resource constraints. 
“Overtime be darned,” he said. “We have a mission to uphold and we’re going to do that. We’ll take care of it on the back end.”
