name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakotans set to decide races for governor, Congress, Legislature and 4 ballot questions
description: Tuesday is Election Day in South Dakota, with races for state and legislative offices, four statewide ballot questions, and a variety of local races and questions. Nationally, control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs, with implications for South Dakota Republican John Thune’s status as U.S. Senate majority leader. Polls are open from […]
text:
Signs identify a polling place in Wanblee, part of Jackson County, ahead of South Dakota's 2026 general election. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Tuesday is Election Day in South Dakota, with races for state and legislative offices, four statewide ballot questions, and a variety of local races and questions.
Nationally, control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs, with implications for South Dakota Republican John Thune’s status as U.S. Senate majority leader.
 Voting and results info

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. Voters can check their registration, locate their polling place and view a sample ballot in the state’s online Voter Information Portal at vip.sdsos.gov. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Identification is required to vote. Acceptable forms include a South Dakota driver’s license or non-driver ID card, a passport or other picture ID issued by the U.S. government, a tribal photo ID, or a current student photo ID issued by a South Dakota high school, college or university.
The South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office will begin reporting results online at electionresults.sd.gov after 8 p.m. Central, 7 p.m. Mountain, when the final polls close in the Mountain time zone on the western side of the state. South Dakota Searchlight’s journalists will report on election returns as they come in throughout the evening.
 Statewide races

Democrats, plus an independent and a Libertarian, are trying to break an 18-year streak of Republicans winning every statewide elected office in South Dakota.
The last Democrats to win statewide elections in South Dakota were U.S. Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin and U.S. Sen. Tim Johnson, who each won reelection in 2008. Herseth Sandlin lost her next reelection campaign to Republican Kristi Noem in 2010, and Johnson’s seat was won by Republican Mike Rounds when Johnson chose not to seek reelection in 2014.


This year’s statewide candidates are:

Governor: Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers
U.S. Senate: Republican incumbent Mike Rounds and independent candidate Brian Bengs
U.S. House: Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley and Democratic nominee Nikki Gronli
Attorney general: Republican Lance Russell, unopposed
Secretary of state: Republican Heather Baxter, Democrat Terrence Davis and Libertarian Tamara Lesnar
Public utilities commissioner: Republican Don Haggar and Democrat Frank Kloucek
State treasurer: Republican Melissa Hull and Democrat Margaret Kuipers
State auditor: Republican Catherine Barranco and Democrat Tom Cool
Commissioner of school and public lands: Republican incumbent Brock Greenfield and Democrat Raeann Mettler

 Legislature

All 105 seats in the South Dakota Legislature are up for election — 35 in the state Senate and 70 in the state House. Voters choose one senator in each district, two representatives in each regular district, and one representative in each of four split House districts. State lawmakers serve two-year terms.
Listen again: All of Searchlight Report’s candidate and ballot-question interviews

This year’s partisan split in the Legislature is 97 Republicans and eight Democrats. That’s the lowest number of Democrats since 1953, when there were two. At least 52 seats are already guaranteed to be held by Republicans in 2027 due to a lack of opposition: 21 seats in the Senate and 31 in the House. 
There are 11 independents running for Legislature this year, which is an unusually high number. At least one is guaranteed a state House seat in District 27, a vast area including the Pine Ridge Reservation, where the ballot has four independents and one Republican vying for two seats.
That will be the first independent elected to the South Dakota Legislature since 2010. If multiple independents serve in next year’s Legislature, it’ll be the first time that’s happened since the 1920s.
 Statewide ballot questions

The four statewide ballot questions are all proposed state constitutional amendments that lawmakers placed on the ballot. Voter approval is required to amend the constitution.
Amendment I would repeal the expanded Medicaid eligibility requirement in the state constitution if the federal government’s share of funding for the expansion drops below 90%. There’s a dispute about whether the amendment would trigger an immediate termination of expanded Medicaid under that scenario, or whether the amendment would merely give lawmakers the opportunity to consider eliminating the expansion in the event of reduced federal funding.
Amendment J would add language to the state constitution specifying that people who are not U.S. citizens are disqualified from voting. The state constitution already includes citizenship as a voting eligibility requirement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amendment K would allow a trust fund containing proceeds from unclaimed property — including abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and more — to be managed by the state Investment Council, like other funds such as the retirement pool for public employees. People could still claim their unclaimed property at any time, but the Investment Council would manage the fund for higher returns, generating more interest to be used in the state budget.
Amendment L would raise the bar for passing state constitutional amendments. If it passes, future amendments would need 60% support from voters, rather than a simple majority.
 Thune’s position, control of Congress

Thune — who is not up for reelection until 2028 — has been traveling the country this fall campaigning for Republican U.S. Senate candidates in an effort to protect the body’s Republican majority. Senate Republicans elected Thune as majority leader two years ago.
Inside Elections, a nonpartisan forecaster, projected Thursday that Democrats would gain enough seats to reach at least a 50-50 split Senate, ranking Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas as tilting Democratic. In a 50-50 Senate, Republican Vice President J.D. Vance would be the tiebreaker in his role as president of the Senate. 
Major forecasts and pollsters more strongly favor Democrats to take the U.S. House, though some experts observe that years of gerrymandering, including Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting, combined with entrenched polarization could stunt the crest of a so-called blue wave. 
 High turnout expectations

Turnout — the percentage of registered voters who cast a ballot — is typically higher in South Dakota than the national average. This is a “midterm” election, because it falls in the middle of President Donald Trump’s four-year term. National turnout for the last midterm election in 2022 was 69.9% in South Dakota and 46.2% nationally.
Statistics are indicating a high turnout for this election. Nationally, voters crossed the high-water mark of 52.7 million early votes cast on Saturday, surpassing the midterm record set in 2022.
South Dakota is also ahead of its advance voting pace from 2022. There were 78,778 ballots cast in the state by Friday, which was more than the 55,377 ballots received through the same period in 2022.


States Newsroom’s D.C. Bureau contributed to this report.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 30 federal observers expected in Pawtucket for Election Day
description: Thirty federal observers are expected to be in Pawtucket Tuesday to ensure each of its polling precincts comply with a Biden-era consent order to assist Spanish-speaking voters, according to the city’s top election official. “They’re arriving here today and tomorrow, that’s all we know,” Pawtucket city registrar Ken McGill said in an interview Monday. A […]
text:
Signs in English and Spanish alert voters how to cast their ballots at St. Theresa's Church in Pawtucket during the 2024 general election. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Thirty federal observers are expected to be in Pawtucket Tuesday to ensure each of its polling precincts comply with a Biden-era consent order to assist Spanish-speaking voters, according to the city’s top election official.
“They’re arriving here today and tomorrow, that’s all we know,” Pawtucket city registrar Ken McGill said in an interview Monday.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately confirm the deployment Monday. The DOJ previously told States Newsroom it would not disclose the full list of monitored locations until Election Day, Nov. 3.
Trump’s DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to 50 states; locations not yet disclosed

The May 2024 consent agreement between the city of Pawtucket and the federal government required local election officials to provide Spanish-speaking voters with election assistance and materials in Spanish. The agreement resolved a voting rights lawsuit brought by the Biden administration.
McGill said the city learned during a call with federal officials ahead of the Sept. 9 primary that the nearly three dozen observers would be coming to Pawtucket. The city has about 300 poll workers spread across its 28 precincts to ensure voters have access to Spanish-language material, he added.
“We’re ready to go,” McGill said.
Pawtucket is one of three jurisdictions where federal observers remain authorized under court orders stemming from voting rights cases. The others are Union County, New Jersey, where a 2023 consent decree addressed Spanish-language election assistance and voters’ right to assistance, and St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, which has been under a federal court order since 1979.
The incoming deployment to Pawtucket comes as the Trump administration prepares to send roughly 1,000 federal election monitors to polling places in all 50 states — the largest such effort in the DOJ’s history. Department officials said the monitors will observe voting and report potential violations of federal law.
But the expanded effort has drawn concern from voting rights advocates who have questioned the department’s role in local elections under the Trump administration.
“This is something we normally don’t worry about,” John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, said. “But given this administration, they don’t get the benefit of the doubt.”
Which is why Marion said Common Cause plans to have about 80 volunteers monitoring polling places around the state and will mark any known issues. That includes Pawtucket where he said the volunteers will keep tabs on the federal observers to make sure they do not overstep their authority.
The DOJ has sent personnel to monitor elections around the country for decades, including in communities not covered by a consent decree. For the Sept. 5, 2023, special congressional primary, the department sent observers to polling places in Central Falls, Pawtucket, Providence and Woonsocket. 
DOJ staff monitors are generally limited to observing polling places from outside unless state or local officials give them permission to enter, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. They document what they see and report potential violations of federal voting rights laws, but cannot interfere with voting or direct election officials. 
Under a court order, federal observers are authorized under the Voting Rights Act to enter polling places and observe election procedures, including how voters are assisted.
Pawtucket will be the only municipality to be under federal observation or monitoring in 2026, Rhode Island Board of Elections spokesperson Chris Hunter confirmed in a text message.
Election observers were also present in the city during the Sept. 9 primary, where  McGill said federal officials found no problems with the city’s compliance with the consent order — a conclusion echoed by Marion after the primary.
Marion said he expects the city’s compliance to remain the same for Tuesday’s general election. 
“Generally speaking, the problems in Rhode Island are hard to predict,” he said. “Problems seem to kind of be distributed randomly.”
For instance, staffing shortages contributed to delayed openings at several Providence polling places during the Sept. 9 primary. The capital city saw an unusually high rate of poll worker no-shows, with some polling places opening more than an hour late.
State election officials told reporters before early voting began in October that they have since worked with universities, state agencies and local election officials to recruit additional poll workers to cover any last minute absences should they happen Tuesday.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: As candidates call to fund IWiLL, some counties ask for local conservation bonds
description: Funding a trust to support Iowa’s natural resources and water has come up repeatedly on the campaign trail ahead of Tuesday’s elections, but some counties have successfully initiated bond referendums to support projects locally.  On Tuesday, Dubuque County voters will be asked to approve an $18 million dollar bond to invest in the county’s natural […]
text:
A family swims in the Raccoon River where it flows through Walnut Woods State Park in West Des Moines in October 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Funding a trust to support Iowa’s natural resources and water has come up repeatedly on the campaign trail ahead of Tuesday’s elections, but some counties have successfully initiated bond referendums to support projects locally. 
On Tuesday, Dubuque County voters will be asked to approve an $18 million dollar bond to invest in the county’s natural resources, parks, trails and water quality.
The county level bond is similar to the statewide Iowa Water and Land Legacy, or IWiLL, constitutional amendment that passed in 2010 to establish a statewide trust that has remained unfunded because lawmakers haven’t raised the sales tax that would fund the trust. 
Joe Jayjack, external affairs director of the Iowa Natural Heritage Foundation, said the county-level bonds, which have passed in a handful of counties, show that “when voters are given the chance, they do want to make these investments.” 
“Nobody likes to pay more taxes, but I think people do like to when they know what it’s going to,” Jayjack said. “I think that’s the really nice thing about these conservation bonds, because the plans are pretty detailed. People can see exactly what’s going to happen over the course of this bond, and it’s the same for the statewide trust fund.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Dubuque County, the $18 million bond, if passed, would support “major projects” managed by the county’s conservation department, which according to the county, has an approved capital expenditure budget that is about 20% of what it had four years ago. 
The county said the bond, with an annual cost to taxpayers of approximately $6.50 per $100,000 of assessed property value, would “provide a potential source of capital funding for major projects that cannot be addressed through routine annual operating funds alone.” 
Examples of projects in the county include shoreline restorations and improvements to parking lots, trails and boat ramps at area lakes and ponds. 
Michael Sertle, a senior advisor for American Rivers Action Fund which has been supportive of the bond in Dubuque County, said the conservation funding helps the community plan for good stormwater infrastructure, safe public access and increased tourism and recreation opportunities. 
“For us — American Rivers — that all really helps with river conservation,” Settle said. “Whether that’s improving water quality, helping address flooding issues, or just getting people out there and to enjoy nature.” 
Dubuque County would need approval from more than 60% of voters to put the 20-year bond in place. The county barely denied a similar effort in 2021 to initiate a $40 million water and land legacy bond, when 59.2% voted in favor of the bond. 
In 2024, Story County passed a similar $25 million bond referendum and Johnson County voters approved a $30 million bond which followed the county’s 2008 bond of $20 million. Polk County has also passed multiple water and land legacy bonds – a $50 million bond referendum in 2012 and a $65 million bond in 2021. Linn and Adams counties have also passed conservation bonds, according to an analysis of the bonds from Iowa Natural Heritage Foundation. 
Dubuque County’s proposal this year is a scaled-back version of its 2021 proposal, and it comes during an election cycle where water quality is a top issue for voters. 
Recent polling from Iowa’s Water and Land Legacy — a coalition pushing for lawmakers to fund the state Natural Resources and Outdoor Recreation Trust Fund — found that 69% of Iowa voters support raising the state sales tax to fund the trust. Iowa’s Natural Resources and Outdoor Recreation Trust Fund, which is broadly referred to as IWiLL, was passed in 2010 with 63% of the statewide vote. 
“It’s neat to see when voters are given the chance, they do want to make these investments, and I think that’s something that we’re optimistic we’ll see at the statewide level because there’s been so much talk about finally funding the Natural Resources and Outdoor Recreation Trust Fund,” Jayjack said. 
Gubernatorial candidates Rob Sand and Zach Lahn have both said they want to see funding in the IWiLL trust as part of their proposed solutions to cleaning up Iowa’s water. 
Jayjack said Iowans are “fed up” over water quality issues and the state’s high cancer rates, which many water quality activists and researchers link. This outlook, plus the conversations happening in the governor’s race, he said, are building a “grassroots movement to put pressure on the Legislature to raise a sales tax and finally fund the trust.” 
He said the county level efforts, like Dubuque’s potential bond, can “work in tandem” with the statewide funds to “amplify the amount of work that can get done and the speed that it can happen.” 
“People are asking for change not in 20 years to our water quality,” Jayjack said. “They want to see it happening now, and I think that having those things working together would really make that a possibility.”

title: Indiana governor denies death row inmate clemency ahead of Thursday execution
description: Gov. Mike Braun denied clemency Monday to death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit, rejecting his request for life without parole three days before his scheduled execution for murdering two children. “I am accepting the Parole Board’s unanimous recommendation to deny clemency for Jeffrey Weisheit,” Braun said in a statement. “The Indiana Department of Correction wi[...]
text:
Jeffrey Weisheit answers questions during his Oct. 16, 2026, clemency hearing at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. Board members questioned him about the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch and whether he could safely serve a life sentence. (Screenshot from livestream)Gov. Mike Braun denied clemency Monday to death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit, rejecting his request for life without parole three days before his scheduled execution for murdering two children.
“I am accepting the Parole Board’s unanimous recommendation to deny clemency for Jeffrey Weisheit,” Braun said in a statement. “The Indiana Department of Correction will continue preparations to carry out the court-ordered sentence of execution on November 5, 2026.”
His statement did not specifically address a separate request from Weisheit’s attorneys for a temporary reprieve to review Indiana’s execution drug purchases and lethal injection safeguards. A reprieve would postpone execution without commuting the sentence.
DOC confirmed Monday that it paid $275,000 for execution drugs and has them in its possession. Weisheit’s execution remains scheduled before sunrise Thursday at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
Weisheit, 50, was sentenced to death in 2013 for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a 2010 house fire near Evansville. Their mother, Lisa Lynch, was working an overnight shift and had left the children in his care.
Braun’s decision followed the Indiana Parole Board’s unanimous Oct. 28 recommendation against clemency. The five-member board heard competing appeals from the children’s parents and testimony about Weisheit’s mental health, remorse and ability to serve a life sentence.
Pharmacy linked to Indiana execution drug invoice faces possible suspension

His attorneys sought life without parole, arguing that evidence of mental illness and brain injuries was not adequately presented during his court proceedings. Prosecutors and investigators urged officials to uphold the sentence.
“The governor has yet to address the central questions emerging from the state’s records,” Weisheit’s defense team said in a statement Monday afternoon. “Why has the state chosen to pay staggering sums to a drugs supplier that the attorney general’s office is simultaneously seeking to shut down and sanction? Why should the public have any belief that the drugs are what they are said to be and not compromised, like the range of medicines the attorney general’s office has found to be in that condition in their efforts to shutdown this pharmacy?”
The children’s father, Steven Lynch, asked Braun to spare Weisheit, saying an execution would inflict another family’s loss without restoring his own.
“What good does it do the memory of my children to put this man to death?” he wrote in a sworn statement.
Lisa Lynch urged the parole board to uphold the death sentence, describing the futures her children lost and the lasting harm of their murders.
“Every single day without them is a struggle,” she told the parole board last month. “Every birthday, every holiday, every landmark moment is marked by their agonizing absence. Time passes, but the weight of losing them never fades.”
During his Oct. 16 clemency interview at the Indiana State Prison, Weisheit apologized but repeatedly struggled to explain why anger toward their mother led him to kill the children.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: On Election Day eve, RI surpasses 17% voter turnout, with record early voting numbers
description: A record-setting number of Rhode Island voters have cast ballots in-person during the 20-day early voting period that ended at 4 p.m. Monday, according to the Rhode Island Department of State’s live voter turnout tracker. The 111,901 people who voted at designated early voting polling places by the end of early voting Monday is more […]
text:
A voter waits to check in for early voting on the second floor of Newport City Hall on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. A total of 2,770 Newport voters had cast ballots in person by Monday, Nov. 2, at 4 p.m. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)A record-setting number of Rhode Island voters have cast ballots in-person during the 20-day early voting period that ended at 4 p.m. Monday, according to the Rhode Island Department of State’s live voter turnout tracker.
The 111,901 people who voted at designated early voting polling places by the end of early voting Monday is more than double the early voting turnout from two years ago. In 2024, 55,700 registered voters took advantage of early in-person voting, while 34,200 did so in the 2022 midterm elections.
Adding in the 25,237 mail ballots received by the Rhode Island Board of Elections as of Monday, total early voting turnout surpassed 137,000, equal to 17.2% of the state’s  registered voters. 
In 2024, more than 227,000 voters cast ballots ahead of Election Day, with mail ballots the dominant choice, used by nearly 172,000 voters. 
Over 17% of Rhode Island registered voters had cast ballots by mail or at early, in-person polling places as of 4 p.m. Monday, the final day before the general election. (Screenshot)
This year, far fewer voters — just over 33,000 — requested mail ballots from state officials, reflecting escalating attacks by the Trump administration. While the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to restrict mail ballots in the midterm elections, the federal administration continues to try to assert authority over the elections, including discounting voters, in a series of federal lawsuits nationwide.
Amid the legal war and public perception problems, Rhode Island election administrators have put special emphasis on the safety and security of the state voting process, including for mail ballots.
“As early voting becomes more well-known and more voters try it, many find it to be a fast, convenient way to cast their ballot,” Secretary of State Gregg Amore said in an Oct. 26 statement on early voting. “I hope to see these high participation levels continue, and encourage every eligible voter to make their voice heard, whether via mail ballot, early in-person, or on Election Day.” 
First offered during the 2020 election cycle due to the pandemic, early, in-person voting and mail ballots were enshrined in state law ahead of the 2022 election cycle. 
More than 71,000 voters cast ballots early in the 2022 midterms, rising to almost 172,000 in 2024.
Mail ballots also grew in popularity, from 34,000 in 2022 to nearly 56,000 in 2024. 
Warwick led the state in total early turnout with 10,616 voters casting ballots as of noon Monday, closely followed by 10,311 voters in Providence. The capital city had also received the most ballots by mail, with 4,277 received as of noon Monday. Warwick had the most people voting early and in-person, with more than 7,942 ballots cast at the city’s designated polling place, the Warwick police station, by midday.
The town of New Shoreham reported the fewest ballots cast early, though the 418 submitted by mail or at in-person early voting represented nearly 37% of the town’s registered voters.
Mail ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day — delivered either to a local board of canvassers, the Rhode Island Board of Elections or a designated drop box. 
Polls open at 7 a.m. on Election Day, with the exception of New Shoreham, which opens at 9 a.m. Polls close at 8 p.m. Information on polling locations and hours is available online.

text:
Des Moines University will set aside seats in its master's of anatomy program for qualifying Bryan College of Health Sciences students. (Photo courtesy of Des Moines University)Des Moines University is expanding its partnership with another health sciences institution to provide a path to further education to students pursuing a healthcare career.
The Des Moines private university announced in a news release it has opened its Master of Science in Anatomy degree to the partnership it holds with Bryan Colleges of Health Sciences, a private institution located in Lincoln, Neb.
“Students are looking for opportunities that allow them to build momentum toward their long-term goals,” said Molly Moeller, Des Moines University senior director of admissions and recruitment, in the release. “This partnership provides a unique pathway that connects undergraduate education, our Master of Science in Anatomy program and the opportunity to continue on to medical school. It’s an exciting way to support student success while preparing future physicians to serve their communities.”

Through the new agreement, qualifying Bryan College students can apply for reserved seats within Des Moines University’s anatomy master’s program once they’ve completed their sophomore year, and then can earn credits toward both their undergraduate and graduate degrees concurrently, the release stated.
The two institutions first established their partnership in January 2025, and since then have offered guaranteed interviews in six different programs, now seven with the master’s program addition. Opportunities for Bryan College students interested in Des Moines University’s doctor of osteopathic medicine program have also grown, with annual reserved seats now available.
Jason States, Bryan College of Health Sciences dean of healthcare studies, said in the release the college is “excited” about the expansion of its partnership with the Des Moines institution and for the new opportunities students will have.
“This pathway provides students with an exceptional opportunity to accelerate their journey to reaching their professional goals,” States said in the release. “By completing coursework that applies toward both their bachelor’s degree and Master of Science in Anatomy, students can save time, reduce costs and build a strong academic foundation for success in medical school.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: This year, everyone is going low: Political groups spend 3 times more on negative ads than positive
description: If you feel like you saw an inordinate amount of negative political ads on your phone or TV the past few weeks, you’re right: Of the $47 million that outside groups have spent on the general election as of Oct. 19, the vast majority has gone to ads attacking opposing candidates rather than touting preferred […]
text:
DFL-aligned Alliance for a Better Minnesota has published ads against Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth's campaign for governor. Restore Sanity, a PAC created for Demuth's campaign, has published ads against her opponent, Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar. (Illustrations from Alliance for a Better Minnesota and Restore Sanity Facebook pages.) If you feel like you saw an inordinate amount of negative political ads on your phone or TV the past few weeks, you’re right:
Of the $47 million that outside groups have spent on the general election as of Oct. 19, the vast majority has gone to ads attacking opposing candidates rather than touting preferred ones.
Outside groups are going negative more this year than ever, spending over $36 million in negative ads in statewide and legislative elections since Minnesota’s Aug. 11 primary election, compared to the $10 million they’ve spent on positive ads. Outside groups refer to political action committees as well as the campaign arms of party groups, such as the DFL Senate Caucus, which have far less restrictive rules for spending on political advertising compared to the candidates, largely thanks to the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United vs. FEC.


Republican-aligned groups have spent over $24 million on negative ads since the primaries, and around $5 million on positive ads, while Democratic-Farmer-Labor-aligned groups have spent over $12 million on negative ads and around $4 million on positive ads.
It’s not always been like this — as recently as the 2018 midterms, both parties spent similar amounts on negative and positive ads.
That dark turn is just one example of the vast changes in the state’s campaign finance landscape in recent years.
Here’s another: For the first time in over a decade, outside groups are spending more money to fuel Republicans in statewide and legislative races compared to Democratic-Farmer-Labor candidates.
That remarkable swap in the campaign spending race, first reported by the Star Tribune, is largely thanks to Restore Sanity, a new super PAC created to boost Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for governor.


Restore Sanity spent $3.8 million to support Demuth in a three-way Republican primary race, and has since poured over $10.3 million for Demuth in her race against Sen. Amy Klobuchar, providing the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican candidate in years.
Restore Sanity is mostly funded by the Restoration of America PAC, which is primarily financed by Wisconsin billionaire duo Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. The Uihleins own one of North America’s largest distributors of shipping and packaging supplies. The unprecedented spending reveals some optimism in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican to a statewide office in two decades.


Minnesota candidates, outside groups, spent big in weeks leading up to Nov. 3 election

In total, Republican outside groups have spent nearly $30 million on statewide office — for governor, attorney general, state auditor and secretary of state — and state House and Senate races, compared to the $17 million spent by DFL outside groups.
The Reformer’s analysis looks at money spent after primary elections for every election since 2016. The exact date of the primary varies each election. For consistency over different election cycles, only spending between Aug. 14 to Oct. 19 of each election year is included in these charts. The campaign finance data released last week includes only spending up until Oct. 19. Contributions received by campaigns and political committees after Oct. 19 are posted on the state’s Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board website.






The second biggest outside group is the Democratic-Farmer-Labor-aligned Alliance for a Better Minnesota, which has spent over $4.7 million on ads against Republican attorney general candidate Ron Schutz, and $3 million on ads against Demuth.
Since the primary election, outside groups have spent $16.9 million on state Senate races, followed by $13.9 million on the gubernatorial race and $10.4 million on the state attorney general race. Significantly less — $5.9 million — was spent on state House races. Voters will choose candidates for all seats in the state’s Legislature on Tuesday.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Groups renew multi-pronged effort to alter Maine’s inclusive trans athlete laws
description: The group aiming to limit what sports and school facilities transgender students can access submitted more than 4,000 new signatures to the Secretary of State’s office on Monday to put the question on the 2027 ballot, after falling short of this year’s deadline.  During a press conference in Augusta on Monday, national conservative legal group […]
text:
Athletes Reagan Wilson and Morgan Clark along with Protect Girls Sports lead petitioner Leyland Streiff submit signatures to the Secretary of State's office. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)The group aiming to limit what sports and school facilities transgender students can access submitted more than 4,000 new signatures to the Secretary of State’s office on Monday to put the question on the 2027 ballot, after falling short of this year’s deadline. 
During a press conference in Augusta on Monday, national conservative legal group Alliance Defending Freedom also announced it is filing a civil rights complaint on behalf of two Maine athletes alleging the state is violating federal protections against sex discrimination. The Title IX complaint is against the State of Maine, two school districts and the Maine Principals’ Association. 
The two actions mark a renewed, coordinated push to roll back Maine’s protections for trans students. One effort seeks to change state law through a ballot referendum; the other threatens legal action against the state and school districts that allow trans students to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity.
Maine has been in the national spotlight since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025 because of its inclusive policies, which protect students from discrimination on the basis of gender identity. ADF has filed lawsuits across the country “against gender ideology” alleging sex-based discrimination against cisgender girls if trans classmates are allowed on sports teams, or in bathrooms and locker rooms aligning with their identity. 
Tavia Bruxellas McAlister, legal counsel for ADF, cited federal investigations by the departments of education and health that found Maine violated Title IX.
Secretary of State invalidates anti-trans ballot question due to improper signature gathering

“Last year, the federal government determined that Maine’s policy of allowing males to compete in female sports was a violation of Title IX,” McAlister said. “As we stand here this morning, Maine has taken no steps to remedy this injustice.”
She said that prompted the national group to get involved and represent Maine athletes who, “despite all of their hard work and their discipline … may be denied the thrill of victory because Maine lets men compete in women’s sports.”
Leyland Streiff, lead petitioner for the Protect Girls Sports campaign echoed that sentiment. “Title IX will be followed in Maine, the question is simply when and how,” Streiff said.
“Either through our ballot referendum in November 2027,” Streiff continued, “or through the crushing legal weight and financial repercussions of civil rights lawsuits that are sure to follow Alliance Defending Freedom’s Title IX complaint if school districts don’t change course and align to federal law.”
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Title IX allows schools to restrict girls’ and women’s sports teams to those assigned female at birth, defining “sex” in this context as biological sex rather than gender identity. Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey said at the time that the state will continue to defend its inclusive policies.
Protect Girls Sports and ADF have both framed it as a girls’ safety issue, although national research from the Williams Institute at the University of California Los Angeles School of Law found no evidence that allowing transgender people access to bathrooms aligning with their gender identity jeopardizes safety and privacy for other occupants.
The two student athletes featured in ADF’s Title IX complaint spoke in support of the ballot measure on Monday, saying they felt competing against trans students is unfair. 
“This is unacceptable and has deprived me and so many other girls of equal opportunity to compete and win,” said Reagan Wilson, a Fryeburg Academy student who said she had competed against trans athletes in soccer and cross country. “Many girls and women are discovering the crushing disappointment that comes from being beaten in their own sports by males who should have never been allowed to compete in the first place.”
Ken Clark, a parent of the other high school athlete listed in ADF’s complaint, accused schools of bullying students by allowing trans athletes to participate in sports.
“It’s time to rattle the cages of the Maine Department of Education, Maine Principals’ Association, principals, coaches, superintendents, athletic directors, athletic trainers in your school, and the school board members,” he said. 
The education department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Renewed ballot initiative 
Protect Girls Sports’ initiative was first approved by the Maine Secretary of State’s Office to appear on this year’s ballot. But following a legal challenge questioning the validity of hundreds of signatures collected by the group, the Maine Supreme Judicial Court in July ultimately backed Secretary of State Shenna Bellows’ determination that the initiative did not clear the threshold.
At issue were hundreds of signatures gathered by out-of-state collectors who did not follow Maine protocols. Streiff told reporters on Monday that the group had spent several months collecting additional signatures to submit ahead of the Feb. 2, 2027 deadline for the November 2027 ballot.
Ultimately, the group will need 67,682 signatures to be validated by the Secretary of State’s Office. The 4,000 submitted Monday will need to be approved before they are combined with the previously validated signatures.
“We’ve obviously paid great attention to make sure that paperwork is done correctly,” Streiff said, noting that the campaign has “not had anyone from out of state come in and circulate petitions for this last round.”
Role of politicians
During the press conference, Streiff stressed the importance of voting in Tuesday’s midterm elections, criticizing several Democratic candidates including gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, Senate candidate Troy Jackson and Matt Dunlap, who is running in the 2nd Congressional District, as well as former candidates Nirav Shah and Graham Platner for their support of trans athletes.
They all “publicly and misogynistically vowed to defeat our referendum and ensure males can continue to have unfettered access to girls’ safe spaces and their competitive courts,” he said. 
The Democrat-led Maine Legislature in 2025 defeated several attempts at restricting the rights of trans students, including bills that attempted to change the Maine Human Rights Act. The final language of the petition mirrors that of one of the defeated bills. 
Streiff said another way supportive Mainers could advance the campaign’s proposed changes to state law is by legislators who back similar restrictions. Last year, all bills attempting to limit trans’ athletes rights were introduced and supported by Republicans.
“Who we elect tomorrow matters, as our girls deserve a Legislature that is willing to do the will of the people and enact this bill immediately,” he said.

title: New Mexico public schools see decline in Native certified teachers, state education data says
description: New Mexico’s public education system saw a steep decrease in Native language and culture teachers over the past year, according to data presented to state lawmakers on Friday.
text:
A New Mexico Public Education Department official with the Indian Education Division told lawmakers on Oct. 30, 2026, that the number of state-certified Native language and culture teachers decreased over the past year. (Photo courtesy of Getty Images)New Mexico’s public education system saw a steep decrease in Native language and culture teachers over the past year, according to data presented to state lawmakers on Friday. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state’s certification program for Native American language and culture allows experts in those fields to teach in New Mexico public and charter schools without a college degree and, if full-time, earn the annual salary of a Level 1 teacher at $55,000. 
Teachers certified in the 520 Native American Language and Culture Certification program play a role in the New Mexico Public Education Department’s action plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit by expanding Native language education and increasing the number of students who graduate with proficiency in English and another language, including Native languages. 
KatieAnn Juanico, assistant secretary for PED’s Indian Education division, highlighted the importance of Native-certified teachers to the interim Indian Affairs Committee, saying: “I was raised on the reservation — without our language, we lose a sense of self, a sense of respect.”
But recent PED data she presented shows a decline in the overall number of 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools statewide. In July 2025, PED reported 234 Native language and culture teachers in public and charter schools, new PED data shows there are now 147—a 37% decline in just over a year. 
Juanico explained that based on feedback she’s received, many 520-certified teachers struggle with the requirements once they enter a public or charter classroom, particularly with classroom loads and developing lesson plans.
The 520-certified Native teachers realize, according to Juanico, “‘Whoa, what did I sign up for?’ with all these students that I have to watch, manage and build lesson plans for.” She added that, “Oftentimes, our 520 teachers, our tribal community members, don’t come to the classroom knowing all those things.” 
Juanico added that PED only tracks 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools and the decrease may also be due to Native teachers with the 520 certification returning to a tribal school after teaching at a public or charter school. Collecting that data “is an opportunity to understand why those teachers are leaving the district and charter schools,” Juanico said. 
To support 520-certified Native teachers, Juanico said the Indian Education Division wants to develop classes for Tribes, Pueblos and Nations to boost Native-teacher success after receiving the 520 certificate, and to work with districts and charter schools to recruit and hire more certificate holders. 
State Rep. Patricia Royal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) highlighted the need for the PED Indian Education Division to collect more information on 520-certified teachers and how they’re addressing gaps articulated in the Yazzie/Martinez case.
“It is important to have that information because we should be modeling and showcasing our tribes as leading the charge in this,” Roybal Caballero said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal judge: Southaven data center gas turbines must have air permits
description: A truck approaches a closed construction site on Tuesday Oct. 6, 2026, where SpaceXAI has had a power plant since August 2025.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A federal judge has denied Elon Musk-owned SpaceXAI’s motion to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the NAACP over its use of gas turbines to power data centers in Southaven and Memphis. 
The lawsuit alleges that the artificial intelligence company’s turbines require a state air permit from the Mississippi Environmental Quality to operate and are “a major source of hazardous air pollutants” that are harming residents.
SpaceXAI, previously known as xAI, argued in its motion to dismiss that the turbines do not require permits because they fall under an exception for “mobile sources,” which the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a letter to the company last year. 
However, on Friday, U.S. District Judge Debra Brown found that turbines are “not a ‘mobile source’ according to the federal regulations” and require permits. She added in her ruling that “the letter does not alter the Court’s determination that the defendants’ turbines are not mobile sources”
The company also argued that the NAACP could not sue under the federal Clean Air Act and that lawsuits brought by the NAACP and other groups are unconstitutional. Brown found that the NAACP does have standing to sue and the case can continue.
Two weeks ago, Brown denied a separate motion to dismiss the case filed by the U.S. Department of Justice. The DOJ said it intervened in the case because Grok, the company’s artificial-intelligence chatbot, is vital for national security. 
“This decision is another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP director of environmental and climate justice in a statement. “The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution. Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits,” 
In March, the state permit board unanimously approved the company’s air permit application to build 41 permanent turbines in Southaven to power its expanding data center presence in the area. Southaven residents appealed that decision and a hearing is scheduled for Nov. 9. 
The project has faced stiff opposition from residents who are concerned about noise and pollution. Some residents have brought a separate class action lawsuit against the company over the “pervasive and inescapable” noise created by the temporary turbines.   
SpaceXAI is constructing six data centers in the Memphis area according to a social media post by Elon Musk on Saturday. The company has said its Southaven operations could amount to an over $45 billion investment. When the project was announced in Jan. 2026, Gov. Tate Reeves said it was the largest economic development in the state’s history and would “transform the region and bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations.” 
The NAACP has requested the court order SpaceXAI to stop operating its mobile turbines until it gets them permitted. The court has not yet ruled on that request. In response, Reeves wrote to the court that such a move would create an “immediate and substantial disruption to the state’s economy.”
SpaceXAI did not respond to a request for comment.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democrats boost early voter turnout, GOP lags ahead of Election Day
description: More than 40% of registered New Mexico Democrats have already cast ballots in the 2026 general election, marking a large increase in their turnout compared with the previous midterm election in 2022, according to the latest figures from the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office.
text:
New Mexico Democratic turnout ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026, has exceeded that of the previous midterm elections in 2022, matching a similar national trend as Democrats seek to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate. (Photo by Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)More than 40% of registered New Mexico Democrats have already cast ballots in the 2026 general election, marking a large increase in their turnout compared with the previous midterm election in 2022, according to the latest figures from the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office.
In total, about 31% of the state’s 1.46 million registered voters have cast ballots ahead of the general election concluding Tuesday, which is on par with the 2022 election. But this year’s figure reflects an increase in Democratic turnout and decrease in Republican turnout. [Voter Guide: New Mexico Primary Election 2026 Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Already this year, 40.7% of the state’s 578,000 registered Democrats have cast ballots, compared with 32.2% of Democrats who voted early or absentee in 2022. Bernalillo and Doña Ana counties largely drove the increase in Democratic turnout, according to a Source NM review. 
On the other hand, significantly fewer Republicans have cast ballots early. In 2022, 36% of registered Republicans had voted ahead of Election Day, compared with 31% of approximately 445,000 Republicans registered in the state as of October of this year. The decrease in early Republican turnout was largest in Bernalillo County, where about 14% fewer Republicans have voted versus 2022. 
The 2026 general election comes after the state’s first-ever semi-open primary, which enabled unaffiliated voters to cast ballots for either a Democrat or Republican for the first time. Their access to the primary ballots coincided with a surge of new registrations of voters who opted not to register with either of the state’s two major parties.
Approximately 107,000 more unaffiliated voters are registered this year than in 2022, making them approximately 28% of the electorate versus 22% in 2022. In both elections, roughly 18% of registered unaffiliated voters cast ballots early or absentee.
The general election also marks the New Mexico Forward Party’s entrance as an official minor party, along with the existing Green and Libertarian parties. In total, voters from the three minor parties have cast less than 1% of the total early and absentee votes. 
Overall, the number of registered voters has risen by approximately 100,000, or 7.4%, since 2022, so the overall number of early and absentee voters — about 456,000 — is greater than it was during the last midterm.
The boost in Democratic turnout ahead of Election Day matches similar trends nationally, with national political observers noting signs of a surge in Democrats hitting the polls. Democrats hope President Donald Trump’s unpopularity will result in both chambers of Congress flipping to Democratic control.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Tuesday’s election in Washington is packed with big decisions for voters
description: Washington’s massive midterm election on Tuesday is nearly here. Voters are weighing in on initiatives to repeal a statewide income tax on high earners and bar transgender girls from competing in girls sports in public schools. They will fill five of the nine seats on the state Supreme Court, a rare opportunity to pick a […]
text:
Trays of ballots await processing in the elections center in Pierce County, Washington on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)Washington’s massive midterm election on Tuesday is nearly here.
Voters are weighing in on initiatives to repeal a statewide income tax on high earners and bar transgender girls from competing in girls sports in public schools.
They will fill five of the nine seats on the state Supreme Court, a rare opportunity to pick a majority of the bench that will soon consider changes to bail rules and could eventually decide the legality of that income tax.
In the Legislature, all 98 seats in the state House and 24 of 49 in the state Senate are up for election. Democrats hold large majorities in both chambers and voters’ decisions could further cement their control.
Washington’s 10 U.S. House seats are on ballots. A lot of eyes are trained on what happens in the 3rd Congressional District in the southwest corner of the state. That’s where two-term Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is dueling with Republican state Sen. John Braun in a match-up that will help decide which party controls the U.S. House next year.
Meanwhile, residents of the 4th Congressional District in central Washington will be getting a new representative. Republican Amanda McKinney and Democrat John Duresky are competing to succeed Republican U.S. Rep. Dan Newhouse, who is retiring after 12 years in office.
Voting ends at 8 p.m. Tuesday. By then, voters need to have put their ballots in a designated drop box, delivered them to an elections office or made sure they are postmarked no later than Nov. 3.
As of Monday afternoon, 1,834,247 ballots had been returned, 35.5% of the state’s registered voters. Statewide numbers will be updated around 5 p.m. Monday. Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said he expects final turnout will exceed 60%.
State and county election officers have urged voters to use one of Washington’s 601 designated drop boxes or cast their ballots in person at one of 64 voting centers. The message is being heard; 71.5% of ballots returned prior to the weekend arrived via a drop box.
Election officials are concerned that as a result of recent changes in its operations, the U.S. Postal Service can no longer guarantee ballots will be postmarked on the day they are put in a mail box. Roughly 20,000 ballots cast in the August primary did not get counted because they arrived too late.
Anyone thinking of mailing their ballot today or on Election Day should go into the post office and request a manual postmark at the counter, officials have said.
It’s not too late to participate. Washington allows same-day voting which means a person can go into an auditor’s office or a voting center, register and cast a ballot up until 8 p.m. Election Day. 
It’s also possible to get a replacement for a lost ballot, or obtain a ballot if you never received one.
Anyone standing in line to vote at 7:59 p.m. — or in a car waiting to use a drop box — will get to vote. Arrive after 8 p.m. you won’t.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

title: Resources available for voters amid flooding in southwest Colorado
description: The Colorado secretary of state’s office is providing resources to support voters in Archuleta and La Plata counties due to rain and the risk of flooding.  Election officials closed the voting center at the Ross Aragon Community Center and the Pagosa Springs Town Hall drop box amid historic flooding, which began in the Four Corners […]
text:
A view of San Juan River flooding in downtown Pagosa Springs on Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Jacque Aragon)The Colorado secretary of state’s office is providing resources to support voters in Archuleta and La Plata counties due to rain and the risk of flooding. 
Election officials closed the voting center at the Ross Aragon Community Center and the Pagosa Springs Town Hall drop box amid historic flooding, which began in the Four Corners region more than a week ago. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Two new voting centers opened at the Archuleta County Courthouse and the Pine River Library at Bayfield. A new mobile drop box opened in the parking lot at 10 Solomon Drive in Pagosa Springs.


Voters can find their county clerk through this tool on the Colorado secretary of state’s website.


No voting centers in La Plata County have closed or moved as of Monday morning. Mobile teams of bipartisan election judges with the La Plata County clerk and recorder’s office will deliver ballots to voters at local emergency management shelters. 
Voters can pick up a new ballot that includes local races as well as state races from their county clerk’s office. Voters can pick up a ballot outside of their home county, but it will include only state races.
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold in a press call Monday told reporters that her office has been in close contact with county clerks in the region, the state emergency management office, the Colorado County Clerks Association and the governor’s office to ensure voters can cast a ballot. 
Voting centers and drop box locations can still change amid the flooding. Griswold said voters can check on her office’s website for the latest information on where they can vote.  
Griswold said that during every election cycle her office hires retired election officials to provide additional support where needed, and a former Grand County clerk is on the ground in Archuleta County to help as necessary. A staff member with Griswold’s office is also in the county to help. 
Both Archuleta and La Plata counties are approaching 50% turnout despite the weather, Griswold said. 
Voters have until 7 p.m. Tuesday to drop off their ballot to their county clerk or be in line to vote in person.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Division of the Arts wins national award for expanding arts access
description: Free programs for veterans and older adults, artist funding, and statewide outreach cited in national recognition The Delaware Division of the Arts has received a national award recognizing its efforts to make arts programs and funding more accessible to people throughout the state. The National Assembly of State Arts Agencies presented Delaware with its 202[...]
text:
Photo courtesy of the National Assembly of State Arts Agencies.
Free programs for veterans and older adults, artist funding, and statewide outreach cited in national recognition
The Delaware Division of the Arts has received a national award recognizing its efforts to make arts programs and funding more accessible to people throughout the state.
The National Assembly of State Arts Agencies presented Delaware with its 2026 Arts Access Agency Award, which honors state or regional arts agencies that expand participation, reduce barriers and extend public investment in the arts to more communities.
Division Director Jessica Ball accepted the award during NASAA’s national conference in Washington, D.C., held Oct. 7-9. The award was announced publicly Monday.
Delaware was recognized for programs that include free arts classes for older adults in libraries and senior centers, free arts programming for veterans, increased direct support for individual artists, free public exhibitions and events, and a statewide calendar connecting residents with arts and cultural activities.
The programs reach communities in all three counties.
Ball credited the Division’s staff and its relationships with community organizations and other state agencies for expanding the agency’s reach.
“I’m proud to accept this on behalf of the Delaware Division of the Arts, but I want to be clear about whose award this is: it belongs to our program officers and our staff,” Ball said.
She said staff members have built relationships throughout Delaware that help residents and organizations understand that state arts funding and programs are available to them.
“People take part when they trust you, and our team has earned that trust,” Ball said.
Bringing arts programs into communities
Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez said the recognition reflects the Division’s effort to bring programming directly to places Delawareans already use, including libraries, senior centers and veterans organizations.
“Delaware is a small state, but this team thinks and delivers big,” Patibanda-Sanchez said. “When the arts come to your neighborhood, they become part of everyday life.”
NASAA President and CEO Pam Breaux called Delaware a national example of how state arts agencies can broaden participation.
“Delaware exemplifies what it means to put access at the center of public arts work,” Breaux said.
She cited the Division’s continuing efforts to reach new audiences and remove barriers that can prevent people from participating in arts programs.
Juan Souki, executive director of Mid Atlantic Arts, said Delaware has demonstrated that arts access can go beyond a policy goal and become part of an agency’s regular programming.
“The Delaware Division of the Arts has shown what it looks like to make access more than a value statement,” Souki said.
Support for artists and organizations
The Division administers grants to arts organizations, community organizations and individual artists throughout Delaware. Current programs include operating support, project funding, arts education grants and artist opportunity grants.
The agency operates with funding provided through state appropriations and support from the National Endowment for the Arts.
Ball has also taken on a larger national role in arts policy. She was elected in 2025 to the NASAA board of directors for a three-year term beginning in 2026.
The Arts Access Agency Award recognizes a state arts agency or regional arts organization that demonstrates an emerging or sustained commitment to expanding access to arts programs and ensuring public arts funding reaches communities throughout its state or region.

name: Daily Montanan
title: 300,000 Montanans have voted, in-person voting kicks off at 7 a.m.
description: With one day left until midterm Election Day polls close in Montana, more than 300,000 votes have already been cast.  The Montana Secretary of State’s office reported that as of Sunday night, 56.6% of the more than 530,000 absentee ballots sent out had been returned, including around 45,000 from Yellowstone County, 41,000 from Missoula County, […]
text:
Montana's new "I voted" sticker. (Secretary of State's Office photo)With one day left until midterm Election Day polls close in Montana, more than 300,000 votes have already been cast. 
The Montana Secretary of State’s office reported that as of Sunday night, 56.6% of the more than 530,000 absentee ballots sent out had been returned, including around 45,000 from Yellowstone County, 41,000 from Missoula County, 34,000 from Gallatin County and more than 31,000 from Flathead County.
Approximately 806,413 Montanans are registered to vote in 2026, according to Monday’s report from the Secretary of State’s office, an increase of 1.8% during the same report in 2024. 
During the last midterm election in 2022, 468,000 Montanans voted, with a voter turnout of 61%. In 2018, the last midterm election held while President Donald Trump was in office, 71.5% of voters turned out — a midterm record of more than 509,000. 
Montana will set a new general election record if just 50% of registered voters who have not yet cast a ballot show up to the polls on Tuesday. 
The large quantity of early voters in the state mirrors a nationwide trend. States Newsroom’s D.C. bureau reported that on Friday, early voters had already set a record for turnout with more than 46 million ballots cast across the county. 
In Montana, voters are casting ballots for a U.S. Senate seat, both U.S. House seats, a state supreme court candidate, two seats on the Montana Public Service Commission and 125 legislative races. Three ballot initiatives are also up for decisions as are numerous local government seats. 
Poll locations in Montana are required by law in most cases to be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., though smaller polling locations may be open from noon to 8 p.m.
Across Montana, weather for those going to the polls in person looks relatively nice. 
Clear skies are expected in Billings, with cloudy and cool weather forecast for Great Falls, Butte, Missoula, and Kalispell. No early wintry conditions are expected this year.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado election leaders hire former Justice Department official to defend against federal meddling
description: Colorado’s top election official hired a former U.S. Justice Department official to lead contingency planning to respond to any attempts to interfere with the state’s elections. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold in a press call Monday told reporters that Colorado voters should not be afraid to cast their ballot and that so far the […]
text:
Jena Griswold, Colorado secretary of state, speaks during a press conference at her Denver office in 2024. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Colorado’s top election official hired a former U.S. Justice Department official to lead contingency planning to respond to any attempts to interfere with the state’s elections.
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold in a press call Monday told reporters that Colorado voters should not be afraid to cast their ballot and that so far the Nov. 3 election has proceeded as usual. 
“We have been working with the attorney general’s office, the governor’s office, the county clerks association, to make sure that we are as prepared as possible for any of the situations that could arise,” Griswold said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Her office has “a wide array of contingencies prepared” in the event that any election observers attempt to interfere with voters, she said. The former Justice Department official she hired has led a small team working for almost two years to prepare for any scenario. Her office declined to identify the former official by name or share details of the work the person has led. 
Justice Department threats against election officials are persistent across the country, Griswold said, and leaders on a bipartisan basis are “standing strong” against any threats of federal interference. The Trump administration has pursued escalating actions to control elections, including its lawsuit to access confidential Colorado voter information and efforts to limit mail-in voting.
“I don’t want Coloradans to hear that they should be scared. They should absolutely not be scared. They should go cast their ballot,” Griswold said. 
The Justice Department’s plans to deploy election monitors to Adams County have raised alarms about potential election meddling, but Griswold said the monitors cannot access any ballot processing locations or interfere with voters. Department monitors must abide by the same rules as any other member of the public and stay 100 feet away from voting centers, Griswold said. 
The department declined terms set by Colorado officials that would have restricted federal election monitor activities inside Adams County election buildings, and the department said the monitors would deploy to election sites but not enter them. The monitors will not be visually identified as Justice observers. 
Congressional observers, which are authorized by federal law to be present in voting centers, are registered with local county clerks’ offices where they intend to observe. Griswold said monitors with U.S. House Republicans will observe in Colorado’s 5th and 8th congressional districts, monitors with House Democrats will observe in El Paso and Adams counties, and U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet’s office will have observers in Adams County.
Griswold’s office will also have workers paired with attorneys from the attorney general’s office in Adams County. Adams County is home to many Democratic voters within Colorado’s competitive 8th Congressional District, a race that could decide which party controls the House.
“I do think if there is any type of misbehavior or concerning behavior, we will know very quickly and then take appropriate steps,” Griswold said.
Voters have until 7 p.m. Tuesday to drop off their ballot to their county clerk or be in line to vote in person. 
Griswold is the Democratic nominee for attorney general.

name: National
title: Many girls, young women try to avoid pregnancy after sex with unproven methods
description: To prevent pregnancy after sex, U.S. teenage girls and young women are more likely to rely on unproven strategies such as prayer, exercise and jumping up and down than they are on evidence-based methods such as Plan B emergency contraception, according to a new study. The study, published in The Journal of Sex Research, is […]
text:
A teacher holds a student’s baby while his class completes coursework at a high school for young parents in Spokane, Wash. A new study finds that many girls and young women try to avoid pregnancy after sex with unproven methods. (Photo by Camilla Forte/The Hechinger Report)To prevent pregnancy after sex, U.S. teenage girls and young women are more likely to rely on unproven strategies such as prayer, exercise and jumping up and down than they are on evidence-based methods such as Plan B emergency contraception, according to a new study.
The study, published in The Journal of Sex Research, is based on a survey of 1,259 girls and women between the ages of 15-29. A quarter of the 633 respondents who reported having sexual intercourse and were not pregnant said they had used a post-coital method to prevent pregnancy.
Of those, about 9% said they’d used evidence-based emergency birth control such as Plan B or a copper intrauterine device.
But about 16% used methods without proven efficacy, including prayer (9.4%), douching (6%), jumping up and down or exercising (3.3%), ingesting something by mouth (1.9%), punching one’s stomach or uterus (1.4%), taking medicine or vitamins (0.9%), inserting something vaginally (0.5%), or using an enema (0.2%). About one-fifth of this group used more than one method — praying and douching being the most common combination.
These types of methods were more common among minors and non-white respondents.
“There is a need to better understand what is underlying these practices or the use of these strategies,” said Riley J. Steiner, an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and one of the authors of the study.
“We really don’t want young people to be seen as misguided or to be judged for these practices,” she said. “They’re trying things, and so how do we best support them to meet what their goals are?”
False birth control claims are proliferating, survey says

The release of the study comes on the heels of the Trump administration cutting and reshaping programs such as Title X and the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program, created to lower the rate of unintended pregnancy and to inform people of safe and effective options for preventing pregnancy.
In August, a federal judge blocked the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services from implementing sweeping changes to grants under the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program, amid an ongoing lawsuit brought by Hennepin County, Minnesota; King County, Washington; an Iowa Planned Parenthood affiliate; and SIECUS: Sex Ed for Social Change, a nonprofit advocacy group. However, grant funding that has already been cut won’t be restored for now, the judge ruled.
The Trump administration has cast doubt on the safety of hormonal contraception, which is increasingly perceived as controversial on social media.
“In our current environment where there’s a lot of mis- and disinformation online and structural constraints that make it hard to access medically evidenced contraceptive methods, it does make sense that people are behaving in broader ways to try to manage that risk,” Steiner said.
But she also noted that the study found the lack of information on contraceptive methods was more likely to drive people to choose post-coital methods rather than concerns about hormones or an inability to obtain clinical care.
Meanwhile, sex education varies widely across the country. And this year several states modified their sex education policies, according to an analysis by SIECUS.
In Alabama, Republican Gov. Kay Ivey signed a law requiring sex education to be focused on promoting “sexual risk avoidance,” updated terminology for “abstinence-only” instruction. The law prohibits sex education before fourth grade and prohibits school districts from partnering with organizations that do not promote “sexual risk avoidance,” as well as organizations that provide or promote abortion.
Instructors are prohibited from teaching students about birth control, but parents can opt out of sex education classes.
Federal judge halts proposed HHS changes to teen pregnancy prevention program

Currently, 15 states offer abstinence-only sex education, according to SIECUS.
In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov. Tony Evers signed a law requiring instruction on adoption as part of sex education. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a bill that would have required instruction on adoption and newborn safe-haven laws whenever contraception or sexually transmitted infections are mentioned. The state already requires instruction to refer to adoption and parenting as the “preferred choice” over abortion.
Three states – Alabama, Louisiana and South Dakota – enacted laws requiring or requesting instruction on fetal development in schools or the viewing of a fetal ultrasound or animated video, such as the “Baby Olivia” video developed by anti-abortion groups.
In California, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills requiring instruction on human trafficking and dating abuse and digital violence.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Early voting in Maine surpasses last midterm election
description: People stood in a line that stretched across the entire second floor of Portland City Hall on the last day of early, in-person voting on Thursday, waiting at times more than an hour to cast their ballots in the midterm election that will decide three congressional seats, the governorship and every seat in the state […]
text:
The line to vote on the last day of early, in-person voting stretches the entire second floor of Portland City Hall on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)People stood in a line that stretched across the entire second floor of Portland City Hall on the last day of early, in-person voting on Thursday, waiting at times more than an hour to cast their ballots in the midterm election that will decide three congressional seats, the governorship and every seat in the state Legislature.  
“Good for us,” one voter remarked. 
Early voting numbers have surpassed the last midterm election in 2022 and are approaching those from the 2024 presidential election. Also, far more voters have cast early ballots in-person than have mailed back absentee ballots, a continuation of a trend seen in recent years. 
As of the latest data from Friday, 290,382 voters had voted early, which includes accepted returned absentee ballots and early votes in the presence of a clerk. 
In 2022, 236,977 absentee ballots were returned and accepted through Election Day. In 2024, it was 378,764.
This year so far, more than 55% of early votes have been cast in-person. Nearly as many Mainers have voted in the presence of a clerk this year than at this point in 2024, and far more than in 2022. 
While the percentage of people dropping absentee ballots in a drop box or with their clerk is about the same as 2024, and down slightly from 2022, the share of voters mailing ballots has decreased significantly — down about 8% from 2022 to 2024 and another 9% from 2024 to 2026.
Thursday also marked the last day to request an absentee ballot. This election, 323,562 absentee ballots have been requested, compared to 388,815 in 2024 and 252,702 in 2022. 
Democrats have cast more early ballots than Republicans, about 47% to almost 23% out of all accepted ballots. Voters who are not enrolled with any political party have also cast more than Republicans, just over 27%. 
This is fairly typical compared with years past. 
There are about 3% fewer Democratic absentee ballot requests compared with 2022, but Democratic requests are up about 5% compared to the 2024 makeup. Requests from unenrolled voters are up more than 4.5% from 2022 and by about 1.5% from 2024. Meanwhile, Republican requests are down a little more than 1% from 2022 and down by about 5% from 2024.
“There’s nothing hugely surprising about this data,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said, noting that historically more Democrats vote early than Republicans. “What’s most exciting about the data is the level of enthusiasm.”
Noting that the primary election in June saw record turnout, Bellows said she is “optimistic that the excellent absentee numbers indicate a strong turnout.” She predicts 70% of all eligible voters will participate in the midterms, which would fall between turnout levels of 2022 and 2024.
