title: Hyde-Smith and Colom make final pitches in Mississippi Senate midterm race
description: Candidates for Mississippi's U.S. Senate seat in the 2026 midterms are, from left, Ty Pinkins, Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom are continuing to travel across Mississippi before Tuesday’s midterm elections and make their final pitches to voters.
READ MORE: What you need to know to vote in Mississippi 2026 midterm elections Tuesday
As voters across the country appear furious over rising prices, Hyde-Smith hopes to weather political headwinds that have sent Republicans scrambling to defend seats even in red states such as Mississippi. Democrats hope to flip the Senate and have begun looking at Mississippi as a dark-horse pickup opportunity.
The race has attracted a string of appearances by national figures hoping to turn out voters. President Donald Trump, former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris have each come to Mississippi over the past two weeks to campaign for their party’s candidate.
Colom has tapped into dissatisfaction with high consumer costs under Trump’s watch, urging Mississippians to send a Democrat to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1982 and promising to lower costs and reverse cuts to social services such as Medicaid. 
Hyde-Smith has promoted her close relationship with Trump and her support in Congress for his agenda, which has included tax cuts and cuts to social safety net programs, a crackdown on illegal immigration and efforts to curb fraud. 
Independent candidate Ty Pinkins is also running, saying voters want a choice neither party is offering.
Hyde-Smith urges voters to show Mississippi remains ‘ruby red’
Over the past week and through the weekend, Hyde-Smith embarked on a bus tour, stopping in Flora, Grenada, Hernando, Holly Springs, Tupelo and Amory. 
“Mississippians know what is at stake in this election, and we’re grateful for the tremendous support and encouragement we have received everywhere we have gone,” said Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager. 
On Sunday evening, she came to Jackson for an event at Martin’s Downtown, a bar where many patrons typically come to watch football and share buckets of beer. 
Hyde-Smith was introduced by U.S. Rep. Michael Guest, Mississippi Republican Party Chairman Mike Hurst and state Transportation Commission Director Brad White. The Republican officials said the race is theirs to win if they turn out voters, and urged supporters not to get complacent.
“We want a big win. We don’t want a little win,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want the rest of this country to know Mississippi is ruby red, and Mississippi is going to stay ruby red.” 
On stage, Hyde-Smith called Colom “literally the most radical liberal” that has “ever run for office in Mississippi,” and said her conservative policies, such as keeping the border secure, would protect jobs and strengthen the economy. 
In a brief interview with Mississippi Today after she walked off stage, Hyde-Smith said voters’ economic pain would be temporary, and that Trump’s war in Iran would keep America safe in the long run. 
“Yes, the prices are high, and yes, the Iran conflict has caused that,” Hyde-Smith said. “We want to get on the other side of that, but today we’re not worried about a nuclear missile about to hit the United States because we took care of that.”
Hyde-Smith also stood by a response she gave in a television interview where she suggested that Mississippians upset over the high cost of beef remember that there are “so many proteins to choose from.” Colom’s campaign seized on the moment, crafting a viral ad that urged voters to “pick another senator” instead of picking another protein. 
Hyde-Smith said her words were taken out of context. 
“You know, gasoline’s expensive, and there’s not a lot of other choices. Or you ride a bicycle. But when a mother wants to feed her family meat, there are several to choose from. I buy gasoline, but there’s one product that’ll make that car go. And I never would take that out,” Hyde-Smith said. “I stand by that every single day.”
Colom repeatedly challenged Hyde-Smith to a debate, which she declined. Asked by Mississippi Today whether she wishes she had accepted the invitations, Hyde-Smith said Colom is “is totally to kill babies in the room. We have nothing to debate.”
Asked for clarification on the senator’s comments, Monssen confirmed she meant “womb” instead of “room” and was talking about abortion. He also said Colom’s policies were too “radical” to merit a debate.    
Colom previously told the Commercial Dispatch that he has always been pro-life, but trusts women “to make the choices that are best for them.”
On Sunday night, Hyde-Smith said she was proud to chair the pro-life caucus in the Senate and said she helped double the number of Republican senators in the caucus.   
Hyde-Smith was set to appear early Monday morning at Ingalls Shipbuilding on the Coast to greet workers during their shift change. She said she stood by her record working on the issues voters have spoken to her about on the campaign trail.
“As I travel throughout the state, there’s one thing that you know: people want a safe border because they want a safe country,” Hyde-Smith said. “People want solid economic policies because they want the dignity of a job. People want to be able to worship the way they want to worship with their families.” 
Colom says he is the fighter Mississippi needs 
Colom over the weekend made final pitches to voters in Ita Bena, Southaven, and Jackson. On Monday, he was scheduled to appear in Meridian, De Kalb and Macon. 
Appearing at a Powers in the Pews event at Anderson United Methodist Church in Jackson on Sunday, Colom repeated his promises to fight for raising the minimum wage, advocate for access to rural healthcare and push back on attempts to weaken voting rights for Mississippians.
In the final days of his campaign, his pitch to Mississippians, including Republicans, was to argue that voters have been betrayed by a president who pledged to stay out of foreign wars, lower gasoline prices and tame the rising cost of goods. 
“My message to every Republican voter in Mississippi is it’s time you got a fighter that’s going to actually hold the president to the commitments he made to Mississippi,” Colom said. 
The Democratic nominee said that politicians like Hyde-Smith and Republican Gov. Tate Reeves have divided Mississippians and disparaged Democrats as a tactic to gain more votes. But he said Mississippi will never reach its full potential unless politicians learn to work together. 
“That’s what they don’t understand,” Colom said. “That division and distraction have always held Mississippi back. We’re only going to reach our potential if we understand that we have to do it together. I truly believe that there’s nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed with what’s right about Mississippi.” 
As a closing argument, he told Mississippi Today that voters should ask themselves which U.S. Senate candidate has tried to earn their vote and lay out a policy plan for the next six years. The Democrat believes he’s the only candidate who has met voters face-to-face, while Hyde-Smith has hidden from them. 
“She has not done one ad or one speech about what she’s said, what she’s going to do for Mississippi. Not one,” Colom said. “It’s clear she hasn’t campaigned. She refused to debate. She lies constantly.” 
Colom was joined by Mississippi Congressman Bennie Thompson, former Massachusetts Congressman Joe Kennedy III, Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, NAACP President Derrick Johnson and Mississippi NAACP President Charles Taylor. 
Kennedy told the crowd he’s invested in the Mississippi Senate race because of his family’s history with the Magnolia State, particularly when his grandfather, U.S. Robert Kennedy, made a historic visit to the Mississippi Delta in the 1960s to shed a spotlight on the abject poverty and malnutrition that Black citizens in the region were experiencing. 
“Almost 60 years ago, my grandfather came to the Delta to see what Mississippi was,” Kennedy said. “On Tuesday, we get to show the world what Mississippi is.” 
If Colom is successful on Tuesday, he will be the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction, and the first Black U.S. senator from the state elected by popular vote. 
Kennedy said that after Reconstruction ended, it slammed the door shut on Black citizens being able to vote and that no Black person has been able to become a U.S. senator since then. But, he said, Mississippi gets to “pry that door open again” on Tuesday.  
The election is Tuesday, and polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware school board members looking to turn a local challenge into a practical project can apply for grants of up to $2,000 through First State Educate’s 2027 Capacity Grants program.
First State Educate announced Monday that applications are open for the program, which helps current school board members work with their superintendents to identify district needs, develop projects and strengthen their ability to govern effectively.
Applications are due Dec. 1, and a virtual orientation for prospective applicants is scheduled for Nov. 9.
Unlike a traditional education grant aimed primarily at classroom programs or equipment, the Capacity Grants focus on the work of school boards — including how members understand issues, engage their communities, evaluate district performance and make decisions affecting students.
The goal is also to make successful projects useful beyond the district where they were developed.
First State Educate says recipients will document their work, results and lessons learned so other Delaware school boards can adapt promising approaches to their own communities.
The organization’s current grant materials describe the program as an effort to move locally developed ideas “from concept to implementation” and eventually create models that can be used by other districts.
Local problems, statewide lessons
Previous grant recipients have addressed issues ranging from literacy and kindergarten readiness to emergency communications, multilingual family engagement and student participation in school governance.
In the Cape Henlopen School District, board member Dr. Alison Myers focused on Science of Reading training designed to improve board members’ understanding of literacy instruction and their oversight role.
In Christina, Y.F. Lou explored emergency communications and the needs of multilingual families, while Monica Moriak examined opportunities for greater collaboration among New Castle County school boards.
Woodbridge board members Rita Hovermale and Timothy Banks pursued projects involving kindergarten readiness and student participation in school governance.
Lou, vice president of the Christina School Board and a first responder, said the grant allowed him to investigate an issue that otherwise might have been difficult for an individual board member to pursue.
“Board members set the guardrails for how a district reaches families in a crisis, but a board member has no resources of their own to put behind a question,” Lou said.
The grant, he said, provided resources for a tabletop emergency exercise involving students and district staff and produced findings the board could use in its governance role.
First State Educate has previously funded projects that developed practical tools involving literacy governance, crisis communication, kindergarten readiness, student engagement and multilingual family communication.
More than the $2,000
The program includes more than the grant itself.
Recipients receive guidance from First State Educate as projects move from an initial idea through planning and implementation. FSE also works with Dr. James Bridgeforth of the University of Delaware to provide additional expertise and technical assistance.
The organization says recipients can receive individualized guidance, peer learning opportunities and assistance with implementation, reporting and problem-solving.
That support is intended to help board members define a manageable project, determine what success should look like and ultimately develop resources that can be shared with other districts.
Those resources could include guides, training materials, community engagement protocols, templates or reports documenting what worked — and what did not.
First State Educate Executive Director Dr. Julia Keleher has described the program as a way to give school boards the resources to move beyond identifying problems and begin testing solutions.
“Stronger governance leads to stronger outcomes,” Keleher said in announcing previous recipients. “These board-designed projects give districts new ways to understand challenges and make decisions that reflect what students and families need most.”
Who can apply
Current Delaware school board members who participate in First State Educate activities are eligible to apply.
Applicants are encouraged to work with their superintendent and other board members to identify a specific issue or opportunity that could benefit from focused attention.
Projects can address areas such as board effectiveness, family and community engagement, student achievement, literacy, STEM education, professional learning or new governance tools and systems.
Proposals do not have to be fully developed when they are submitted. First State Educate says it will work with selected recipients to refine their plans and develop appropriate measures for evaluating the work.
The application deadline is Dec. 1. Award notifications and grantee orientation are expected between Dec. 16 and Jan. 5.

Rebecca “Becky” Jane GiudiceSeptember 11, 1953 – October 28, 2026Worland, WyomingShared by: Bryant Funeral HomeRebecca “Becky” Jane Giudice, 73, passed away on October 28, 2026, at her home in Worland, Wyoming, with her husband by her side.
Becky came from Cornhusker country, Nebraska. She was born on September 11, 1953, in Cozad, Nebraska, the youngest of five children. Shortly after her birth, her family relocated to Colorado, where Becky grew up in Longmont.
A hard worker from an early age, Becky served as a yearbook editor during high school while also working as a carhop at the local hamburger stand. She later worked at Mr. Steak Restaurant, where she was promoted to floor supervisor.
During her senior year of high school, Becky met Gary Giudice through a mutual friend on December 19, 1970. The two quickly became inseparable. Money was often tight in those early days, but they always found creative ways to spend time together. They didn’t need much to have a good time, just each other’s company.
Becky and Gary were married on October 16, 1971, beginning a marriage that would span 55 years. Following their wedding, Becky left Mr. Steak and began working for the local newspaper. When their first child arrived in October 1973, she stepped away from work to care for their growing family. Their second child followed in May 1975, and Becky later returned to the newspaper as a rural route carrier.
Between working and raising her children, Becky always managed to make time for softball. She loved the game, and no matter how busy life became, the ball field was somewhere she wanted to be. Give her the chance to hear someone yell, “Play ball!” and she was ready.
In the spring of 1980, Becky and Gary packed up their family and moved to Worland, Wyoming, sight unseen. Worland became home, and Becky soon found herself busy with work, family, and the friendships she made along the way. She worked as a checker at Safeway, Go Gas and later waited tables at the Elks and Ranchito. Becky genuinely enjoyed serving others, and waitressing gave her the opportunity to do something that came naturally to her: take care of people and make them feel welcome.
Their family grew again with the birth of their third child in 1981 and fourth in 1983. With four children to raise, a household to manage, and jobs to work, Becky certainly had her hands full. Still, she found time for the softball games she enjoyed so much.
Throughout her years in Worland, Becky worked for Larry and Anne Hill at Rolling Hills Trucking, where the working relationship grew into a lasting friendship for both Becky and Gary. She also worked as a receptionist at Basin Clinic and later at NGP. Eventually, she joined the Washakie County Clerk’s Office, handling accounts payable and payroll. She retired after 12 years of service.
In 2015, Becky began dealing with an unknown illness that would bring years of challenges and uncertainty. Through it all, she leaned on her faith in God, facing each day with determination and trusting in the promises of her Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.
Becky’s Christian faith was an important part of who she was, particularly during the difficult years of her illness. She looked forward to the day she would hear the words, “Well done, my good and faithful servant.” Her family finds comfort in knowing that she is now at peace and resting in the presence of her Heavenly Father.
Becky was preceded in death by her parents, Robert and Lois Scott; sisters, Vivian McCann and Virginia Glen; and brother, Raymond Scott.
She is survived by her husband, Gary Giudice of Worland; sons, Jason (Maralee) Giudice of Worland and Anthony Giudice of Orofino, Idaho; daughters, Patricia Knopp of Laurel, Montana, and Christina Giudice of Worland; and sister, Marean Dyer of Hastings, Nebraska; grandchildren, Jerome, Tyler (Amanda), Garrett (Elizabeth Carver), Kyleigh (Raven) Heflin, Rhidge (Shayden), Brooks, Sabrina Knopp, Chloe (Noah) Shirley, Haylee (Juan) Giudice Lopez, Tate, Riley, and Bexley; six great-grandchildren, with two more on the way.
A memorial service will be held at 10:00 a.m. on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at the Worland Community Center Complex Conference Room. Memorial donations may be made to the Worland Senior Center, please send checks to PO Box 524 Worland, Wyoming 82401. 
Online condolences may be made at Bryant Funeral Home.

Kent George ProfitApril 21, 1944 – October 29, 2026Big Piney, WyomingShared by: Covill Funeral Home & CrematoryKent George Profit was born on April 21, 1944, to George Reginald Profit and Patricia Annette O’Brien in Seattle, Washington. He passed away peacefully at his home in Big Piney, Wyoming, on October 29, 2026, surrounded by loved ones here on earth and those that welcomed him in Heaven.
Kent’s family roots in Wyoming ran deep. His great-grandparents homesteaded in LaBarge, Wyoming, in 1912, and Kent spent his first-grade year there. His family later moved to Idaho, where he graduated from Middleton High School with the Class of 1962. No matter where life took them, the family always made their way back to the T.E. O’Brien Ranch in Big Piney. Those visits helped establish a lasting connection to the area Kent would eventually call home.
On September 26, 1970, Kent married Judith Ann Smith. Together, they welcomed two daughters, Tanya in September 1972 and Cheryl in January 1975.
Kent wore many hats throughout his life, but hard work was always a constant. He began his career as a truck driver at just 18 years old, an occupation he carried with him throughout his life. He eventually founded KP Trucking in the early 2000s and worked as an owner-operator across numerous industries. A man of exceptional work ethic, Kent was never intimidated by a challenging job. He took tremendous pride in what he did, and even in his later years, he could be found putting in a hard day’s work and tackling whatever project was in front of him. He was simply not one to sit still.
Kent’s life was filled with adventures and hobbies. In his younger years, he earned his private pilot’s license and shared plenty of stories about his flying adventures. He also spent time team roping, a passion he would enjoy even more in his later years. One of his proudest moments came when he and his partner, Bob Bing, competed in Rock Springs for a chance to qualify for the World Series of Team Roping in Las Vegas. With the top 50 teams qualifying for the payout, Kent and Bob finished 51st out of more than 300 teams. It was an accomplishment he was proud of and a memory he cherished.
In 1998, Kent earned one of his most treasured titles when he became Pa with the birth of his first grandson, Tanner Kent Elliott. He was soon joined by Mathiew Sage Pierce in 1999, Teagan James Elliott in 2002, and Ruby Judith Pierce in 2003. Known affectionately as Pa to his grandchildren, it didn’t take long before he became Pa to just about every kid who crossed his path.
Kent was one of his grandchildren’s biggest fans. Distance was never an excuse, and he made every effort to be there for their activities, games, and milestones. Even after his grandchildren graduated, his loyalty to the Big Piney Punchers never wavered. He continued traveling to away games and cheering from the stands at as many home games as he could. He was a proud grandfather, and his family always knew they had someone in their corner.
Kent was preceded in death by his parents, George and Annette Profit; his wife, Judy; his brother, Mike Profit, and sister-in-law, Ilene Profit; his sister, JaNeane Hays; and his grandson, Tanner Kent Elliott.
He is survived by his daughters, Tanya (Steven) Greenwell and Cheryl (Vince) Pierce; his grandchildren, Mathiew (Hannah) Pierce, Ruby Pierce, Devon Eddie, Teagan Elliott, Lainee Andersen, Ryan Hristco, Kimberly (Eric) Tuten, KC Greenwell, Tyler Greenwell, Trevor (Jenny) Greenwell, Shelby Greenwell, Sadie Greenwell, and Colter (Misty) Stene; his great-grandchildren, Athena and Aurora Tuten, Marshall Swett, Autumn and Kenna Pierce, Myles Kent Elliott, Jesalie, Mia and Jackson Greenwell, Blaze and Brody Oakley, Rosalie Greenwell, and Tatum, Harper, Raelynn, and Barrett Stene; his sisters, Toni David and Laurel Profit; along with several nieces and nephews.
It is nearly impossible to condense Kent’s big, full life into a few paragraphs. His work history alone could fill pages, and his adventures and stories could keep a room entertained for hours. But those who knew Kent don’t need an obituary to tell them who he was. They know the stories, the laughter, the determination, and the unmistakable presence that came with him.
Kent never met a stranger. He was genuinely interested in people, never missing an opportunity to hear someone’s story, strike up a conversation, or lend a helping hand. He lived life on his own terms, worked hard, played hard, loved his family, and left his mark on countless lives along the way.
He was a hardworking man, a proud father and grandfather, a loyal friend, and a cowboy through and through. His stories will be told for years to come, his presence will be deeply missed, and his legacy will live on through the many lives he touched.
Heaven gained one hell of a cowboy.

Rebecca “Becky” Jane GiudiceSeptember 11, 1953 – October 28, 2026Worland, WyomingShared by: Bryant Funeral HomeRebecca “Becky” Jane Giudice, 73, passed away on October 28, 2026, at her home in Worland, Wyoming, with her husband by her side.
Becky came from Cornhusker country, Nebraska. She was born on September 11, 1953, in Cozad, Nebraska, the youngest of five children. Shortly after her birth, her family relocated to Colorado, where Becky grew up in Longmont.
A hard worker from an early age, Becky served as a yearbook editor during high school while also working as a carhop at the local hamburger stand. She later worked at Mr. Steak Restaurant, where she was promoted to floor supervisor.
During her senior year of high school, Becky met Gary Giudice through a mutual friend on December 19, 1970. The two quickly became inseparable. Money was often tight in those early days, but they always found creative ways to spend time together. They didn’t need much to have a good time, just each other’s company.
Becky and Gary were married on October 16, 1971, beginning a marriage that would span 55 years. Following their wedding, Becky left Mr. Steak and began working for the local newspaper. When their first child arrived in October 1973, she stepped away from work to care for their growing family. Their second child followed in May 1975, and Becky later returned to the newspaper as a rural route carrier.
Between working and raising her children, Becky always managed to make time for softball. She loved the game, and no matter how busy life became, the ball field was somewhere she wanted to be. Give her the chance to hear someone yell, “Play ball!” and she was ready.
In the spring of 1980, Becky and Gary packed up their family and moved to Worland, Wyoming, sight unseen. Worland became home, and Becky soon found herself busy with work, family, and the friendships she made along the way. She worked as a checker at Safeway, Go Gas and later waited tables at the Elks and Ranchito. Becky genuinely enjoyed serving others, and waitressing gave her the opportunity to do something that came naturally to her: take care of people and make them feel welcome.
Their family grew again with the birth of their third child in 1981 and fourth in 1983. With four children to raise, a household to manage, and jobs to work, Becky certainly had her hands full. Still, she found time for the softball games she enjoyed so much.
Throughout her years in Worland, Becky worked for Larry and Anne Hill at Rolling Hills Trucking, where the working relationship grew into a lasting friendship for both Becky and Gary. She also worked as a receptionist at Basin Clinic and later at NGP. Eventually, she joined the Washakie County Clerk’s Office, handling accounts payable and payroll. She retired after 12 years of service.
In 2015, Becky began dealing with an unknown illness that would bring years of challenges and uncertainty. Through it all, she leaned on her faith in God, facing each day with determination and trusting in the promises of her Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.
Becky’s Christian faith was an important part of who she was, particularly during the difficult years of her illness. She looked forward to the day she would hear the words, “Well done, my good and faithful servant.” Her family finds comfort in knowing that she is now at peace and resting in the presence of her Heavenly Father.
Becky was preceded in death by her parents, Robert and Lois Scott; sisters, Vivian McCann and Virginia Glen; and brother, Raymond Scott.
She is survived by her husband, Gary Giudice of Worland; sons, Jason (Maralee) Giudice of Worland and Anthony Giudice of Orofino, Idaho; daughters, Patricia Knopp of Laurel, Montana, and Christina Giudice of Worland; and sister, Marean Dyer of Hastings, Nebraska; grandchildren, Jerome, Tyler (Amanda), Garrett (Elizabeth Carver), Kyleigh (Raven) Heflin, Rhidge (Shayden), Brooks, Sabrina Knopp, Chloe (Noah) Shirley, Haylee (Juan) Giudice Lopez, Tate, Riley, and Bexley; six great-grandchildren, with two more on the way.

Kent George ProfitApril 21, 1944 – October 29, 2026Big Piney, WyomingShared by: Covill Funeral Home & CrematoryKent George Profit was born on April 21, 1944, to George Reginald Profit and Patricia Annette O’Brien in Seattle, Washington. He passed away peacefully at his home in Big Piney, Wyoming, on October 29, 2026, surrounded by loved ones here on earth and those that welcomed him in Heaven.
Kent’s family roots in Wyoming ran deep. His great-grandparents homesteaded in LaBarge, Wyoming, in 1912, and Kent spent his first-grade year there. His family later moved to Idaho, where he graduated from Middleton High School with the Class of 1962. No matter where life took them, the family always made their way back to the T.E. O’Brien Ranch in Big Piney. Those visits helped establish a lasting connection to the area Kent would eventually call home.
On September 26, 1970, Kent married Judith Ann Smith. Together, they welcomed two daughters, Tanya in September 1972 and Cheryl in January 1975.
Kent wore many hats throughout his life, but hard work was always a constant. He began his career as a truck driver at just 18 years old, an occupation he carried with him throughout his life. He eventually founded KP Trucking in the early 2000s and worked as an owner-operator across numerous industries. A man of exceptional work ethic, Kent was never intimidated by a challenging job. He took tremendous pride in what he did, and even in his later years, he could be found putting in a hard day’s work and tackling whatever project was in front of him. He was simply not one to sit still.
Kent’s life was filled with adventures and hobbies. In his younger years, he earned his private pilot’s license and shared plenty of stories about his flying adventures. He also spent time team roping, a passion he would enjoy even more in his later years. One of his proudest moments came when he and his partner, Bob Bing, competed in Rock Springs for a chance to qualify for the World Series of Team Roping in Las Vegas. With the top 50 teams qualifying for the payout, Kent and Bob finished 51st out of more than 300 teams. It was an accomplishment he was proud of and a memory he cherished.
In 1998, Kent earned one of his most treasured titles when he became Pa with the birth of his first grandson, Tanner Kent Elliott. He was soon joined by Mathiew Sage Pierce in 1999, Teagan James Elliott in 2002, and Ruby Judith Pierce in 2003. Known affectionately as Pa to his grandchildren, it didn’t take long before he became Pa to just about every kid who crossed his path.
Kent was one of his grandchildren’s biggest fans. Distance was never an excuse, and he made every effort to be there for their activities, games, and milestones. Even after his grandchildren graduated, his loyalty to the Big Piney Punchers never wavered. He continued traveling to away games and cheering from the stands at as many home games as he could. He was a proud grandfather, and his family always knew they had someone in their corner.
Kent was preceded in death by his parents, George and Annette Profit; his wife, Judy; his brother, Mike Profit, and sister-in-law, Ilene Profit; his sister, JaNeane Hays; and his grandson, Tanner Kent Elliott.
He is survived by his daughters, Tanya (Steven) Greenwell and Cheryl (Vince) Pierce; his grandchildren, Mathiew (Hannah) Pierce, Ruby Pierce, Devon Eddie, Teagan Elliott, Lainee Andersen, Ryan Hristco, Kimberly (Eric) Tuten, KC Greenwell, Tyler Greenwell, Trevor (Jenny) Greenwell, Shelby Greenwell, Sadie Greenwell, and Colter (Misty) Stene; his great-grandchildren, Athena and Aurora Tuten, Marshall Swett, Autumn and Kenna Pierce, Myles Kent Elliott, Jesalie, Mia and Jackson Greenwell, Blaze and Brody Oakley, Rosalie Greenwell, and Tatum, Harper, Raelynn, and Barrett Stene; his sisters, Toni David and Laurel Profit; along with several nieces and nephews.
It is nearly impossible to condense Kent’s big, full life into a few paragraphs. His work history alone could fill pages, and his adventures and stories could keep a room entertained for hours. But those who knew Kent don’t need an obituary to tell them who he was. They know the stories, the laughter, the determination, and the unmistakable presence that came with him.
Kent never met a stranger. He was genuinely interested in people, never missing an opportunity to hear someone’s story, strike up a conversation, or lend a helping hand. He lived life on his own terms, worked hard, played hard, loved his family, and left his mark on countless lives along the way.
He was a hardworking man, a proud father and grandfather, a loyal friend, and a cowboy through and through. His stories will be told for years to come, his presence will be deeply missed, and his legacy will live on through the many lives he touched.
Heaven gained one hell of a cowboy.

If you can’t be there in person, then please donate to a charity of your choice.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Pohutsky calls Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers a ‘betrayal’ of reproductive rights
description: For state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), the decision by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for U.S. Senate was a “betrayal” and “unconscionable,” a feeling shared by many Democrats — especially in terms of Rogers’ stance on abortion policy. “You either support reproductive rights or you support Mike Rogers. You can’t do both,” […]
text:
Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) speaks ahead of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signing the last bill in the Reproductive Health Act in Lansing on Dec. 11, 2023. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)For state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), the decision by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for U.S. Senate was a “betrayal” and “unconscionable,” a feeling shared by many Democrats — especially in terms of Rogers’ stance on abortion policy.
“You either support reproductive rights or you support Mike Rogers. You can’t do both,” she told Michigan Advance on Monday, a day after Stevens stunned her Democratic colleagues and appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church and endorsed his candidacy over that of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
Pohutsky said she and Stevens represented overlapping areas before Michigan’s 2022 redistricting, and she noted in an interview that “even after we no longer had overlapping geographical areas, we would frequently run into each other at reproductive rights events.”
That makes her endorsement of Rogers “a complete reversal on her position,” Pohutsky continued.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), tours the UA Local 333 training facility in Lansing, Mich. April 6, 2026 | Photo By Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
An attempt was made by the Advance to contact Stevens for comment, but was unsuccessful. If a comment is received, this story will be updated. Her chief of staff resigned on Sunday after Stevens endorsed Rogers, and said many other staffers had also quit.
Stevens has historically been an advocate for reproductive rights in her time as a legislator. A Planned Parenthood Action Fund endorsement page from her 2020 congressional campaign called her a “champion for reproductive health care.” She received a 100% score from Reproductive Freedom For All, and an “F” rating from anti-abortion group SBA Pro-Life America. And in a competitive 2022 primary following the U.S. Supreme Court decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, Stevens put her gender at the forefront of the race in her support of abortion rights.
But now one of those same groups, Reproductive Freedom For All, is describing Stevens’ decision as “giving cover” to Rogers, a vocally and historically anti-abortion legislator.
The group’s president and CEO, Mini Timmaraju, said in a statement criticizing Stevens “Nothing can erase Mike Rogers’ votes or make him any less dangerous to our reproductive freedom.”
Rogers was condemned by Democrats for a radio interview with conservative Christian talk radio host Bob Dutko in October in which he pointed to his “100% pro-life rating” while previously in Congress, and assured Dutko that there was no concern that he would join Democrats on social issues in the Senate, including abortion rights. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While Democratic Party leaders called it proof that Rogers would vote for a nationwide abortion ban, Rogers quickly pushed back on social media, reposting a video in which he said that when it comes to abortion, “Michigan voters have already decided the issue, and I respect that decision.”
Though Michigan enshrined reproductive rights in its state constitution in 2022, many have warned that a constitutional convention — which is a ballot measure, Proposal One, in Tuesday’s election — could open the door to reversing that.
“This is a battle that we are never going to have to stop fighting. I think that if we learned anything from the Dobbs decision, it’s that this is never going to be over,” Pohutsky said. “Just because we’ve enshrined it in our constitution, we can’t let our foot off the gas. Between Mike Rogers and Proposal 1 being on the ballot, there are existential threats to reproductive rights right now this election cycle, and I don’t think that’s going to change anytime soon.”
On Stevens supporting Rogers and supporting abortion rights, Pohutsky said, “Those two things cannot exist in the same space.”

title: Commentary: Rural South Dakota’s growth strategy has to start under a roof
description: On any given day in Sisseton, Milbank or Winner, you will pass an employer with a hiring sign in the window, or you will see an advertisement on social media or in the local newspaper. Some have been advertising for six months. Some for a year. The applicants are out there, and they’re interested. The […]
text:
One of the ways Lakota Tech High School is finding housing for teachers is using state grant funding to help build homes like these for teachers on the Pine Ridge Reservation. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)On any given day in Sisseton, Milbank or Winner, you will pass an employer with a hiring sign in the window, or you will see an advertisement on social media or in the local newspaper. Some have been advertising for six months. Some for a year. The applicants are out there, and they’re interested. The shift schedule is written. What is missing is the second half of the equation: somewhere for those workers to live.
That gap is the most consistent story I hear throughout rural South Dakota. Our economy is doing its part. Our housing has stopped keeping up with what that economy is asking of it.
Founded in 2007, GROW South Dakota is a statewide nonprofit advancing rural housing, community development and economic opportunity across South Dakota. Each year, we provide down payment assistance, mortgage lending and housing counseling to hundreds of families, and help rural school districts, agricultural employers and manufacturers address one of their newest strategic challenges.
New program provides 5% down payment for qualifying South Dakota homebuyers

Housing challenges look different in rural South Dakota. Often, it’s a home that is too expensive to repair for what it’s worth, a contractor driving hours to reach a job site, or a lender without enough comparable sales to finance a modest home in a small town. Distance becomes part of the cost of housing, even if it never appears on a closing statement.
Those challenges also affect our employers. Manufacturers, health care providers, schools and agricultural businesses tell us their employees struggle to find housing. In my conversations with nearby communities, I consistently hear that they need additional homes to keep up with the people who want to live and work there. We’ve seen nurses and teachers accept positions, only to discover there isn’t a home available within a reasonable commute. Housing is an economic development issue as much as a community development one.
The challenges are even greater for many of our tribal communities, where decades of limited access to mortgage financing have made homeownership hard to achieve. That’s why partnerships matter. Organizations like Lakota Funds, the NeighborWorks Dakota Coalition and the South Dakota Native Homeownership Coalition are helping expand opportunity through collaboration, patient investment and trusted local relationships. Building homeownership on tribal land doesn’t happen overnight. It takes time, persistence and people who are committed to showing up year after year.
GROW SD is part of the NeighborWorks America network, a national platform of nearly 250 community-based housing organizations working in almost every state, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. Closer to home, we are one of four members of the NeighborWorks Dakota Coalition, which serves rural and Native communities across South and North Dakota.
In fiscal year 2025, coalition members helped 117 households become homeowners. That same year, our four organizations used $1.59 million in NeighborWorks America grants to leverage more than $213 million in total investment, or $134 for every grant dollar. In our state of South Dakota, where the margins on any single project are thin and the distances between projects are long, that multiplier is not a talking point. It is the difference between a project happening this year or not happening at all.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
What is needed is the right type of financing tools that are built for towns our size, technical support designed for rural areas and partners patient enough to measure success in years rather than quarters.
We know many of the solutions because we’ve seen them work. When housing is part of an economic development conversation from the beginning, communities are better positioned to grow. When builders, lenders, employers and local leaders work together, they can create opportunities that wouldn’t happen alone. Rural communities have always found ways to solve problems by working together, and housing is no different.
The hiring signs you see in Sisseton, Milbank, Winner and communities across South Dakota tell us employers believe in the future of rural America. Our responsibility is to make sure families find a place to live when those opportunities come. That’s how communities grow. Not all at once, but one home, one family and one neighborhood at a time.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Supreme Court upholds ruling keeping nonprofit out of PSC docket
description: The Alabama Supreme Court Friday upheld a lower court ruling preventing a nonprofit organization from weighing in on how Alabama Power charges customers for fuel used to generate electricity. The court said that the Public Service Commission acted within its jurisdiction in denying  Energy Alabama, which advocates for more renewable energy use in the state, [...]
text:
The Heflin-Torbert Judicial Building in downtown Montgomery, Alabama, seen on January 24, 2023. The Alabama Supreme Court Friday upheld a lower court ruling preventing a nonprofit from intervening in a docket on the costs Alabama Power charges customers for fuel used to generate electricity. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Supreme Court Friday upheld a lower court ruling preventing a nonprofit organization from weighing in on how Alabama Power charges customers for fuel used to generate electricity.
The court said that the Public Service Commission acted within its jurisdiction in denying  Energy Alabama, which advocates for more renewable energy use in the state, the ability to intervene in a docket to decide the rate ECR (Energy Cost Recovery) that Alabama Power gets to charge its customers.
“The Legislature did not establish an all-purpose right of intervention into any and all commission business,” Associate Justice Will Parker wrote in the ruling issued Friday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Daniel Tait, executive director for Energy Alabama, said Friday in a statement “we’re not deterred” even with the ruling.
“We will keep pushing for lower bills and more transparency at the commission,” he said. “Alabama Power customers cannot continue paying some of the highest bills in the country. We believe that the public deserves a seat at the table.”
A message was sent to Alabama Power on Monday seeking comment.
ECR is the amount that the power company is allowed to charge customers when it buys the fuel it needs to generate electricity. Alabama Power submits a filing each month that the PSC uses to decide the appropriate rate. The rate fluctuates based on the price of fuel at the time.
The PSC first set the rate in 1981, but then opened other proceedings in 2005 and 2008 and increased the “factor” both times, according to the ruling. The PSC may also issue consent orders to adjust the rate ECR, which the agency has done using the most recent docket in 2008.
In March 2024, shortly after Alabama Power submitted its monthly filing for rate ECR, Energy Alabama sought to intervene in the 2008 docket. However, the PSC denied Energy Alabama in August because “there is no pending Rate ECR ‘proceeding’” in which Energy Alabama may intervene.
Energy Alabama appealed the decision to the Montgomery Circuit Court in December 2024. Montgomery Circuit Court Judge Brooke Reid ruled against Energy Alabama in August 2025, saying that the PSC did not make its decision based on fraud or reach a decision that did not align with the evidence.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Lawsuit accuses Mercer County of illegally housing children in adult jail
description: Mercer County officials illegally housed a 16-year-old boy in the adult jail, where he got pepper-sprayed and strip-searched, the suit says.
text:
The Mercer County Correction Center on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A 16-year-old Mercer County boy spent several weeks incarcerated in an adult jail, where he endured strip searches and got pepper-sprayed while naked, all in violation of state law and his constitutional rights, a new lawsuit charges.
A state judge twice sent the boy to the Mercer County Correction Center after his August 2024 arrest even though the state Youth Justice Commission twice warned officials the placement was illegal, ordered his transfer to a juvenile facility, and told them to “immediately cease” detaining youth in the adult jail, according to the civil rights lawsuit filed Monday in state Superior Court.
The New Jersey Code of Juvenile Justice prohibits placing anyone under 18 in any prison, jail, or other adult lockup and prioritizes rehabilitation over punishment.
Yet the boy, who is identified only as W.H. in the lawsuit, spent two two-week stints in October and November 2024 at the county jail and said he heard and saw another underage boy there too.
Repeatedly detaining children in adult jails, especially after receiving written notice from the state not to do so, suggests the court and county have a policy, practice, and custom of violating the constitutional rights of children in their custody, attorneys Alexander Shalom and Jennifer Bagger Jamerson wrote in their complaint. It also amounts to deliberate indifference and cruel and unusual punishment, especially given that W.H. was being held pretrial and hadn’t been adjudicated delinquent, the attorneys added.
Children in the youth justice system, as some of the state’s most vulnerable residents, require more protection — and are given it under state law, which recognizes that children are more susceptible to harm and more capable of rehabilitation, Shalom said.
“New Jersey has had for many years a law in the books that says you can’t house children in adult jails, and that’s for darn good reason,” Shalom said. “Notwithstanding that, they held a 16-year-old in an adult jail, which is just so anathema to our code of youth justice, which is supposed to be for the betterment of the child and for their rehabilitation. We know that’s not what adult jails are about. We think that’s crazy, and that our client is entitled to recompense for their flagrant violation of the law.”
The lawsuit names as defendants Judge Rodney Thompson, who presides over family court in Superior Court’s Mercer County vicinage and signed the orders under which W.H. was placed in the county jail; Mercer County Executive Dan Benson; and Timothy Friel, the jail’s warden. Spokespeople for the county and courts did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Mercer County Correction Center on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Mercer County doesn’t have a juvenile detention facility and typically houses in-custody youth in neighboring counties that do, like Middlesex County.
After W.H. got arrested, Thompson sent him to Mercer House, a youth shelter, according to the lawsuit. He ran away a few weeks later, police found and rearrested him, and Thompson ordered him to be placed in the adult jail, the lawsuit says. Conditions are so bad in the century-old jail, an 871-bed, mixed-custody men’s facility just outside Lambertville, that inmates have sued and officials began calling for its closure a decade ago.
W.H. spent two weeks at the county jail before officers took him back to the youth shelter, but he got into a fight there and landed back to court, where Thompson returned him to the county jail for another two weeks, the lawsuit says. He later got transferred to juvenile detention facilities in Middlesex and Essex counties before being released to a relative in February 2025, the lawsuit says.
Thompson and other officials “went beyond what was necessary to accomplish any legitimate penological objective,” Shalom and Jamerson wrote. They shouldn’t have illegally placed him in an adult jail, but once they did, they shouldn’t have strip-searched and pepper-sprayed him, held him alone in a cell that had no mattress or pillow the first night, and placed him where he could see and hear adult inmates, who he found intimidating, the attorneys said.
Those traumatic, degrading experiences left him with lasting emotional and psychological injuries, they wrote.
They want a judge to declare both W.H.’s 2024 detention and the practice of placing children in adult jails an unconstitutional violation of state law and prohibit officials from placing any other youth in adult lockups.
W.H.’s placement in the adult jail came at a time when the state was struggling with a shortage of juvenile detention space. Only seven counties in New Jersey have juvenile detention facilities — Atlantic, Bergen, Camden, Essex, Middlesex, Morris, and Ocean. The other 14 counties typically contract with those seven counties for their youth detention needs.
In a lawsuit filed in September 2024, Atlantic County accused the Youth Justice Commission of shirking its duty to manage where youth charged with crimes should be housed and booting that responsibility to the counties. Atlantic County officials complained that overcrowding led to riots and delays in youth placements.
A judge ruled in the county’s favor in December 2024, declared the commission solely responsible for youth detention statewide, and ordered commission officials to take charge.

title: Few apartments are open for low-income renters, but cost drops in some cities
description: Fewer than 1 in 20 rental listings across the largest U.S. cities are flagged as reserved for renters under an income limit, according to new data from Apartments.com. But average income-restricted rent fell year over year in 13 of the 50 markets, compared with three for market-rate rent. Just 4.6% of listings across the 50 […]
text:
Few rental listings across the largest U.S. cities are flagged as reserved for renters under an income limit, according to a new analysis. (Wyatt Gordon/The Virginia Mercury)Fewer than 1 in 20 rental listings across the largest U.S. cities are flagged as reserved for renters under an income limit, according to new data from Apartments.com.
But average income-restricted rent fell year over year in 13 of the 50 markets, compared with three for market-rate rent.
Just 4.6% of listings across the 50 largest metro areas were listed as “income-restricted” in the third quarter of this year, whether through public housing, a housing voucher or as a tax-credit property, the report by the rental listing site said. 
The finding was based on a sample of more than 70,000 active listings out of the site’s full inventory of over a million apartments.
Feds encourage public housing authorities to impose work rules, time limits

Washington, D.C., while being one of the most expensive housing markets in the country, has the most available income-restricted units at 227, the report said. 
San Antonio, Texas, had the highest share of income-restricted listings, at 12.4% of its total listings, followed by Austin at 11.7% and then two Virginia cities: Richmond and Norfolk at 10%.
On the other end of the spectrum, the San Francisco Bay area stood at 4.2%.
Income-restricted rents average $988 per month in Detroit, the lowest price among the 50 markets measured. Averaged across all 50 metros, income-restricted rent came to $1,448 a month in the third quarter. Market-rate rent averaged $1,756.
Proposed changes to federal housing assistance programs could further affect the income-restricted market.
Stateline previously reported that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has proposed allowing public housing authorities and certain property owners to impose work requirements and time limits on some rental assistance recipients.
Stateline reporter Robbie Sequeira can be reached at rsequeira@stateline.org.

Dover Police Arrest 18-Year-Old in Shooting That Struck Home With Child Inside
POLICE LOG – November 2, 2026
DOVER, DE — Dover Police have arrested an 18-year-old man in connection with a shooting that damaged an occupied home and a parked vehicle in the 500 block of River Road on October 27, 2026.
The shooting occurred at approximately 4:22 p.m. near River Road and Sussex Avenue. Police said gunfire struck a second-story window of a residence where a 10-year-old girl was inside. A parked, unoccupied vehicle was also struck. No injuries were reported.
Officers recovered multiple shell casings during a search of the area. Investigators initially described three male suspects wearing dark clothing.
Through their investigation, detectives identified the 18-year-old as one of the suspects involved in the shooting.
On October 30, officers took the suspect into custody during a traffic stop near East Water Street and New Castle Avenue in Dover.
The suspect was charged with possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, possession of a firearm by a person prohibited, possession of ammunition by a person prohibited, first-degree reckless endangering, discharging a firearm at a vehicle, and two counts of criminal mischief under $1,000.
He was committed to Sussex Correctional Institution (SCI) on a $29,500 cash bond.
Police have not released the suspect’s name in accordance with Delaware’s House Bill 59, which restricts the release of certain identifying information about individuals charged with crimes.
The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information about the shooting is asked to contact the Dover Police Department at 302-736-7111.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio voters cast more than 1.7 million ballots early, surpassing 2022 totals
description: Ohioans cast more than 1.7 million ballots early this year, either in person, through the mail, or a drop box. That total is 17% higher than the early vote total for the last midterm election in 2022. Democratic voters outpaced Republicans slightly — casting roughly 468,000 ballots to the GOP’s 432,000. Unaffiliated voters, being the […]
text:
Early voting in Ohio at the Franklin County Board of Elections. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal) Ohioans cast more than 1.7 million ballots early this year, either in person, through the mail, or a drop box. That total is 17% higher than the early vote total for the last midterm election in 2022.
Democratic voters outpaced Republicans slightly — casting roughly 468,000 ballots to the GOP’s 432,000. Unaffiliated voters, being the vast majority of Ohio voters, swamped them both, with nearly 807,000 ballots.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The distribution of those votes looks pretty different than it did just four years ago.
In 2022, voters cast absentee ballots through the mail or a drop box at a nearly 2-to-1 rate. In that election, 918,333 Ohioans voted by mail compared with roughly 550,092 who showed up early in person.
This year, that relationship has nearly flipped. Almost 1.1 million voters showed up in person at the county board, while only 632,254 Ohioans voted at their mailbox.
That trend persists at the county level, too. Comparing the final tallies between 2022 and 2026, every county reported an increase in voters showing up to vote early in-person.
In nearly a third of Ohio counties, the 2026 figure was double or more than the early in-person total from 2022. At the same time, no county matched its mail voting totals from the last election.
Cuyahoga County came closest to meeting its 2022 mail voting totals. The nearly 107,000 ballots voters returned amounts to 78.29% of the number returned in 2022.
The biggest fall off was in deep-southern Ohio’s Lawrence County. Voters there mailed in just 57% as many ballots as they did in 2022. Meanwhile, Lawrence’s early in person vote increased more than three-fold — the biggest jump in the state.
The shift away from mail voting is significant but perhaps not that surprising.
University of Akron political scientist David Cohen chalked it up to President Trump railing against mail voting “for the last 20 months.”
“He has tried to put in place things with the U.S. Postal Service that will make it, potentially more difficult for people to vote by mail, or may put their ballots at risk if they do end up voting,” Cohen said.
The president’s effort to leverage the postal service was ultimately turned away by the U.S. Supreme Court. Center of Election Innovation and Research Executive Director David Becker praised that decision in September.
“These rules would have done nothing for election integrity,” he said, “but would have imposed a vast and expensive new bureaucracy on the states, given massive new responsibilities to a Postal Service already overwhelmed by its current core responsibilities, and disenfranchised thousands if not millions of eligible voters.”
Also, in the lead-up to this election, Ohio lawmakers nixed the state’s absentee ballot grace period, meaning any ballots arriving after Election Day will not be counted.
How to vote now
Despite a significant uptick in early voting this election cycle, there are still millions of Ohioans who have yet to cast a ballot.
If you plan to vote in person on Election Day, you can find your polling place through your county board of elections; this tool on the Ohio Secretary of State’s website will get you there quickly.
Also, don’t forget to bring along an unexpired, approved photo ID, like a driver’s license, military ID, or U.S. passport.
According to Ohio Secretary of State data, more than 104,000 Ohioans who requested an absentee ballot haven’t returned it yet. If you’re one of those voters, you shouldn’t put your ballot in the mail. Instead, your best bet is to bring your ballot to your county board of elections on Election Day. To be counted, all absentee ballots must to be in the hands of county election officials by 7:30 pm on Election Day.
Voters who previously requested a mail ballot but show up to vote on Election Day anyway, will have to vote provisionally, to ensure only one ballot gets counted.
If you put your ballot in the mail already, you can track it here.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Three authors sue over Alabama library restrictions on transgender content
description: Three authors and a free-speech organization Friday filed a federal civil lawsuit against the state board overseeing Alabama’s libraries, alleging  a rule that limits minors’ access to books with transgender-related content violates the First Amendment. The plaintiffs argue the code changes approved by the Alabama Public Library Service last November amount [...]
text:
Books in the young adult section of the Ozark - Dale County Library Wednesday, Aug. 30, 2023 in Ozark, Ala. A lawsuit filed by three authors and a nonprofit alleges that Alabama Public Library Service administrative code changes restricting books with LGBTQ+ themes violates the First Amendment. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)Three authors and a free-speech organization Friday filed a federal civil lawsuit against the state board overseeing Alabama’s libraries, alleging  a rule that limits minors’ access to books with transgender-related content violates the First Amendment.
The plaintiffs argue the code changes approved by the Alabama Public Library Service last November amount to content-based discrimination.
“I think that having a small group of people decide what is right, not only for their own children but for the children and the families of every family in Alabama, is unconstitutional,” said Kit Rosewater, an author and one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, in an interview Monday. “I think it violates the First Amendment, freedom of speech, which I believe includes the freedom to read. Whether appointed or not, I think this level of power is outside of the position that anyone should hold of dictating what access families have to different literature.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A message seeking comment was sent to APLS Board Chair John Wahl, the Republican nominee for Alabama lieutenant governor, on Monday. APLS had not filed a response as of Monday afternoon.
Rosewater authored a book called “Buried Feelings,” published in July. The book is about the friendship between two high school students, one of whom is a transgender boy. However, Rosewater said that one library told her it feared stocking the book, named a Junior Library Guild Gold Standard Selection, because of the Board’s restrictions on transgender content.
APLS voted to change the administrative code to prohibit library materials with transgender-related content in the children’s section of libraries last November.
The board added language stating that “any materials regarding transgender procedures, gender ideology, or the concept of more than two biological genders shall be considered inappropriate for children and youth.”
Board members did not define the meaning of gender ideology in the proposed changes.
It marked the second time since 2023 that APLS modified its administrative code to limit minors from having access to specific library materials. In May 2024, APLS revised the code to require local libraries to create policies that prevent books that are either obscene or considered “sexually explicit or other material deemed inappropriate for children or youth” from areas in libraries designated for minors.
Two other authors are also plaintiffs in the case. Page Powars wrote “But I Hate Him,” which features that features two teen boys locked in an academic rivalry at an elite summer camp. Phoenix McDonald wrote “The Hidden Continent,” which has LGBTQ+ characters.
Plaintiffs allege in the lawsuit that the rule is unconstitutional because it violates the First Amendment rights of specific groups, like members of Read Freely Alabama, a grass-roots organization whose members are unable to borrow library books with transgender-related content, and hinders the financial interests of authors who write books about transgender issues.
The lawsuit also states the language in the administrative code is vague and overly broad. One example cited in the complaint is “Twelfth Night” by William Shakespeare because “the character Viola disguises herself as a young male page and falls into a love triangle in which the other two characters mistake Viola’s gender.”
“Readers, specifically young readers, who walk into places like libraries, look around and either not see themselves reflected if they identify as a transgender person, or they are just not going to see the mention of transgender people,” Rosewater said of the APLS rules. “Culturally, we lose empathy, we lose compassion, and then we lose support and validation of a very small part of the population who has already been picked on from every possible angle.”

Photo: Getty Images Crime. For decades, it’s long been a tried-and-true election tactic of the American political right to campaign under the “get tough on crime” banner.
The model was cynically perfected during the 1988 presidential campaign in the infamous and racially charged “Willie Horton” ads crafted by supporters of then-Vice President George H.W. Bush to attack Democratic nominee Michael Dukakis.
That said, the practice goes back at least as far as the 1968 presidential campaigns of Richard Nixon and George Wallace and has continued right through to the present day.
You’ve seen and know these ads. An ominous sounding narrator describes a horrific crime allegedly attributable to the “soft” policies of the attacked candidate. Frequently, the ads play the race card by highlighting situations in which the crime victim is white, and the perpetrator is a person of color. In the ‘88 campaign, it was Bush’s top campaign aide Lee Atwater who even went so far as to rename the offender in question — William Horton — as “Willie” in a blatant effort to play up racist stereotypes.
Of course, it must be said that there has sometimes been more to the political right’s crime-oriented politicking than mere campaign ads. Conservative politicians have also often followed up on the ads by enacting new laws and policies that lengthen criminal sentences, limit the rights of people accused of crimes, and even militarize law enforcement.
Some of these “get tough” policies have probably made a modest difference in some places and some situations, while many – think of the ill-fated and disastrous “war on drugs” and President Trump’s cruel ongoing war on immigrants — have done little more than erode the Constitution cause our prisons to overflow and become breeding grounds for hopelessness and more crime.
If, however, there’s a most maddening aspect to the right’s longstanding obsession with “crime” – one that fuels the suspicion that the whole thing is more about stoking the fears of white voters, abetting misogyny and winning elections than effectively addressing the issue – it’s the way conservative politicians have so often ignored and undermined the kinds of unsexy policies that can make a real difference.
A recent report authored by NC Newsline journalist Greg Childress – “Worrisome domestic violence statistics aren’t declining in NC” — serves to highlight this sobering reality.
As Childress reported, “In 2025, more than 63,000 people in North Carolina reported being victims of a crime committed by current or former spouses, partners or family members, according to a report released this week by the state’s Criminal Justice Analysis Center.”
The story goes on to report this truly remarkable fact: “Domestic and family violence in 2025 accounted for the majority of murders of women and girls in the state, and more than half of reported kidnappings and simple assaults, according to the report.”
In view of such large and disturbing numbers, you’d think that supporting programs and policies that target domestic violence and aid its victims would be a top, if not the top, law enforcement priority for elected officials.
Unfortunately, that’s not been the case. As Childress also reported, funding for programs that combat domestic violence has declined significantly under the budgets crafted by Republicans in Washington and Raleigh in recent years.
This is from the story:
“Elizabeth Sager, director of evaluation at the N.C. Coalition Against Domestic Violence, said the reduced funding has caused several domestic violence organizations to close over the last three years. ‘Other agencies have had to take on neighboring counties to cover that population, and there’s one right now that just launched a GoFundMe campaign so that they can try to keep their doors open,’ Sager said.”
Think about that for a moment. A domestic violence program – the one to which Sager referred is a Greenville-based program that serves Pitt, Martin and Washington counties – is having to beg for online donations to stay open at the same time that conservative politicians who’ve been crafting our state and national budgets are waving the “tough on crime” flag.
It’s hard to imagine a more obvious and disturbing bit of political hypocrisy.
Of course, the hard and sad reality is that it’s not possible to mobilize the right’s political base – which tends to tilt white, male and macho – with ads or policies that promote funding for programs largely run by women for women and children seeking to escape abusive partners.
Especially during weekend football games, it’s better to run ads that play to racial and gender fantasies and stereotypes. Never mind that given the widely accepted connection between big games and violence toward women, a more accurate anti-crime ad might feature promises to “get tough” on beer-swilling knuckleheads who take out their frustrations over their favorite teams’ performances and their gambling losses on their wives and kids.
The bottom line: criminal behavior is and always has been a vexingly complex problem that cries out for dispassionate and bipartisan policies grounded in data and backed by adequate funding. Right now, this is an area in which North Carolina is falling well short.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn took campaign gifts from TVA board nominees while backing their candidacies
description: This story was originally published by The Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis.
