A veteran Memphis healthcare executive, Graves had been nominated by President Trump to serve on the board of the Tennessee Valley Authority, and Black[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, photographed at an August 2026 event, is one of several senators who received campaign donations from nominees to the Tennessee Valley Authority Board of Directors. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)This story was originally published by The Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis.
Marsha Blackburn brimmed with enthusiasm when she introduced Mitch Graves at a Senate confirmation hearing last fall.
A veteran Memphis healthcare executive, Graves had been nominated by President Trump to serve on the board of the Tennessee Valley Authority, and Blackburn left no doubt she was solidly behind the president’s pick.
“He represents the best of Tennessee’s business and civic leadership,’’ Senator Blackburn told her colleagues in formally introducing Graves, the CEO of the West Cancer Center & Research Institute. “And I’m confident that his experience and dedication will continue to serve our state and nation well.”
What Blackburn didn’t say is that days earlier, she had accepted more than $58,000 from Graves and five of his associates at the West Cancer Center for her then recently opened campaign for Tennessee governor.
Though legal, the campaign donations trouble critics who say these types of financial gifts give the appearance that our government is for sale, eroding the public’s faith in our democratic system.
“It taints government officials as to who they’re paying attention to,’’ said Craig Holman, a legislative representative for Public Citizen, a left-leaning government ethics watchdog group.
“They’re supposed to work in the public interest, but when they have to rely on money from private individuals and private sources, they lose sight of the public interest. And now they’re promoting really the private interests of whoever gives them the most amount of money. And that will not be the American public.”
The Senate later confirmed Graves, who now serves as the influential board chairman at TVA, the federally owned power company that provides electricity to some 10 million people across Tennessee and six other states. Board members earn a reported $60,000 to $70,000 a year.
Graves isn’t an isolated case.
Tennessee Valley Authority Board Chair Mitch Graves (Photo from TVA.com)
An analysis of federal and state campaign finance reports by the Institute for Public Service Reporting found that four of President Trump’s nominees to the TVA board made generous campaign contributions to a series of Republican politicians, including three GOP senators, while their senate confirmation proceedings were underway. Two of the three senators who accepted these campaign contributions — Blackburn and her fellow Tennessee senator Bill Hagerty — had pushed Trump to fire several TVA board members, creating vacancies on the board.
In one case, Randall Jones, an insurance agent and nominee from Alabama, gave $20,000 in donations to the gubernatorial campaign of that state’s Republican senator, Tommy Tuberville. Tuberville endorsed Jones with high praise at his confirmation hearing. Jones’ company, Randy Jones & Associates, gave another $5,000 to Tuberville on October 27, 2025, five days after the senate hearing and while the confirmation process was still underway.
The Institute’s analysis also found that Knoxville lawyer Jeff Hagood, another Trump nominee who joined the TVA board in January, gave Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign $10,600 last October. That donation came less than three weeks before the Oct. 22, 2025 hearing of the Senate’s Environment and Public Works Committee, where Blackburn spoke glowingly of both Graves and Hagood.
Graves, Hagood and Jones were confirmed by the Senate on December 18.
A fourth nominee, former Nashville auto executive Lee Beaman, gave Blackburn’s campaign $10,600, records show. That same day — Aug. 21, 2025 — Beaman’s wife Julie gave another $10,600. Those donations came about 15 weeks before Blackburn introduced Beaman to the Senate committee that December, saying he had “demonstrated a longstanding commitment to giving back financially to causes that support Tennesseans, and make their lives and our communities better”.
A major Republican donor who over the years has given more than $170,000 to Blackburn’s political campaigns, Beaman failed to win Senate confirmation amid strong opposition from Democrats.
The Institute made multiple attempts to seek comment from Blackburn, Hagerty, Tuberville, Graves, Hagood, Jones, Beaman and others mentioned in this article but none responded. A phone message and email left for Tennessee Republican Party Chair Scott Golden, who once served as then-Congresswoman Blackburn’s deputy chief of staff, also went unanswered. The White House, too, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A similar review of contributions to the gubernatorial campaign of Democrat Jerri Green, who faces Blackburn in Tuesday’s governor’s election, found no contributions from current TVA board members or the recent nominees.
Lee Beaman, Nashville businessman and conservative donor gave U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn $10,700 a few months before she introduced him as a nominee to the Tennessee Valley Authority board. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
 Series of payments before hearing

In addition to Mitch Graves’ long career in the healthcare industry, he had served since 2016 on the board of Memphis Light, Gas & Water, TVA’s largest customer.
On July 1, 2025, Trump nominated Graves to the TVA board along with Hagood and Beaman, stirring instant applause from Blackburn and Hagerty.
“The Tennessee Valley Authority is a critical part of our nation’s energy security, and we are pleased that President Trump has nominated three competent and visionary Tennesseans to the board who will help achieve America’s nuclear renaissance and deliver affordable and abundant energy,’’ the senators said in a joint statement. “These nominees are a strong departure from the Biden-era TVA board which failed to meet the moment. We urge colleagues to swiftly confirm President Trump’s TVA board nominees to make certain the United States leads the world in next-generation nuclear and wins the global race for energy dominance.”
Then the campaign donations started pouring in.
Over eight days that October, Graves and his colleagues at the West Cancer Center made a series of contributions to Blackburn.
On October 7, West Cancer Center’s chairman emeritus Kurt Tauer and chief medical officer Sylvia Richey gave Blackburn $10,600 each, the maximum allowed under Tennessee law. Five days later, on October 12, chief financial officer James Cagle gave $10,600 and oncologist Jason Chandler gave $5,300. Then, on October 14, Graves and chief operating officer Candace Wilder donated $10,600 each.
The limit for an individual’s contribution to a candidate running for a statewide election in Tennessee, such as the governor’s race, is $10,600 — $5,300 for the primary and another $5,300 for the general election.
Graves and the other West Cancer Center employees and officials have made campaign contributions to politicians in the past, but the contributions made in 2025 to Blackburn’s campaign stand out in their scale. The campaign contributions made by Graves and his five colleagues, to all candidates in federal races or statewide elections in Tennessee, totaled $31,300 in 2023 and $17,500 in 2024. In contrast, in those eight days in October 2025, Graves and his five colleagues contributed $58,300 to Blackburn’s campaign.
According to Public Citizens’ Holman, the contributions also stand out for their timing.
“The timing of it is very funny,’’ said Holman, who favors replacing the country’s private campaign contribution system with public financing of elections. “The timing of it reveals exactly what the purpose of private campaign contributions are all about. And that is to curry favor with public officials. That’s exactly what’s going on here. These individuals and businesses are actually endearing themselves to Blackburn with very sizable contributions.”
Graves joined TVA’s board of directors in January. In March, the TVA announced that the board had selected him to become its chair through April 1, 2027. Hagood was appointed the chair-elect, and is scheduled to succeed Graves as chair, serving in the role through May 2029.
Longtime TVA critic Stephen Smith said news of the contributions Blackburn accepted doesn’t surprise him. Though he hasn’t seen anything quite like this in his 30 years of studying TVA, times have changed, he said. Trump has set a new tone of questionable conduct in government, and loyalists like Blackburn are simply following his lead, he said.
“It’s all pay for play now with Trump,’’ said Smith, executive director of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, a Knoxville-based nonprofit. “So, they’re just going along with the zeitgeist of the day… Marsha Blackburn is so allegiant to Trump. She is probably one of the tightest MAGA acolytes of Trump.’’

 Contributions to Hagerty, Kustoff

Plans to retool TVA’s board stretch back to the early days of Trump’s second presidency.
On March 20, 2025, senators Blackburn and Hagerty published an op-ed in Power Magazine calling on President Trump to revamp the board.
“The presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed, TVA Board of Directors lacks the talent, experience, and gravitas to meet a challenge that clearly requires visionary industrial leaders,’’ Blackburn and Hagerty wrote in the article. “The group looks more like a collection of political operatives than visionary industrial leaders.”
Two days earlier, on March 18, Graves had made a campaign contribution of $800 to Hagerty. His wife Kelly Jo had made another contribution — $5,000 — to the senator on the same day.
Trump responded to the appeal by the Tennessee senators by firing three of the TVA’s board members. On July 1, 2025, he nominated four new members — Graves, Hagood, Beaman, and Jones.
Since then, TVA has reversed several changes from the Biden era and earlier. It has backed away from renewable energy and reversed the planned closing of major coal plants.
The TVA board’s role has assumed greater political significance in recent months as it sets electricity rates for a burgeoning number of data centers in these states. For instance, in February, the TVA board of directors that included Graves and Hagood, voted unanimously to double the amount of electricity Elon Musk’s xAI data center operations in Memphis can take from the TVA grid. In August, the TVA board imposed a 10% increase in electricity rates for AI data centers.
In October 2025, Hagerty helped introduce Graves and Hagood to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, alongside Blackburn. Hagerty said, “Mitch Graves and Jeff Hagood understand the responsibility before them. They recognize that TVA’s role in deploying advanced nuclear technologies is central to not just Tennessee’s prosperity, but to America’s national security and global competitiveness.”
While the Senate confirmation proceedings were still underway, on November 10, Graves made a $4,000 contribution to Hagerty’s campaign.
David Kustoff, a Republican member of the U.S. House from Tennessee, also supported Graves’ nomination and submitted a formal letter in support of him. During the hearing, Graves thanked Kustoff for his support. On March 19, the day after Graves and his wife had made campaign contributions to Hagerty, Graves contributed $5,000 to Kustoff. That same day, Graves’ colleague and the CFO of West Cancer Center, James Cagle, also gave $3,500 to Kustoff.
On December 9, 2025, less than two weeks before the Senate was to vote on Graves’ nomination, West Cancer Center’s chairman emeritus Tauer donated $2,000 to Kustoff.
Graves was confirmed by the Senate, along with Hagood, on December 18.
In a press release the following day, Kustoff congratulated Graves on the appointment. He wrote, “I applaud the U.S. Senate’s vote today confirming Mitch Graves to the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA)’s Board of Directors. President Trump made an outstanding choice nominating Mitch Graves for the TVA Board of Directors.” Kustoff concluded, “Thank you to Senator Marsha Blackburn and Senator Bill Hagerty for their support of this important nomination.”

title: Green Party secretary of state candidate charges Republican impersonated him in text message
description: Pete Karas, the Green Party candidate in the race for Wisconsin secretary of state, filed a complaint Monday against Republican candidate Jay Schroeder, charging that Schroeder’s campaign impersonated Karas in text messages sent to voters over the weekend. The complaint, filed with the Wisconsin Elections Commission,  alleges that Schroeder’s campaign violat[...]
text:
Pete Karas, left, the Green Party candidate for Wisconsin secretary of state, has filed a complaint charging that Republican candidate Jay Schroeder, right, impersonated him in campaign text messages sent over the weekend. (Campaign photos)Pete Karas, the Green Party candidate in the race for Wisconsin secretary of state, filed a complaint Monday against Republican candidate Jay Schroeder, charging that Schroeder’s campaign impersonated Karas in text messages sent to voters over the weekend.
The complaint, filed with the Wisconsin Elections Commission,  alleges that Schroeder’s campaign violated a Wisconsin law against publishing “a false representation pertaining to a candidate or referendum which is intended or tends to affect voting at an election.”
Karas said the messages appeared to be intended to draw votes from the Democratic candidate in the race, JoCasta Zamarripa.
Schroeder did not respond immediately Monday to phone, email and text messages seeking comment about the allegations and the Wisconsin Elections Commission complaint that Karas filed.
According to the complaint, over the weekend text messages went out to voters with an image of Karas, a headline “Not a duopoly candidate,” and urging people to “Vote Pete Karas for Secretary of State on November 3.”
A screenshot showing that the campaign of Jay Schroeder for secretary of state replied to an opt-out message in response to a text purportedly from the campaign of Pete Karas. (Text message screenshot included in complaint to Wisconsin Elections Commission)
A screenshot shows that when a person replied “Stop” to the message, the reply came back, “Jay for Wisconsin: You are now opted-out and will receive no further messages.”
Schroeder is running on a platform focused almost exclusively on eliminating the elections commission and moving election administration back into the secretary of state’s office. The job of running elections in Wisconsin was moved out of the secretary of state’s office in 1974.
Schroeder has claimed the change would restore “integrity” to the administration of elections. His assertions have largely been rejected by the other candidates, elections commission officials and outside observers.  
“What he did was dishonest and lacks integrity, and he’s talking about election integrity,” Karas said in an interview Monday. “I don’t know how we can trust him to run honest elections when he behaves like this in a campaign.”
One of Schroeder’s chief complaints has been the state’s practice of retaining information about voters who are removed from the state’s registration list rather than deleting their records entirely.
Election commission officials have pointed out that the law does not allow records to be deleted, and that a voter whose record is converted to “inactive” is no longer on the lists used to make up poll books of registered voters. Deleting the records would remove a safeguard against voter fraud, according to Don Millis, the Republican chair of the Wisconsin Elections Commission.
Karas said his own campaign has not sent any text messages to voters. He said he learned about the messages over the weekend from reporters.
“I was distraught about that, obviously. It’s really low of Jay [Schroeder] to do that,” Karas said. “It looks like what he’s trying to do is take votes from JoCasta [Zamarripa].”
The presence of three candidates in the general election as well as Schroeder’s focus on rewriting Wisconsin’s election administration law has alarmed Zamarripa and other Democrats, who cite the possibility that Karas’ campaign could divide voters, enabling Schroeder to get elected with less than 50% of the vote.
Karas said the weekend texts don’t lend credence to that concern. “I think this hurts me more than it helps me,” he said.
The message refers to healthcare costs and education costs — issues that Karas said he has not been centering because they have nothing to do with the secretary of state’s race.
“The message that he sent out in my name — ‘The one we’ve been waiting for’ — how presumptuous was that type of statement? If the intent was to take votes away from JoCasta, what he sent out was not a good representation of my cause.”

title: Governor predicts good results for Republicans in North Dakota but maybe not everywhere else
description: North Dakota’s governor cast his ballot Monday, telling reporters he expects good results for Republicans in the state but not necessarily nationally. “I think we’re doing well here. I think we have reasonable, rational legislators that have put the state on a great path,” Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong told reporters. Armstrong, a former congressmember, sa[...]
text:
North Dakota Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong takes a receipt to get his ballot from a poll worker at the Bismarck Event Center during early voting on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s governor cast his ballot Monday, telling reporters he expects good results for Republicans in the state but not necessarily nationally.
“I think we’re doing well here. I think we have reasonable, rational legislators that have put the state on a great path,” Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong told reporters.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Armstrong, a former congressmember, said he expects national Republicans “are going to be asking some tough questions tomorrow.” He said he has friends across the country who are facing some tough races. Armstrong said he campaigned for former House Republican colleagues Tom Tiffany for Wisconsin governor, U.S. Reps. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin and Brad Finstad in Minnesota.
In Congress, Democrats are expected to take control of the House from Republicans, but the GOP-led Senate is a tossup. 
Armstrong arrived in the rain at the Bismarck Event Center with his wife, Kjersti, an aide and a member of his security detail. The couple shuffled through the line for early voting just after polls opened at 9 a.m.
A poll worker shows North Dakota Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong a touch-screen voting machine during early voting at the Bismarck Event Center on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
The governor presented an ID to a poll worker who asked him standard questions for every voter, including whether he is at least 18 and a U.S. citizen and whether he had lived at his provided address – the governor’s residence on the state Capitol grounds – for at least 30 days.
The Armstrongs soon made their way to a cluster of touch-screen voting machines – (“It’s a lot easier for me to touch a screen than it is to fill in the bubbles,” the governor told reporters) – where he affixed his eyeglasses and began making his choices like other voters around him.
After a few minutes, he rose, turned in his ballot and picked up a red “You Betcha I Voted” sticker, which he stuck to his lapel. He said the voting process was quick, easy and convenient.
“We got here at 9, it took us six minutes and you’re interviewing me already,” he told reporters as voters came and went. He encouraged everyone eligible to turn out. 
Early in-person voting in North Dakota begins as group looks to encourage Native voters

Early in-person voting is available in some counties Monday. Polls open on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m., depending on location. Polls will close at 7 p.m. local time. Absentee ballots must be received by 7 p.m. Tuesday. Absentee ballots are not accepted at polling places, but can be dropped off with the county auditor or county dropbox.
Armstrong supported more than two dozen North Dakota Republican statewide and legislative candidates with endorsements and more than $430,000 in campaign contributions, mostly before the June primary.
He also appeared in a video ad supporting Measure 1 for a 60% voter threshold to amend the state constitution. He opposed Measure 2 for free school breakfast and lunch for K-12 students.
Armstrong said he planned to work on his state budget blueprint on Monday, then spend Tuesday hunting and later watching election results.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Not registered to vote? New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. Here’s how to do it.
description: New Hampshire is one of 24 states (plus Washington, D.C.) that allows citizens to register to vote on Election Day, so Granite Staters who haven’t yet registered can still cast their ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Under state law, to register on Election Day voters need to bring to the polls proof of: identity (driver’s […]
text:
Nashua voters check in at their polling station on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin) New Hampshire is one of 24 states (plus Washington, D.C.) that allows citizens to register to vote on Election Day, so Granite Staters who haven’t yet registered can still cast their ballot in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Under state law, to register on Election Day voters need to bring to the polls proof of:

identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID or passport serve that purpose);
age (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID or passport also work for this);
U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport or naturalization papers work; if you have none of these or forget them, you can sign a sworn affidavit);
and domicile (government-issued ID with an address or documentation containing an address, such as a utility bill or lease).

New Hampshire’s polls open at varying times on Tuesday morning, depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot.
Who’s going to be on the ballot?
The highest profile races are those for Congress. U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, a Democrat, and former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican, are competing for an open U.S. Senate seat. Former Portsmouth City Councilor Stefany Shaheen, the Democratic nominee, is battling car dealer Anthony DiLorenzo, the Republican nominee, for the 1st Congressional District. And in the 2nd Congressional District, incumbent Rep. Maggie Goodlander is facing a rematch against Republican challenger Lily Tang Williams.
Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, is facing her first reelection challenge against former Democratic Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington. Additionally, every state representative and state senator across the state is up for election (all New Hampshire elected state offices have two-year terms). Finally, all five members of the Executive Council — an elected body unique to New Hampshire that serves as a check on the governor — are up for reelection.
There will also be a number of county-level positions, such as sheriff, treasurer and county attorney, on ballots.
Also on the ballot are two questions
The first of the two ballot questions is a rather bureaucratic one. Mandated by the New Hampshire Constitution, every New Hampshire county elects a register of the probate. The position, which is currently defunct, used to complete administrative tasks for the courts. But in 2011, during a major overhaul of the court system, its job functions were absorbed by other staff. However, because it’s still in the Constitution, the position still appears on the ballot every two years and the winner accepts an annual $100 salary to do nothing. Ballot Question 1 would eliminate the position completely if more than 60% of voters vote “yes.”
Two questions, shown here in a screenshot of a sample Manchester ballot from the Secretary of State’s Office, will be on the ballot for New Hampshire voters in the Nov. 3, 2026 midterm elections. This is how they’ll look on your ballot. (Screenshot)
The second is a more consequential question. Question 2 on the ballot asks whether the voter would like to vote in a tax cap for their local school district — and impose a spending limit on their local school administrative unit.
Voting yes on Question 2 means voting to limit the school district’s “tax levy” — the total amount raised in property taxes each year — for the next two years. The limit would restrict the tax levy to the total levy of the year prior, plus an adjustment for inflation and for any new property construction in the school district that would increase the property tax base in that district. 
If imposed, the tax cap would require the district’s school board to propose a budget that keeps the total tax haul below that level. Question 2 requires 60% of voters across the school district to vote in favor in order for the tax cap to apply. Should a district adopt the tax cap, it would apply for tax years 2027 and 2028. However, any tax cap could be overridden for a specific annual district budget if 60% vote to do so at the district’s annual school meeting in spring. 
Question 2, if approved, would also make another change: It would require the voter’s School Administrative Unit costs to amount to less than 6% of the voter’s school district’s total budget. 
Unlike the tax cap, which applies only to individual school districts, the SAU 6% limit applies to the entire SAU. SAUs can consist of one or more school districts. Thus, the 6% limit will not be put into force unless 60% of all voters in all school districts within that SAU vote to approve it.

name: California
title: Cuidado con el “espejismo rojo” si los republicanos de California obtienen ventaja la noche de las elecciones
description: En California, el recuento de votos puede tardar semanas, lo que puede dar lugar a "espejismos rojos" y "cambios demócratas".
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Sucede en contiendas reñidas en casi todas las elecciones importantes. Los primeros resultados en California muestran a los republicanos ganando o, al menos, obteniendo mejores resultados de lo esperado. Luego, a medida que se cuentan los votos en los días siguientes, los resultados se inclinan a favor de los demócratas.
 Este “giro azul” o “espejismo rojo” no es resultado de que los demócratas de California “encuentren votos” o manipulen las elecciones, como han afirmado repetidamente el presidente Donald Trump y sus partidarios.
 Trump y sus aliados en el gobierno federal ya están sentando las bases para cuestionar los resultados electorales, al tiempo que se embarcan en un ataque sin precedentes contra las elecciones de California, lo que podría derivar en un enfrentamiento sobre los fundamentos de la democracia estadounidense. Los expertos les instan a no dejarse engañar por sus afirmaciones de elecciones “amañadas” basadas en los primeros resultados.
 Según los expertos, las variaciones en los primeros recuentos son simplemente el resultado de cuándo y cómo suelen votar los demócratas y los republicanos, así como del tiempo que tardan los funcionarios electorales de California en contar millones de votos.
Ejemplos del “desplazamiento al azul” y del “espejismo rojo”
 Este fenómeno se ha descrito al menos desde 2013, pero los términos cobraron fuerza en torno a las polémicas elecciones de 2020.
 Hace seis años, los resultados de la noche electoral mostraban a Trump por delante de Joe Biden en varios estados clave, pero a medida que los condados de todo el país contaban los votos en los días siguientes, Biden terminó ganando en los estados que le dieron la victoria en el Colegio Electoral.
 En las últimas semanas de su primer mandato, Trump hizo afirmaciones, que han sido desmentidas repetidamente , de que le habían robado las elecciones. Miles de sus seguidores irrumpieron en el Capitolio de los Estados Unidos durante los disturbios mortales del 6 de enero de 2021.
 California ha experimentado sus propios espejismos republicanos en elecciones congresionales y locales a lo largo de los años. En 2018, por ejemplo, cuatro candidatos republicanos a la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos parecían ir por delante la noche de las elecciones, pero terminaron perdiendo ante sus oponentes demócratas cuando se contabilizaron todos los votos.
 En las primarias de junio, Spencer Pratt, un republicano que fue estrella de un reality show, parecía estar superando a la progresista concejala de Los Ángeles, Nithya Raman, según los primeros resultados de la contienda por la alcaldía de Los Ángeles. Sin embargo, Raman terminó aventajando a su oponente y pasó a las elecciones generales para enfrentarse a la alcaldesa en funciones, Karen Bass. Este cambio llevó a Trump a calificar los resultados de “fraudulentos” y a otros miembros de la derecha MAGA a declarar que había maniobras demócratas detrás.
 Los expertos y los funcionarios electorales dicen que no hay que creer esas afirmaciones. 
 ¿Por qué cambian los recuentos de votos?
 Primero, aclaremos lo obvio: California es el estado más poblado. Hay 23 millones de votantes registrados en California; eso es más votantes que la población total de los 16 estados menos poblados juntos. El condado de Los Ángeles, el más poblado del país, cuenta con casi 6 millones de votantes registrados . En California también hay muchos republicanos, aunque los demócratas los superan ampliamente en número.
 ¿Quieres sorprender a tus amigos en tu próxima fiesta? Pregúntales qué condado de EE. UU. tuvo la mayor cantidad de votantes de Trump, en cifras absolutas, en las elecciones de 2020. La respuesta: el condado de Los Ángeles , tradicionalmente demócrata, donde Biden obtuvo una victoria aplastante.
 ¿Y cómo se traduce eso en un espejismo rojo? En las elecciones a la alcaldía de Los Ángeles celebradas en junio, los republicanos de la ciudad entregaron sus papeletas antes que los demócratas.
 Había tanta incertidumbre de última hora sobre la gran cantidad de candidatos demócratas a gobernador que aparecían en la misma papeleta que muchos votantes liberales esperaron mucho tiempo para devolverlas.
 Eso significó que se reportaron más votos republicanos en la primera tanda de resultados electorales, un espejismo rojo que desapareció una vez que se tabularon por completo los votos demócratas. Eso bien podría ocurrir en las diversas contiendas partidistas que figuran en las papeletas electorales de California, incluidas aquellas que podrían determinar qué partido controla el Congreso.
 Y, como de costumbre, el resto del país podría tener que esperar semanas para conocer los resultados de California y obtener una respuesta. 
 Sí, California tarda mucho tiempo en contar los votos.
 No hay vuelta de hoja: el proceso de recuento de votos en California es lento , y eso da más tiempo para que se enquisten las dudas sobre los resultados de las elecciones. “Esto socava la confianza de los votantes y abre la puerta a la desinformación y las falsedades electorales”, declaró Kim Alexander, presidenta de la Fundación de Votantes de California, en una rueda de prensa la semana pasada. “Provoca amenazas y críticas contra nuestro personal electoral… Y acorta el tiempo necesario para una transición de poder ordenada”.
 Pero existen razones por las que California avanza tan lentamente en el recuento.
 Durante la pandemia, California comenzó a enviar por correo una boleta electoral a cada votante registrado. El procesamiento de las boletas enviadas por correo requiere mucho más tiempo que el de las boletas entregadas en persona. Además, muchos votantes guardan sus boletas hasta el día de las elecciones.
 Además de las demoras en el recuento, California otorga a los votantes un período de gracia de siete días para que las papeletas con matasellos del día de las elecciones lleguen y sean contabilizadas.
 California también tiene el plazo más largo del país para subsanar las papeletas que presentan problemas, como firmas que no coinciden, lo que obliga a los funcionarios electorales a contactar a los votantes para corregirlas. Este año, los votantes tienen hasta el día anterior al Día de Acción de Gracias para subsanar sus errores, según Alexander.
 El estado solo exige que los condados cuenten las papeletas durante al menos seis horas al día, y no están obligados a contarlas los fines de semana ni los días festivos.
 Alexander afirmó que muchos condados van más allá, pero que la decisión final recae en cada oficina electoral. A menudo, la elección depende de si el condado cuenta con suficientes trabajadores electorales, puede pagarles horas extras y dispone de espacio para que trabajen, factores que dependen de los presupuestos locales.
 Los recientes cambios en la ley de California buscan acelerar el recuento, y este año los legisladores destinaron 29 millones de dólares a los condados para la compra de más máquinas de conteo de votos o la contratación de más personal. Aun así, Alexander indicó que algunas contiendas reñidas podrían permanecer sin definirse durante semanas. Los condados tienen 30 días para certificar oficialmente los resultados.
 Ben Gips, de Protect Democracy, una organización sin ánimo de lucro y no partidista dedicada a combatir el autoritarismo, instó a los votantes de California a no dejarse engañar por quienes pretenden utilizar tales retrasos para sembrar dudas sobre un proceso electoral que, si bien se está desarrollando con lentitud, está funcionando según lo previsto. “Estos retrasos realmente pueden dar más que hablar a esa estrategia y facilitar mucho ese engaño”, dijo Gips.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: A tip of the hat to all the election workers
description: Thinking of this election, I began to remember the election of 1964. I was living in San Francisco. It was my first time voting, and not only that, it was my first time serving as an election judge. It made an enormous impression on me, and I remembered how proud I was not just of […]
text:
Early voters line up at the Midtown Mall in Anchorage, Alaska, on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Yereth Rosen photo/Alaska Beacon)Thinking of this election, I began to remember the election of 1964. 
I was living in San Francisco. It was my first time voting, and not only that, it was my first time serving as an election judge. It made an enormous impression on me, and I remembered how proud I was not just of America, but of all the people who voted at my assigned precinct and all the people who were my fellow poll workers. The polling place was in a garage under one house of a solid block of older three-story buildings. It was a small, two-car space that had been cleaned up and made ready for business by the owner. This was in a somewhat poor neighborhood, mostly Black, white and Asian. We poll workers elected who was going to do what at the voting place and I was elected to whatever the top position was called. I often wondered whether it was because I was young and white, but I will never know. I was then, and am now, grateful to my fellow poll workers for their trust because it gave me the honor and the privilege of delivering the tallied ballots to San Francisco’s City Hall, which had a big dome and was about as big as Montana’s Capitol building.
I left the polling place at about 9 at night with the official papers tucked under my arm and took a city bus down to City Hall which seemed strangely empty and quiet, sort of church-like, and delivered them to the proper office. I remember feeling very proud, very much a part of the process of democracy and very responsible. I remember how carefully we did the initial tally of the ballots in the small garage, how well we got along, and how proud we all seemed to be in exercising our responsibility. It has colored my lifelong trust and confidence in our voting system.
In Trout Creek, we voted at the school. I almost always voted in person because it seemed so much like a community event. We all knew each other and visited as we stood in line. Shirley McLinden would be the first poll worker. She would make a mark next to our names and hand us over to Linda Kiester who would give us our ballots. The voting process changed over the years and when we were first required to show picture identification I remember laughing when Shirley said, “Hi Jim, could I please see your ID?”
I remember one clerk and recorder originally being against mail-in ballots and then a couple of years later being for them. I never doubted the honesty of the people who ran the elections even if they were of the opposite party. Then, in the 2020 election, they seemed to be the most distrusted people in America because of the false claims of ballot manipulation. I hope those days are ending.
In my 25 or so years in Montana politics, 16 in the Legislature, I have worked with many elections officials and trusted all of them to follow the laws impartially. I appreciate the work they all do. Many people are suspicious of public workers having a political bias that they take into their on-the-job decision making. I have found that to be very, very, rare—non-existent, even.
So now, having cast my ballot in my umptieth election, I want to thank all the election administrators, all the poll workers and watchers, and not least, all the voters who safeguard our American democracy.
My hat is off to you.

name: California
title: ¿Necesitas más ayuda financiera para la universidad? Esta nueva ley te facilitará solicitarla
description: Una nueva ley de California exigirá que las universidades informen claramente a los estudiantes sobre cómo solicitar ayuda financiera adicional si consideran que la cantidad otorgada no es suficiente. Las instituciones también deberán publicar cómo calculan los costos de asistencia, que se utilizan para determinar la cantidad de ayuda financiera que reciben [...]
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Pronto, las universidades tendrán que facilitar a los estudiantes la solicitud de más ayuda financiera, así como ser más transparentes en cuanto a cómo calculan el coste de la matrícula.
 Una nueva ley firmada por el gobernador Gavin Newsom en septiembre exige que las universidades e instituciones de educación superior muestren claramente cómo los estudiantes pueden solicitar ayuda financiera adicional si consideran que la cantidad otorgada no cubre suficientemente sus gastos. Las instituciones también deben publicar cómo calculan los costos de asistencia, que se utilizan para determinar la cantidad de ayuda financiera que reciben los estudiantes.
 El proyecto de ley 2251 de la Asamblea, presentado por las asambleístas demócratas Celeste Rodriguez del Valle de San Fernando y Marc Berman de Menlo Park, exige que las escuelas implementen los cambios para el otoño de 2027.
 La legislación vigente ya exige que los campus publiquen estimaciones de costos, que incluyen no solo la matrícula y las cuotas, sino también el alojamiento, el transporte, la alimentación y otros gastos probables. Según los defensores de los estudiantes, con los nuevos requisitos, ahora les resultará más fácil encontrar soluciones cuando sus gastos superen dichas estimaciones.
 “California tiene un historial muy sólido en la búsqueda de nuevas formas de mejorar la asequibilidad de la educación superior, y la ley AB 2251 es un ejemplo más”, afirmó Laura Szabo-Kubitz, asesora principal de políticas del Instituto de Acceso y Éxito Universitario, una organización que aboga por la asequibilidad de la educación superior. “Es un paso hacia otras iniciativas de promoción para cerrar la brecha de asequibilidad”. 
Los estudiantes pueden apelar su beca de ayuda financiera
Junely Merwin, ahora consultora de The Foster Youth Pre-College Collective, recibió una beca completa para asistir a Cal State Fullerton en 2015. Pero como ex joven tutelada (en foster care) y madre joven, necesitaba ayuda adicional para cubrir los gastos de cuidado infantil.
 “Mi dinero se fue a pique en el cuidado de los niños y en lo caro que era”, dijo Merwin. “Incluso con la beca completa, no fue suficiente”.
 En busca de más apoyo financiero, Merwin encontró el proceso que su escuela tenía para revisar el costo de su matrícula. Sin embargo, el sitio web no era claro y, cuando se comunicó con la oficina de ayuda financiera para hacer preguntas, la derivaron a varios miembros del personal.
Tras completar finalmente el proceso de apelación, el costo de la matrícula de Merwin se ajustó para incluir sus gastos de cuidado infantil. Esto le permitió acceder a una mayor cantidad de becas. Más de la mitad de las universidades estatales utilizan estimaciones inferiores a lo que los estudiantes realmente pagan para asistir a la universidad, y algunas las subestiman en más de 10,000 dólares, según una investigación de 2024 de John Burton Advocates for Youth, principal promotora de la ley. Esta organización californiana defiende los derechos de los jóvenes sin hogar y los jóvenes tutelados.
 Los estudiantes no pueden recibir más ayuda financiera —incluidos préstamos, subvenciones y algunas becas— que el costo estimado de la matrícula calculado por la universidad. Esto puede llevarlos a trabajar horas extras y tomar menos clases para compensar la diferencia, según una investigación del Instituto para el Acceso y el Éxito Universitario.
 Cuando los gastos de los estudiantes superan los calculados por su universidad, pueden solicitar un ajuste en el costo de la matrícula. Sin embargo, a menudo los estudiantes desconocen que esta opción está disponible. 
Oficina de Ayuda Financiera y Becas en el edificio administrativo Joyal de la Universidad Estatal de Fresno, el 3 de septiembre de 2026. Foto de Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters.
 Según un informe de marzo de John Burton Advocates for Youth, casi la mitad de las universidades del estado no informan adecuadamente a los estudiantes sobre los recursos y las opciones disponibles para ellos al solicitar ajustes en la ayuda financiera.
 Estos ajustes pueden ser especialmente útiles para estudiantes de bajos ingresos y jóvenes que estuvieron bajo tutela estatal, quienes a menudo reciben la ayuda máxima pero aún necesitan más, explicó Jessica Petrass, directora de educación de la organización. Debido a esto, los estudiantes suelen tener que rechazar ayuda adicional a la que de otro modo tendrían derecho.
 Según un informe de la organización John Burton, dedicada a la defensa de los derechos de la juventud, los representantes de los programas universitarios que brindan apoyo a jóvenes en hogares de acogida en los tres sistemas de educación superior del estado no encuentran accesibles los procesos de ajuste de costos. La mayoría de los encuestados afirmó que la información en los sitios web de los campus es insuficiente y poco clara.
 “Por eso considero que la ley AB 2251 es tanto una cuestión de transparencia como de acceso para los estudiantes, porque no basta con tener una política establecida”, dijo Merwin. “La información debe comunicarse de forma clara y coherente, de manera que los estudiantes puedan comprenderla y utilizarla”. 
Las universidades deben explicar claramente el proceso de adaptación
 Las universidades varían enormemente en la forma y el lugar donde explican cómo solicitar un ajuste en el costo de la matrícula y el límite de ayuda financiera. Mientras que algunas instituciones detallan claramente los costos en sus sitios web, otras guían a los estudiantes a través de un laberinto de enlaces y documentos.
 Según la nueva ley, los campus deben publicar información clara sobre cómo un estudiante puede presentar una solicitud de ajuste, cuánto tiempo podría tardar y con quién debe comunicarse. Esta información deberá aparecer en la misma página que los detalles sobre el costo de la matrícula. 
La estudiante Jackie Cordero frente a la oficina de Programas de Oportunidades Educativas en UC Santa Cruz, el 27 de octubre de 2026. Foto de Jessica Parga para CalMatters.
 Jackie Cordero, estudiante universitaria de primera generación en la UC Santa Cruz, está tramitando una solicitud de ajuste en su matrícula. Cordero eligió la UC Santa Cruz por el generoso paquete de ayuda financiera que le ofrecieron. Sin embargo, tras la lesión de su padre, que le impidió seguir trabajando, tuvo que buscar la manera de cubrir los gastos que su ayuda financiera no cubría.
 Tras investigar por su cuenta y contactar directamente con la oficina de ayuda financiera, descubrió que solicitar más ayuda era una opción. Sin embargo, no ha sido fácil. Cordero explicó que los documentos que le pidió la universidad —que detallaban la rescisión del contrato laboral de su padre y los ingresos de su madre— no existían en formato físico. Ha tenido dificultades para completar esa documentación y, en su lugar, ha tenido que redactar cartas explicando la situación financiera de su familia.
 “Probablemente debería haber un poco más de ayuda para las personas que quieren hacer un ajuste en el costo de la matrícula”, dijo. “Todavía estoy un poco confundida con el proceso y contactar con la oficina de ayuda financiera puede ser un poco difícil”.
 Según la ley federal, los estudiantes no están obligados a presentar documentación para los ajustes en el costo de la matrícula, pero las universidades casi siempre la solicitan antes de otorgar becas adicionales. 
Las universidades varían en sus fuentes de cálculo de costos
 En los tres sistemas públicos de educación superior, el personal de John Burton Advocates for Youth descubrió que el 83 % de los campus no detallan el costo total de cada categoría de gasto, como alojamiento y transporte, en sus sitios web. Esta información permite a los estudiantes comprender mejor si sus gastos superan los costos calculados y si podrían ser elegibles para un ajuste en el costo de asistencia.
 “En definitiva, estos presupuestos son una estimación… Se trata de hacer la mejor estimación posible para obtener el promedio que mejor represente las circunstancias únicas de cada estudiante”, dijo Petrass.
La mayoría de los campus no citan las fuentes de datos que respaldan sus estimaciones. Según la organización de defensa de los derechos de la juventud, solo el 17 % de las universidades de California (UC), el 26 % de las universidades estatales de California (Cal State) y el 22 % de los colegios comunitarios explican cómo elaboran estas estimaciones. Cada sistema calcula los costos de manera diferente. Las universidades de la UC utilizan una encuesta realizada por su Oficina del Presidente. Los campus de Cal State y los colegios comunitarios utilizan una combinación de datos, incluidos los del Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de los Estados Unidos y las estimaciones de encuestas de la Comisión de Ayuda Estudiantil de California. 
 Lo que la nueva ley no hace
 Si bien la ley garantiza un nuevo estándar de transparencia en materia de ayuda financiera, no proporciona nuevos fondos para dicha ayuda, ni garantiza que se aprueben los ajustes en el costo de asistencia de ningún estudiante.
La Comisión de Ayuda Estudiantil de California estima que el estado podría gastar entre 805,000 y 2.3 millones de dólares adicionales en becas Cal Grant debido a solicitudes de ajuste que de otro modo no se habrían presentado. Esto supone un aumento del 3% al 5% en el número de ajustes aprobados anualmente, según la comisión.
 Aunque se acepte la solicitud de un estudiante para un aumento de ayuda financiera, muchos sitios web de ayuda financiera de las universidades indican que la ayuda adicional generalmente se otorga en forma de préstamos. La ley tampoco modificará el proceso, a menudo complicado, de ajuste de costos, ni la forma en que las universidades calculan el costo de la matrícula.
 “Creo que todavía hay áreas en las que California podría seguir modificando sus políticas para fortalecer este proceso”, dijo Petrass. “También creo que existen oportunidades para reducir los requisitos de documentación para los estudiantes, con el fin de lograr un proceso más ágil que se ajuste a los requisitos federales mínimos”.
 Mariam Farag y Max Guerra colaboran con la Red de Periodismo Universitario, una iniciativa conjunta de CalMatters y estudiantes de periodismo de toda California. La cobertura de CalMatters sobre educación superior cuenta con el apoyo de una beca de la Fundación College Futures.

name: California
title: Los residuos nucleares de San Onofre están almacenados en la playa: ¿Aceptará otra comunidad hacerse cargo de ellos?
description: Los residuos nucleares de San Onofre han estado almacenados en una playa durante años. Este legislador quiere encontrar una comunidad dispuesta a recibirlos.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Si la propuesta del representante Mike Levin sigue adelante, el combustible nuclear gastado almacenado en la playa de San Onofre se guardará y procesará en uno de los varios complejos potenciales ubicados en otros estados.
 Levin, congresista demócrata que representa a partes de San Diego y el condado de Orange, expuso su plan la semana pasada desde un punto situado sobre la central nuclear de San Onofre.
 “Desde que estoy en el Congreso, retirar este combustible nuclear gastado de nuestras costas ha sido una de mis principales prioridades”, dijo Levin, con vistas al océano Pacífico y a los contenedores de acero y hormigón que albergan las barras de combustible nuclear. “Llevo ocho años luchando contra esta inacción respecto al combustible nuclear gastado”.
Levin está impulsando la creación de instalaciones denominadas Campus de Innovación del Ciclo de Vida Nuclear en comunidades que desean reciclar parte del combustible gastado y almacenar los residuos restantes, a cambio de oportunidades de desarrollo económico.
 El Departamento de Energía afirmó que los campus podrían “atraer inversiones significativas, expandir la manufactura nacional y crear miles de nuevos empleos bien remunerados en sus respectivas regiones”. Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Luisiana e Idaho se han postulado como posibles sedes para estas instalaciones.
 Finlandia y Canadá han emprendido iniciativas similares para localizar instalaciones de residuos nucleares, con el consentimiento y la colaboración de las comunidades locales, según un informe de la oficina de Levin . Finlandia prevé deshacerse definitivamente de los residuos nucleares el próximo año.
 Levin afirmó que instalaciones similares en Estados Unidos podrían comenzar a operar a finales de la década de 2030, y está presionando para que la planta de San Onofre sea una prioridad para la eliminación y el almacenamiento de residuos nucleares.
 La central de San Onofre dejó de funcionar en 2013, tras el fallo de un generador de vapor recién instalado, lo que dejó la planta inoperativa. Las autoridades comenzaron el desmantelamiento de la planta en 2020.
 Desde entonces, se han retirado del lugar 700 millones de toneladas de material de construcción, y las barras de combustible gastado se trasladaron de las piscinas de refrigeración a un depósito en seco en la playa, dijo Levin.
 Sin embargo, no existe un depósito permanente para el combustible nuclear gastado, tras la fuerte oposición que suscitó una propuesta anterior para almacenar los residuos.
 “El gobierno federal aún no ha cumplido lo que prometió hacer allá por 1998, por lo que comunidades como la nuestra se han quedado con el combustible”, dijo Levin.
 El gobierno federal había designado previamente el depósito de residuos nucleares de Yucca Mountain en Nevada como el lugar de almacenamiento permanente de desechos nucleares. Sin embargo, el expresidente Barack Obama canceló ese plan en 2010, tras una fuerte oposición de ambientalistas, grupos locales y tribus indígenas.
 Al carecer de un depósito de almacenamiento permanente, el combustible nuclear gastado ha permanecido en las instalaciones de San Onofre , donde su ubicación en la costa, cerca de fallas sísmicas y junto a Camp Pendleton, hace que los residuos sean vulnerables a desastres naturales o amenazas a la seguridad nacional.
 Para abordar estos riesgos, Levin presentó la Ley de Priorización del Combustible Gastado, con la colaboración del representante Darrell Issa, republicano de San Diego, y el representante Young Kim, republicano del condado de Orange. Esta ley priorizaría la eliminación y el almacenamiento de combustible en instalaciones nucleares con alto riesgo sísmico, gran población y que representan un riesgo para la seguridad nacional, como San Onofre. El proyecto de ley está pendiente de рассмотрение en el Comité de Energía y Comercio de la Cámara de Representantes, según el informe de Levin de 2026 sobre San Onofre.
Otro desafío se refiere al transporte de combustible nuclear gastado. Levin indicó que el próximo año un tren especialmente diseñado, denominado Sistema de Automotores Atlas, completará las pruebas y transportará las primeras barras de combustible gastado desde Virginia hasta Idaho. El Atlas es un automotor de 12 ejes equipado con sensores y sistemas de monitoreo, capaz de transportar casi 225,000 kilogramos de combustible nuclear gastado, según el Departamento de Energía. Su construcción duró diez años y costó 33 millones de dólares.
 Levin también ha presentado proyectos de ley para crear una administración de residuos nucleares, para exigir que los contenedores de residuos nucleares duren 100 años en lugar de los 40 años actuales, y para aumentar la participación pública y mejorar la inspección de seguridad en las centrales eléctricas en proceso de desmantelamiento.
 “No declararé la victoria hasta que el último contenedor haya salido de San Onofre”, dijo.

name: California
title: ¿Por qué los miembros del consejo escolar no se presentan a la reelección? “Mucha desilusión”
description: Miembros de consejos escolares citaron una serie de razones para no presentarse a la reelección, entre ellas la preocupación por los recortes presupuestarios y los conflictos laborales, las redadas de inmigración que afectan a las escuelas y a los jóvenes, y un clima político hostil en general.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
La papeleta del 3 de noviembre es extensa y está repleta de contiendas trascendentales. Pero hay algo que la mayoría de los votantes de California no verán: mucho revuelo en torno a las juntas escolares.
 Según un informe reciente de la USC , es muy probable que aproximadamente la mitad de los candidatos a las juntas escolares de California se presenten sin oposición, lo que genera una falta de escrutinio público justo cuando se están produciendo enormes cambios en la educación primaria y secundaria a nivel estatal y federal.
 « Necesitamos más gente, más opciones, más debate público», afirmó Julie Marsh, profesora de educación de la USC y una de las autoras principales del informe. «De lo contrario, se abre la puerta a que los grupos de interés intervengan y adquieran un poder desproporcionado».
 Los miembros del consejo escolar citaron numerosas razones para no presentarse a la reelección, entre ellas la preocupación por los recortes presupuestarios y los conflictos laborales, las redadas de inmigración que afectan a las escuelas y a los jóvenes, y un clima político hostil en general. Además, las jornadas laborales son largas, el sueldo es bajo y los amigos escasean.
 “Muchos no previeron lo agotador que puede ser emocionalmente este trabajo”, dijo Marsh. “Vimos mucha desilusión”. 
 Incertidumbre y tumulto
 El control local ha sido un pilar fundamental de la gestión escolar en California durante más de una década, desde que el estado adoptó la Fórmula de Financiamiento de Control Local, que otorga a los distritos escolares mayor libertad en el gasto y la toma de decisiones. Sin embargo, actualmente el estado está transfiriendo más poder a la oficina del gobernador y la administración Trump está cerrando el Departamento de Educación de los Estados Unidos , lo que genera incertidumbre y confusión entre las juntas escolares.
 Las guerras culturales no han ayudado. Las disputas sobre el currículo que incluye la historia LGBTQ+, los derechos de los estudiantes transgénero y otros temas han agitado las reuniones de las juntas escolares en regiones indecisas durante los últimos años. Pero esas preocupaciones palidecen en comparación con el estrés relacionado con las huelgas de maestros , el cierre de escuelas y los problemas presupuestarios , según descubrieron Marsh y sus colegas.
 En los últimos años, grupos de interés como los sindicatos y los grupos políticos conservadores han intentado, con cierto éxito, colocar a sus miembros en las juntas escolares. Si se presentan sin oposición, estos candidatos resultan elegidos fácilmente, con escaso escrutinio público. 
 ¿El dinero ayuda?
Se están realizando algunos esfuerzos para hacer más atractivos los puestos en las juntas escolares. El proyecto de ley 1390 de la Asamblea , aprobado el año pasado, permite a los distritos escolares pagar a los miembros de la junta hasta 4,500 dólares al mes, dependiendo del tamaño del distrito. Actualmente, la mayoría de los miembros de las juntas escolares reciben un pequeño estipendio, generalmente de unos pocos cientos de dólares al mes.
 Pero incluso un salario más alto no se acerca a una compensación justa por un trabajo que a menudo implica 40 horas semanales, dijeron los miembros de la junta escolar. Y, de todos modos, la mayoría no lo hace por dinero.
 “Si me presento a la reelección, no será por dinero ni por beneficio personal”, dijo Nick Caston, quien ganó un puesto en la junta escolar de Santa Rosa City Schools en 2024 y se convirtió en presidente de la junta el año pasado. “Será por el beneficio a largo plazo de los estudiantes, el personal y la comunidad”.
 Caston, padre de tres hijos y consultor de estrategia empresarial, afirmó que el trabajo ha sido mucho más estresante y exigente de lo que esperaba. Inicialmente, el distrito pensó que tendría que cerrar una escuela primaria para equilibrar su presupuesto, pero pronto la cifra se redujo a seis.
 Dijo que la indignación pública fue difícil de soportar.
 “Uno siente que es el rostro tangible de cosas que suceden fuera de su control”, dijo Caston. “Puede ser muy estresante”.
 Otro esfuerzo por retener a los miembros de las juntas escolares ha sido mejorar su capacitación. La Asociación de Juntas Escolares de California ofrece una gama cada vez mayor de seminarios web, talleres y un programa de “maestría en gobernanza” de 40 horas que abarca temas como la negociación colectiva, las relaciones con la comunidad, la Ley Brown y la financiación escolar.
 Pero esas capacitaciones no son obligatorias. El único requisito estatal para los nuevos miembros de la junta escolar es un curso de ética de dos horas. A partir del próximo año, también deberán tomar un curso de finanzas de cuatro horas . En el informe de la USC, la mayoría de los miembros de la junta dijeron que necesitaban más capacitación, especialmente en el uso de las redes sociales, la comprensión de si los programas o planes de estudio son efectivos y cómo manejar las tensiones políticas.
 «La capacitación no puede eliminar todas las fuentes de estrés, pero puede ayudar a los miembros de los consejos escolares a ser más seguros, eficaces y eficientes en su trabajo», dijo Troy Flint, portavoz de la asociación de consejos escolares. «Nuestro objetivo es garantizar que tengan las herramientas para tener éxito sin tener que afrontar estos desafíos solos». 
Más latinas aspiran a cargos
 A medida que disminuye el interés por postularse para la junta escolar en general, un grupo parece estar en auge: las latinas. En 2023, las latinas representaban al menos el 20 % de los miembros de las juntas escolares de California en distritos con un gran número de estudiantes latinos, según una encuesta realizada por Hispanas Organized for Political Equality, una organización sin fines de lucro con sede en Los Ángeles. En Los Ángeles y la Costa Central, la cifra se acercaba al 30 %. La junta del Distrito Escolar de Oxnard estaba compuesta íntegramente por latinas.
 “Se trata de mujeres, muchas de ellas de primera generación, que se preocupan por sus comunidades y quieren contribuir a ellas”, dijo Helen Torres, directora ejecutiva de la organización.
 El grupo de Torres capacita a mujeres latinas para el liderazgo cívico, incluyendo la postulación a cargos públicos. En sus 35 años de historia, el grupo ha capacitado a más de 2500 personas, entre ellas María Anguiano, presidenta de la Junta de Regentes de la Universidad de California; Yammilette Rodríguez, fideicomisaria de la Universidad Estatal de California; la senadora estatal Sasha Renée Pérez, presidenta del Comité de Educación del Senado; y la senadora estatal Monique Limón, presidenta del Senado estatal y exmiembro de la junta escolar. Torres también mencionó a otras mujeres latinas que han alcanzado puestos de alto nivel en el ámbito educativo del estado: Daisy González, directora de la Comisión de Ayuda Estudiantil de California, y Mildred García, rectora del sistema de la Universidad Estatal de California.
 La representación latina es importante, afirmó Torres, porque más de la mitad del alumnado del estado es latino, y es probable que los miembros latinos de las juntas escolares aboguen por programas que beneficien a las familias inmigrantes y trabajadoras, como los programas para estudiantes de inglés y las actividades extraescolares. El informe de Marsh reveló que, en general, los miembros de las juntas escolares en California tienden a ser blancos, mayores y adinerados. 
 Superar la inercia y la apatía
 Nabil Kherfan, miembro de la junta escolar del distrito Central Unified de Fresno, siente pasión por las escuelas públicas y por servir a su comunidad. Pero tras un solo mandato, ya ha tenido suficiente.
 No fueron las disputas en las reuniones del consejo escolar ni la angustia de los recortes presupuestarios lo que lo disuadió. Fue el compromiso de tiempo: servir en el consejo y, al mismo tiempo, hacer campaña.
 “Después de haber pospuesto muchas cosas en mi vida personal durante cinco años, tengo muchas ganas de avanzar en mi carrera y, con suerte, formar una familia”, dijo Kherfan.
 Kherfan es uno de los primeros estadounidenses de origen palestino elegidos en California y, a sus 30 años, uno de los miembros más jóvenes de la junta escolar del estado. Creció en Fresno, asistió a escuelas del distrito escolar Central Unified y espera volver a postularse para un cargo público algún día.
 Pero el tiempo que requiere puede resultar abrumador para alguien que ya trabaja a tiempo completo.
 “Todos queremos un cambio, pero puede haber resistencia a modificar el statu quo”, dijo Kherfan. “Abordar la desigualdad sistémica y la apatía lleva tiempo”.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: State officials ask WV Supreme Court for more time on school funding lawsuit, cite upcoming session
description: West Virginia officials are asking the state Supreme Court to wait until next spring to consider a lawsuit that alleges inadequate public school funding. The time gap could give the state Legislature time to rework the state’s school funding formula, which is the crux of the lawsuit.  The state’s seven-step school funding formula, which hasn’t […]
text:
West Virginia officials are asking the state Supreme Court to wait until next spring to consider a lawsuit that alleges inadequate public school funding.West Virginia officials are asking the state Supreme Court to wait until next spring to consider a lawsuit that alleges inadequate public school funding.
The time gap could give the state Legislature time to rework the state’s school funding formula, which is the crux of the lawsuit. 
The state’s seven-step school funding formula, which hasn’t been updated for years, largely relies on headcount to determine funding. West Virginia is dealing with a population loss and a wave of school closures; school officials largely point to the funding formula’s outdated method.
A new filing by the West Virginia Attorney General’s Office on behalf of leaders in the legislative and executive branches asks for delay in the school funding lawsuit until next April. 
Lawmakers’ next 60-Day session will begin Jan. 13, 2027.
“Petitioner asks this Court to order the political branches to rewrite West Virginia’s school aid formula. But the political branches are already engaged in discussions. The Department of Education has delivered an overhaul of the formula to the Governor and legislative leadership. The Joint Standing Committee on Education plans to hear the Department out on Nov. 9,” said the attorney general’s filing.
Consideration of the school funding formula is expected during the session, the attorney general’s office added. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey has already said that public school funding issues will “dominate the next legislative session” in January. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia filed a lawsuit in September over the funding formula, asking the the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals to require lawmakers to correct it. The suit was filed on behalf of a sixth grader in Lincoln County Schools, and Lakin Patten, the student’s parent.
The group believes that the state is not following a state Constitutional mandate that it provide a thorough and efficient education due to the current funding formula. 

The lawsuit listed the state school board, State Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt, House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, Senate President Randy Smith and others as respondents.
In response to that suit, school board members last month approved a motion that the board’s attorney advance their position that the current school funding formula is inadequate.
The state Attorney General Office said in its filing that holding off in the case will “give lawmakers the opportunity to evaluate whether and what adjustments to the education system are appropriate.”
“The Governor and Legislature, including State Officer Respondents, deserve the chance to discuss any proposed amendments without juggling litigation deadlines tied to a record subject to additional factual development,” the filing said. 
Lawmakers ended the 2026 regular session in March without making any changes to the school funding formula despite numerous bills to make changes to it. Many of those proposed changes had more than $100 or $200 million price tags, creating a hangup for lawmakers’ approval. 
The state school board has recently shared its proposal for restructuring the school funding formula to address declining enrollment along with monetary needs in special education, high poverty areas, rural schools and more. 
The board hasn’t released a total cost for its school funding proposal; their special education reform piece alone would cost $190 million.
Last week, Berkeley County Schools Superintendent Ryan Saxe said it will file its own lawsuit against state officials over the school funding formula. School officials believe the current funding formula does not reflect the responsibilities the county is required to fulfill in education, especially in serving special education students.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Miners file case against West Virginia coal safety officials over silica dust
description: The United Mine Workers of America and 52 miners have filed a lawsuit against the state Board of Coal Mine Health and Safety, asking it pass a limit on the amount of silica dust being produced in coal mines.
text:
Exposure to mixed coal mine dust that contains silica — a carcinogen — can lead to the development of pneumoconiosis, commonly known as black lung disease. (Getty Images)The United Mine Workers of America and 52 miners have filed a lawsuit against the state Board of Coal Mine Health and Safety, asking it pass a limit on the amount of silica dust being produced in coal mines. 
The union and the miners filed an emergency petition with the West Virginia Supreme Court on Oct. 29 to mandate that the board pass regulations limiting the amount of silica dust in coal mines. 
The suit is the latest salvo in a decades-long fight to limit the dust, which has driven the number of cases of black lung to a high not seen since the 1970s. 
Attorney Sam Petsonk, representing the miners, said silica dust rules were supposed to be passed in the state back in the 1980s, but didn’t come to fruition.
“The industry found one way after another to prolong and delay and distract and dodge any trick in the book,” he said. “They have fought dust regulation with a fiery vengeance.” 
The petition describes miners, some as young as their 30s, developing pneumoconiosis, due to the mining of thin-seam coal, which requires more sandstone to be cut in order to be extracted. 
Pneumoconiosis is when dust — from coal and rock — are breathed in over a prolonged amount of time, slowly destroying the lungs. 
History buffs may recall cutting sandstone led to the Hawks Nest Tunnel Disaster, in which hundreds of men died from inhaling silica while cutting a tunnel in Fayette County back during the Great Depression. 
Compounding that, the suit states coal operators have a financial incentive to mine thin-seam coal due to a tax credit passed in the 1990s, which charged a reduced severance on the coal. 
In 2024, federal regulators with the Mine Safety and Health Administration passed a rule to limit the amount of silica dust in the air, with it set to take effect in 2025. But after President Donald Trump won a second-term, the agency reversed course and indefinitely delayed implementation. 
Petsonk said the lawsuit is a way to kick the process into gear, in light of federal inaction. He said past efforts have seen the state be pushed to adopt new safety standards, and in turn the MSHA followed suit. 
“That’s what, unfortunately, may have to happen at this time as well, given MSHA’s abandonment of the silica rule,” he said. 
Thomas Clark, the administrator of the Coal Health and Safety Board did not respond after being left a voicemail. John F. Willems, assistant state attorney general representing the agency, forwarded a request to comment to media liaison, noting that person would not be in the office until Friday. 
Jared Hunt, spokesman for the West Virginia Supreme Court, confirmed the case has been docketed, but said it would likely be heard next year.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: A wastewaster manager faces 3 years in prison for hiding 3 years of E. coli contamination from SC
description: A South Carolina wastewater treatment plant manager pleaded guilty to federal Clean Water Act violations for concealing an E. coli contamination.
text:
Matthew J. Perry Jr. U.S. Courthouse in Columbia, where John Lorick, senior manager for the Saluda Commission of Public Works, pleaded guilty Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, to federal Clean Water Act violations. (File photo by Abraham Kenmore/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A South Carolina wastewater treatment plant manager pleaded guilty to federal Clean Water Act violations for concealing E. coli contamination.
John Lorick, senior manager for the Saluda Commission of Public Works, entered a guilty plea in federal court Thursday. He faces a maximum penalty of three years in federal prison and fines between $5,000 and $50,000 per violation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Investigators found the 45-year-old from Ninety-Six diluted water samples to hide E. coli levels elevated due to an inoperative chlorination system.
On dozens of occasions over more than three years, the town of Saluda’s plant released raw, untreated sewage directly into the Little Saluda River, which flows into Lake Murray.
“The defendant not only completely failed to treat sewage many times but also falsified records and reports to hide these failures. EPA will ensure that those who endanger public health and lie to the government to evade detection of their wrongdoing are found out and held accountable,” Charles Carfagno, special agent in charge of EPA’s criminal enforcement program in South Carolina, said in a statement.
The town of Saluda has a permit allowing the plant to release of set levels of pollutants, but without a working chlorination system, the E. coli levels violated that permit.
Lorick knowingly allowed this to happen 10 to 12 times a year between 2022 and March 2025, federal prosecutors said. One such release, which occurred from July 27-28, 2025, killed approximately 1,529 fish about a mile downstream from the plant, leading to the investigation.
“South Carolina’s natural resources are one of the many gems of our state. Lorick’s actions were harmful to the environment, the wildlife that rely on the Little Saluda River and potentially anyone who recreated in the water,” U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling for South Carolina said in a statement.
Lorick took no steps to repair the system or notify regulators of the issue.
“The intentional pollution of our state’s natural resources, especially our essential water resources, can never be tolerated,” Myra Reece, the director of the state Department of Environmental Services, said in a statement.
United States District Court Chief Judge Sherri Lydon accepted the guilty plea and will sentence Lorick at a later date.
Lorick’s plea came in the same week that York County officials reported a massive sewage spill into Lake Wylie. The spill happened Oct. 26, after a pump station overflowed, dumping 500,000 gallons of sewage into Little Allison Creek on the southwest end of the lake.
Unlike Lorick, however, county staff reported the issue to state environmental regulators.

name: VTDigger
title: Universal primary care will strain a shrinking doctor workforce
description:
Free care would drive up demand for appointments faster than Vermont can train or recruit clinicians.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Universal primary care will strain a shrinking doctor workforce.
text:
Dear Editor,
As someone who has worked in Vermont’s healthcare financial advisory sector over the past year, I think Olivia Gieger’s recent VTDigger report does a great service by highlighting universal primary care, a goal both gubernatorial candidates view as important for Vermont. However, turning this vision into reality requires overcoming substantial structural and financial challenges.
On the care side, our delivery system is under immense strain. With nearly a third of our primary care doctors over 60 and 16% planning to retire, leave Vermont or reduce hours soon, eliminating cost-sharing will spike demand before capacity exists. Expanding access will likely force greater reliance on nurse practitioners rather than doctors. While nurse practitioners are vital to our system, studies show that relying on them to fill physician shortages can inadvertently drive up downstream costs through higher diagnostic testing and specialist referral rates. 
Actual 2027 program costs will certainly exceed the outdated cost estimate of $281.9 million projected in 2015. Grown at the same rate as hospital budgets over the period — which have averaged over 3% annually, tracking medical inflation — the $281.9 million initially projected by state analysts for 2017 could be closer to $400 million by 2027, if the scope remains constant. However, if we look at total Vermont healthcare costs in 2024, which I calculate at $7.5 billion, and use Maine as a composition proxy for primary care at 10% of the total, Vermont’s program would be closer to $750 million. We will also have to pay a premium to induce new doctors to relocate and fill our current shortages, creating additional expenses.

READ MORE

On the financing side, the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act barrier is our primary obstacle. Because federal ERISA preemption bars Vermont from mandating that self-insured employer health plans, which make up about three-quarters of employer plans, join a state-funded risk pool, taxpayers face an unfunded $80 million to $100 million gap based on my estimate of 135,000 to 145,000 self-insured lives at an annual conservative cost of $600 to $700 per person. 
Additionally, bypassing a Medicaid waiver would needlessly forfeit around $107 million in Medicaid funding, much of it federal. Induced demand will likely outpace provider access at all levels, and offering free primary care may incentivize some to drop comprehensive insurance altogether, potentially increasing uncompensated emergency care and eliminating any projected emergency department savings, at least in the short term.
Total program costs without physician relocation bonuses would be $400 million to $750 million per year, and indirect costs of ERISA preemption and the Medicaid waiver would bring the total to $587 million to $957 million per year. Attempting to fund this project with almost $1 billion of taxpayer liability and cost shift using a targeted high-earner surtax is risky. 
The tax relies on about 3,500 filers who already generate over 30% of state income tax revenue, according to the Vermont Department of Taxes, meaning the tipping point for cannibalization of our general fund from out-of-state migration is only a few hundred departures. One billion dollars of total cost for universal primary care spread over the high-earner cohort would result in an average tax increase of $285,714 per filer per year. 
The numbers above are order of magnitude only. These challenges are formidable, but they may be solved. I look forward to seeing how Vermont meets this new moment in healthcare.
Myers MermelManchester, Vt.
