text:
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — Key Democrats said Sunday they would not let Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers divide the party ahead of Tuesday’s election.
Stevens, a sitting member of Congress, was all but formally exorcized by her party after she publicly endorsed Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, whom she had previously endorsed and pledged to support through the general election, despite lingering tensions from their August primary.
Over the past few weeks, the congresswoman has changed her position on supporting El-Sayed, moving from a position that was critical of the nominee but still supportive of the overall ticket, to outright joining Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday where she heaped praise on Rogers for supporting some of her campaign platforms involving housing and Black-owned businesses.
Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers called a ‘disgrace’ at Detroit unity roundtable

Later, on CNN, Stevens said that she found El-Sayed’s campaign to be getting “angrier” against those who opposed him, and cited what she felt were instances of antisemitism from the campaign. Stevens said that ranged from campaigning with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker to his lack of condemnation of an ad purchased by a political action committee run by Piker’s uncle.
“Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier, and I was just trying to help,” Stevens told CNN. “I endorsed him, and that ad was very painful. There are so many Democrats who want to vote for the Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told this is a party you don’t belong in. This is a campaign you don’t belong in. … I’m making a decision here, and that’s just where I landed on.”
Stevens could not, however, pinpoint an exact moment on when it was that she changed her mind, saying the decision had been building up for her and that Sunday’s turn to Rogers represented “a weight off her shoulders.”
Before Stevens decided to support Rogers, which appeared to be a snap decision earlier Sunday morning, as she told CNN, Stevens was set to attend a church service with El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, a former Stevens supporter who was backing El-Sayed after he became the nominee. The engagement was brokered by U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Ann Arbor, who had played the intermediary between El-Sayed’s campaign and Stevens.
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) and state Rep. Alabas Farhat (D-Dearborn) listen to speakers at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)State Rep. Stephanie Young (D-Detroit) speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
The congresswoman had agreed but put conditions on the visit, including a call that El-Sayed disavow the ad produced by Ugyur, and other examples of rhetoric El-Sayed used to question the U.S. relationship with Israel. A major platform of El-Sayed’s campaign is acknowledging Israel has been committing a genocide in its war against Hamas in Gaza.
While that determination remains controversial, it is backed up by multiple international organizations including Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders and a United Nations commission.
El-Sayed did not budge and asked Stevens’ campaign to stay out of the race through Tuesday’s election. Stevens repeatedly told CNN that being disinvited from the church event marked a turning point. It was reported that several of her staff were waiting for her at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, where El-Sayed and Clyburn were holding a Souls to the Polls event on Sunday.
Instead, Stevens showed up at the Perfecting Union church, led by Pastor Marvin Winans of gospel music fame, to take in a morning of worship with Rogers, his wife, and Stevens’ fiance, attorney Jason Turkish.
Gongwer News Service reported that former Michigan. Gov. Jim Blanchard said he had spoken to Stevens Saturday night and she said she would support El-Sayed. Blanchard told the outlet that Turkish, who had openly supported Rogers over the last few weeks, may have had a strong influence on Stevens’ decision.
“He was all distraught,” Blanchard told Gongwer. “He was all strung out about Abdul. I let her know, he’s not a good influence.”
Either way, the move sent shockwaves across the political universe in Michigan and beyond. 



Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Mike Rogers was despicable, and she must be removed from the House Democratic Caucus, @hakeemjeffries.
We will double down our efforts to elect @AbdulElSayed on Tuesday. Joint statement from @IfNotNowOrg @MPowerAction & @OurRevolution: https://t.co/iWZrrCKVP4
— Yasmine Taeb (@YasmineTaeb) November 2, 2026

Several national Democrats, including those who had openly supported Stevens in the primary, said her endorsement of Rogers was a betrayal, including one of her biggest national surrogates, Neera Tanden.
“Standing with Miker Rogers is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career,” Tanden said in an X post. “It’s also a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her.  I hope Abdul El-Sayed has a strong victory on Tuesday and that all Democrats and like-minded independents support vote for him.”
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel wrote in an X post that Stevens was no longer a Democrat and she had no opportunity to run as a Democrat in the future after her stunt with Rogers.
The party removed Stevens from its elected officials page entirely, taking down both her name and her photo from the list.
Instead of going all in on Stevens, El-Sayed took the higher ground, called her antics a distraction, and urged members of the media to stay focused on his campaign messages rather than the drama of the race. 
“At the end of the day, I don’t think about Haley Stevens,” El-Sayed said. “None of this matters.”
In a media scrum outside the church on Sunday afternoon, El-Sayed was adamant that he would only take questions that had to do with his campaign and its policy points and that he would end the press availability if any “horse race” questions emerged.

.@AbdulElSayed calls @HaleyforMI’s maneuvering today “a distraction” from the issues in the race. “None of this matters,” he said of the distraction. “I don’t think much about Haley Stevens. https://t.co/S8vEyUpvd8
— Ben Solis (@bensolis1) November 1, 2026

Those types of questions were immediately shouted at El-Sayed, and he promptly ended the press event to begin his event with Clyburn.
Clyburn praised El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens on Sunday.
“We have been doing what we possibly can to make this great country of ours accessible and affordable for all of our citizens,” Clyburn said. “This campaign is about making healthcare and education accessible for all our citizens. It’s about making housing, and energy affordable for all of our citizens. And it’s about having candidates for office who will be accountable to all of our citizens.”
Clyburn said he was pleased to be in Detroit with El-Sayed and to stand “in solidarity” with his campaign.
Dingell, whose voice was hoarse, strained and dry by Sunday evening, was the one of several main speakers at a unity event held outside of UAW headquarters in downtown Detroit.
She also urged the national media to not become distracted by what she called drama in the 11th hour of the race.
“I’m just going to say it straight,” Dingell said Sunday. “There has just been too much drama created by national media and not enough attention on the people I talk to every day. If you’re worried about the direction that the country is going in, and what we have done to the African American community … Do you think that Mike Rogers, a Republican senator, will support us in doing any of that?”
Other speakers included state Sen. Jeremy Moss of Bloomfield, who is running for Stevens’ 11th District seat, state Rep. Donavan McKinney of Detroit, who is running to replace U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar in the 13th District, and former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin, who was defeated by Stevens in the 2022 primary.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak, who had been in the race for the U.S. Senate before she dropped out, also spoke about the stakes of the election and called out Stevens — without naming her — for the dustup she caused on Sunday morning.
“The message that I hope you heard today is that we are locked in,” McMorrow said. “Are we ready to ignore all of the nonsense? Because let me tell you, my phone has been pretty busy today. I don’t know if you saw some news, but here’s the thing: a lot of those texts and a lot of those phone calls were not from Michiganders, they are from reporters all across the country who are treating this election like an episode of Real Housewives of Michigan.”
McMorrow was adamant that this was “not a reality TV show” or about “people’s emotions” or someone trying to get “their last 15 minutes before they no longer have a title.”
“This is about Michiganders, because today, while all of those messages were coming in, I heard from people in church this morning … who said what do we do to stop this president?” McMorrow said. “I want to answer all the reporters who texted me to ask, ‘is this going to change anything?’ Are we divided? No. Are we united? Yes. Are we going turn out every vote? Yes. Are we going to lock in and send Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate? Yes.”

title: School counseling becomes issue in Alabama state school board races
description: The Alabama State Board of Education votes on a resolution at the board meeting in the Gordon Persons Building in Montgomery, Alabama, on Aug. 14, 2025. Two Republican candidates for the board have called for limits to social-emotional learning in schools, which aims to teach learners compassion and community participation. Their Democratic opponents support[...]
text:
The Alabama State Board of Education votes on a resolution at the board meeting in the Gordon Persons Building in Montgomery, Alabama, on Aug. 14, 2025. Two Republican candidates for the board have called for limits to social-emotional learning in schools, which aims to teach learners compassion and community participation. Their Democratic opponents support the measure. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Two Republican nominees for Alabama State Board of Education have called for changes to the state’s school counseling program. 
Cathi Bradford, the GOP nominee for Alabama State Board of Education District 6, and Emily Jones, the Republican nominee for Alabama State Board of Education District 8, have both called for limits to a process known as social-emotional learning. 
Advancing Students Forward, an organization working to give underserved students access to education and academic success support, describes social-emotional learning as a process where students learn “how to manage emotions, problem solve, and create positive relationships with others.” According to the United Nations Education, Scientific and Cultural Organization, SEL aims to allow learners to process emotions effectively, develop compassion, form a sense of identity and become engaged members of society.
Jones said in a recent interview that she thinks SEL has a space in certain educational areas but would place limits on it.
“It does not need to be integrated into science class, history class, whatever it is,” Jones said. “We need academic courses to focus on academics, and SEL does not have a space there, but if it’s a counseling class, I think that’s kind of the expectation, and parents can decide that.”
Multiple messages seeking comment from Bradford were left unanswered. According to her website, Bradford opposes “expanding classroom-based social-emotional learning frameworks that move schools beyond their core mission— to educate.”
Angela Morgan, the Democratic nominee for State Board of Education District 6, said in a recent interview that some students need social-emotional learning because of their environment outside of school.
“I taught high school, and I had a lot of students that had really tough home life,” Morgan said. “You can’t say that education is only about teaching arithmetic and English and history. Education is also teaching about hope. And there are children who come to school traumatized because life is beating them down. And if you’re not there to give them support the way they need it, then I do not think you’ve done your job as an educator.”
Shatika Armstrong, the Democratic nominee for State Board of Education District 8, said in a statement Thursday afternoon that social-emotional learning does have a space in classrooms.
“We cannot expect students to perform at their best academically if they do not know how to manage emotions, resolve conflicts, communicate effectively, or make responsible decisions,” Armstrong said. “As a parent and someone who has worked in education, I understand that children bring more than backpacks into our classrooms. They bring real life experiences and challenges.”
The Alabama School Counselor Association Leadership Team said in a statement lat week that school counselors are “student advocates, and they are important partners in empowering students to become successful civic citizens.”
“School counselors provide counseling, crisis intervention, and collaborative services, which are all designed to help create an equitable and accessible world in which all students thrive, regardless of their background or circumstance,” the statement said. “School counselors work in tandem with teachers, administrators, and parents/families to improve access to opportunity and achievement for students and also to address foundational wellness challenges.”
Jones said she thought the plan needed to be “looked at, revamped, brought up to speed” and many of her concerns predated the new counseling plan.
“There were a lot of things in there that I thought needed to be removed,” she said. “So that’s really the big thing with getting the standards updated to be more reflective of the times that we’re living in.”
The counseling plan was last updated in 2003. The Alabama State Board of Education voted in March to update the Comprehensive School Counseling Program Model for Alabama Public Schools.
Under the new counseling plan, sensitivity —  which includes collaboration with parents and guardians to “ensure students’ continued success, promoting accessibility, transparency, and advocacy” — is considered a foundational skill. The model also states that transparency is key for establishing and maintaining relationships with families.
The ALSCA said because the updated plan is new, the full benefits have yet to be seen.
“As school counselors across the state become more familiar with the model through professional development and implementation, its positive impact is expected to grow,” the statement said. “Ultimately, the model is intended to strengthen the effectiveness of school counseling programs and ensure that students, families, and school communities better understand and benefit from the services that school counselors provide.”
Some of the benefits the ALSCA said benefits they anticipate seeing are “greater clarity regarding the role of the school counselor within the school, stronger collaboration between school counselors and other school professionals and increased parental involvement and family engagement in the comprehensive school counseling program.”
One issue Jones had with the previous code was language it used surrounding gender identity.
Under the new model, students in public K-12 schools have foundational and wellness standards which include teaching children to identify and respect differences among others. Jones said if the new standards start “breaching beyond that” into gender identity, there could be an issue with not following state law.
“So there was some stuff in the prior standards that had talked about, … just kind of (being) open and accepting,” she said. “Well, Alabama law’s changed on a lot of these things. Alabama law defines sex as male and female, and it cannot change. So we need to make sure that the standards we have, especially around these topics, are in line with that.”
Jones and Armstrong agreed on the need for communication and transparency between counselors and parents.
 “Schools should clearly communicate what counseling services are available, what requires parental consent, and how families can ask questions or review information,” Armstrong said. “At the same time, we must make sure students have access to appropriate support when they need it. Communication and trust between schools and families are essential.”

title: US Supreme Court to hear arguments in latest debate over LGBTQ+ protections in Colorado
description:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Attorneys representing Colorado education officials and two Catholic preschools will face off at the U.S. Supreme Court Tuesday to determine if Colorado’s universal preschool program can require religious educational institutions to include LGBTQ+ children and parents.
It’s the [...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Attorneys representing Colorado education officials and two Catholic preschools will face off at the U.S. Supreme Court Tuesday to determine if Colorado’s universal preschool program can require religious educational institutions to include LGBTQ+ children and parents.
It’s the latest in a fraught history of the nation’s highest court weighing in on the balance of state anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people and religious exemptions.
The Archdiocese of Denver and the Catholic preschools allege in a lawsuit that they were unable to participate in Colorado’s universal preschool program, known as UPK Colorado, because the state will not allow the institutions to exclude LGBTQ+ children and parents. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton and the St. Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood both operate preschool programs that were not part of UPK, because the state requires providers to accept applicants without regard to the family’s religion, sexual orientation or gender identity. 
The schools applied for public funding through the universal preschool program and were denied when they requested religious exemptions from the state’s equal-opportunity requirement. They claimed their exclusion violated their rights under the free exercise clause of the First Amendment.
Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, which represents the plaintiffs in the case, says Catholic families like plaintiffs Dan and Lisa Sheley are forced to pay thousands of dollars out of pocket for Catholic preschool since their schools of choice are excluded from the program. It said enrollment in schools run by the Archdiocese of Denver have fallen by 20%, and two schools closed since the UPK program began. 



Quotation







Colorado's rule is simple: If you take public money to teach kids, you serve every kid.


– Jax Gonzalez, political director at One Colorado


A U.S. District Court of Colorado judge ruled in June 2024 that the UPK requirement that prohibits discrimination against LGBTQ+ families is valid. The Denver-based 10th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the district court’s decision in October 2025, and the Supreme Court accepted the case in April. The church and schools filed the lawsuit against Lisa Roy, executive director of the Colorado Department of Early Childhood. 
The Supreme Court will weigh in on aspects of a 1990 ruling in another case that raised the question of religious exemptions to state laws. The court held in Employment Division v. Smith that a person’s religious beliefs are not an automatic exemption from compliance with a law against conduct the state is free to regulate.
Dozens of organizations have filed court briefs for one or the other side of the case. Several Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., filed a brief in support of Colorado, while Republican-led states filed a brief urging the court to overturn the lower court rulings. The Trump administration also filed a brief in support of the preschools. 
Not the first Colorado discrimination case at Supreme Court
Jax Gonzalez, political director at LGBTQ+ advocacy organization One Colorado, said no school should use taxpayer dollars to turn away kids because of who their family is. 
“Colorado’s rule is simple: If you take public money to teach kids, you serve every kid,” Gonzalez said. “Religious freedom matters to all of us, including LGBTQ Coloradans of faith.”
The organization did not file a brief in the case, but Gonzalez said One Colorado supports briefs that support Colorado. 
More than 79 faith-based schools have taken part in the UPK program and agreed to the nondiscrimination parameters, Gonzalez said. Colorado voters approved the program to ensure a strong start for all children. 
“A ruling for Colorado keeps that promise,” Gonzalez said. “A ruling against Colorado would let schools take public money and turn kids away, and it could open the door to discrimination of any protected class with taxpayer dollars in healthcare, shelters, food pantries and other services.”
The initial lawsuit made several references to past court cases related to LGBTQ+ discrimination in Colorado that made their way to the nation’s highest court. That includes a case in which the Supreme Court said a Colorado web designer does not have to make websites for same-sex couples, and another in which the court said a cake shop owner could deny a same-sex couple a wedding cake based on religious beliefs. 
Most recently, the court sided with a Christian counselor against Colorado’s law that bans licensed providers from conducting “conversion therapy,” a discredited practice of trying to change a person’s sexual orientation, such as to eliminate same-sex attraction, or gender identity.

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Clinton Township has joined the ranks of Michigan communities with a temporary moratorium on data centers. Anne Snabes of The Detroit News reports that the township’s Board of Trustees voted 6-0 to approve a 180-day pause on accepting and processing permitting applications and site plans for data centers within Clinton Township.
The Lansing Economic Area Partnership on Tuesday announced a partnership with Lighthouse Sustainability to begin community engagement with the goal of constructing a $10 billion data center at a site in Holt and Delhi Township, Beth LeBlanc reports for The Detroit News. The group intends to work with community members over the next six months to develop a framework for what an acceptable data center would look like, with one of the developers penning a poem outlining his vision of a facility negotiated alongside residents.


One of the developers wrote a two-page poem that he read at a press conference announcing the process. https://t.co/aisFiYCGi2
— Beth LeBlanc (@DNBethLeBlanc) October 27, 2026


In a statement released the following morning Delhi Charter Township Manager Tracy Miller announced that the township was ending its membership in the Lansing Economic Area Partnership. The township approved a 12-month data center moratorium last April
On Friday, the Delhi Charter Township Board of Trustees unanimously approved a resolution in opposition to data center development within the community.

Updates

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel is challenging the Michigan Public Service Commission’s decision to approve special contracts allowing DTE Energy to supply power to a hyperscale data center planned by Google in Van Buren Township. Filing a petition for rehearing, Nessel argues that the public service commission should accept a series of recommendations she proposed to strengthen DTE’s cost recoveries from Google and ensure costs do not fall on DTE’s existing customers, or reject the contracts outright.
Members of the Pittsfield Township Board of Trustees approved an ordinance regulating data centers and other high-resource demand facilities after about a year of discussion on guardrails, WEMU’s Kevin Meerschaert reports.

News of Note

Ahead of Election Day, the Sierra Club’s Michigan chapter has launched a data center position tracker asking sitting state lawmakers and candidates three questions: Will you vote for a temporary moratorium if it is put up for a vote; will you vote for permanent regulations to protect our water, energy grid, transparency, community benefits agreements, and require union labor, if put up for a vote; and will you vote for data center tax incentive repeal, if put up for a vote?
Bridge Michigan’s Kelly House recaps a panel discussion centered on data centers held as part of Bridge’s inaugural Michigan Issues Summit. Panelists discussed the backlash against data centers and how this pushback is reshaping the state’s policy landscape.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Proposal would issue up to $500M in bonds for Arkansas’ aging water infrastructure
description:
(Getty Images)Supporters of a ballot measure that would allow the state to issue up to $500 million in bonds for water and wastewater improvements say it’s needed to address Arkansas’ aging infrastructure, but opponents are concerned about borrowing money to finance the projects.
Issue 4 is one of four ballot measures being considered by voters, and it’s the[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Supporters of a ballot measure that would allow the state to issue up to $500 million in bonds for water and wastewater improvements say it’s needed to address Arkansas’ aging infrastructure, but opponents are concerned about borrowing money to finance the projects.
Issue 4 is one of four ballot measures being considered by voters, and it’s the only measure that wouldn’t require amending the Arkansas constitution. [Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The state’s majority-Republican Legislature referred all four proposals to voters. Issue 4 was created through legislation sponsored by Republicans Sen. Bart Hester and Rep. Howard Beaty and approved by the General Assembly in 2025. 
The ballot measure would authorize the Arkansas Natural Resources Commission to issue up to $500 million in general obligation bonds to finance or refinance water, waste disposal, water pollution control, abatement and prevention, drainage, irrigation, flood control, and wetlands and aquatic resources projects. 
No more than $165 million could be issued for the development of irrigation facilities. The state would also be prohibited from issuing more than $60 million in bonds during any two-year period without prior approval from the General Assembly. 
The proposal comes as communities have struggled to maintain water and wastewater systems, which has resulted in Arkansans losing access to water in places like Helena-West Helena.
Arkansas Rural Water Association CEO Chris Harris said work on an updated state water plan indicates it will cost more than $20 billion to address the needs of water and wastewater utilities. 
Plan or penalty: The next step in Arkansas city’s path to better water infrastructure

“A lot of them are at the end of their lifespan and it’s going to take a massive amount of money to even begin to start replacing some of this,” he said. 
Harris also serves as treasurer of The Committee for Water Infrastructure Now (WIN) for Arkansas, a ballot question committee that supports Issue 4. Since forming in March, the ballot question committee has spent nearly half of the $83,000 it’s raised on polling, according to finance reports.  
Issue 4 is also supported by Water Infrastructure for AR, another ballot question committee that formed this month. The committee hasn’t raised any money, according to a finance report. A representative for the group said they had no public comment for this story.
Harris said Issue 4 allows utilities to access loans from the state at a lower rate than they could through private banks. Utilities that receive a loan would pay a small fee to the state, and that money can be used to access additional federal funding, he said. 
The proposed ballot measure wouldn’t increase taxes, but ratepayers would cover the cost of paying the loans back to the state, Harris said.  
Issue 4 supports a program that’s been in place since 1980 and a tool that the state has used to help fund utilities, Harris said. Arkansans have considered similar proposals in the past, most recently in 2008 when voters approved up to $300 million in bonds to finance water projects.
Voters are being asked to approve up to $500 million now because of inflation and because more projects need financing, Harris said.  
While no formal group has formed in opposition to Issue 4, critics of the proposal have said its broad language raises questions about who could benefit from taxpayer-backed bonds, according to the Public Policy Center at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. 
In recent years, discussion over water infrastructure has been tied to data centers, which require a lot of water to cool servers. Data center projects have faced pushback from communities across the state because of concerns over environmental effects and utility costs.
MAP: More Arkansas communities putting data centers on hold

Harris said there’s no economic development intention behind Issue 4, but acknowledged that a utility could say it’s installing a water line to serve dozens of local residents, and then sell the land to a data center project. 
“You can’t stop a bad actor, but that’s not what this is designed to be used for,” he said. 
Opponents of Issue 4 have also pointed to the billions of dollars the state has accumulated in reserves, and noted that borrowing through bonds will mean paying interest at a time when rates are higher than they were several years ago, according to the Public Policy Center.
Harris said there’s not sufficient funding in the state’s reserves to address all of Arkansas’ water and wastewater infrastructure needs. 
The League of Women Voters of Arkansas, a nonpartisan voting rights organization, opposes the other three legislatively referred measures on noncitizen voting, gun rights and economic development. But the group took a neutral stance on Issue 4. While Issue 4 aligns with the national organization’s stance on water and water quality, Executive Director Kristin Foster said there were concerns about public input and accountability. 
“That’s why we decided not to take a position because those two pieces of it were in conflict with our national guidance on it,” Foster said. 
If approved by voters, Issue 4 would be effective July 1, the start of the new fiscal year. 
You can read the ballot measure in its entirety here.

text:
The Snake River runs through Idaho Falls. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho has periodically faced serious threats to its water sovereignty from an overreaching federal government. 
In the early 1950s, when Len Jordan was Idaho governor, the feds wanted to build a massive dam on the Snake River in Hells Canyon. That would have usurped Idaho control of its upstream waters. Jordan stopped the proposal, opting instead for the three existing Idaho Power company dams in order to protect Idaho’s control of those waters.
The next water fight occurred after I was elected as Idaho attorney general in 1982.
Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights

Idaho Power had just received an erroneous decision from the Idaho Supreme Court, giving the company practical control of Snake River waters above its Swan Falls Dam in Ada County. Gov. John Evans and I were able to work together behind the scenes and across the political aisle to defeat that threat. 
When we were able to get the conflict settled to the state’s advantage, the next federal threat raised its ugly head.
In December 1987, Congress was on the verge of approving legislation that would have given the feds the ability to control the flow of Snake River waters above Deer Flats Wildlife Refuge in Canyon County. 
The matter was being handled behind closed doors in congressional offices. When my staff members learned that a political deal was being made to compromise the state’s interests, I blew the whistle, the Idaho water community erupted in anger, and the threat was brought to a screeching halt. 
Anyone interested in the details can check out pages 337-345 of my book on the subject – “A Little Dam Problem.”
The latest threat to Idaho’s water sovereignty surfaced less than two months ago.
 Shortly after it was announced that the Idaho National Laboratory had been selected as a finalist for designation as a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, the Trump administration launched an extremely troubling lawsuit challenging Idaho’s ability to “administer” the federal water right at the INL. 
In practical terms it means that, if there is a water shortage involving water rights in the INL vicinity, any reduction or mitigation would fall wholly upon the shoulders of other Idaho water users — farmers, fish producers and other folks dependent on those waters. The INL would be exempt.
Trump administration’s lawsuit claiming ‘supremacy’ over our water is a gut punch to all Idahoans

The lawsuit was filed against Idaho in the federal court in Boise on Sept. 11, without any attendant publicity from either side. 
While the allegations focus primarily upon the INL water right, the complaint seeks much broader relief. The Trump administration wants “a declaration that the Idaho Department of Water Resources lacks the authority to administer federal water rights” and “an order permanently enjoining the Director of IDWR from exercising his authority” under any state law as to the United States or its agencies. 
In short, the administration is asking the court to prevent Idaho from administering federal water rights anywhere within state borders. This is wholly without precedent and contrary to the determination of rights in the Snake River Basin Adjudication.
The agreement settling the Swan Falls water right fight called for filing a case in state court to adjudicate all water rights to Snake River Basin waters. That is, to quantify and prioritize those rights in court proceedings. 
Idaho specifically sought and received approval to include all federal water rights under a federal law, called the McCarran Amendment, that permits federal claims to be determined in a state court adjudication.
Idaho’s petition in the Snake River Basin Adjudication sought both adjudication and administration of water rights in the Snake River Basin. Former Gov. Cecil Andrus and I signed the agreed-upon water right for INL in June 1990. The final unified decree entered by the judge in the Snake River Basin Adjudication recognized administration as an element of the decree.
A distressing fact about the current threat is that state officials have failed to alert the public about the danger of the federal lawsuit. Idahoans deserve to be informed of the nature of the suit and the challenge it presents to Idaho’s control of its water resources. 
In years past, such a bald-faced federal intrusion into Idaho’s natural resource affairs would have been met with outrage by our state leaders. Quiet acquiescence to the water grab is unacceptable. Bipartisan public outcry could stop it. 
Idaho’s water community and public land users deserve to get the facts, to understand how the lawsuit could affect their interests and to consider seeking intervention into the lawsuit to protect those interests.
The state must strongly oppose the suit. Our chances of prevailing, based upon the entire record, are excellent. There should be no political settlement that would endanger Idaho’s control of its vital water resources. 
The economic future of the Gem State depends on defeating this unwarranted federal threat.
Complaint in United States v. Idaho

title: 3 years after fight over LGBTQ+ books, an Arkansas community takes up vote to cut library money

text:
The Mabel Boswell Memorial Library, part of the Saline County Library System, in Bryant, Arkansas on May 18, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)The Saline County Library’s newest branch lives in a rented unit in an East End strip mall near a hair salon, an optometrist’s office and some restaurants.
Renting the space costs the library system $56,000 per year. Some Saline County residents fear the branch will close if the typically Republican county votes Tuesday to reduce how much property tax money funds public libraries, Lela Chism said.
Chism is a member of the nonpartisan Saline County Library Alliance, which has been leading the charge against the proposed tax reduction. Alliance members met a few library patrons in August who weren’t aware of the measure, which is printed on Saline County ballots as Issue 5.
But awareness has grown as Election Day has grown closer, Chism said Friday. The Saline County Library Alliance crowdfunded pro-library merchandise, including yard signs, T-shirts and a billboard on Military Road in Benton.
Lisa Bergren and Lela Chism, members of the Saline County Library Alliance, attend a May 18, 2026 Saline County Quorum Court meeting. Both urged the court not to place a measure on the November ballot to reduce the property tax millage funding the county library system. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)
“We’ve had multiple candidates that are running from both sides come out and say that they do not support [Issue 5] and told their people that they would not vote for it,” said Chism, who’s running for a Shannon Hills city council seat.
Saline County has been a primary battleground over Arkansas libraries’ funding and content in the past few years, part of a larger fight libraries around the country have faced over efforts to restrict access to books addressing race, sexuality or other controversial subjects. The vote comes three years after Saline County’s library director was fired in a standoff with conservatives who wanted books about LGBTQ+ topics removed from shelves. 
The library’s Facebook page includes information about voting, but no mention of Issue 5.
“If a ballot initiative had been run by citizens… the library could have come out and defended itself,” Chism said. “They can’t do anything when it’s their own elected officials doing it.”
The all-Republican Saline County Quorum Court voted 10-2 in May, after much public pushback, to allow the public to vote on reducing the Saline County Library’s millage to 1.1 mills. The library currently receives 1.7 mills, or $1.70 for every $1,000 of assessed property tax in the county of more than 131,000 people.

2026 Saline County library funding cut proposal 
If voters approve Issue 5, the library is expected to lose $1.4 million per year, or about one-third of its projected $5.7 million operating budget for 2027.
Josh Curtis and Keith Kellum, two of the three quorum court members who introduced Issue 5, have been promoting it on Facebook. Curtis said the library potentially losing funding and cutting services “is simply not true,” and Kellum said the property tax revenue “has outgrown the library system that it supplies,” citing Saline County’s growing population.
“This issue is about being better stewards with our tax dollars,” Kellum wrote. “This [is] not about defunding the library or retaliation from any book issues in 2023.”
 How Saline County got here

Three years ago, Saline County Republicans decried the county library for having books about LGBTQ+ topics, sex education and systemic racism within children’s reach. In 2024, members of the Saline County Republican Women circulated a petition to reduce the library’s tax millage from 1.7 to 0.9 mills.
Republican County Judge Matt Brumley rejected the 2024 petition on a technicality. This year, he has been one of the most vocal supporters of Issue 5.
Brumley defended both stances during a candidate question-and-answer forum last month in Bryant. He said he gave the library’s governing board advance notice that there would be another proposed millage cut after 2024.
Saline County is not the first Arkansas county to have the people vote on library funding. Craighead County narrowly voted in 2022 to cut its library funding in half.
Craighead County citizens who opposed the library’s LGBTQ+ book display in 2021 shifted their message the following year and claimed the library was overfunded. Saline County residents started to make similar claims in 2023, but that message has died down, Chism said.
Jon Newcomb holds a copy of “All Boys Aren’t Blue” by George M. Johnson which he claims is pornographic, as he speaks to the Saline County Quorum Court on April 17, 2023. He spoke in favor of a resolution that aims to keep certain books out of the reach of children. (Photo by John Sykes Jr./Arkansas Advocate)
“It hasn’t been like it was last time, where you had all those people showing up [at public meetings] and holding books up and screeching about queer kids,” Chism said.
Such materials have been the focus of efforts nationally to restrict access to library books. The American Library Association last year tracked more than 4,200 titles that were challenged in public, school and academic libraries. 
Libraries have also faced efforts to withhold or threaten funding over such materials. The Arkansas State Library Board is expected to vote next week on new rules that hinge public libraries’ funding on ensuring patrons age 16 or younger cannot check out materials that depict or describe sexual contact and behavior.
The Craighead County Jonesboro Public Library reduced its hours and laid off employees to accommodate the loss of about $2 million in operating funds. An effort to restore some of the library’s funding failed in 2024, while voters in neighboring Lawrence County rejected a library defunding measure the same year.
Saline County’s Issue 5 is Arkansas’ only ballot measure concerning library funding this year. Elsewhere, voters in a New Jersey city will decide Tuesday whether to dissolve their local library.
On Oct. 19, the first day of early voting in Arkansas, some Saline County residents said they voted against Issue 5. Others said they supported Republican candidates and had not been paying attention to ballot measures.
As of 1 p.m. Friday, more than 26,000 Saline County residents had voted, according to a Facebook post from county clerk Doug Curtis, who is Josh Curtis’ father.
Voter turnout is typically lower in a midterm than in a presidential election year, but Curtis said Saline County’s 31% voter turnout after 11 days of early voting is a county record for a midterm.
Republican voters tend to favor policies framed as tax cuts, Chism said, but both the high voter turnout and the opposition to Issue 5 she’s heard from Saline County residents and candidates give her hope that the library will keep its funding.
“I have not run into anybody who wants to defund it, so it’s very promising,” she said.

What Arkansans said on the first day of early voting for the midterm election


 Potential future ballot measure

One of the two quorum court members to oppose putting Issue 5 on the ballot was Pat Bisbee, who represents East End. Over more than a decade in office, Bisbee used to be the quorum court’s appointed liaison to the county libraries, and he has kept acting in this role even though it is no longer an official position.
Earlier this year, Bisbee suggested to Brumley that the quorum court put a measure on the ballot that would allow the library’s property tax revenue to be used for capital improvements, such as building a permanent East End location, instead of solely for operations.
“We decided to hold off on that because having both issues on the ballot at the same time could be confusing to some people,” Bisbee said in a Friday interview.
He said he hopes the measure will be on the November 2028 ballot, since holding a special election before then costs taxpayer money.
The other quorum court member to oppose Issue 5 was Clint Chism, a cousin of Lela Chism. He was among the quorum court members who said in 2023 that he considered certain books dangerous to children, but he said in May that his constituents urged him to oppose the funding cut.
Later in 2023, Clint Chism joined 10 other quorum court members in voting to give Brumley hiring and firing power over library employees. Bisbee was one of two members to vote no.
Brumley proceeded to fire Patty Hector, who had been the Saline County Library’s executive director for seven years and had refused to relocate LGBTQ+ books at the quorum court’s urging.
Hector sued Brumley and the county, saying they violated her First Amendment right to free speech. The county paid Hector a $275,000 settlement in August.

Arkansas librarian fired after opposing book ban efforts to receive $275K in settlement

title: Drug pricing program changes worry West Virginia clinic

text:
Pharmacist Sherry Witters looks over prescriptions at Cabin Creek Health Systems’ West Side Clinic on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)Using a federal drug discount program, Cabin Creek Health Systems offers their uninsured patients income-based prices. It writes off some or all of their prescription costs. 
The 340B drug pricing program requires pharmaceutical companies that are covered under Medicaid and Medicare to offer discounts to healthcare organizations like Cabin Creek Health Systems, which is for low income and uninsured patients, allowing them to stretch limited resources to care for patients. 
“A great deal of our medications that we offer, we’re able to give to our patients for $5 or $6,” said Angela Stone, the health system’s director of pharmacy. “And if they can’t afford that, this affords us to be able to say, ‘We can write this off for you. We’re not going to let you go without your medication.’”
Beginning next year, though, Trump administration changes to the federal program will increase the purchasing and administrative costs for Cabin Creek Health Systems and other eligible clinics, which will have to pay up front for the drugs and seek rebates from drug manufacturers. 
The changes — part of a pilot program set to begin Jan. 1 — are coming at a time when thousands of West Virginians and millions across the country are expected to lose their healthcare coverage. 
For Cabin Creek Health Systems, a drug that cost 30 cents this year could cost them $1,500 to $5,000 to pay for upfront under the 340B rebate model, Stone said.
“Our purchasing costs could go from $100,000 to three quarters of a million dollars, and that’s just for the drugs that are affected by this rebate program, where we won’t get our discount upfront,” she said. “We will have to seek the discount from the manufacturer for every prescription that we dispense.” 
Having a rebate model for the program will require the pharmacy staff to spend time applying for rebates, without a clear timeline on when they’ll get the money paid back. 
“I would say that it could be someone’s full time job to keep up with it,” Stone said. 
According to the Health Resources and Services Administration, which oversees the program, the 340B Program has grown substantially in size and complexity over the last 15 years. The rebate pilot program is meant to improve transparency and program integrity, the agency said.
“Unlike the current upfront discount model, which provides limited visibility into individual 340B transactions, a rebate model requires claims-level identification of each transaction, allowing verification to occur before a rebate payment is issued,” HRSA said on its website about the program changes. “This approach helps address compliance concerns proactively, rather than relying primarily on retrospective reviews, audits and dispute resolution processes. 
“It also supports compliance with statutory non-duplication requirements under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program,” the agency said. “The claims-level data is also expected to support better-informed oversight and long-term stewardship of the program.”
At least 33,000 West Virginians will be affected by new work requirements going into effect Jan. 1, according to an estimate by the Department of Human Services. The work requirements are a part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Act, which Trump signed into law last year. 
Healthcare analysts and insurance officials predict that people — including those who are eligible – will lose their healthcare coverage as they struggle to keep up with paperwork associated with the work requirements.
Amber Crist, chief operating officer for Cabin Creek Health Systems, said the 340B changes may mean some patients will be prescribed alternative medications other than the ones they need or that will work best for them. 
“It’ll just make healthcare that is already hard in the state increasingly more difficult,” Crist said. 
About a third of Cabin Creek’s patients are covered by Medicaid. Crist said it’s difficult to predict how many of them will still be enrolled in Medicaid in the coming months. 
“Coupled with what we’re going to experience with the 340B rebate model, it just makes projecting your budget increasingly difficult,” Crist said. 
Rebate model program challenged in court
The American Hospital Association and the Maine Hospital Association filed a lawsuit Oct. 9 against the Department of Health and Human Services over changes to the drug pricing program. The organization alleges that changes to the program will lead to $1 billion in increased annual administrative costs for hospitals that are already-strapped.
Tony Gregory, interim director of the West Virginia Hospital Association, said the 340B program is especially important in places like West Virginia, where hospitals face significant financial challenges and patients may have limited healthcare options.
The program is supported through discounts from drug manufacturers, so no direct state or federal tax dollars go into it, Gregory said. 
“(The program) helps hospitals maintain essential healthcare services and support their community,” Gregory said. “The program has been an important resource for West Virginia hospitals for a long time. It’s helped eligible hospitals stretch those limited resources, and in turn, it’s helped us provide care to vulnerable patients and communities.”
Matt Walker, a lobbyist who represents federally qualified health centers in West Virginia, said if the 340B rebate model works flawlessly, health centers will be delayed in saving money on the drugs. At the rebate model’s worst, companies could deny rebates to health care organizations.
“If you’re asking me personally, I think that hospitals and health centers will lose billions of dollars statewide as a result of this change, at least,” Walker said. “And they will certainly be delayed in collecting their rebate dollars, which has a negative impact on them because they can’t put those dollars to good use on the programs that they’re supposed to subsidize when they don’t have the dollars yet.”
Pending legislation would address drug pricing program, delay changes
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., is one of six members of Congress who are sponsoring the Sustain 340B, a bill that would reform the program while keeping the discounts at the point of sale. The members make up the Senate’s 340B Bipartisan Working Group. 
“We have received invaluable input from stakeholders throughout our process, and the legislation we are introducing reflects that feedback by aiming to provide greater stability, clarity, and transparency in the 340B program,” the group wrote in a statement in August. 
“The SUSTAIN 340B Act makes comprehensive reforms to the program while preserving its critical benefits that support eligible healthcare providers and the patients they serve throughout the country. By continuing to work together in bipartisan fashion, we are committed to strengthening the 340B program and helping make certain it remains accessible to serve patients and communities for years to come.”
The bill is pending in the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. 
Other legislation would delay the start of 340B becoming a rebate program. 
Both the Senate and the House of Representatives are in recess until after the midterm elections. 
Crist, with Cabin Creek Health Systems, said her staff is starting to come up with ideas about how to deal with next year’s budget with a lot of unknowns. The clinic may open a line of credit, she said. 
“Our main goal is to keep all of our doors open and keep all of our staff employed, and continue to take good quality care of patients,” she said. “It’s just requiring us to kind of think outside the box a little bit, the best way to continue to do that.”

title: Republican, Democratic Governors Associations put $2.5M into Nebraska governor’s race
description: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont are the 2026 Republican and Democratic candidates for Nebraska governor. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — In the final weeks of the race for Nebraska governor, the Republican and Democratic candidates have received some of their largest donations from their re[...]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont are the 2026 Republican and Democratic candidates for Nebraska governor. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — In the final weeks of the race for Nebraska governor, the Republican and Democratic candidates have received some of their largest donations from their respective governors’ associations.
The candidates have also received boosts from President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat who chairs the DGA.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, top right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, bottom left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
A PAC for the Republican Governors Association gave incumbent Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus $1 million on Oct. 6, followed by $500,000 each on Oct. 19 and Oct. 26. The Democratic Governors Association, meanwhile, gave former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont $7,500 on Oct. 9 and $500,000 on Oct. 21. Both associations operate in Washington, D.C.
In total, Pillen and Walz have raised just shy of $20 million heading into Tuesday’s election, and by the last reporting period, ending Oct. 19, the two had together spent more than $17.1 million.
The dynamics are different from what typically ruby-red Nebraska has seen for gubernatorial races for nearly 30 years, where spending is often centralized in GOP primaries.
In 2022, Pillen was part of a heated primary to succeed term-limited Gov. Pete Ricketts. Republicans brought in $26 million in the primary, but in the general, when Pillen faced then-state Sen. Carol Blood of Bellevue, a Democrat, the duo brought in just $2.3 million more.
Nebraska Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly of Lincoln, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection alongside Gov. Jim Pillen. The Republican ticket faces Ben Steffen of Humboldt, top right, and former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont for the Democratic Party; Keenya “Ruby” Barnes of Omaha, bottom left, with Rick Beard of Omaha for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party; and Michael Picard of Omaha with former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The 2022 contest is, for now at least, the most expensive race in state history. The second-most expensive gubernatorial race came in 2014, when Ricketts first won an open seat for governor. That race cost $17.7 million in total.
Ricketts and former University of Nebraska Regent Chuck Hassebrook, a Democrat, spent $6.1 million after the primary. This year, Walz and Pillen have spent $13.6 million in the general election period, and it’s the third-most expensive race behind Ricketts and Hassebrook already. Walz has raised more than any Democrat seeking the governorship in Nebraska history, and Pillen, across his two campaigns, has done the same on the Republican side.
The last Democrat to win the governor’s seat was former Gov. Ben Nelson, who won reelection in 1994. He had unseated then-Gov. Kay Orr, a Republican, in 1990 despite being outspent.
‘Full steam ahead’
Pillen, in a statement last week, said his team has been “full steam ahead for months now.” Yet, in just over the past week, he said he held more than 40 public events in every corner of the state. He said he’s talked with thousands and thousands of voters to ensure they vote. 
“That’s what it takes to win — and I’m the only candidate putting in that type of work,” Pillen said.
President Donald Trump praises Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, who is running for reelection, during a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Trump headlined on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Trump, when he visited Grand Island on Oct. 5 in part to help Pillen, praised Pillen for signing major income tax cuts in 2023. The president derided Walz as a “crazy relative” of “disgraced” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who he said is “probably the worst governor in history.
“She’s a disaster just like her uncle or whatever the hell he is,” Trump said then. “They come from a bad bloodline.”
Lynne Walz is a distant cousin of Tim Walz related through marriage. Lynne Walz has noted that her husband, Chris, is a Republican.
Of Pillen, Trump said he is “very tough” and often seeks money for Nebraska after storms.
“He’s a fantastic governor. He loves you like crazy. He works like hell,” said Trump.
Pillen and other Republicans have repeatedly leaned into voter turnout this year. They argue that if conservatives stay home, they’ll help Democrats.
“Republicans and commonsense Nebraskans know just how critical this election — up and down the ballot — (is) to keep far-left radicals from gaining a foothold in our state,” Pillen said. “We’re going to win — and we’re going to keep building on the success and progress we’ve made over the last four years.”
‘You give me hope’
Walz said she has traveled the state, too, and has probably put 40,000 miles on her car visiting communities statewide. Her running mate, Ben Steffen of Humboldt, an ex-Republican farmer, has also flown or driven across Nebraska. She’s criticized Pillen’s “mismanagement” of the state budget, which sits at a $1.2 billion deficit through mid-2029, which must be addressed next year.
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, center, speaks at a get-out-the-vote event in Omaha on Nov. 1, 2026, with former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, center right, and her running mate, Ben Steffen of Humboldt, at left. To Walz’s left is her husband, Chris. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Walz said after every listening session, she feels “more obligated to finish this race and finish it strong, because people are really counting on change.”
“Every single time I finish a town hall, somebody says, ‘You give me hope. I am walking away finally having some hope,’” Walz said. “I think what that means to people is that, No. 1, they have somebody who will listen to them and empathize with them.”
She described those feelings as a desire for more opportunity and to make Nebraskans’ lives easier, around healthcare, childcare, housing and education, all with a lean toward kindness.
At an event Sunday, Beshear, the Kentucky governor eyed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, told an Omaha crowd he is “living, breathing proof that Democrats can win anywhere.” He said Democrats should be fighting everywhere.
“Just imagine the message we are going to send to this country when Nebraska turns blue,” Beshear said. He predicts voters will also keep Kansas blue and flip governorships in Nevada and Georgia.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and the tools you need to cast your vote in Nebraska’s Nov. 3 general election.]
Speaking with reporters after the event, Beshear said Walz “earned” the DGA’s support, which comes later in the cycle than other races but was made possible with record fundraising. Beshear credited Walz and Steffen for making the Nebraska race competitive.
“Nebraska has a governor right now that cares more about the approval of one individual than the well-being of families in this state,” Beshear said. “Lynne is for those families. She’s going to deliver, and I’m just really excited for her.”
The next four years
National pundits, pollsters and political insiders have focused attention on Nebraska’s U.S. Senate race, the 2nd Congressional District and other federal races, but the governor’s race has started to take more attention and funding, as indicated by the national governors associations.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, right, meets with reporters after hosting a kickoff event where he confirmed he is sticking with his running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, for another four years on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Walz said she does feel momentum and is confident she’ll win, telling the Nebraska Examiner, “I feel that there are a lot of people who are praying for us and just backing us.” She said her closing message is that she’ll govern for all Nebraskans statewide, regardless of party.
“It’s been an honor for us to listen and bring people in on conversations to hear your ideas,” Walz said. “This campaign, and this future administration, will be about the people of Nebraska. It will not be about party. It will be how we can provide as much opportunity for the people of Nebraska as possible.”
Pillen told the Examiner that everywhere he goes, Nebraskans have also come up and told him and his wife, Suzanne, that they’re praying for them, which he said is “just extraordinary.” 
He said his focus is on lowering taxes, ensuring a ballot measure passes to constitutionally protect a state law governing girls’ and women’s sports participation, and standing up for family farms and ranches.
“My final message today is one of gratitude to Nebraskans: It’s the privilege of a lifetime to serve this state, and I’d be honored to earn your vote,” Pillen said.
Third-party candidates
The governor’s race is also complicated by two third-party candidates: Rick Beard of the Legal Marijuana NOW Party and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of the new America First Party.
Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, right, and Humboldt farmer Ben Steffen, the 2026 Democratic nominees for Nebraska governor and lieutenant governor, respectively, host a private roundtable on property tax policy in Lincoln on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The new Nebraskans for Cannabis Future PAC formed in early October to support Beard. The group has spent $65,000 on mailers, a webpage and digital ads. Beard, who has frequently spoken against money in politics, said he has had no involvement with the group.
The treasurer of the cannabis PAC is the same as Nebraska United, a conservative PAC that has spent nearly $1.3 million this election cycle, including $675,000 to support Pillen as recently as Sept. 3.
Beard said he never would have expected an outside group to boost him, and he said running has shown him how “corrupt” the process can be and how difficult it is while facing millions spent otherwise. He estimated he probably spent $500 in his entire race.
“I had no idea or nothing to do with this,” Beard said of Nebraskans for Cannabis Future.
Lindstrom, meanwhile, is running under the “America First” label that Republicans have worried could pull votes from Pillen. He had not filed a required disclosure report detailing funds raised or spent between Sept. 30 and Oct. 19 as of Nov. 1. That report was due Oct. 26.
A PAC known as Preserve the Good Life, which has predominantly supported Democrats and Democratic-endorsed nonpartisans and opposed Republicans, has been the primary funder of the America First Party, based on available campaign disclosure records. The party has partnered with Lindstrom to spend $90,000 to run ads against Pillen.
Lindstrom has repeatedly denied that he’s a spoiler candidate to help Walz. He says he’s the right alternative who can win.
“I’m offering a different approach based on what I’ve learned and what I’ve actually done. You don’t have to agree with it, and you certainly don’t have to vote for me,” Lindstrom said in a Friday post on Facebook. “But I believe there’s a better way to work together, solve problems and move Nebraska forward. That’s what I’ve been trying to do all along.”
Voting ends at 8 p.m. Central time Tuesday. Early voting is underway.

text:
Voters stream into a Clarksville poll during the last day of the early voting period for the midterm elections, Oct. 29. 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)More than 1.28 million Tennessee voters cast their 2026 midterm ballots during early voting, outpacing the 2022 midterm early voting turnout by 45%. But the total fell about 98,000 votes short of equalling early voting turnout for the 2018 midterms.
All counties except Johnson recorded more early votes cast than in 2022, according to data collected by the Tennessee Secretary of State’s office.
Early voting turnout in Shelby and Williamson counties — both key to the outcome of congressional races — fell just short of 2018, when Democrats performed their best statewide in any election since 2006 (though Democratic candidates failed to flip any Congressional seats).
Turnout in West and Middle Tennessee could be particularly influential on the outcome of congressional races since the Tennessee legislature redrew district maps in May to give Republican candidates better odds.
U.S. House District 9, which historically has included the majority of Memphis, now stretches from the Memphis airport along Tennessee’s southern border and then up to encompass a portion of Williamson County. Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson is fighting to keep the seat blue despite the new boundaries against Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor.
Early voting turnout for 9th district counties was a mixed bag compared to 2018. The district now includes portions of Shelby, Fayette, Williamson, Maury counties, a small sliver of Rutherford County and several rural counties. 
Shelby County tallied 183,896 early votes, falling 2.5% behind 2018’s turnout (and up over 52% from 2022). Fayette County exceeded 2018’s turnout by 0.45% with 9,593 early votes. Williamson, a reliably Republican stronghold, logged 73,450 votes this year, 1.4% behind 2018. Maury County outpaced 2018 by 1.2% with 19,870 votes, and Rutherford recorded 2.5% more votes than in 2018 with 67,625.
Moore and Bedford counties both came out slightly ahead of 2018 early voting turnout. But the rest of the district — Hardeman, McNairy, Hardin, Wayne, Lawrence, Giles, Lincoln and Marshall counties — fell behind.
The new 5th congressional district includes parts of Shelby, Tipton, Montgomery, Maury and Williamson counties in addition to rural Northwest and Middle Tennessee counties.
Montgomery County reported a 4.8% bump up from 2018 early voting turnout with 32,636 votes. But the district’s rural counties lagged 2018 from anywhere between 2% to 23.5%.

The concern over data centers[...]
text:
The construction site for the Serverfarm data center in Clarksville, Arkansas on July 13, 2026. Construction on it began earlier this year. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)All politics is local, as the adage goes. In Arkansas, this year’s midterm campaigns are revealing that data center politics is primarily local too.
The concern over data centers has prompted a local backlash in Arkansas, with several communities enacting measures to block their construction or impose new restrictions. 
But unlike in states like Ohio and Texas where data centers have become one of the leading issues in the midterm election, the political fallout in Arkansas hasn’t been as prominent in top races for governor, Congress or the Legislature. Data centers and artificial intelligence have mostly come up in local races. [Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The lack of campaign resources for Democrats has likely played a role, said Jay Barth, a professor emeritus of politics at Hendrix College.
“It is interesting that there has not been more engagement on that issue,” Barth said. “I think that is an issue that I think would have probably popped up more assertively if there had been more expansive campaigns.”
Data center construction has accelerated amid a race by major technology companies to develop AI models and products. That data center blitz has run into local worries about energy and water use, and suspicions about the promises of large numbers of jobs or tax revenue for local schools.
That’s not to say that opposition to the data centers has lessened. Polling of likely voters in the 2nd Congressional District conducted by Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College in August found that more than half of Arkansans are strongly opposed to a data center being built in their community, with nearly 19% somewhat opposed.
The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points.
The sentiment in Arkansas has largely mirrored national trends, said Robert Coon, a strategist and consultant for Republican campaigns.
When data centers come up on the campaign trail, Democrats have mostly been on the attack — though opposition to data centers is bipartisan. Democratic challenger Hallie Shoffner has gone after Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton on the topic, and said she wants to be on the Senate Energy Committee in response to the concerns about data centers. Shoffner’s campaign stops have included Clarksville, where a $6.6 billion data center project is under construction. 
It’s also come up in at least one race for the state legislature. Former Republican Rep. Debra Hobbs, who is running to represent Clarksville as an independent, has taken aim at data centers too — as well as her opponent’s support of tax incentives for building the projects. Incumbent Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington of Knoxville is a prominent supporter of the data centers, becoming the executive director of the Arkansas Connected Communities Association, a pro-data center and pro-AI advocacy nonprofit, earlier this year. 


Let us know what you think...


 

Data centers have resonated more at the local level. Former circuit and appeals court Judge Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County’s top executive office, spearheaded a monthslong fight to pass land-use regulations for the centers in unincorporated Pulaski County. The regulations were spurred by community anger over a planned data center. In Conway, residents have been pushing for the ouster of some city council members in part due to anger over a data center proposal in the area.
Griffen was a regular presence at quorum court meetings, speaking forcefully and at length during public comment about his belief that the regulations were necessary. 
His Facebook posts on the topic were equally detailed. At one point, Griffen posted on Facebook an “independent transparent analysis” of the proposed regulations that he said was generated by ChatGPT, an AI model — the development of which by companies like Google, Anthropic and OpenAI is a primary driver of the rapid data center buildout nationwide. 
“Judge Griffen did a good job of becoming an advocate for (regulations) in a very visible way, and that kind of elevated the issue in the midst of that campaign,” said Barth. But overall, data centers aren’t having the campaign impact here that they’re having in states like Ohio and Texas, he added.
Griffen’s opponent, Republican Michael Rushin, said he was neither “for nor against” data centers “as a category” when weighing in on the debate recently. He took issue with the regulations authored by Griffen because he believed it would get the county sued — which happened two days after the quorum court overrode the current county judge’s veto on them.

Several Arkansas cities pull plug on Flock cameras


Other AI-related issues have also been playing out at the local level, sometimes in unusual ways. In the Little Rock mayor’s race, City Director B.J. Wyrick appeared to make Flock cameras an issue in her bid to unseat incumbent Frank Scott. A 40-second video Wyrick posted on social media depicts floating eyeballs as a parody of the Rockwell song “Somebody’s Watching Me” plays and refers to thousands of Little Rock cameras. According to the Little Rock Police Department’s Flock transparency portal, it operates 114 Flock cameras. 
Coon said candidates who support the centers likely aren’t bringing them up on the campaign trail. When the centers do come up, he said, it’s likely not the facilities themselves that move the needle.
“I think that, from a messaging standpoint, I think it’s probably easier for people to leverage impacts rather than just saying, you know, a candidate is pro-data center versus anti-data center,” Coon said. He pointed to Cotton’s proposed DATA Act, which would make it easier for data centers to produce their own electricity, as an example.
“I think Sen. Cotton in particular has a really interesting proposal that he’s put out, which probably has helped insulate him from some criticism over data centers,” Coon said. “For someone who likes the idea of data centers, you’re taking away a large chunk of controversy when you’re talking about, ‘Why can’t data centers bring their own power to the grid,’ right?”
MAP: More Arkansas communities putting data centers on hold

Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has expressed support for data centers in the past but has also touted her efforts to preserve state-level AI regulations alongside other governors last year. Sen. Fred Love, the Democratic candidate challenging her, pushed for a non-binding resolution to encourage a statewide moratorium in August. It was referred to a committee and hasn’t been voted on.
In the same way that data centers themselves aren’t always the topic moving the needle, Coon said they aren’t always the “bad guy.” The way Entergy Arkansas has handled a utility rider to build several new power generation plants — including one that will power Google’s West Memphis data center — is a good example, he said.
“Affordability right now is such a hot issue, and making sure that people are not feeling like they’re subsidizing (data centers),” Coon said. “In many cases, I think people can feel that that’s the case.”
Barth said that while data centers may not be animating top races in Arkansas, changes to the Generating Arkansas Job Act, which allows utilities to begin charging ratepayers a rider to pay for power generation projects before they are built, and laws that municipalities have said tie their hands when it comes to regulating data centers will be among the biggest topics tackled by legislators next spring.
“I think it’s going to be the battle,” he said, alongside efforts to rein in spending on the state’s school voucher program. “I think it will be on that front, with the cost issue, and then I think it’s going to be a local control issue.”

Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine control of both chambers of Congress. 
In Mississippi, a U.S. Senate race tops the ticket, which includes contested general elections for all four of the state’s U.S. House districts.

We want to make sure Mississippians have all the information they need to vote. That’s why we’ve answered some frequently asked questions about voting and election day. 
When can I vote on election day? 
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday. Anyone in line by 7 p.m. can still vote after closure time.
What do I need to bring to the polls? 
All Mississippi voters are required to present a photo ID. If you do not present an acceptable form of photo ID, you are entitled to cast an affidavit ballot, but must then present an ID at your local circuit clerk’s office within five business days. For voter ID information or help obtaining valid identification, call 1-800-829-6786.
Mississippi 2026 midterm elections guide: Who’s running? What are the issues?
How do I find out where I vote?
 To find your polling location, view sample ballots and see who your current officeholders are, go the the secretary of state’s My Election Day page.
How do I check to see if I’m registered to vote?
 You can check your voter registration status through this portal on the Secretary of State’s website. You can also contact your county circuit clerk’s office for registration verification. For your circuit clerk’s address and contact information, go to the secretary of state’s County Election Information page here.
CHECK YOUR STATUS: Counties have purged some voters from their rolls recently. Confirm your status as a registered voter here through the secretary of state’s office.
How do I vote absentee?
 Absentee voting began on Sept. 19. Mississippi does not have standard early voting like many other states do, but the state allows for absentee voting in person and by mail under certain circumstances, including for students attending schools away from their homes, people who will be away from their residence due to work or “any qualified elector who is required to be away from his or her residence within the county on election day for any reason.” Those who are 65 or older also can vote absentee by mail or in person. For more information on how to vote absentee, go to this page on the secretary of state’s website.
Who do I contact if I experience problems while trying to vote?
 You can call the Mississippi Secretary of State’s Elections hotline at 1-800-829-6786 
You can also email ElectionsAnswers@sos.ms.gov.
