State treasurer
Democrat Ted Lauzen vs. Republican Mike Ramone
Treasurer Colleen Davis, a Democrat, is not on the ballot. She won the office in 2022 with 53.6% of the vote.

Ted Lauzen of Wilmington is campaigning as a financial expert.  He is an investment manager, a former Marine combat pilot and the board treasurer of the Delaware YMCA, according to his campaign. At an Oct. 8 forum hosted by the Wilmington Rotary Club, he said the treasurer’s main job is to protect public money as the state’s fiduciary, and he pledged to make public how the office chooses banks and investment partners. He won the Sept. 15 Democratic primary with 45.3% of the vote over Mike Miller and Michael Alexander Smith.
Mike Ramone of Newark is campaigning as the best chance for transparency and accountability for the voters’ money. He represented the 21st District in the state House from 2008 to 2024 and led House Republicans as minority leader. He has owned businesses for more than four decades, according to his campaign. At the same forum, he said the treasurer should be an independent watchdog on state spending, since Democrats control the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly. He was the Republican nominee for governor in 2024 and lost to Democrat Matt Meyer, 56.1% to 43.9%. He had no primary opponent.

Why it matters: It’s the only statewide office on Tuesday’s ballot with no incumbent. As of Sunday afternoon, 76,769 registered Democrats and 40,343 registered Republicans had voted early or by absentee ballot statewide.
Senate District 15: western Kent County
Democrat Nisha Lodhavia vs. Republican Emily A. Thompson
Republican state Sen. Dave Lawson is leaving after four terms. He was first elected in 2010 and had no opponent in 2022. In 2020, he won with 55.3% of the vote.

Nisha Lodhavia taught at Delaware Technical Community College’s Terry Campus and at Wesley College, and raised her two daughters in Camden-Wyoming, according to her campaign. She is running on lowering costs, public schools, health care, small businesses and farming. She had no primary opponent.
Emily A. Thompson lives on her family’s farm in Hartly and has worked in state government for nearly a decade, overseeing programs for children and families, according to her campaign. She holds a doctorate in prevention science from Wilmington University. She is running on supporting farms and small businesses, early education for children, and responsible government spending. Lawson endorsed her. She had no primary opponent.

Why it matters: This seat hasn’t had a contested general election since 2020. Republicans have about 3,100 more registered voters, but as of Sunday afternoon, more registered Democrats (2,465) than registered Republicans (2,378) had voted.
House District 4: Long Neck, Oak Orchard and Angola
Democrat Gregg Lindner vs. Republican Dan Zitofsky
Republican state Rep. Jeff Hilovsky is leaving after two terms. He was elected in 2022 as the first legislator to serve this district after redistricting moved it to Sussex County.

Gregg Lindner led a media and marketing business operating in the United States and Latin America and served on an elected school board, according to his campaign. He ran for this seat in 2024 and lost to Hilovsky, 58% to 42%. He is running on roads and schools, controlled growth and public education. He had no primary opponent.
Dan Zitofsky is a Navy veteran of the Persian Gulf War and a retired New York City police officer who responded on 9/11, according to his campaign. He is running on making large developments pay for roads, drainage and emergency services before residents move in. He had no primary opponent.

Why it matters: Lindner is running for this seat again, this time with no incumbent in the race. Republicans have about 1,300 more registered voters, but as of Sunday afternoon, more registered Democrats (4,181) than registered Republicans (3,757) had voted.
House District 33: Kent County
Democrat Joshua Pennington vs. Republican Morgan Hudson
Republican state Rep. Charles S. Postles Jr., a poultry grower and former Milford School Board president, is leaving after five terms. He was first elected in 2016 and had no opponent in 2022 or 2024.

Joshua Pennington of Magnolia has spent several years in nonprofit work advocating for people with disabilities, according to his campaign. He grew up in Bowers, where his family has served with the Bowers Volunteer Fire Company, and he was a cadet there. He is running on supporting first responders, people with disabilities and seniors, education and mental health. He had no primary opponent.
Morgan Hudson of Milford is vice president and head of human resources at her family’s construction cleaning business, manages rental properties, is vice chair of the Kent County Board of Adjustment and is president of the Frederica Senior Center board, according to her campaign. She is running on small businesses, family farms, seniors, education, health care and public safety. She won the Sept. 15 Republican primary by seven votes, 1,017 to 1,010, over Matt Bucher.

Why it matters: Of the districts on our list, it has the smallest gap between registered Republicans and registered Democrats: Republicans are ahead by about 350 voters. As of Sunday afternoon, more registered Democrats (1,503) than registered Republicans (1,334) had voted.
House District 38: Bethany Beach to Fenwick Island
Democrat Maureen Madden vs. Republican Carlie Carey
Republican state Rep. Ronald E. Gray, an engineer, is leaving after seven terms. He was first elected in 2012 and had no opponent in 2020, 2022 or 2024. The district includes Bethany Beach, Fenwick Island, Selbyville and Ocean View.

Maureen Madden of Dagsboro retired from federal service after nearly 23 years at NASA and more than seven at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), where she was a deputy director of a satellite research center, according to her campaign. She is running on slowing overdevelopment, affordable housing and adding voting and reproductive rights to state law and the state constitution. She had no primary opponent.
Carlie Carey grew up in the district and graduated from Indian River High School, according to her campaign. She and her husband opened a farm-to-table restaurant in Fenwick Island and sold it in 2022. She now owns a ceramics studio and works on the couple’s 16-acre farm. She is running on supporting small businesses, protecting the environment, and affordable, reliable energy. Gray endorsed her. She had no primary opponent.

Why it matters: As of Sunday afternoon, 5,525 registered Republicans and 4,450 registered Democrats had voted, the largest gap in favor of registered Republicans among the seven races. Still, a larger share of registered Democrats (59%) than registered Republicans (48%) has voted.
House District 41: Sussex County
Democrat Ryan Stuckey vs. Republican John Atkins
Republican state Rep. Richard G. Collins, a farmer and former insurance business owner, is leaving after six terms. He was first elected in 2014. In 2024, he won with 64.4% of the vote.

Ryan Stuckey was born in Sussex County, was raised by a single mother and owns a coffee shop on Main Street, according to his campaign. He says he served on a planning and zoning commission and rewrote local rules to control development and protect forests. He is running on roads, schools and slowing development. He had no primary opponent.
John Atkins campaigns through a Facebook page and does not have a campaign website. He won the Sept. 15 Republican primary with 48.7% of the vote, 67 votes ahead of Doug Conaway.

Why it matters: Collins won this seat by 28 points in 2024. As of Sunday afternoon, more registered Republicans (2,302) than registered Democrats (2,004) had voted.
New Castle County Council, District 3
Democrat Kira Alejandro vs. Republican Melissa S. Brayman
Republican Councilwoman Janet Kilpatrick, first elected in 2010, is retiring after 16 years. She had no opponent in 2022. The district covers the Pike Creek, Hockessin, Yorklyn and Newark areas.

Kira Alejandro of Yorklyn has worked for about a decade in specialty coffee and small local businesses and has never held elected office. At an Oct. 7 forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of New Castle County, she said she would protect people on fixed incomes from county tax increases, wants a pause on approving new data centers, and takes no money from developers, land use attorneys or corporations. She won the Sept. 15 Democratic primary with 68.8% of the vote over Kyle R. Grantham.
Melissa S. Brayman of Pike Creek is director of administration and finance at the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce and has never held elected office. At the same forum, she pledged to vote against any new county tax increase, said she opposes data centers in residential areas but would not back a pause if defending it costs taxpayers money, and said she has not taken money from developers. She had no primary opponent.

Why it matters: At the forum, both candidates named affordability as the county’s most urgent problem. As of Sunday afternoon, 5,471 people in the district had voted: 3,098 registered Democrats, 1,207 registered Republicans and 1,166 everyone else.
What happens next
When the new General Assembly meets in January, at least 14 of its 62 seats will have a new lawmaker. That includes the 13 departing members’ seats plus House District 23, because Rep. Mara Gorman is running for Sokola’s Senate seat instead of her House seat.
Lawmakers will then decide whether to give final approval to eight proposed amendments to the state constitution that the current General Assembly has already passed once. They cover topics including early voting, absentee voting, marriage and the death penalty. Each one needs a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate again, so it matters whether either party has enough seats to pass or block them on its own.
Voting Tuesday
Polls are open Tuesday, Nov. 3, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. You vote at your own polling place. Not sure which districts you’re in or where to vote? Delaware LIVE’s 2026 Voters Guide has your polling place and every name on your ballot. It will also have election results Tuesday night.

title: Fazio, Lamont and others make final push as Election Day nears
description:

Jahana Hayes and her challenger Chris Shea were in Meriden and Middlebury in an effort to turn out voters in the 5th Congressional District in the waning days of their campaigns.
Lamont and Fazio offered closing[...]
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, state Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, came closest to crossing paths Sunday in Enfield, while U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes and her challenger Chris Shea were in Meriden and Middlebury in an effort to turn out voters in the 5th Congressional District in the waning days of their campaigns.
Lamont and Fazio offered closing arguments in the swing town on the Massachusetts border that Lamont carried with 50.2% of the vote four years ago.
“It’s a hardworking, middle-class town,” Fazio said. “People on both sides of the aisle, they’re common-sense people. They’re not ideological or partisan people. They believe that you should be able to work hard, follow the rules and be able to pay your bills. And in this state, after eight years of the Lamont administration, it’s harder than ever to get by.”
Fazio campaigned at the Country Diner with two Republican incumbents in difficult races, Sen. John Kissel and Rep. Carol Hall, and Marie Pyznar, the GOP challenger to Rep. John Santanella, D-Enfield. 
Less than two miles away, Lamont gave a pep talk in Santanella’s kitchen to volunteers.

Gov. Ned Lamont speaks to state Senate candidate David Kiner during a campaign stop at a home in Enfield on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“We’ve come a long way in the last eight years. We were hurting a bit back in the 2010s,” Lamont said, recalling the budget shortfall and debt he inherited from his predecessor, Gov. Dannel P. Malloy, when he took office eight years ago.
“I think a lot of people were losing some confidence, losing a little bit of confidence in the state.”
Lamont, a Democrat seeking a third term, is favored by double digits in every recent public poll, and the time for persuading voters to choose a candidate is over. The focus is getting the base to turnout on Tuesday, though hundreds of thousands already have voted in early voting and by absentee.
At Santanella’s house, Lora Rae Anderson corralled volunteers for door knocking, assuring them the task involved no hard sell.
“We’re talking to friendly voters. We want to make sure that we’re turning people out,” said Anderson, a Lamont administration official and the volunteer manager of David Kiner’s campaign to unseat Kissel, who was elected 34 years ago.
Kissel, after surviving for so long in a district that leans Democratic, likened him to a cat who has expended his nine lives.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio laughs with state Sen. John Kissel, R- Enfield, during a campaign stop at Country Diner in Enfield on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“I’m at absolutely the last of my nine lives on my second cat,” Kissel said.
He told Fazio he was grateful for the visit.
Fazio seemed content to drop back to his key message that voters should hold the Democratic governor and not the Republican president responsible for the high cost of living in Connecticut after making an issue of the governor pushing away the camera phone of a person who challenged him about an aide’s traffic ticket.
The governor’s campaign ignored the episode, while Fazio’s promoted the woman’s brief video, as did the conservative radio host, Reese on the Radio. His campaign called it a “criminal confrontation.”
Fazio campaigned later Sunday with Rep. Jill Barry, D-Glastonbury, who is running on the Independent and Republican ballot lines after losing the Democratic endorse. He was closing with a rally in Bristol.
Hayes and Shea in the 5th District
In the sprawling 5th Congressional District in the western part of the state, Hayes and her Republican opponent Shea sought to capitalize on the last day of early voting and convince voters not to sit out of a midterm election.
Democrats are buoyed by a favorable political environment, but the candidates focused on a closing message that called on voters to not get complacent during a high-stakes election year.

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, who’s running for reelection in Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, speaks to a group of volunteers in Meriden ahead of canvassing on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

“You want to turn the news off. Everything is negative, everything is ugly. Working people are getting hit the hardest,” Connecticut state Treasurer Erick Russell said at a gathering in Meriden. “What you all have to remember is all of that is on the line right now this election cycle.”
“I know I’m preaching to the choir, but the main thing here is we got a couple of days left, and we can’t leave anything on the table, because this is an opportunity not only for us to win but win big,” he continued. Russell faces a challenge from Republican Fred Wilms.
Russell was joined by Hayes and state legislative candidates who gathered in Meriden before supporters went out to go door-knocking on a sunny and mild autumn day. He touted Connecticut’s legislature as a “back stop” to what’s coming out of Washington.
Hayes, who’s seeking a fifth term in Congress, delivered a forceful response to a room packed with a few dozen volunteers. She painted a picture much larger than the 5th District seat but of what she sees as the consequences nationally.
“It matters, every single election, because what we are seeing is a slow burn, chipping at the edges, eroding our democracy, intimidating the right to vote, doing all of these little things, which by themselves don’t seem significant, but all together is the recipe for disaster and where we are heading,” Hayes said. “So we have two days. Everything is on the line.”
Hayes brought up the H.R. 1, Republicans’ tax legislation that passed last year and was dubbed by Trump as the “big beautiful bill.” She argued that “the most damaging parts haven’t even gone into effect,” pointing to changes to Medicaid eligibility that’ll lead to cuts in the state and across the country.
“Give them a reason to make the issues that you care about a part of whether it be the Democratic priorities or the Republican priorities, it doesn’t matter,” Hayes said. “Let them know this seat is not yours to have. You don’t get to keep it. You have to work for it every single time.”
Midterms are challenging in general because turnout lags compared to presidential election years. On top of that, the party in power historically faces headwinds in a midterm year.

Republican Chris Shea, who is running for Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, campaigns alongside local Republicans in Middlebury on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026.  Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

Shea, meanwhile, spent the morning with about two dozen local Republicans in Middlebury. They stood on the side of a main road, waving campaign signs for a number of GOP candidates running up and down the ballot on Tuesday.
Shea, a firefighter and retired Navy SEAL, said he’s working to get lower-propensity voters out to the polls.
“We’re feeling good, we’re working real hard on getting the word out and getting after folks — the presidential-year-only voters. There’s a ton of those registered,” Shea said, as he waved to cars that honked in support or drivers that flashed a thumbs up. “You get after a chunk of those and a couple other cities, it makes a big difference.”
Shea is a first-time candidate but noted that he has long ties to the 5th District compared to the past Republican candidate running for the seat. He’s hoping that’ll materialize into more support, along with his career in the military and his work at the Pentagon.
The 5th District is still considered the most competitive congressional race in the state. This cycle, election analysts who rate competitive races moved the 5th District much closer to Democrats.
National attention has shifted away from the district as outside groups in both parties look to other U.S. House races in the battle for control of Congress. That has largely dissipated, though both candidates got an 11th-hour boost from political action committees.
“I think they could have gotten more bang for their buck by investing a little bit here, which would have made the Democrats try to pump in two or three times as much,” Shea said about more involvement and financial support from Republicans at the national level.
“Based on what everybody says, I’m a pretty darn good candidate, based on my background, no criminal history, no nonsense, serving the country, serving locally,” he added. “That’s a pretty appealing candidacy to put in front of people.”
John Calabrese, chairman of the Middlebury Republican Town Committee, spent the morning alongside Shea and others to boost turnout.
“The base has to get out. That’s the bottom line. Even in Connecticut,” Calabrese said. “Connecticut has to draw independents. Republicans, we don’t have enough. But if we can draw some of the independents, I know we can pick up something.”
Calabrese said one of the bigger challenges for the party is getting younger voters into the political fold. “We have to get those people motivated to come out to an event like today, to spend some time,” he said.
The news about U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy’s stroke sent a shockwave throughout the campaign trail in Connecticut on Sunday.
Murphy “has been all over this country working for Democratic candidates up and down the ballot, because he understands it’s not just about what happens to those small things, it’s about making sure that those big things are also taken care of,” she said. “It’s about making sure that we have Democratic majorities in the House and in the Senate. He’s going to be OK,” she said to applause.

title: Federal judge rejects Trump administration attempt to pause Alaska’s US Senate election

On Oct. 22, Trump ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to file a lawsuit that would prohibit anyone but Sullivan from being certified as the winner of the U.S. Senate election. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)A federal judge has dis[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a rally featuring President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Wasilla. On Oct. 22, Trump ordered the U.S. Department of Justice to file a lawsuit that would prohibit anyone but Sullivan from being certified as the winner of the U.S. Senate election. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration that sought to block the state of Alaska from declaring a winner in the state’s U.S. Senate election.
In a 20-page order issued Sunday morning, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason said the federal government failed to explain how it has the authority to bring its lawsuit.
“Therefore, this court lacks jurisdiction and the United States’ amended complaint must be dismissed,” Gleason wrote.
Legal experts had expected the result because the federal government’s arguments were legally questionable.
President Donald Trump said last week he ordered the filing of the case, which asked a judge to stop the state from declaring anyone but incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan the winner. 
Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins

Gleason is an appointee of President Barack Obama and the most senior federal judge in Alaska.
Polling averages indicate Democratic candidate Mary Peltola is slightly ahead of Sullivan in a race that could help determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate.
A New York Times article on Wednesday said Democratic campaigners sought to recruit spoiler candidates in the race, including Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg. 
Dan J. Sullivan and Republican Gerald Heikes of Palmer are the third and fourth candidates in the four-person Senate race.
The Alaska Beacon has not independently verified the Times’ reporting.
Peltola denied personal involvement after the Times reporting indicated she was aware of the recruitment, which involved an intermediary. Since the Times published its article, the federal government and the state have announced criminal investigations but have not said what crime may have been committed or whom they are investigating.
Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy had been challenged earlier this year in state court, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in his favor. 
Peltola denies knowledge of spoiler candidate plan at Juneau rally

No way to preserve ballot secrecy, Gleason says
In written arguments filed since last week, attorneys representing the federal government had argued without evidence that Alaska voters might be confused by the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan and sought an order that would require the state to set aside all votes for Dan J. Sullivan, pending further investigation.
The state of Alaska, Peltola’s campaign, a national Democratic group and two nonpartisan voting organizations opposed that request. 
In written filings, they said the action requested by the federal government would not prove any possible confusion.
“No pattern of ballot markings will reveal any voter’s reason for voting for Daniel J., regardless of how the voter ranks the candidates on the ranked-choice ballot,” state attorneys wrote. “And the ballot markings will be the only evidence of voters’ intent. Ballots cannot be associated with voters to allow the state or federal government to follow up with Daniel J. voters about their true intentions. Like every state in the union, Alaska protects the secrecy of the ballot by law, and such an investigation would require violating that secrecy.”
In response, the federal government could not explain how it would keep Alaskans’ votes secret. 
“The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling,” Gleason wrote. “Simply, the Court cannot grant the United States the relief it seeks because the United States has failed to establish the redressability prerequisite for Article III standing.”
Federal attorneys suggested the state could segregate votes for Dan J. Sullivan to allow the counting of others, “but requiring the segregation of ballots cast by voters for Daniel J. Sullivan so that these voters can be further investigated by law enforcement is not a remedy that this Court can or should order as it clearly (violates) Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot,” Gleason wrote.
Ordinarily, a plaintiff could amend a rejected legal complaint to show how it has standing, but in this case, Gleason said that would be unfair to Alaska because the election is so near.
As Alaskans vote, state’s top federal prosecutor confirms criminal investigation of Dem groups

Appeal is possible but may be moot
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which was named in the Times article as one of the organizations recruiting spoilers, had intervened in the lawsuit alongside the Peltola campaign and the state of Alaska.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said DSCC executive director Devan Barber in an emailed statement.
The federal government may appeal Sunday’s rejection to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, but action in that court may not take place until after Election Day. 
If incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan wins the election, or if Peltola wins by a margin that is larger than the number of votes received by Dan J. Sullivan, an appeal could be moot.
In addition, there is some indication that the 9th Circuit may be unwilling to overturn the rejection. On Oct. 26, a three-judge panel from the 9th Circuit rejected a separate lawsuit filed by the federal government against California elections officials. A lower court had also dismissed the federal lawsuit against California.
In that ruling, the panel wrote, “On balance, given the record and because Plaintiff has offered no workable plan of any kind as to how the remedy it seeks could be accomplished in practice without potential catastrophic consequences to California’s ongoing election, the equities between the parties and the public’s interest do not weigh in favor of granting the requested relief.”
Through Saturday, almost 15% of registered Alaska voters had already cast ballots for the general election. Turnout is expected to be near 50%, based on trends over the past two midterms.

title: Something wrong at the polls? What Delaware voters should know and do!
description:
From malfunctioning voting machines and registration disputes to suspected fraud and intimidation, voters have several ways to document concerns and seek help from state, federal and political party officials
DOVER — When Delaware voters head to the polls Tuesday, Nov. 3, most will cast their ballots without difficulty. But what happens when something doesn’[...]
text:
From malfunctioning voting machines and registration disputes to suspected fraud and intimidation, voters have several ways to document concerns and seek help from state, federal and political party officials
DOVER — When Delaware voters head to the polls Tuesday, Nov. 3, most will cast their ballots without difficulty. But what happens when something doesn’t seem right?
Voting machines that stop working. Registration records that don’t match. Voters turned away. Questions about whether ineligible individuals are voting. Allegations of intimidation or interference.
Concerns about these issues have surfaced in previous elections, raising questions about election security, voter access and accountability.
While an allegation does not establish wrongdoing, legitimate concerns deserve examination, not dismissal.
Election integrity requires ensuring that every eligible voter can cast a ballot while preventing illegal voting or misconduct from compromising the process.
Just as important, voters need to know how to report problems, who is responsible for investigating them and how to preserve evidence.
When voting machines fail
Malfunctioning voting machines can create long lines, delays and questions about whether voters will have an opportunity to cast their ballots.
Delaware has contingency procedures, including the use of paper ballots when voting machines are unavailable.
Ballot shortages and other disruptions present additional challenges that election officials are responsible for resolving.
A machine failure does not automatically mean fraud has occurred. However, repeated problems, unexplained delays or irregularities involving ballots deserve examination.
When voters are turned away
Registration disputes are another potential Election Day problem.
A voter may be told their name is missing from registration records, their information does not match or they are at the wrong polling location.
Delaware has procedures for handling registration discrepancies, identification questions and provisional ballots.
A documented example occurred during Delaware’s 2024 primary election, when the Department of Elections acknowledged a clerical error affecting 764 voter registration records.
The error involved party affiliations recorded incorrectly during automatic voter registration. State officials said they corrected the problem and that no voters were prevented from voting because of the error.
The incident demonstrated that administrative mistakes can occur — and why identifying, correcting and explaining them matters.
What about illegal voting?
Concerns about election integrity also include allegations that unregistered individuals are voting, someone is impersonating another voter or a person is attempting to vote more than once.
Delaware law prohibits fraudulent voting, including impersonation and knowingly casting multiple ballots.
But suspicion alone does not establish a violation.
Someone being unfamiliar at a polling location does not mean that person is ineligible. Registration disputes also do not necessarily indicate fraud.
Credible allegations require investigation and evidence before conclusions can be reached.
Intimidation and interference are serious offenses
Threats, harassment, coercion and attempts to interfere with voting can violate Delaware law.
The Delaware Department of Justice has identified voter intimidation, interference with election officers, impersonating law enforcement and improper questioning of voters among activities that may constitute election offenses.
Delaware also restricts certain campaign activities within 50 feet of polling place entrances.
These protections apply to voters of every political affiliation.
What is Delaware doing?
Attorney General Kathy Jennings, Gov. Matt Meyer and State Election Commissioner Anthony Albence outlined the state’s Election Day preparations in an Oct. 30 announcement.
The preparations include trained election officers, statewide investigators, attorneys available to assist election officials and coordination with law enforcement.
The Department of Justice’s Division of Civil Rights and Public Trust will help investigate allegations of voter intimidation and criminal interference.
The Department of Elections and Department of Justice also plan to jointly staff a voter hotline at 302-739-4277.
But preparation alone is not enough. Public confidence depends on how effectively problems are addressed and whether officials explain what happened.
What should voters do if something goes wrong?
Voters who encounter problems at their polling place should notify an election officer and seek assistance.
State guidance identifies several circumstances in which additional procedures may apply:




Voting machines unavailable: Paper ballots may be used.






Missing registration records: Provisional ballot procedures may be available.






Registration discrepancies: Election officers can review applicable records and procedures.






Voters in line at 8 p.m.: Those already in line are entitled to vote.






Suspected fraud or intimidation: Concerns can be reported to election authorities. Immediate threats should be reported to 911.




The statewide voter hotline is 302-739-4277.
Why documenting an incident matters
An important step in addressing suspected election irregularities is creating an accurate written account.
A telephone call can alert authorities to an immediate problem, while a written report provides a record that investigators can review afterward.
An incident report should identify the polling location, date and approximate time of the incident, individuals involved, potential witnesses and a factual description of what occurred.
Supporting information may include lawfully obtained photographs, documents or communications. Voters should observe restrictions on recording inside polling places and avoid interfering with voting or compromising ballot secrecy.
Reports should distinguish between something personally witnessed and information received from someone else.
People submitting complaints should retain copies, supporting materials, email correspondence and any acknowledgment from election officials.
Delaware provides an online Complaints & Issues form.
For formal administrative complaints covered by the federal Help America Vote Act, Delaware has additional requirements. These complaints must be submitted in writing, signed, sworn and notarized. An ordinary email or online issue report does not automatically satisfy those requirements.
Where can voters report concerns?
The Delaware Department of Elections oversees polling locations, voting equipment, registration records and election administration.
Its county offices can also receive concerns about election procedures.
The Delaware Department of Justice investigates potential violations of state law, while federal authorities may investigate violations of federal voting rights laws.
The U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division maintains a reporting system at civilrights.justice.gov/report and a toll-free number, 800-253-3931.
Reports involving threats or violence should be directed to emergency services when immediate assistance is needed.
Both political parties offer additional contacts
Delaware’s two major political parties also provide ways for voters and election observers to contact their organizations about election concerns.
The Delaware Republican Party can be reached through DEGOP.gop and its published headquarters number, 302-668-1954. A separate number, 302-397-8074, has been supplied as a Republican election-integrity contact, although Delaware LIVE has not independently confirmed its current hotline designation.
The Delaware Democratic Party can be reached at 302-328-9036 and through DelDems.org. Its website identifies that number as its state headquarters contact.
At the national level, the Republican National Committee operates Protect the Vote, an election-integrity initiative involving election observers, volunteers and legal efforts.
A similarly named website, protectthevote.org, redirects to a nonpartisan Election Protection organization and is not affiliated with the RNC.
Political party reporting channels provide additional points of contact but do not replace complaints submitted directly to government election authorities.
Delaware LIVE wants to hear from voters
Voters who believe they have witnessed a problem or irregularity at their polling place can also contact Delaware LIVE at Editor@DelawareLIVE.com.
Readers are encouraged to include the polling location, approximate time, a factual description of what occurred and any supporting information.
Delaware LIVE may follow up on credible reports as part of its Election Day coverage, seeking independent confirmation and responses from appropriate election officials.
Contacting the newsroom does not replace reporting concerns to election authorities or law enforcement.
Accountability matters
A fair election protects eligible voters from being denied their ballots while ensuring that only legally qualified individuals vote.
It also protects election workers from harassment and requires credible allegations of misconduct to receive appropriate scrutiny.
Not every equipment failure is fraud. Not every registration discrepancy is an attempt at illegal voting. But legitimate concerns should not be ignored simply because officials believe their preparations are adequate.
Written documentation, timely reporting and transparent investigations all contribute to public confidence.
Delaware voters deserve an election system that is fair, responsive and accountable.
The ultimate measure of election integrity is not whether officials promise a secure election, but how effectively they address problems when they occur.

BILOXI — Five hundred or more people gathered on Biloxi’s southeastern waterfront Sunday morning and then marched to Ocean Springs, demanding justice for Nolan Wells.
The Ocean Springs teen went missing during a July 4 trip to Horn Island with a group of friends. The group traveled to the barrier island on three boats, but the friends returned without Wells, saying he stayed behind to talk to a girl.
Two days later, on July 6, authorities found Wells’ body in the water off Horn Island, a barrier island about 10 miles from the mainland.
Marchers gathered Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, after crossing into Ocean Springs from Biloxi, calling for justice for Nolan Wells. Credit: Tim Thorsen/Sun Herald
A Jackson County grand jury later found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Wells’ friends, who had traveled to Horn Island that day to celebrate the Fourth of July.
The official cause of his death remains undetermined.
Wells’ parents, Elmore and Christine Wonsley, hired civil rights attorney Ben Crump to do an independent investigation into their son’s death.
They have called on the Department of Justice to do an independent investigation. The protesters came from the Mississippi Coast and beyond, including New Orleans, Atlanta, Chicago and other places.
The event was billed as part of a 50-state march.
Vanessa Diggins and Jennifer Matthews drove from New Orleans to the Mississippi Coast to take part in a mass protest Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, over the death of Nolan Wells and others who have died under questionable circumstances. Credit: Margaret Baker/Sun Herald
“It’s important for us to come out here today because this is a concern for all people, not just Black people,” said Jennifer Matthews, who drove from New Orleans. “This didn’t just happen to Nolan Wells. It’s been going on with three or four other Black kids, and we need to get to the bottom of it.
“Mississippi is a very prejudiced state, and it’s 2026, and I want to be a part of the change that needs to happen,” she said.
Sandra Wyche, of Gulfport, echoed the sentiment.
She said she came to the protest “because we’re tired of our children being murdered and killed, and tired of the people that are over these communities.
“If it was a Caucasian baby that was a part of this, somebody would have been in jail today,” Wyche said of Wells’ death. “And color does matter. Now, as far as me being prejudiced, I’m not. But right is right, and wrong is wrong.”
Protesters march across the Biloxi Bay Bridge in a mass protest Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, calling for justice for Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old from Ocean Springs, who was found dead after a July 4 trip to Horn Island. Credit: Margaret Baker/Sun Herald
The speakers at the protest talked about other Black lives cut short, including Kohen Wiley, a 1-year-old shot to death by police in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia after a report of shoplifting by women who were with Kohen, and Andrew Joseph III, a 14-year-old who was struck and killed on an interstate after being kicked out of the Florida State Fair in 2014.
Tonya Brown, of Biloxi, said she came out like the others who made the nearly four-mile walk to Ocean Springs and back to “support these families that are in dire need of knowing what happened to their babies. We need justice, and the killing needs to stop. We all need to come together as one to support these families.” 
Another protester, Carolyn Ruff, of Chicago, is founder of Black Lives Matter Women of Faith and described herself as an activist fighting for justice for Nolan Wells and others. 
“We know Nolan Wells did not drown,” Russ said. “We’re here because we know they will find the truth eventually.” 
Protestors chanted, “Justice for Nolan Wells,” and “Nolan did not drown,” among other slogans calling for justice for those who died under questionable circumstances.

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized after experiencing a stroke, his office confirmed on Sunday.
Murphy, 53, experienced symptoms on Saturday while attending his son’s hockey game and was taken to a hospital. He was later transferred to another hospital and is expected to make a full recovery.
“Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game,” Murphy chief of staff Allison Herwitt said in a statement on Sunday.
“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she said. “He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
Murphy, who is not on Tuesday’s ballot, has been campaigning the past several weeks in Connecticut and a handful of swing states on behalf of Democratic candidates competing in the midterm elections. He was supposed to be in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who’s running for Senate.

text:
(Eric Harkleroad/KFF Health News)Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds.
But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. 7.
Robert Travis Scott of Abingdon, Virginia, did just that in late October after he received a notice that his AARP-UnitedHealthcare Medicare drug plan premium would be increasing from $39.60 a month in 2026 to $121.90 in 2027. With just a little work checking prices online, Scott found a Humana plan for $19.30 with similar benefits.
“Yes, I am quite happy about that,” he said of the new plan he just found. He said he was stunned his existing plan was going up so much and worried that other seniors won’t shop for plans to save money. He estimates he saved himself about $1,000 for next year.
“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” said Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and the director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, which conducted the analysis. KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
Rising drug costs are among the litany of affordability issues angering voters ahead of November’s midterm election. President Donald Trump, whose approval rating in some polls has dipped to the lowest level of his two terms in office, claims his administration has succeeded in negotiating lower prices from drug manufacturers.
“What we’re doing great with is pharmaceuticals, hundreds of billions,” Trump said at a campaign rally in Ohio on Oct. 28, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. “You should win just on this, everybody running. We have the lowest drug prices anywhere in the world. We went from the highest drug prices, we now have the lowest drug prices, favored nations, anywhere in the world.”
How much people actually pay for drugs varies widely, depending on what medicines individual patients need and their insurance coverage.
Medicare beneficiaries who get their drug coverage as part of private Medicare Advantage plans, which replace traditional Medicare coverage, will see much lower premium increases. The KFF analysis found these enrollees will pay an average of $9 for drugs as part of their overall monthly premium in 2027, or an increase of less than $2 per month.
More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage health plans, which usually include a drug benefit, instead of the traditional program.
Nearly 25 million people are enrolled in Medicare stand-alone prescription drug plans, according to KFF. About 31 million get drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans.
Premiums are just part of the higher costs Medicare enrollees are facing.
Most enrollees who buy a stand-alone drug plan or get drug benefits through Medicare Advantage plans will also have an annual deductible for drug coverage in 2027.
The average deductible in 2027 will be $643 for stand-alone plans, according to the KFF analysis, up from $540 in 2026. Drug deductibles will average $489 for those with Medicare Advantage plans, up from $360 in 2026.
In addition, most Medicare enrollees with drug coverage next year will have to pay coinsurance rather than copayments, the KFF analysis found. That can mean less predictable out-of-pocket costs because coinsurance requires paying a percentage of the cost of a drug, not a fixed amount.
One possible cause of the projected premium hikes is the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ decision in July to end early a three-year pilot program designed to keep down stand-alone premiums. The program paid subsidies to stand-alone plans in 2025 and 2026.
KFF said CMS’ decision to end that subsidy program after only two years could cause stand-alone premiums to rise in 2027.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has called the subsidy program an insurance industry bailout.
KFF noted its analysis differs from CMS’ projection for a $1 increase in the national average premium, from $35 to $36, based on September 2026 enrollment. It said that CMS did not explain its calculation methods and that it’s possible CMS assumed people would switch to lower-cost plans.
CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the KFF findings.
About 10.4 million Medicare enrollees, or 76% of enrollees in stand-alone drug plans who don’t get low-income subsidies, will pay a higher monthly premium in 2027 if they stick with the same plan, KFF found.
This includes 4.1 million enrollees who are currently in a zero-premium plan. They’ll automatically pay more in 2027, because there will be no zero-premium plans available, the KFF analysis found.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

text:
Dear Editor,
As a parent and a teacher, I urge local leaders to demand accountability for data centers. Right now, big polluters are profiting while our families foot the bill. Data centers take up acres of much-needed land that could otherwise be used for affordable housing, education or agriculture. We need our rural landscapes to keep protecting wildlife and providing clean air and water. 

READ MORE

The rush to power data centers is driving new fossil fuel development, threatening climate progress and bringing more toxic pollution to communities. Instead, we could be powering our lives with clean energy that protects our wallets, our climate and our health. The progress we have made in the last 20 years in restricting emissions and reducing pollution will be reversed, especially if data centers are gas powered.
This shouldn’t be a difficult choice. Let’s hold data centers accountable with common-sense guardrails now. 
Anne D’Olivo
Manchester, Vt.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: In an Alaska House district known for low voter turnout, the candidates present stark contrasts
description: A Government Hill Elementary School student walks on Oct. 29, 2026, on the overpass adjacent to the school and near the Government Hill gate of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. Federal law prohibits candidates from campaigning on military bases, but many candidates, including House District 18 hopeful Cliff Groh, have posted signs in strategic spots near the[...]
text:
A Government Hill Elementary School student walks on Oct. 29, 2026, on the overpass adjacent to the school and near the Government Hill gate of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. Federal law prohibits candidates from campaigning on military bases, but many candidates, including House District 18 hopeful Cliff Groh, have posted signs in strategic spots near the base. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)In the Alaska House district with chronic low voter turnout and high resident turnover, how do legislative candidates connect with voters?
Democrat Cliff Groh and Republican Dan Sager are trying to answer that question in the race to represent House District 18.
The vast majority of the territory in the district spans Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, or JBER, and more than half of the voters are listed as base residents. Federal law prohibits campaigning on military bases, so Groh and Sager are using phone calls, texts and online communications to try to reach them.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
It is not an easy task, according to Groh, who represented the district in the state House in 2023 and 2024 and hopes to return to the seat.
Military personnel around the country vote at lower rates than the U.S. average, he noted, and the JBER residents fit that pattern. Additionally, some voters considered JBER residents are not actually in Anchorage when he tries to contact them.
“That’s because some of the people who have addresses on JBER wake up every morning in Germany or Alabama,” Groh said. “I have called Hawaii, California, Rhode Island, Texas. I’ve called for people, I think, in Turkey and South Korea, too.” Some have not answered, but he has reached people all around the country who are absentee voters, he said.
Sager, who is running for the seat for the first time, also faces the challenge of JBER voter lists that quickly become obsolete.
Sager said the transient nature of military service quickly makes JBER voter lists obsolete. He mentioned his last list. “I got it, and then they said, like, “‘Don’t even contact numbers, you know, 700 through whatever because we already know that they’ve moved on,’” he said.
Like other candidates, he has chosen some strategic and eye-catching sites just outside JBER’s gates to post campaign signs.
The low voting propensity of enlisted personnel and their family members shows up in election statistics.
 

Democratic candidate Cliff Groh stands on a sidewalk on Oct. 28, 2026, in the Ship Creek area, part of the eclectic state House district he represented in 2023 and 2024 and hopes to represent again. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	In the Aug. 18 open primary, in which Groh took over 67% of the vote, turnout in House District 18 was only 9.2%. That was, by far, the lowest turnout in the state, and it compares to a statewide turnout of about 27% for the primary election, according to Alaska Division of Elections records.
The district has been at the bottom in turnout in other years. In the 2022 general election, in which Groh beat then-incumbent Republican David Nelson, turnout was just 18.7% in the district, compared to the statewide rate of about 44%, according to state records.
It is not just JBER that is transient and less politically engaged than Alaska as a whole – or less accessible to door-knocking candidates.
The district includes a slice of downtown Anchorage, mostly with industrial properties along Ship Creek, and a piece of the Muldoon neighborhood in the northeastern part of town.
Overall, House District 18 ranks near the bottom in the state for household income, and many residents have difficulty affording even the substandard housing that is available to them, Groh said. They are also coping with underfunded schools, among other issues that give them little time to engage with candidates and voting options, he said.
“There are a number of working families in this district who don’t feel like they have the luxury to follow politics,” Groh said. “They’re often hard-pressed and struggling.”
Off-base, Groh and Sager noted, many residents live in buildings with locked entries, either apartments or senior housing, posing another challenge to on-the-ground campaigning.
There is one part of House District 18 that is stable, easily walked by candidates and home to some of the city’s more economically comfortable residents: Government Hill. As Anchorage’s oldest neighborhood, it has tight community ties and strong civic spirit. For the most part, however, district residents face difficulties, Groh said.
Groh and Sager both live in Government Hill; Sager said he was drawn to the neighborhood by its “charm,” and he and his wife enjoy the easy access to parks, trails and the city’s downtown district.
 

Republican Dan Sager, a candidate for Alaska’s House District 18, holds his baby daughter Liberty outside his Government Hill house on Oct. 29, 2026. Government Hill is Anchorage’s oldest neighborhood, and some converted military Quonset huts, like those in the background, remain in use. The House district is dominated by Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson but also includes part of the Muldoon neighborhood in East Anchorage and a mostly industrial slice of downtown Anchorage around Ship Creek. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	They might be neighbors, but Groh and Sager are vastly different candidates.
Groh, 72, is a lifelong Alaskan with decades of experience in politics and government policy. His father, also named Cliff, served as a Republican state senator in the 1970s. In the 1980s, the younger Cliff was a legislative aide — and specifically worked on the legislation that created the wildly popular Alaska Permanent Fund dividend. His campaign website features a photo of him with former Gov. Jay Hammond, an Alaska political icon generally credited with creating the dividend program.
Groh holds a bachelor’s degree from Harvard, and after receiving a law degree from the University of California Berkley, he returned to Alaska and worked as a prosecutor and municipal attorney in Sitka and Anchorage, as well as in private practice. He has also worked as a special assistant in the Alaska Department of Revenue. He has authored academic books and articles about Alaska policy issues, taught about public policy at the university level and, since the 1990s, served on the board of Alaska Common Ground, a non-profit civic organization.
This is his third time running for the House seat. After he beat Nelson in 2022, during the first election season under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, he lost to Nelson in 2024 by a mere 23 votes.
Groh said he is excited about the opportunity to be in a legislative majority with a potential Democratic governor. When he served previously, he was in the minority. A victory by him could boost the ranks of the now-slim bipartisan House majority.
“I very much hope that there can be what is called a ‘trifecta’ of a good House majority, a good Senate majority, and that my preferred candidate, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, wins the governorship so that we can make some progress in the state on a whole host of issues for which we have stagnated,” Groh said, naming the Democratic candidate for governor.
For Sager, who has been a participant in the Government Hill Community Council since he bought a house in the neighborhood in 2020, this is his first attempt at elective office.
He is 39, the new father of a 5-month-old girl named Liberty and has lived in Alaska for 13 years. He campaigns in between his duties taking care of his daughter while his wife is at work and attending to his own job as a territorial sales manager in the building materials industry.
Sager stepped into the race after Nelson, the incumbent representative, mentioned that he would not be seeking reelection. Sager said he tried to talk others into running to represent a Republican viewpoint.
 

A campaign sign for Cliff Groh, who is running to represent state House District 18, is seen in Anchorage’s Muldoon neighborhood on Sept. 23, 2026. As a legislative aide in the 1980s, Groh worked on the bill that created the Alaska Permanent Fund dividend, and his slogan reflects that personal history. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“I am worried about the implications of what would happen if we don’t have a Republican majority in the House and not a Republican governor,” he said. “I think that it’s guaranteed a bunch of taxes, income taxes. And I’m afraid they’re not going to be very friendly to the energy industry that we really need.”
He said he entered the race after failing to convince anyone else to do it. The prospect of serving in the legislature turned out to be unappealing to those he tried to convince to run, he said.
“You’re away from home for, you know, five to six months. And it’s just a hard job,” he said.
District problems and common concerns
Despite their philosophical differences, Groh and Sager are in agreement on some of the problems and needs in the district.
There are some common citizen concerns, such as education and public safety, they said. But in the Muldoon part of the district, residents regularly bring up some hyper-local and immediate problems.
Sager said he learned that when he was door-knocking there. “Everything was sidewalks and speed bumps. That’s what everybody wanted to talk about,” he said.
A particular trouble spot is Duben Avenue, a thoroughfare on the Muldoon edge of the district that Groh dubs “Dangerous Duben.” Pedestrians, including children attending Muldoon Elementary School, have to navigate Duben, but there are no sidewalks.
Sager said he has seen the problem firsthand. “I’d go knock on people’s doors and they’d be talking about it, and then a car would fly through,” he said.
Groh, who believes he was the first legislative candidate this cycle to start door-knocking, has also seen the traffic problem firsthand.
 

Campaign signs for Republican candidates, including state House candidate Dan Sager, are seen on Oct. 29, 2026, in the parking lot of a strip mall just outside the Government Hill gate of Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	He considers Duben to be the most dangerous road in the district, but he said there are other bad spots. He has engaged with residents concerning road dangers for years, as both a legislator and a candidate, he said. Just this week he wrote a letter to Anchorage Mayor Suzanne LaFrance relaying a citizen complaint about another road in the neighborhood, Boundary Avenue.
Groh said residents call on him to help them in other ways, and he is able to tap into his long years of government and public policy experience.
One example is his work with people struggling to find or keep homes. “A substantial percentage of the homeless population in Anchorage wake up every morning in my district, and there’s a number of people also in my district who are on the cusp of homelessness who slip in and out of it,” he said.
He has kept in contact with district residents he met as far back as 2022 who are struggling with homelessness, he said.
This year, even in struggling House District 18, residents cannot help but be aware of the ongoing election. Sager said he has encountered some people who are disengaged, mostly young military people, but only a few people who say they definitely will not vote.
The downside of that awareness is the dominance of the federal elections in Alaska, particularly the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. It is considered one of the races that will decide the control of the Senate. That U.S. Senate race has drawn national attention and massive amounts of money for a small-population state like Alaska.
“The federal (election) is taking a lot of the oxygen out of the room,” Sager said. 
That leaves state legislative candidates much overshadowed, he said
“So then all us House and Senate people are just fighting for, like, ‘Hey, don’t forget: We actually affect you a little bit more than that, you know. More directly anyway,’” he said.
Vehicles travel on Oct. 29, 2026, on rain-slicked Duben Avenue in Anchorage’s Muldoon neighborhood. Residents have complained about pedestrian safey along the street, which lacks sidewalks. Both candidates seeking to represent House District 18 in the state legislature cite Duben Avenue as a constituent concern. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

text:
Daniel Houghton, who teaches industrial design at Middlebury College uses the free Midd Tel phone in downtown Middlebury. Photo by Norah Khan/The Middlebury Campus

This story by Norah Khan was published by the Addison Independent on Oct. 29, 2026.
MIDDLEBURY — In Cannon Park across from Ilsley Public Library sits a citrine yellow payphone with a hand-painted logo that reads “Midd Tel.” The phone — which is completely free to use — was born out of Middlebury College’s Makerspace.
Daniel Houghton, who teaches industrial design and manages the Makerspace in the Christian A. Johnson Memorial Building, was the driving force behind the Midd Tel project.
Always interested in doing stuff and in helping people learn new things, Houghton gained inspiration this past summer after learning about the work of Patrick Schlott, an engineer in Randolph. Schlott, encouraged by others with similar ideas, created the company RandTel, which aims to connect people by installing free-to-use phones in rural areas.
That idea deeply resonated with Houghton.
“I thought that would be cool in Middlebury. There’s tons of upgrades you can do to the town of Middlebury, and (the phone) was one of them that felt within reach. It would cost a bit, but not a ton. It would take a bit of learning, but not years and years, and it would last for a while,” Houghton said. “This town is so well structured for walking around in. So that bit of connectivity felt cool. Something that’s not that black rectangle as not your only portal into life was fun to think about.” 
Houghton enlisted two interns to help him make the project come to life, Helena Goskreutz, a visiting intern from California, and Middlebury sophomore Noah Klompus.

Remi Beauharnois ’27 makes a phone call using the new Midd Tel in town. Photo by Norah Khan/The Middlebury Campus

Over the summer, Klompus met with Schlott, who personally donated the phone that would turn into Midd Tel. “He was super kind, and he donated the phone that is now in town, along with its components, which was pretty incredible,” Klompus said.
The team then had to present and propose the project to a Middlebury town board and enlist the help of an electrical company to source the Wi-Fi and organize who would pay for electricity.
Klompus, like most students on Middlebury’s campus, did not grow up with payphones and feels that this project is a great way for younger generations to communicate.
“It’s a total novelty,” Klompus said. “I’d never seen, much less used, a payphone. I think that in itself is super cool. I think the movement as a whole is a pretty interesting and neat way to get kids involved and, like, actually allowing for communication that’s not entirely cellphone based.”
Klompus’ experience over the summer was a special way for him as a student to have a positive impact on the town.
“It was a pretty cool opportunity, the town just being really supportive with having a couple of kids in an internship to come in and get experience putting (the phone) in an actual piece of infrastructure for the town. It was cool to be able to feel as a student that I was doing something that will stay and be intact,” he said.
As a parent, Houghton was motivated to create ways to communicate outside of smartphones.
“(Midd Tel) basically started as a bit of silliness and then genuine consideration for what it feels like to be a father of two kids who are of an age where I want them going out into the world, but I don’t want them to have a cellphone yet because I don’t think it’s the best thing for them. The existence of some way to make contact just feels like a way to release some of those feelings of anxiety that you might feel as a parent,” Houghton said.
Midd Tel has taken off.
It is easy to use. Anyone can pick up the handset, punch in a phone number — anywhere — and it will connect the call. Someone has posted a laminated sheet with important phone numbers: a 24/7 crisis line, Charter House shelter, bus service.
Within the first two weeks after it was installed in September, 300 people made calls. That hit a threshold of allotted calls that the initial calling plan imposed. But Houghton and the town upgraded to an unlimited business plan, so there’s no longer a call limit at all. The phone is fully operational to anyone.
He has heard that some in the library are telling youngsters they can use the Midd Tel phone to call parents or others, which, for Houghton, is one of his motivations behind starting it.

Middlebury College Makerspace Director Daniel Houghton makes a free call on an old-style, publicly accessible telephone posted in Canon Park in the heart of downtown Middlebury. Although Houghton was the force behind setting up the phone, anyone can use it anytime. Photo by Independent photo/John S. McCright

The project was funded and supported by the Makerspace, but Houghton aims to turn ownership and operation completely over to the town.
The cost of all those calls? Very little to the organizers and free to anyone who picks up the handset and punches in a phone number.
“You can just pick (the phone) up and talk. That’s all being supported by the Makerspace for now, and then the town will take over. But so far the phone bill has been $3. It’s a penny a minute.”
The location of the phone was a thoughtful choice for the Makerspace team. Houghton feels that for Midd Tel to be an actual social project that lasts, it must be publicly owned and considerate of the heavily felt division between the college and the town.
Editor’s note: Norah Khan is the editor-in-chief of the Middlebury Campus newspaper, where this story first appeared.

text:
Ohio Democratic governor candidate Dr. Amy Acton at the Franklin County Board of Elections. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). In the wake of a controversial attack ad, Ohio Democratic governor candidate Dr. Amy Acton said her opponent Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is a “danger to my state.” 
“I just think (the ad) is a travesty,” Acton said to reporters speaking outside the Franklin County Board of Elections on Friday afternoon. 
“There is no bar too low apparently for my opponent, he will say and do anything. … I think it was absolutely despicable to do this. I really hope everyone is held accountable for their behavior in this.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ramaswamy is no longer airing the controversial attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother. 
“It ran to completion, and we’ve put up 4 other ads,” he told reporters Thursday.
The ad features Acton’s biological mom, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a liar. Court documents show Acton’s stepfather was arrested for raping her as a child, and Arthur lost custody. The couple fled the state to avoid a trial. Acton said she has not seen her mother in nearly 50 years.
“We’ve had such an incredible amount of love and support, and I will tell you also, over the last week, so many people have been coming up at the rallies, at the rope lines, sharing their stories,” Acton said. 
“I’ve always said that I am not the only one who has seen a thing or two in my childhood, and that’s why I do what I do. That’s why we’re fighting to make sure every kid gets a fair shot.”
Politicians on both sides of the aisles, including Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, called on Ramaswamy to take the ad down. 
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended Ramaswamy over the ad. 
The Cook Political Report labeled the Ohio governor race as “Lean Democrat” as of Thursday.
Election Day is Nov. 3 and polls will be open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

title: New Burlington police chief will face tall order
description:
New Watervliet Police Chief Anthony Geraci speaks after being sworn in to the department at the Watervliet Senior Center on Thursday, July 25, 2019 in Watervliet, N.Y. Anthony retired from the Albany Police Department where he was a lieutenant to accept the appointment. File photo by Lori Van Buren/Times Union

Shoring up the beleaguered Burlington police de[...]
text:
New Watervliet Police Chief Anthony Geraci speaks after being sworn in to the department at the Watervliet Senior Center on Thursday, July 25, 2019 in Watervliet, N.Y. Anthony retired from the Albany Police Department where he was a lieutenant to accept the appointment. File photo by Lori Van Buren/Times Union

Shoring up the beleaguered Burlington police department won’t be easy but residents and leaders said they are hopeful the newly selected chief, Anthony Geraci, could make headway — especially if he takes the time to understand the Burlington community. 
“It’s important to me to have someone who can really come in, do an evaluation, address this,” said Burlington City Councilor Melo Grant (P-Central District), who was on the 12-person hiring committee. 
A 25-year law enforcement veteran, Geraci has served multiple police departments in upstate New York and held leadership positions in Watervliet and Newburgh. He most recently worked for a Texas-based recruitment firm.
He began his career in 1998 with the New York City Police Department before a stint of about 15 years with the Albany Police Department. He later served as police chief of nearby Watervliet and, more recently, Newburgh.
Grant said she appreciated that Geraci has tackled tough issues in Newburgh, a city with a high crime rate, and a department with operational and accountability issues. “So we are dealing with someone who’s not going to be faint of heart with regards to what they see here,” she said.
According to a public safety report presented to the Police Commission earlier this month, the Burlington Police Department is down to 54 officers and has 19 vacancies. It is currently looking to fill several other positions including community service officers and emergency communications specialists. A 2024 internal survey indicated the police department was understaffed and in crisis, with officers routinely burnt out and overwhelmed by a growing number of high-priority incidents.
Progressive Mayor Mulvaney-Stanak recently selected Geraci as the finalist after a months-long search. He is slated to replace Burlington’s Interim Police Chief Shawn Burke who has been serving since former chief Jon Murad resigned in April, 2025. 
The mayor declined to comment at this time. Geraci could not be reached for comment.
The City Council is expected to vote on the mayoral appointment on Nov. 9.
Mark Bouchett, owner of the Homeport store and chair of the Church Street Marketplace District Commission, said he believes recruiting should be a priority. “We have half a police department right now,” he said. 
Bouchett, who was on the hiring committee, said Geraci has dealt with the social problems Burlington is facing and he has “a lot of enthusiasm and energy.”   
FaRied Munarsyah said he believes the new chief should focus on rebuilding relationships with the community.  
“We’ve witnessed the way BPD operates long enough to know that it’s gonna take much more than a new chief to rebuild both the BPD as well as the public’s trust,” said Munarsyah, a city resident and co-organizer of The People’s Kitchen, a mutual aid effort that serves free hot meals and essential supplies at City Hall Park. 
Several residents, including Munarsyah, called for greater external accountability and pointed out roadblocks, such as the police chief having final say over the investigation, discipline and termination of officers. Voters have long pushed for greater civilian oversight but police and the union have opposed efforts to give civilians more oversight. 
Residents also pointed to a recent $150,000 city settlement stemming from a 2021 incident and lawsuit claiming Burlington police restrained and sedated a Black teen with disabilities. 
The Burlington Police Commission unanimously disagreed with the chief’s decision to exonerate the officers, finding that they violated several department policies in their handling of the incident. But the commission’s recommendations were rejected by then-chief Jon Murad, according to court documents.
“The community wants a chief who is open and cooperative with civilian oversight of policing,” said Stephanie Seguino, a former member of the city’s police commission and an economist at the University of Vermont who has long studied racial disparities in traffic stops.
“There’s a lot of research that suggests that civilian oversight has the possibility of improving police-community relations. And one of the areas that civilian oversight usually steps into is reviewing citizen complaints and having input into decisions about how those complaints are dealt with,” Seguino said.
Former community safety advisor to the city Ingrid Jonas said she admires the willingness of the new person to step into the role and hopes he will be given the opportunity to succeed. 
“I think he should begin by getting a clear understanding of what the community is dealing with in terms of public safety needs, and then taking an honest account of the department’s capabilities, just given the lower numbers, on record. And then he should make a plan to strengthen and or develop partnerships because that’s going to be the best way to address the array of problems,” she said.
Jonas, who was hired by the mayor last September, has since left. A retired member of the Vermont State Police, she said she helped start the Situation Table — a multi-disciplinary group including police, social services workers, substance abuse interventionists, and community members with different perspectives to collaboratively approach the complex challenges facing the city.
She said she believes policing can’t solve all of the problems Burlington is facing. Partnerships and a method to evaluate progress are also important, she said.
Catherine Davis, president and CEO of the Lake Champlain Chamber of Commerce, said an employee this week reported witnessing a drug deal across from the downtown office and that needles were spotted littering the walkway this week. 
“One of the biggest priorities needs to be hiring, recruiting new officers and retaining our existing officers, building the police force back up to the numbers that it needs to be at,” she said. “The demands being placed on the current officers who have stayed in Burlington, I think, are a real challenge. So I’m hopeful that the new chief will really be able to focus on that.”
She said she is excited the new chief has experience in other cities that can be applied to Burlington. Having someone new on board could also energize people to work together to make progress, she said. 
“I’m hoping that he can bring some fresh ideas,” Davis said. “In terms of advice, I would say really listen to the folks who want to help, maybe listen really carefully to the folks who might not want to help, and really listen to the officers as well.”
Patrick Brown, executive director of the Greater Burlington Multicultural Resource Center, and a longtime resident and organizer, also recommended the new recruit start with a non-political listening tour to gather broad perspectives of people across the city, including those who have led or worked in the police department.
“The mayor or city councilors cannot set the stage for him. He needs to be the person setting the stage,” Brown said. “It’s going to take the entire community, he said.
